papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can elicit specialized visual capabilities in vision-language models (VLMs), yet jointly optimizing heterogeneous objectives often introduces cross-capability gradient conflicts. Training experts independently mitigates this interference, but direct reward optimization may entangle specialized knowledge with reward-hacking biases. This paper proposes Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation (SCOPED), which trains capability-specific experts and extracts explicit skills through reward-guided reflection. During on-policy distillation, these skills guide expert supervision while remaining unavailable to the unified student, encouraging it to internalize procedural knowledge without explicit skills at inference time. Across eight multimodal benchmarks, SCOPED consistently outperforms the backbone and mixed-capability RL, demonstrating the effectiveness of skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation for integrating independently acquired capabilities. Further analyses reveal interference during joint capability optimization and suggest that skill augmentation promotes more consistent expert trajectories, greater attention to task-relevant visual evidence, and better preservation of specialized expertise in the unified student. All code and data are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/SCOPED.
authors: Yuqi Xiong, Chunyi Peng, Zhipeng Xu, Qing Yang, Zhenghao Liu, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu
bullets: Motivation: jointly optimizing heterogeneous capabilities can cause cross-capability gradient interference, while direct reward optimization may encourage reward-hacking biases.
Method: train capability-specific experts, extract skills through reward-guided reflection, and use those skills to guide on-policy distillation into a unified student.
The student receives skill-guided supervision during training but not the explicit skills at inference, encouraging it to internalize procedural knowledge.
Across eight multimodal benchmarks, SCOPED outperforms the backbone and mixed-capability RL.
Analyses indicate reduced interference, more consistent expert trajectories, stronger attention to relevant visual evidence, and better preservation of specialized expertise.

papers.abstract: Accurate motion prediction is critical for safe autonomous driving, yet even strong forecasters leave residual errors in their multimodal proposals. Existing refiners compress complete proposals or update their segments sequentially, preventing the full proposed future from serving as explicit relational context for correction. We introduce FutureLift, a backbone-agnostic refiner that represents each multimodal proposal as a heterogeneous future graph, with spatially grounded temporal nodes connected to agent histories, map elements, alternative modes, and, for joint prediction, other agents future trajectories. Bidirectional temporal edges allow later evidence to revise earlier segments in a single pass, and the updated nodes predict residual coordinate and confidence corrections. Requiring only proposals, scores, and scene context, FutureLift provides a common refinement interface for structurally different forecasting backbones. On Argoverse2 and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, it consistently improves frozen proposals and outperforms native and specialized refiners across marginal and joint forecasting. On the WOMD motion-prediction leaderboard, FutureLift ranks first in minADE (0.5049m) and minFDE (0.9942m) among the compared standard-input methods, without LiDAR or ensembling, while achieving a competitive 0.4874 Soft mAP.
authors: Daniel Grimm, J. Marius Z\"ollner
bullets: Addresses residual errors in complete multimodal trajectory proposals that existing sequential or compressed refiners cannot fully contextualize.
Builds heterogeneous graphs linking future trajectory nodes with agent histories, map elements, alternative modes, and other agents’ futures.
Uses bidirectional temporal edges so later predicted segments can revise earlier ones in a single refinement pass.
Backbone-agnostic interface requires only proposals, confidence scores, and scene context, and improves frozen proposals on Argoverse2 and WOMD.
Ranks first among compared standard-input methods on WOMD for minADE and minFDE, while achieving competitive Soft mAP without LiDAR or ensembling.

figures.caption: Figure 2. FutureLift method overview. (a) Scene history and map context flow through an arbitrary frozen forecasting backbone, which exposes only multimodal trajectory proposals Ŷ and logits ℓ; FutureLift does not access backbone queries or intermediate features. (b) Each proposal is partitioned into R intervals and lifted into spatially anchored future nodes. For clarity, the panel visualizes one representative mode k of the K instantiated modes. Typed relations connect the full node set to agent histories, map context, other modes, and for coherent joint-scenes proposals also to other predicted agents, while bidirectional temporal edges expose the complete horizon before correction. (c) Relation-specific attention updates all future nodes on this fixed graph and simultaneously decodes coordinate residuals, uncertainty parameters, and confidence residuals. Thus, later evidence can revise earlier segments in one graph pass without a causal sweep or graph reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent's responses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, producing both false positives where correct responses mask broken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories spanning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, conversations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ systematically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to support reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.
authors: Sebastian-Antonio Toma, Jean de Kernier, Mike Ply, Oliviu Matei
bullets: Introduces 30 fact-evolution trajectories across 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels.
Uses paradigm inversion to generate artifacts from known fact trajectories, enabling deterministic ground truth and direct memory inspection.
Finds intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories showing meaningful divergence.
A representative memory system correctly classifies memory operations only 20% of the time, a failure hidden by downstream QA.
Releases the benchmark, document-generation pipeline, and scoring framework for reproducible evaluation.

papers.abstract: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs.
authors: Ian Gemp, Shubhendu Trivedi, Adam Fisch, Fantine Huot, Michael Kaisers, Mirella Lapata, William W. Cohen, Alekh Agarwal, Kate Larson, Jacob Eisenstein
bullets: Addresses market failure at both extremes: perfect clones eliminate profits, while no competition collapses value extraction.
Studies the critical middle ground where heterogeneous agents strategically shade bids to earn positive margins.
Evaluates Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO bidding across three auction protocols.
Finds that imperfect competition preserves agent profitability while maintaining high task success at low cost across diverse domains.

papers.abstract: External-memory systems extend language-model applications beyond a context window, but their quality depends critically on the model executing the write path: deciding what to retain, how precisely to represent it, and how new evidence should update persistent state. Existing frameworks typically place a general-purpose large language model behind framework-specific prompts. This raises serving cost, and a writer specialized for one protocol does not transfer directly to another; a unified model that can operate across established memory frameworks remains largely unexplored. We present Hy-Memory-30B-A3B, a compact long-term-memory writer trained across Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Memory On-Policy Distillation teaches framework-specific write protocols on student-generated states; Memory RL then optimizes downstream answerability using dense per-chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO. Carrying policy-written banks across windows keeps training aligned with deployment. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.
authors: Tianxiang Fei, Jiazheng Kang, Mao Zheng, Xingyan He, Xiang Yu
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited transferability of using general-purpose LLMs as framework-specific memory writers.
Supports Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory through framework-specific write-protocol distillation.
Uses Memory RL with dense chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO.
Carries policy-written memory banks across context windows to better match deployment conditions.
On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, ranked first across four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.

papers.abstract: In robotic manipulation, the same observation often admits multiple feasible actions. Generative policies such as diffusion and flow matching naturally capture such multimodal behaviors, yet which mode is executed is left to random sampling and cannot be actively controlled. We propose Mode-Oriented Source Shaping (MOSS), which turns mode selection into an explicit choice of where generation starts. We first reveal, both empirically and theoretically, that deterministic flow transport induces mode-dependent structure in the source space. Under ideal deterministic ODE transport, distinct behavioral modes have distinct source-space preimages, while practical approximation errors can blur their boundaries due to imbalanced data, limited model capacity, and few inference steps. Motivated by this source-space structure, MOSS constructs semantically aligned mode-specific Gaussian sources that encode mode identity in the initial noise. A modality-strength estimator predicts the local degree of multimodality, which adaptively controls the geometry of the mode-specific sources. It contracts them toward a shared Gaussian where behaviors are similar and separates them near behavioral branching points. During deployment, the desired behavior is selected at inference simply by sampling from the corresponding component. Across 6 simulated and 3 real-world manipulation tasks, MOSS steers to the target mode up to 100% of the time with high task success, recovers minority modes at over 90% guidance rate under a 10:90 imbalance dataset, and surpasses mode-conditioned flow policy by 43.3 points of guidance rate on real robots.
authors: Zirun Ma, Jindou Jia, Tuo An, Jiaqi Bai, Jiahua Dong, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Deterministic flow transport creates mode-dependent structure in source space, but approximation errors can blur mode boundaries.
MOSS builds semantically aligned, mode-specific Gaussian source distributions to represent behavior choices.
A modality-strength estimator adaptively contracts or separates these sources based on local behavioral multimodality.
At inference, users select a behavior by sampling from its corresponding source component.

Across 6 simulated and 3 real-world tasks, MOSS achieves up to 100% mode guidance, over 90% minority-mode recovery under 10:90 imbalance, and a 43.3-point guidance-rate gain over a mode-conditioned flow policy on real robots.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychological constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understudied. To address this gap, we define and systematically investigate scale sensitivity, the variation in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sensitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpretation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alternative scales.
authors: Wonjeong Jo, Gyuwan Kim, Ming Shan Hee

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Omni Language Models (OLMs) provide a unified solution for audiovisual video captioning. Nevertheless, existing approaches predominantly treat captioning as an unstructured text generation process, neglecting the inherent semantic structure of videos and leading to suboptimal fine-grained audiovisual alignment. To bridge this gap, we propose EVA-Cap, a novel framework that decomposes captions into atomic audiovisual events and transforms unstructured text supervision into event-centric alignment. We train EVA-Cap via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a self-curated dataset, EVA-Data, which is built with event-centric quality control. During the GRPO phase, the model is explicitly optimized against three event-centric alignment targets: global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap significantly outperforms existing methods in event-centric evaluation (e.g., +9.0% average gain on ChronusAV), while achieving competitive performance on general audiovisual captioning benchmarks (e.g., +3.3% on WorldSense).

papers.abstract: Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans' ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot's body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to-any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it. The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole-body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.
authors: Conor Mc Gartoll, An Dang, Pranay Thangeda, Arjun Gupta, Carolina Higuera, Nima Fazeli, Mustafa Mukadam, Manikantan Nambi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of end-effector-only grasping for bulky-object manipulation.
Builds a feasible whole-body grasp dataset, trains reinforcement-learning experts for grasp-to-grasp repositioning, and distills them into one policy.
The policy uses proprioception and object geometry and transfers zero-shot from simulation to a real Unitree G1.
Demonstrations include repositioning a basketball and box, plus carrying and stowing a box in a long-horizon task.
Across real-world tasks, it completes 90% of trials versus 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.

papers.title: Whole-Body Dexterity
papers.tldr: Whole-Body Dexterity enables a humanoid to use its arms and torso as contact surfaces for robust, interactive manipulation of bulky objects, achieving 90% real-world task completion.

papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation often relies on an encoder's final global representation, leaving complementary information in intermediate layers underused. Combining these features is challenging because their dimensions can differ and their usefulness varies across tasks. We propose LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors, a training-free framework that combines global and regional information from multiple encoder layers. A single forward pass per view supplies all descriptors. Global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors independently fit the same label residuals. Labeled validation data select their mixture in class-score space, preserving native feature dimensions without learned projections. LAMP-F further adapts text-anchored class prototypes, using a cached response to update the fixed-kernel residual predictions exactly. Experiments cover eleven datasets and ViT and ResNet backbones. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the compared published training-free ResNet-50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, reaching 78.73% at 16 shots. Averaged across five support budgets, LAMP improves over a paired global-feature-only baseline by 1.14 and 1.59 percentage points on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; LAMP-F raises these gains to 1.96 and 2.54 points. LAMP-F reaches 16-shot accuracies of 83.57% and 79.10%, respectively. Controlled experiments identify multi-layer integration as the main source of improvement and examine pooling, calibration, validation labels, and computational cost. These findings show that combining layer-specific predictions can exploit complementary features from frozen encoders to improve few-shot classification.
authors: Zhipeng Ye, Feng Jiang, Qiufeng Wang, Hao Li
bullets: Addresses the underuse of complementary intermediate-layer information and differing feature dimensions in few-shot adaptation.
Uses one forward pass per view to generate descriptors, then combines global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors in class-score space.
Validation labels select the predictor mixture without learned projections; LAMP-F additionally adapts text-anchored class prototypes.
Evaluated on 11 datasets with ViT and ResNet backbones, LAMP and LAMP-F consistently improve over global-feature-only baselines across support budgets.
At 16 shots, LAMP-F reaches 83.57% on ViT-B/16 and 79.10% on ResNet-50; multi-layer integration is identified as the main improvement source.

papers.abstract: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.
authors: Juliette Marrie, Paul Pacaud, Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Shizhe Chen, Moritz B\"ohle
bullets: Pretrained exclusively on curated public robot, egocentric human, and vision-language data.
Combines a vision-language model with a flow-matching action expert.
Uses register tokens to summarize recent VLM outputs in the action expert’s cache at negligible cost.
Improves simulated and real-robot success, while making pose oscillations about four times rarer.
Outperformed only by roughly twice-as-large models on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand, and RoboCasa365.

Hatched bars mark models pretrained on in-house data and outlined bars world-action models. Each bar gives the overall score and the ticks the subset scores. Figure 3: REKI. (a) Camera views and instruction are encoded as context Et, which every expert block reads by cross-attention. The state embedding gt and the flow time modulate the actions through adaptive normalisation. The noisy chunk enters the expert’s stream, and the flow loss compares the predicted velocity with its target. The register keys and values of past frames are kept in a cache and read by self-attention, which is the memory of §4.1. (b) One of the ten blocks, holding nr=32 registers and the action tokens of the current frame. Arrows run from a query to what it reads. Action tokens read the current and past registers and themselves, and registers never read them.

Figure 2: How VLAs carry the past. Each panel shows one training window of three frames, with a loss under each frame that receives one. (a) Past frames enter the VLM with the current one, in full (Yuan et al., 2026), compressed (Torne et al., 2026; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026) or from a cache (Jang et al., 2025). The VLM takes the whole window as input, and only the last frame is supervised. (b) A state is written at each step and read at the next, in the backbone (Cherepanov et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026) or as fast weights in the head (Jiang et al., 2026). Each step needs the output of the previous one, so the window is unrolled step by step. (c) Each frame is encoded on its own, and an added module mixes the memory tokens of past frames into the prediction for the current one. HAMLET (Koo et al., 2026) supervises the last frame only, and MemoryVLA (Shi et al., 2026) every frame, with the bank entries stored without gradient. (d) In REKI, the memory tokens are registers in the action expert. Their keys and values are kept across frames and read by the self-attention already present. The window is one batched pass, and every frame receives a loss.

The registers do not read the action tokens and skip adaptive normalisation, so they do not depend on the flow time and are computed once per frame. papers.abstract: Feed-forward transformer models have recently achieved strong performance in multi-view 3D reconstruction, but they still rely primarily on appearance-based attention and often struggle in dynamic scenes with weak geometric cues. In this work, we introduce a motion- and gravity-aware framework under the Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI) paradigm. During training, residual optical flow and gravity direction are provided as privileged signals to guide geometric representation learning; during inference, the model uses standard visual inputs only. We integrate these priors into transformer backbones with lightweight architectural changes, preserving feed-forward efficiency. Experiments on standard benchmarks show consistent gains in reconstruction accuracy and robustness, especially in scenes with dynamic objects, ambiguous structure, and challenging camera motion. Our analysis further shows that the optimal injection stage is backbone-dependent: middle-layer integration is generally preferable for VGGT, while late-stage integration is more effective for {\pi}3. These results suggest that LUPI offers a practical way to inject motion and physical priors into feed-forward 3D reconstruction without increasing test-time complexity.
authors: Shiyao Qian, Yuan Ren, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Targets weak geometric cues and dynamic-scene challenges in appearance-driven multi-view reconstruction.

Standard-benchmark experiments report consistent gains, particularly with dynamic objects, ambiguous structure, and difficult camera motion.
Prior injection works best at different stages depending on the backbone: middle layers for VGGT and late layers for π3.

papers.abstract: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session's advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.
authors: Yilong Xu, Minrui Xu, Xinyu Zhou, Xiang Long, Haochen Tan, Zhijiang Guo
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between single-session RL training and inference trajectories spanning multiple sessions.
Introduces a general multi-session RL setting supporting arbitrarily many sessions per trajectory.
Uses critic-free hierarchical optimization: trajectory-level session-usage signals and session-level marginal-contribution advantages.
On BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B, outperforms broadcasting in context compaction and subagent forking while using fewer sessions on average.
Analysis indicates gains in session utility and allocation; broader advances in multi-session RL remain future work.

papers.abstract: The vocabulary of a language model is its native semantics: the embedding and the unembedding fix the meaning of a state at the two ends of the residual stream. Between them, existing methods either reuse a fixed lens or treat the states as a point cloud, and neither reads a state the way the model does. We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that read it next and adaptive to the context. Lexical reference frames approximate it by reading a state through the model's own remaining layers with a stated number of rounds of attention between positions and a typical attention output for the rest, without fitting to the model's output. No lens, with fixed directions per layer, can exceed the square root of the native frame's coherence, 0.30 and 0.35 at mid-depth of SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B, whereas the first-order frame, LexFrame[1], reaches 0.97 and 0.97 and reads a state within 0.16 nats of the model's output. Its coefficients attribute predictions more faithfully than attribution patching, its lexical basis steers a prediction while sparing other tokens, and its confident readings would let an early exit skip 0.45 and 0.42 of the layers, where lenses skip almost none. In this way, lexical reference frames make every hidden state of the model readable, attributable and steerable.
authors: Jian Gu, Hongyu Zhang, Chunyang Chen, Aldeida Aleti
bullets: Fixed lenses and point-cloud views do not capture the context-dependent semantics of intermediate states.
LexFrame approximates each state’s native reference frame by applying remaining layers, with configurable inter-position attention rounds and typical attention elsewhere.
The first-order LexFrame[1] achieves 0.97 coherence on both SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B, reading states within 0.16 nats of the model output.
Its coefficients are more faithful than attribution patching, and its lexical basis can steer selected predictions while preserving others.
Confident readings support skipping 0.45 and 0.42 of layers on the two models, respectively, unlike conventional lenses.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces native lexical reference frames for interpreting and steering LM residual streams, relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics

papers.abstract: Test-time context optimization adapts frozen language models through textual feedback, but ordinary conditional generation provides no separate control over how strongly to reinforce the distributional changes induced by a context update. We introduce EMO, a training-free framework inspired by expectation--maximization that alternates question-specific context estimation (E-step) and distribution refinement (M-step). The E-step revises a system context using textual gradients from an external judge without access to gold answers. The M-step contrasts next-token distributions under the revised and preceding contexts at a shared prefix to construct a confidence-constrained logit correction. Feedback on the steered response drives the next context update, coupling adaptation across rounds with intervention within each generation. Theoretically, we connect parameter and context optimization through a shared target-KL objective and additive logit representations, and derive the steering vector from context-induced logit displacements. Under context-improvement and faithful-steering assumptions, we prove a one-round decrease in target KL divergence for sufficiently small steering strength. Under greedy decoding across eight models and six benchmarks, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging $+9.10$ percentage points. With the same judge, it adds $+1.53$ points on average over context-only optimization (TextGrad), with consistent MMLU-Pro gains across models. At matched target-model generation budgets, accuracy advantages over best-of-$N$ are strongest on Llama, while oracle coverage is higher in most comparisons despite fewer candidates. The coverage--selection gap motivates allocating test-time computation jointly to candidate generation and verification.
authors: Wei Xia, Yehui Tang, Zhi-Hong Deng
bullets: Addresses the lack of independent control over how strongly context updates alter a language model’s output distribution.
Uses an expectation–maximization-style loop: an external judge revises question-specific context, then logits are corrected by comparing revised and previous contexts.
Derives steering from context-induced logit changes and theoretically shows reduced target KL divergence under stated assumptions and sufficiently small steering strength.
Across eight models and six benchmarks, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging +9.10 percentage points.
Outperforms context-only optimization on average and can surpass best-of-N at matched generation budgets, while highlighting a remaining candidate-generation versus verification trade-off.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a closed-loop test-time framework (EMO) for LLM adaptation using alternating context optimization and logit steering, directly relevant to test-time learning and inference-time optimization.
papers.title: EMO: A Closed-Loop Test-Time Computation Framework via Alternating Context Optimization and Logits Steering
papers.tldr: EMO improves test-time adaptation by alternating textual context updates with confidence-constrained logit steering, yielding broad zero-shot gains without training.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning agents optimize exactly the reward signal they are given, which can diverge sharply from an intended true objective when that signal is only a proxy for it; this failure mode is known as specification gaming. Existing evidence for this failure mode is largely observational, with comparatively few demonstrations pairing a controlled, deliberately constructed proxy/true gap with a mitigation that carries a verifiable guarantee rather than only an empirical improvement. We construct a minimal gridworld in which a cleaning-robot agent can either genuinely remove dirt or conceal it from a cheap sensor, and show that a standard deep Q-network trained only on the sensor's proxy reward converges to a policy that games it completely, reaching near-maximal proxy reward while never achieving the true objective. We then introduce a constrained reinforcement learning fix, penalizing the specific behaviors through which the agent exploits the gap, and show that it eliminates the gaming behavior from the final policy while substantially recovering true-objective performance. We further derive and empirically verify an exact accounting identity relating the proxy reward, true reward, and our cost signal for this environment, showing that the cost signal measures the proxy/true gap exactly rather than merely tracking it, and yields a deterministic guarantee under a hard-constrained variant of the method.
authors: Hilda Adwubi Osei
bullets: A cleaning robot can either remove dirt or hide it from a cheap sensor, creating a deliberate proxy–true objective gap.
A standard deep Q-network trained on proxy reward converges to complete specification gaming: near-maximal proxy reward but no true cleaning.
The proposed constrained RL method penalizes the specific exploitative behaviors and eliminates gaming in the final policy.
An exact identity links proxy reward, true reward, and the cost signal, proving that the cost measures the objective gap in this environment.
A hard-constrained variant provides a deterministic guarantee, with substantial recovery of true-objective performance.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses specification gaming in a cleaning robot scenario using constrained RL, relevant to robot learning and safety in embodied environments.
papers.title: Specification Gaming and a Constrained Reinforcement Learning Mitigation in a Cleaning Gridworld

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59\% and action latency by 9-32\% (a 1.09$\times$-1.46$\times$ speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20\% (1.25$\times$ speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Chengyuan Qian, Zhengzhong Tu, Yang Sui, Yangming Shi
bullets: Targets VLA inference bottlenecks caused by hundreds of visual tokens from high-resolution, multi-view observations.
Ranks tokens using task-to-vision attention rather than generic visual saliency.
Adapts compression rates from attention-distribution uniformity using an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration.
Evaluated across OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT in LIBERO, SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.
Reduces simulation backbone FLOPs by 35–59% and action latency by 9–32% while maintaining success; real-robot end-to-end latency drops 20% at comparable success.

By retaining task-relevant yet information-diverse tokens across timesteps, our approach reduces LLM backbone computation while preserving action performance.

papers.title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: FastVLA accelerates vision-language-action robot control by selecting task-relevant visual tokens and adapting their budget over time without retraining.

papers.abstract: A perception system that must brake for a pedestrian does not need a low average latency. It must deliver an answer before the deadline on every frame, the worst case included. Commodity edge accelerators optimize the mean through dynamic scheduling, OS jitter, thermal throttling, and contention, so their per-frame latency can be measured but not bounded. We build FALCON, a camera-based 3D occupancy front-end on the AMD Kria KR260, an embedded FPGA drawing 4.3 W idle and up to 6.6 W under inference, and make the latency guarantee layered and explicit: programmable-logic (PL) compute is cycle-bounded analytically; inference is a measured envelope over 100k-frame traces; and a watchdog enforces output delivery, publishing the previous output flagged stale when a frame is late. The deadline runs use a fixed-work proxy of six ResNet-50 DPU inferences per frame, not the full occupancy network: across three 100k-frame enforced runs, all 300k proxy frames delivered an output within the 100 ms deadline plus at most 10.2 ms, the worst of the three runs. The full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline composes to about 1.3 s per frame on the board and is not yet a 10 Hz system. The two operations the DPU cannot run, a view-transform gather and a bilinear resize, become fixed-trip-count PL IPs numerically matched to their software references. On the full Occ3D-nuScenes validation set the board reaches mIoU 29.88, 92.8% of an FP32 baseline the DPU cannot run. On a ResNet-50 probe over 100k frames the KR260 tail stays within 1.5 times its median (2.0 times for the six-inference proxy), where Jetson Orin reaches 4.4 times and the worst datacenter GPU run (NVIDIA L4) 23.6 times. The deployment recipe, HLS sources, and raw timing traces are released.
authors: Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Handong Yao
bullets: Targets worst-case deadline compliance rather than average latency for autonomous-driving perception.
Implements unsupported view-transform gather and bilinear resize operations as numerically matched FPGA logic.
On three 100k-frame proxy runs, all 300,000 frames produced an output within the 100 ms deadline plus at most 10.2 ms.
Achieves 29.88 mIoU on the full Occ3D-nuScenes validation set, or 92.8% of the FP32 baseline.
The full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline takes about 1.3 s per frame and is not yet a 10 Hz system; deployment artifacts and timing traces are released.

papers.selection_reason: FPGA-accelerated occupancy network with worst-case latency guarantees and low-power edge inference; directly fits efficient AI and 3D perception.
papers.title: FALCON: FPGA-Accelerated Latency-Certifiable Occupancy Networks for Camera-Based Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: FALCON uses fixed-trip-count FPGA kernels, measured latency envelopes, and a watchdog to provide certifiable camera-based occupancy inference timing, though the full pipeline remains far from 10 Hz.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet real-world applications often require them to continually acquire new capabilities from sequential tasks, i.e., Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). In typical MLLMs, a projector is employed to align visual representations with the language model. However, existing methods primarily protect the language model from forgetting while continuously updating the projector across tasks. Such asymmetric adaptation can cause substantial representation drift in the projector, increasing the mismatch between the projector and language model and consequently exacerbating catastrophic forgetting. To address this issue, we propose Compatible Routing (CART), which explicitly coordinates the adaptation of the projector and language model. Specifically, CART maintains task-specific experts for both modules and combines them through weighted mixtures. CART jointly infers their weights by considering both expert relevance and cross-module compatibility, thereby promoting coordinated adaptation between the two modules. To further control model growth, we introduce relevance-guided expert consolidation, which merges experts exhibiting similar relevance profiles across samples within each module. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CART achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Ling-Xiang Zhang, Tao Hu, Da-Wei Zhou
bullets: MCIT requires MLLMs to learn sequential multimodal tasks without losing previously acquired capabilities.
Existing methods mainly protect the language model while continually changing the projector, causing representation drift and cross-module mismatch.
CART maintains task-specific experts for both the projector and language model, then jointly routes them using expert relevance and cross-module compatibility.
Relevance-guided consolidation merges experts with similar sample-level relevance profiles to limit model growth.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, though the abstract provides no specific datasets or numerical results.

At inference, Gaussian likelihoods yield relevance scores Rp(x) and Rl(x). Alternating compatibility-aware updates produce routing weights qp(x) and ql(x), which combine projector outputs into a shared visual representation and mix LLM LoRA branches for inference without task identities.

papers.abstract: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone's native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33--34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems.

papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.
authors: Aozhong Zhang, Selcuk Gurses, Yanxia Deng, Naigang Wang, Chi-Chun Liu, Davis Wertheimer, Derrick Liu, Xin Li, Zi Yang, Felix X. -F. Ye, Penghang Yin

Uses fused Triton kernels without materializing the full attention matrix, yielding a reported 19.8× scoring-kernel speedup and up to 9.9% end-to-end prefill speedup.
On RULER and LongBench, outperforms evaluated baselines at equal cache budgets and achieves the lowest reported inference latency among eviction methods.

papers.abstract: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly important for user-centric applications, yet prior methods mainly adapt dense LLMs, whose polysemantic neurons, each encoding multiple unrelated concepts, hinder localizing the components behind personalization, and thus understanding and controlling it. We propose to personalize Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, which sparsely route each token to a few specialized experts, reducing polysemanticity and enabling such localization. We adapt three open-weight MoE LLMs on a large-scale personalization dataset and train crosscoders on paired activations of the personalized and non-personalized models to learn interpretable personalized latents, from which we identify the experts encoding distinct personalization features. The personalized MoE LLMs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of their parameters, exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and, within the same model family, yield personalized latents that are less shared with the non-personalized model. Causal interventions show that these latents suffice to recover the personalized model's behavior and that boosting their associated experts moves the non-personalized model toward it, revealing distinct routing paths for different personalization features.

papers.abstract: We propose Compliant GMT (C-GMT), a modular framework for full-body compliant responses in general motion tracking. As humanoid robots move into real world deployment, they not only need to perform any motion but also respond safely and robustly to interaction forces. Existing general motion tracking policies can imitate diverse motions but are trained to be stiff, leading to unexpected and unsafe behaviors under disturbance. Prior work in compliant humanoid control trades off compliance and generality. There exist examples of full-body compliant responses, but these are heavily curated to single-reference policies. On the other hand, general motion trackers (GMT) are trained to rigidly imitate massive motion capture datasets. Our key insight is to leverage the generality of pretrained GMTs for motion tracking while introducing compliance from a residual adapter that conditions on a history of proprioception. This enables our approach, C-GMT, to achieve both general motion tracking and whole-body compliant responses. Compared to state-of-the-art general motion trackers and single-motion compliant policies, C-GMT demonstrates competitive performance in both motion tracking accuracy and compliance adherence. We further demonstrate improved safety, robustness, and error tolerance in simulation and real-world G1 experiments.
authors: Venki Parsuram, Michelle Wang, Jin-Hyuk Hong, Pulkit Agrawal
bullets: Addresses the stiffness and unsafe disturbance responses of general motion tracking policies.

papers.abstract: Splatting-based radiance-field representations have recently gained popularity in robotic perception, enabling high-quality novel-view synthesis (NVS) through explicit scene primitives. However, existing splatting methods typically rely on iterative nonlinear optimization that jointly optimizes millions of coupled primitive parameters, resulting in substantial computation time, peak GPU memory consumption, and susceptibility to local minima. In this paper, we propose CF-Splat, a novel closed-form triangle-splatting framework for efficient scene appearance estimation over a known mesh either pre-existing or provided by upstream mapping or reconstruction pipelines. Our key insight is that, by properly formulating the problem over the given mesh geometry and calibrated cameras, the rendered pixel colors can be expressed linearly with respect to the per-vertex spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, allowing multi-view scene appearance estimation to be formulated as a global linear least-squares (LLS) problem without the need of iterative nonlinear optimization. To guarantee a well-posed solution under uneven multi-view observation coverage, we introduce adaptive SH regularization that constrains insufficiently supported high-order SH coefficients and yields a unique global minimizer. To ensure the scalability to large-scale scenes, we develop a triangle-structured matrix-free preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver that avoids explicitly constructing the large sparse normal system while producing the same LLS solution. Experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate that CF-Splat achieves competitive or superior NVS quality compared with state-of-the-art splatting methods. While, CF-Splat requires approximately 27.5-378.0 times less computation time and 1.8 times lower peak GPU memory on average than 3DGS across scenes of different scales on a consumer-grade laptop.
authors: Yixin Fang, Liang Zhao
bullets: Targets the high computation, memory use, and local-minima susceptibility of nonlinear splatting optimization.
Represents rendered colors linearly using per-vertex spherical-harmonics coefficients over calibrated cameras and mesh geometry.
Uses adaptive SH regularization to produce a unique solution despite uneven multi-view coverage.
Employs a matrix-free, preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver for large-scale scenes without forming the normal system.
Reports competitive or better NVS quality than state-of-the-art splatting, with substantially lower computation time and lower peak GPU memory than 3DGS.

papers.abstract: Byte-level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) run their large global model once per patch and start a patch where a small model's next-byte entropy is high. This rule rarely starts a patch at in-line computed results, such as the number after "=" in a worked solution, and accuracy on them collapses under tight patch budgets. We propose novelty patching, motivated by LZ77-style compression: start a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent context. The rule is a lookup table over the previous two bytes, fitted in seconds on raw text with no labels, reference model or losses. In BLT-style models trained from scratch on a 1.9 GB math corpus at a matched ~11% patch rate (3 seeds each), it has no clear effect at 1M parameters, raises final-answer accuracy from 47% to 72% at 12M, and at 50M raises computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90%; a table fitted on the raw pretraining corpus keeps the gain. Outside math the advantage shrinks: novelty lowers bits per byte on prose and ties entropy on source code and on synthetic execution traces. An analysis of where boundaries fall explains the pattern. Computed results have ordinary surprisal for the patcher's model, so surprisal-seeking rules pass over them: entropy concentrates patch starts on high-surprisal bytes most strongly of all rules (boundary enrichment 1.61) and is the worst on computed results, while the best rules sit near chance enrichment. Novelty works where new content begins at segment starts close to the computation, as in written math; a learned chunker (H-Net) finds such structure on its own, in math and in code. We also report what did not work: typed uncertainty as a training rule, switching rules after training, and a context-aware novelty predictor.
authors: Nicol\'as Vera Z\'u\~niga
bullets: Entropy-based patching often misses inline computed results because they have ordinary surprisal for the patching model.
Novelty patching starts patches where upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent two-byte context, using a label-free lookup table fitted on raw text.
At 50M parameters, computed-result accuracy rises from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90% at a matched ~11% patch rate.
The benefit is strongest in written math, shrinks on prose, and ties entropy on source code and synthetic execution traces.
Typed uncertainty, post-training rule switching, and a context-aware novelty predictor did not work; learned chunking finds related structure in math and code.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models expose an inference-time choice: which positions become visible after each denoising pass. Many existing decoding methods use hand-designed rules or require visibility to grow monotonically. We present a $\textbf{T}$iny $\textbf{I}$nference-time $\textbf{P}$olicy for $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{TIPS}$), an approximately $600$K-parameter controller that learns both unmasking and remasking while keeping the underlying language model frozen. TIPS uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select which tokens should be visible, while a fixed schedule controls the expected visible fraction. We train the controller through supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards. On GSM8K and MATH-500 with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the full-canvas and two-block TIPS variants achieve $58.46\%$ and $57.97\%$ micro-averaged accuracy at a budget of $32$ decoder evaluations, exceeding the strongest baseline in our main comparison by $12.1$ and $11.6$ percentage points, respectively. Both variants are trained at a budget of $32$ evaluations and remain competitive at higher budgets without retraining. These results demonstrate that learning when to reveal and reconsider tokens can improve the accuracy-compute trade-off without updating the decoder backbone.
authors: Ya-Shi Zhang, Jian Tang, Pierre-Andr\'e No\"el, Oleksiy Ostapenko
bullets: Addresses the limitation of hand-designed or monotonically expanding visibility schedules in masked diffusion language models.
Uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select token visibility, with a fixed schedule controlling the expected visible fraction.
Trains a roughly 600K-parameter controller using supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards.

With LLaDA-8B-Instruct at 32 decoder evaluations, TIPS reaches 58.46% and 57.97% micro-averaged accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500, respectively, outperforming the strongest cited baseline by 12.1 and 11.6 percentage points.
The full-canvas and two-block variants remain competitive at higher inference budgets without retraining.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language pre-training supports zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis, but standard objectives treat every off-diagonal image-report pair in a batch as a negative. In radiology, recurring findings across patients mean that instance mismatch need not imply semantic incompatibility, creating false-negative supervision that we term a semantic conflict. A training-trace audit shows that pair-observations selected by the online mask used during training are enriched for report-derived finding agreement, although this proxy analysis does not establish clinical equivalence. Fixed thresholds can become miscalibrated as similarity distributions evolve, while soft reweighting leaves residual repulsive gradients. We therefore propose Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning (SCCL), which tracks modality-specific similarity distributions with exponential-moving-average (EMA) statistics, derives adaptive thresholds, and hard-masks flagged candidates before softmax normalization. Inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) rules define two SCCL teachers, whose bidirectional cross-modal rankings are consolidated through standard distillation into a single deployable student, SCCL-DT. Across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, SCCL-DT achieves a mean zero-shot AUC of $0.850$, compared with $0.837$ for the strongest evaluated baseline in our comparison. Code will be made publicly available soon.
authors: Ting Liu, Haoran Lai, HaobinChen, Ming Liu, S Kevin Zhou
bullets: Addresses false-negative supervision caused by treating all mismatched image-report pairs as incompatible.
Uses EMA-tracked modality-specific similarity distributions to set adaptive thresholds and hard-mask conflicting candidates before softmax.
Combines inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) teachers through bidirectional ranking distillation into a deployable student.
Reports mean zero-shot AUC of 0.850 across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, versus 0.837 for the strongest evaluated baseline.
The agreement signal is proxy-based and does not establish clinical equivalence; code is planned for public release.

papers.abstract: Aerial robots operating near people must treat a pedestrian, a parked car, and a wall differently, yet conventional perception--planning stacks reduce all of them to occupied geometry---a \emph{human-aware safety gap} in which category-specific clearance is unavailable to the planner and temporary occlusions remove pedestrian-specific constraints from its map. We present a modular, fully onboard pipeline that closes this gap by turning visual observations into context-dependent safety constraints for real-time UAV navigation. A shared BLIP encoder drives scene captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, which is fused with depth to localize obstacles in 3D. Obstacle-specific risk is inferred by a lightweight LLM (Qwen-2.5-0.5B) stabilized with retrieval-augmented generation and grammar-constrained decoding that restricts its output to a planner-compatible JSON schema. The LLM reasons once per object category rather than per frame: its verdicts are cached per class, so previously seen categories are resolved without inference and new ones trigger a fresh retrieval-grounded query; detections are additionally given persistent identities and held in the map across occlusions. The perception pipeline runs at 10\,Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, while fallback LLM queries take approximately 0.8\,s and remain off the control-critical path. In Gazebo, low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles shows a roughly $3\times$ reduction in collision events over a geometric planner, and semantics-aware landing among moving actors raises success from 34\% to 96\%. The 224-pixel encoder input limits reliable small-object perception at range; conservative pedestrian margins and short-term persistence mitigate this limitation during navigation.
authors: Siwei Cai, Yuwei Wu, Vijay Kumar, Lifeng Zhou
bullets: Addresses the human-aware safety gap: pedestrians, vehicles, and walls receive different clearance requirements instead of being treated as generic occupied geometry.
Fuses BLIP-based captioning and text-conditioned segmentation with depth to localize obstacles in 3D.
Uses a lightweight Qwen-2.5-0.5B LLM with retrieval grounding and grammar-constrained JSON outputs; category-level verdicts are cached and detections persist through occlusions.
Runs perception at 10 Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, with fallback LLM queries kept off the control-critical path.
In Gazebo, collision events decrease by roughly 3×, while semantic landing success among moving actors increases from 34% to 96%; small-object perception at range remains limited.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning datasets remain overwhelmingly English-centric and commercially restricted, as their content is frequently generated by proprietary models whose terms of service forbid training competing systems. We introduce Multi-SFT, a commercially permissive collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs across five European languages, built via translation and regeneration pipelines for tasks where translation is insufficient. Human evaluation yields inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages. Fine-tuning nine models from three different families (EuroLLM, OLMo 2, Qwen3; 1B-32B) and evaluating them on 13 benchmarks shows that Multi-SFT alone is competitive with larger augmented mixes and official instruction-tuned releases, with decisive advantages on safety tasks.
authors: Daniela Baiamonte, Kamyar Zeinalipour, Elena Fano, Stefano Simonazzi, Andrea Zugarini
bullets: Addresses the lack of open, commercially usable multilingual supervised fine-tuning data.
Contains 502,818 instruction-response pairs in five European languages.
Uses translation and regeneration pipelines, with regeneration for tasks where direct translation is insufficient.
Human evaluations report inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across datasets and languages.
Fine-tuning nine models across three families and evaluation on 13 benchmarks show competitiveness with larger mixtures and official instruction-tuned releases, with clear safety-task advantages.

papers.abstract: Neural networks offer critical adaptability for controlling complex systems where nominal modeling proves intractable. However, when offline-trained neural networks are deployed within closed-loop control systems, their actions fundamentally alter the state distribution upon which they were trained. This paper introduces a unified taxonomy to categorize these sequential failure modes: the initial Closed-Loop Identification Error, the deployment-induced Action Error, and the continuous Tracking Error. Through discrete-time sensitivity analysis, this work formalizes how offline-learned parameters locally guarantee a trajectory divergence upon deployment, degrading performance due to local loss geometry. To mitigate this distribution shift, we propose actionable design policies centered on time-scale separated online adaptation. These mechanisms are validated through ablation studies on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator, demonstrating that bounded continuous learning successfully mitigates trajectory divergence whereas static deployments fail, offering concrete guidelines for practitioners deploying machine learning components in safety-critical feedback systems.
authors: Vittorio Lippi
bullets: Identifies three sequential failure modes: Closed-Loop Identification Error, deployment-induced Action Error, and continuous Tracking Error.
Uses discrete-time sensitivity analysis to formalize how local loss geometry can cause deployment trajectories to diverge from those seen during training.
Proposes time-scale-separated online adaptation policies to mitigate deployment-induced distribution shift.
Ablations on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator show bounded continuous learning mitigates trajectory divergence, unlike static deployment.
Targets safer deployment of learned control components in safety-critical feedback systems.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that depth recurrence can be retrofitted into pretrained language models. In this work, we adapt this paradigm for visual understanding, using depth recurrence to reduce the parameter footprint of a pretrained vision-language model (VLM). To this end, we prune layers from the language backbone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. At each step of the loop, a linear adapter merges the block's output with the token representations from the preceding layers and projects the fused representation back into the block. As the pruning impacts the original model performance, we propose a three-stage recovery training: first, we leverage a language-only pretraining to recover the performance of the language backbone, followed by an alignment of the vision-language projector, and a full fine-tuning of the model via visual instruction tuning. In the first and the last stage, we distill the outputs of the pretrained non-recurrent model into the recurrent model, which further improves the recovery. We evaluate the proposed approach on the TinyLLaVA-1.4B backbone without introducing any new vision-language data during retrofitting. Our experiments demonstrate that the retrofitted recurrent model outperforms the unpruned baseline trained with the same recovery data while storing 23.3% fewer language parameters. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup of converting a recurrent LM into a VLM on the same data. Additionally, our ablations show how design choices, such as the adapter between recurrences and a larger recurrent block, lead to the improved performance of our approach. Finally, we find that our proposed model gains on reasoning-oriented benchmarks, whereas its performance on basic visual understanding benchmarks remains on par with the baseline.
authors: Madhav Iyengar, Andreas Geiger, Hilde K\"uhne
bullets: Prunes the language backbone and repeatedly applies a subset of its layers, using linear adapters to merge representations across recurrences.
Uses three-stage recovery: language-backbone training, vision-language projector alignment, and visual instruction tuning.
Distills outputs from the original non-recurrent model during the first and final recovery stages.
On TinyLLaVA-1.4B, the retrofitted model outperforms an equally recovered unpruned baseline without adding vision-language data.
Improvements are strongest on reasoning benchmarks; basic visual understanding remains comparable to the baseline.

papers.abstract: Many hierarchical byte-level language models group bytes into patches using a learned boundary predictor whose view of the next codepoint depends on encoding and lookahead. In UTF-8, codepoints of many scripts take three bytes: 8 of 24 bits mark length and continuation, and the first byte carries only 4 high codepoint bits. After the same left context, a mark extending a grapheme cluster and a letter starting the next can thus share their first byte. Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE) keeps one- and two-byte UTF-8 encodings but writes these codepoints as two UTF-16 bytes, low byte first, so its first symbol carries 8 low codepoint bits that can distinguish such continuations. We train small causal predictors on matched FineWeb-2 text and evaluate on FLORES-200 under UTF-8, UBE, and UBE's same-length big-endian variant. At one-symbol lookahead, balanced grapheme-boundary error at codepoint boundaries across 17 languages in 13 Brahmic scripts is 8.76% with UTF-8, 8.62% with the big-endian variant, and 0.06% with UBE. When the target instead retains a parent tokenizer's subword cuts at grapheme boundaries, UBE lowers the mean error relative to UTF-8 at the same lookahead by 72.91% in Korean, 35.29% in Chinese, and 67.32-99.55% in eight more scripts. In the seven of them whose main Unicode block fits on one 256-codepoint page, the big-endian variant stays within 3.0% of UTF-8, so the gain follows byte order, not length. In Korean and Chinese, UBE's mean error falls below UTF-8's final mean error after only 25% and 37.5% of training. Which byte comes first thus affects how much lookahead a byte-level boundary predictor needs.
authors: Hyunsik Kim
bullets: UTF-8 can make a grapheme continuation and a following letter indistinguishable from their first byte in many scripts.
Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE) retains short UTF-8 encodings but represents longer codepoints as low-byte-first UTF-16.
Across 17 languages and 13 Brahmic scripts, one-symbol balanced boundary error was 0.06% with UBE versus 8.76% with UTF-8.
For parent-tokenizer subword boundaries, UBE reduced mean error by 35.29–99.55% across the reported scripts, including Korean and Chinese.
The comparison with a big-endian variant indicates that byte order—not encoding length—drives the improvement; scope is focused on boundary prediction and the evaluated multilingual text settings.

papers.title: The Right Byte First: How UTF-16 Helps Multilingual Boundary Prediction
papers.tldr: Putting the low UTF-16 byte first substantially improves multilingual grapheme-boundary prediction compared with UTF-8 at the same lookahead.

papers.abstract: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
authors: Zhuoming Liu, Jinhong Lin, Lin Zhang, Yiwu Zhong, Yin Li
bullets: Addresses the context bottleneck caused by memory methods that retrieve or append historical video observations to current inputs.
Uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to consolidate incoming observations into fixed-size LoRA parameter updates while keeping current observations as input.
Introduces MaLoW-Instruct, a streaming-video instruction dataset with 381K question-answer pairs across 56K videos.
Achieves 3.9%–11.8% higher performance than prior memory approaches on OVO-Bench’s backward split, with modest latency overhead.
Also improves action success on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%, suggesting applicability to vision-language-action models.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can act unsafely when individually benign images and texts are interpreted jointly. Beyond implicit reasoning risk, where reasoning drifts toward harm, we identify intent-level risk, where cross-modal ambiguity silently commits the model to a hazardous premise that path-level optimization alone cannot correct. We propose SAFE-PRO, which uses a Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty (RCU) signal, combining predictive entropy with a learned cross-modal risk score, to decide when to ask safety-grounded clarifying questions and where to apply path optimization, under a reward that prioritizes safety and penalizes over-refusal. We also build SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision, and theoretically analyze gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk under RCU. Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, SAFE-PRO consistently improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves its over-refusal, and surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.
authors: Wei Cai, Jian Zhao, Yuchen Yuan, Xuelong Li
bullets: Identifies intent-level risk: benign images and text can jointly imply hazardous premises that ordinary reasoning optimization may miss.
Uses Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty to trigger safety-grounded clarification and guide path optimization.
Introduces SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision.
Theoretically analyzes RCU’s effects on gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk.
Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves over-refusal, and exceeds GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.

papers.title: When Reasoning Is Not Enough: Proactive Inquiry for Cross-Modal Safety in Multimodal Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Long-context language models support ever longer context windows, and evaluations typically treat context length as the main indicator of difficulty. However, context length alone cannot explain why models fail on long-context tasks that require reasoning over complex information. Contexts of equal length can pose very different challenges: a task may be solvable from a single local passage, or it may require integrating evidence distributed across the full context. We quantitatively characterise this difficulty through three properties: evidence scope, how much necessary information must be found; evidence dispersion, how widely that information is scattered within the context; and reasoning depth, how many dependent steps are needed to derive an answer from it. We construct LURCH, a multi-domain question-answering benchmark of 6,550 instances with supporting evidence and reasoning graphs, enabling all three properties to be quantified. Evaluations of proprietary and open-weight models show that: (1) at fixed context length, all our three properties are strongly negatively correlated with model performance; (2) as context length increases, performance degrades sharply on samples with dispersed evidence, whereas it remains relatively stable on samples with localised evidence; and (3) difficulty compounds across properties, as questions with moderately high values on all three are harder than those with an extreme value on just one. These findings establish evidence scope, dispersion and reasoning depth as measures of long-context reasoning difficulty that complement context length.
