papers.abstract: Given a state and a set of options, such as intents, tools or interface elements, System One decision models return a distribution over the options in one forward pass, without generated reasoning. Web systems increasingly build them by reading decisions from language models. Two axioms of rational choice are natural requirements for such decisions, because in web systems the listing and the option set are determined by other components and can change or be manipulated: the order in which the options are listed should not matter, and adding an option should not change the relative odds of the others (Luce's choice axiom). We test the standard reads, namely single-choice question (SCQ) prompting, with shuffled-order training, order averaging or sorted options, and invariant set architectures, and find that each violates at least one axiom: one shuffle changes 12-20% of SCQ answers, sorting only freezes an arbitrary convention, and a well-chosen added option steers 4-34% of decisions. By Luce's theorem, a read satisfies both axioms only if it is a softmax over scores that each depend on one option alone, so in a transformer they hold by construction only if no token that scores an option sees another. We implement this as Prism-1 (Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models): every option is read in its own block at shared positions, with the model's usual left-to-right attention, in one forward pass. On five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, SCQ prompting trained on the same data still changes 7% of its answers under one shuffle, and an added irrelevant option steers 12% of its decisions. Prism-1 stays within one point of that baseline's accuracy and is 2-4 points more accurate once only answers that survive a reordering are counted, while no shuffle changes any of its answers and no added irrelevant option moves its choice among the others.
authors: Yao Long Teng, Jianguo Huang, Yanchen Deng, Jiayi Cai, Bo An
bullets: Web System One models should be insensitive to option order and to adding competing options, as required by rational-choice axioms.
Standard SCQ prompting, even with shuffling, sorting, or invariant architectures, violates at least one axiom.
Prism-1 scores each option independently in separate blocks at shared positions, using one forward pass.
Across five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, Prism-1 had no changes under shuffling or irrelevant-option additions.
Its accuracy stayed within one point of the baseline and was 2–4 points higher when counting only reorder-stable answers.

papers.abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long-term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning-based approaches often depend on pre-defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low-level control policies, while reward-based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high-level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask-oriented, fine-grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low-level reward generation, inspired by potential-based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM-based planning and reward methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/deng-ai-lab/PRM4RL.
authors: Xiuhui Zhang, Ning Gao, Xingyu Jiang, Yihui Chen, Yuheng Pan, Mohan Zhang, Yue Deng
bullets: Addresses sparse rewards and the difficulty of learning long-term tasks with conventional RL.

Uses a progress function to construct dense rewards inspired by potential-based reward shaping.
Provides theoretical optimality and convergence guarantees for policy optimization.
Outperforms existing LLM-based planning and reward methods on robotics control tasks, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion. We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific execution characteristics from planned-executed trajectory pairs and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while keeping the original planned trajectory unchanged. The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen. On NAVSIM, ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across unseen controller configurations and multiple frozen world-model planners, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes where execution mismatch more strongly affects candidate evaluation.
authors: Danqi Zhao, Keyu Chen, Wenchao Sun, Minglei Huang, Jianhe Zhang, Yan Zhu, Hao Cheng, Zifan Cao, Sifa Zheng
bullets: Problem: Different downstream controllers can execute the same plan differently, causing a gap between imagined and actual outcomes.
Naively substituting predicted or observed execution trajectories improves fidelity but does not reliably improve planning decisions.
Method: Infer controller-specific execution characteristics from planned–executed trajectory pairs and adapt the planner’s native ego latent rollout.
The world model, planner, and reward head remain frozen; the original planned trajectory is preserved.
On NAVSIM, the method consistently improves planning across unseen controllers and multiple frozen planners, especially in challenging driving scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Architecture of ExecutionBridge. (a) Controller Encoder. Given a support set of planned–executed trajectory pairs Sc, the Controller Encoder summarizes these observations into a compact controller representation ec that captures persistent controller-specific execution characteristics. An auxiliary execution decoder predicts the execution of a held-out query trajectory for training supervision and is discarded at deployment. (b) Controller-Conditioned Latent Bridge. For each candidate, the frozen world model first produces its native rollout from the original planned trajectory. Conditioned on ec, the Latent Bridge predicts a gated correction to the ego latent, which is bounded by a trust-region projection before being injected into the rollout. The resulting controller-conditioned rollout is evaluated by the unchanged reward model for candidate scoring.

Fig. 2. Planning–execution gap and motivation for ExecutionBridge. (a) The same planned trajectory can lead to different executions at deployment from those implicitly assumed by the frozen world model, causing its imagined future to deviate from the future actually encountered. (b) Directly substituting the planned trajectory with its executed counterpart improves execution fidelity, but introduces a plan–execution semantic mismatch: the executed trajectory can still be interpreted through the model’s implicit plan-to-motion mapping, and therefore does not necessarily improve candidate ranking. (c) ExecutionBridge instead retains the original planned trajectory as the conditioning input and uses controller-specific execution evidence to adapt the imagined future used for candidate evaluation.

Fig. 4. Representative planning results under the standard NAVSIM setting. Compared with frozen WoTE, ExecutionBridge yields trajectory selections that are better aligned with controller-dependent execution in representative collision and drivable-area failure cases.

Fig. 1. Evolution of end-to-end planning paradigms. Model-free planners predict or score trajectories directly from the current scene, without explicitly modeling their future consequences. Model-based planners additionally use a learned world model to imagine candidate-conditioned futures for trajectory evaluation. Conventional model-based planning typically assumes that candidate trajectories are executed according to the planto-motion relationship learned during training. Execution-adaptive modelbased planning further incorporates controller-specific information, allowing candidate futures to be evaluated under deployment-specific execution.

Fig. 6. Adaptation under representative controller styles. We show four representative controller configurations, including aggressive, conservative, steering-lag, and steering-gain behaviors. Controller-conditioned candidate evaluation consistently improves both PDM and Time to Collision (TTC) across these diverse controller styles. Examples on the right illustrate safetycritical cases in which accounting for controller-specific execution changes the selected trajectory and avoids failures under frozen evaluation.

Fig. 5. Planning under unseen controller shifts. Performance of the frozen planner and ExecutionBridge across ten unseen deployment controller configurations. (a) ExecutionBridge consistently improves PDMS across controller styles (mean: 87.98 → 88.59, +0.61). (b) It also improves TTC (mean: 94.53 → 94.86, +0.33). (c) The improvement is substantially larger on the low-score subset, where PDMS increases from 32.04 to 46.13 (+14.09). These results indicate that controller-conditioned adaptation is particularly beneficial in challenging driving scenes where candidate evaluation is more sensitive to execution differences.

Fig. 7. Execution fidelity does not imply decision fidelity. (a) Predicted and exact controller execution substantially reduce geometric execution error. (b–c) Nevertheless, candidate-ranking fidelity changes only marginally on the frozen-defined difficult-scene subset. (d) Direct execution substitution improves selected-candidate quality, but ExecutionBridge performs best by preserving the original plan and adapting its imagined future. Pairwise-oracle PDMS in (d) is a candidate-level diagnostic distinct from final navtest PDMS.

papers.abstract: Current heterogeneity-aware training systems for large models balance workloads by assigning unequal numbers of layers across pipeline stages, a strategy aimed at equalizing execution time through a unique pipeline configuration. However, this approach fails to address critical memory constraints and suffers from inherently coarse balancing granularity. In this paper, we propose Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism (HPP), a novel approach enabling efficient and fine-grained data balance across heterogeneous pipelines. To address HPP's key challenges, prohibitive search overhead for optimal configurations and high communication overhead from asymmetric All-Reduce, we design the ETH training system. ETH employs a hierarchical workload balance framework that jointly optimizes balance across heterogeneous pipelines and within individual pipeline stages. To mitigate asymmetric communication costs, ETH implements block-wise gradient aggregation. Furthermore, it integrates specialized optimizations that dramatically reduce HPP configuration search overhead. Evaluations demonstrate ETH achieves up to 2x training speedup while reducing configuration generation overhead by up to 56x compared to state-of-the-art systems. The code is available at https://github.com/YuMJie/ETH.
authors: Mianjie Yu, Zhongmin Zhao, Zizhao Mo, Jianxiong Liao, Wenxuan Li, Yulin Qiao, Huanle Xu, Wenquan Yang, Yongqiang Yang, Zeren Li, Ruifeng Tang, Chengzhong Xu

papers.abstract: Self-evolving language models train on tasks they generate, so every round must decide which updated model the next round inherits. Current loops such as R-Zero, Agent0, and Skill Self-Play make this decision through the task, admitting tasks that look learnable and inheriting every resulting update. We identify a selection-to-update gap in these loops, where a task that looks learnable need not produce a useful update. Most updates on verified tasks fail to make correct answers more likely, yet these loops inherit them all. HeirCommit freezes the updated model and uses fresh evaluation questions to decide whether to inherit it or retain the current model. EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, using current and archived experience to repair failures and preserve successes before final confirmation. Our analysis characterizes selection-induced optimism and decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors. HeirCommit cuts the harmful share of accepted updates by 68-83% relative to random inheritance at the same acceptance rate. Across four backbones, EvoHeir achieves the best mathematics and general-reasoning averages, raising the math average by 5.3% relative to the strongest baseline, Agent0. The framework lets useful experience persist even when the model that produced it is not inherited.
authors: Haoyi Yang, Kshitij Mishra, Nils Lukas, Salem Lahlou
bullets: Self-evolving loops often inherit updates from tasks that appear learnable, even when those updates do not improve correctness.
HeirCommit evaluates frozen candidate models on fresh questions before deciding whether to inherit them.
EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, allowing useful experience to persist despite rejecting its originating model.
The analysis decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors and characterizes selection-induced optimism.
HeirCommit reduces harmful accepted updates by 68–83%; EvoHeir obtains the best reported mathematics and general-reasoning averages across four backbones.

papers.abstract: Learning from demonstration is an effective strategy for endowing robots with manipulation capabilities but requires training on datasets comprised of massive amounts of demonstrations. Existing demonstration collection approaches either require constant human involvement, for example, via teleoperation or are specialized for a single task. Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems are able to autonomously solve and therefore generate demonstrations for general-purpose tasks; however, learning from their demonstrations has proven difficult due to multi-modality in their solutions. In this work, we build on recent work leveraging GPU acceleration for TAMP and propose DemoStream, a TAMP system that optimizes demonstration quality in order to improve behavior cloning success rates. First, we introduce batched TAMP sampling operations along with a new TAMP algorithm that correspondingly performs batched constraint satisfaction in order to explore many solutions in parallel. We conduct simulation experiments ablating different action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes to analyze the effect of these choices on downstream policy success rates. Finally, we show that we can leverage the safety guarantees of TAMP to directly collect real-world demonstrations at an average rate of 66 demos per hour. See our website for policy rollout videos: demostream.github.io.
authors: Caelan Garrett, Neel Jawale, Fabio Ramos
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, autonomous demonstration collection beyond teleoperation or task-specific systems.
Introduces batched TAMP sampling and batched constraint satisfaction to explore many solutions in parallel.
Optimizes demonstration quality to mitigate multimodal solutions and improve behavior-cloning success rates.
Evaluates action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes in simulation, and collects real-world demonstrations at an average of 66 per hour.
Scope: Results are presented through simulation ablations and a real-world demonstration-collection demonstration; the abstract does not specify broader task coverage or policy performance details.

papers.abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.
authors: Soumye Singhal, Joseph Jennings, Ka Shun Shum, Alexander Bukharin, Khushi Bhardwaj, Zirui Liu, Venkat Srinivasan, Jonathan Li, Yash Jain, Kezhi Kong, Markus Kliegl, Olivier Delalleau, Sanjeev Satheesh, Mostofa Patwary
bullets: Addresses the underexplored midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, where short-context pretraining and synthetic-heavy SFT may limit agentic capabilities.
Trains at 256K context on hundreds of billions of tokens from repositories, pull requests, commit histories, build logs, and a small amount of agent traces.
After identical SFT, gains appear across SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-bench Pro, and the long-horizon DeepSWE benchmark on two Nemotron models.
The recipe also improves robustness across agent harnesses.
Proxy metrics from base models were unreliable; the authors instead use short fixed SFT runs and report supporting ablations.

papers.abstract: Arabic calligraphy is a high-stakes cultural visual domain for Muslim communities, yet VLM evaluations rarely test its fine-grained script traditions. We audit 12 VLMs on a cleaned 1,195-image six-way benchmark using numeric, visual-cue, and Diwani-first prompts. In this closed-set setting, the best numeric-prompt accuracy is 60.9% for closed/API models and 47.2% for open-weight models. The main failure is default-label collapse: every numeric run is dominated by a single label taking 33-63% of predictions, against an 18.8% majority-class baseline. For 8 of 12 models the default is Thuluth; GPT-4o labels 52.9% of all images as Thuluth although it is only 18.1% of the set. Prompting helps unevenly: visual cues move accuracy by more than 10 points for some models but hurt others, and foregrounding Diwani often relocates the default rather than removing it. Arabic calligraphy recognition is therefore a compact, culturally grounded stress test for VLM robustness and for measuring which visual traditions become legible to automated systems.
authors: Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Evan Maksud, Reyana Shahid
bullets: The audit evaluates 12 VLMs on a cleaned 1,195-image, six-way Arabic calligraphy benchmark.

Prompt strategies have inconsistent effects: visual cues help some models by over 10 points but hurt others, while Diwani-first prompts often shift rather than eliminate the default.
The benchmark serves as a culturally grounded stress test for VLM robustness and the visual traditions recognized by automated systems.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to interpret religious, educational, and culturally sensitive visual content, yet their reliability on citation verification remains underexplored. We introduce Visual Sanad, a controlled benchmark for testing whether VLMs falsely accept incorrect Qur'anic verse attributions when the same quote-reference pair is rendered under different visual framings. The benchmark contains 2,400 rendered images built from 100 English Qur'an verses, four factual states per verse, and six visual conditions ranging from plain text to decorative and authority-framed layouts. All quote-reference pairs were source-checked and human-audited before rendering. Across 24 full model-prompt runs, we observe a sharp capability split. Proprietary API-served VLMs range from near-perfect citation verification to moderate false acceptance, whereas recent open-weight VLMs often show weak discrimination and default to VALID on most images. De-biased prompting can reduce false acceptance, but often by shifting the decision threshold toward INVALID rather than by producing strong citation discrimination. Visual Sanad therefore exposes a culturally grounded multimodal factuality failure: fluent VLMs may treat displayed religious citations as self-authenticating unless they have strong citation-verification ability.
authors: Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Reyana Shahid, Evan Maksud
bullets: Introduces a controlled benchmark of 2,400 rendered images based on 100 English Qur'an verses and four factual states.
Tests citation verification across six visual framings, from plain text to decorative and authority-framed layouts.
Finds a sharp capability split: proprietary VLMs range from near-perfect verification to moderate false acceptance, while many open-weight models default to VALID.
De-biased prompting can lower false acceptance but may simply shift models toward INVALID rather than improve discrimination.
Highlights a culturally sensitive multimodal factuality failure: displayed citations may be treated as self-authenticating.

papers.abstract: Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) is an essential capability for intelligent robots in human-robot collaboration, requiring an agent to follow a designated target person in dynamic environments relying solely on egocentric visual perception. However, persistent pedestrian occlusions in dynamic scenes pose critical challenges to existing EVT methods. Lacking proactive visibility preservation, reactive tracking methods frequently experience prolonged target loss under severe occlusions. Therefore, we propose VP-EVT, a framework that treats target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control rather than a by-product of following. Acting on this objective requires understanding both what obstructs the target and how robot motion can change that obstruction. VP-EVT therefore uses language-guided perception to extract separate target and pedestrian observations. When occlusion makes current observations incomplete, VP-EVT combines visual history with ego-motion to maintain estimates of their relative positions and motion. Using these estimates and the current following waypoints, VP-EVT predicts whether continued following will sustain the obstruction. When the predicted risk is low, the original following motion is retained; otherwise, a recurrent controller combines updated estimates with maneuver context from preceding decisions to coordinate viewpoint adjustment and the return to stable following. Moreover, we introduce OccEVT-Bench for closed-loop evaluation of persistent occlusion and collect expert demonstrations for training. On its Risk split, VP-EVT improves success rate by 121.4% relative to a competitive baseline and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%, respectively.
authors: Yanci Wen, Tianle Zeng, Jianwei Peng, Weixi Situ, Hanjing Ye, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses prolonged target loss caused by pedestrian occlusions in dynamic environments.
Uses language-guided perception to separate target and occluder observations, then combines visual history with ego-motion to estimate relative motion during partial visibility.
Predicts whether continued following will maintain occlusion and selectively triggers viewpoint-adjustment maneuvers through a recurrent controller.
Introduces OccEVT-Bench and expert demonstrations for closed-loop evaluation and training.
On the Risk split, improves success rate by 121.4% and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%.

papers.abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.
authors: Xueli Sun, Yuxiang Lu, Yantong Liu, Xianzhe Fan, Xi Chen, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Addresses failures caused by committing to a poor action sample during fine-grained manipulation.
Uses two initial samples to detect critical states from within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance.
When triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicted future latent states and task-progress changes.
Improves average real-world completion from 50.8% to 65.5% across pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement, with 326 ms added per triggered decision.
Also reports consistent simulation gains across RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO; verification is applied selectively rather than at every decision.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting trajectories that remain safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi-agent interactions, yet robust closed-loop decision making in planning-critical scenes remains challenging. Existing diffusion- and RL-based planners often rely on generic rewards and use relational structure mainly for representation, limiting how planning-critical rollouts shape policy improvement. We present GRID-Planner, a graph--reward integrated diffusion planning framework that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals. Specifically, GRID-Planner combines graph-aware importance weighting, a time-indexed relational reward surrogate, and an advantage-weighted diffusion objective with on-policy self-distillation, forming a rollout-return-advantage-update loop without explicit likelihoods. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that, compared with the diffusion-only baseline, GRID-Planner reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8\%, 60.8\%, and 27.4\%, respectively, and improves the planning score by 3.4\%. Project website: https://github.com/yangzhaojason/GRID-Planner.
authors: Zhao Yang, Zezhong Qian, Yinan Shi, Longjun Liu, Yawei Jueluo
bullets: Targets safer, rule-compliant, and more comfortable planning in complex multi-agent scenes.
Combines graph-aware importance weighting, time-indexed relational reward surrogates, and advantage-weighted diffusion training.
Uses on-policy self-distillation to form a rollout–return–advantage–update loop without explicit likelihoods.
On nuPlan and interPlan, reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8%, 60.8%, and 27.4%, respectively, while improving planning score by 3.4% over a diffusion-only baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall framework of GRID-Planner. We address the mismatch between semantically flat imitation signals and rare planning-critical scenarios through two components, graph-aware importance weighting (GA-IW) and relational reward surrogate (RRS), which are unified in the final graph-reward integrated diffusion objective.

Figure 1: Overview of GRID-Planner. Traditional diffusion planning may miss planning-critical relational semantics, whereas GRID-Planner combines Graph-Aware Importance Weighting and RRS to prioritize high-risk trajectories and evaluate safety, lane/route consistency, and comfort.

The baseline (top) results in collisions, while our method (bottom) navigates the same scenes. The ego vehicle is highlighted in yellow and collisions are shown in red.

Along the candidate trajectory 𝜏 , a time-indexed scene graph 𝐺𝑡 is queried at each step to evaluate safety, rule-compliance, and comfort terms. Selected steps are shown for illustration, and the per-step scores are aggregated over the horizon to form the dense trajectory-level reward RRRS (𝜏).

Figure 3: Illustration of the graph-aware weighting mechanism. CentFeat is computed from a snapshot interaction graph at 𝑡 = 0 and map-element counts, while CollProb is estimated from future proximity and TTC. They are combined to form the importance weight𝑤 (𝜏) in Eq. (5).

Figure 7: Training dynamics of the unified on-policy objective. The full graph-reward integrated objective shows faster convergence and lower collision rate than offline diffusion and partial ablations, demonstrating better sample efficiency and more stable closed-loop adaptation.

Figure 6: Training dynamics of GAIW. The full GAIW design with clipping and mean-normalization achieves higher closed-loop score (left) and lower collision rate (right) than variants without clipping or mean-normalization, indicating improved training stability in planning-critical scenarios.

papers.abstract: Learning from experience requires recovering reusable knowledge and determining when it applies to a new situation. We introduce OntoAct, a hypothesis-based neuro-symbolic framework built on ontological abstraction. OntoAct turns individual experiences into axioms over entity types, relations, and conditions, making their underlying patterns reusable across situations. A large language model (LLM) uses this world knowledge to propose hypotheses and actions, while a symbolic verifier assesses their supporting conditions against current observations. Verification identifies missing evidence, and new observations and intervention outcomes update hypothesis assessments and guide subsequent actions. We also introduce Tacit-FLE, a benchmark built on the Factorio Learning Environment (FLE) for diagnosing and repairing hidden faults in existing factories using inherited operational records. Its synthetic maintenance corpus distributes evidence across records, and an executed repair may leave the fault unresolved, requiring agents to reassess their diagnoses through interaction. Across Tacit-FLE, Mars, and ALFWorld, OntoAct achieves leading task performance with efficient interaction and inference.

papers.abstract: Biological visual navigation achieves remarkable robustness at extremely low power, whereas frame-based robotic systems relying on artificial neural networks remain limited in both respects, particularly for energy-constrained micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) operating in complex environments. Inspired by the event-driven, sparse, and asynchronous principles of biological visual systems, neuromorphic sensing and computation provide a promising alternative for robust and energy-efficient navigation. In this paper, we propose the first end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic paradigm for MAV visual navigation in complex environments by integrating neuromorphic vision, spiking neural networks, and neuromorphic processors. The proposed method first extracts the environmental representation from event streams using a spiking perceptual representation module. This representation is fed into a spiking navigation module, where guidance learning and population coding enable efficient policy learning with few time steps. The navigation module then outputs a waypoint converted into executable trajectory points. Experiments show that the proposed neuromorphic method achieves navigation performance comparable to ANN-based methods while markedly reducing power consumption. The spiking perceptual module consumes only 19.57% of the power of its ANN counterpart, while the spiking navigation module deployed on Intel Loihi consumes only 12.37% of that required by its ANN counterpart running on NVIDIA Orin NX. Beyond prior neuromorphic systems focused mainly on relatively simple navigation subtasks, we demonstrate a complete neuromorphic visual navigation system spanning simulation and real-world deployment. Our results establish the feasibility of the neuromorphic paradigm for autonomous navigation and provide a bio-inspired pathway toward robust and low-power MAV navigation.
authors: Junjie Jiang, Ankang Zhou, Zheng Fang

figures.caption: Figure 2: End-to-end event-driven neuromorphic MAV navigation system. (A) Architecture of the proposed end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic navigation system. The system comprises a spiking perceptual representation module and a spiking navigation policy module. The perceptual module converts event streams into compact, geometry-aware features, while the navigation policy module maps these visual features, together with the robot state and goal direction, to navigation actions. (B) Key hardware components of the neuromorphic system. The platform consists of a neuromorphic vision sensor (Prophesee EVK4), an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, an x86 host computer, a neuromorphic processor (Intel Kapoho Bay), and a micro aerial vehicle. The NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX communicates wirelessly with the x86 host computer. (C) Deployment and communication pipeline of the proposed system. Owing to the limited neuron models supported by Intel Kapoho Bay, the spiking perceptual representation module is deployed on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, whereas the spiking navigation policy module is deployed on Intel Kapoho Bay. The Jetson Orin NX acquires the event stream and transmits control commands to the Pixhawk flight controller. The Jetson Orin NX and the x86 host computer exchange system information wirelessly. The x86 host computer exchanges spike trains with Intel Kapoho Bay through NxSDK.

Figure 3: Training pipeline of the proposed end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic navigation method. Continuous grayscale image sequences are first transformed into asynchronous event streams using an event simulator. Depth estimation is then introduced as an auxiliary task to enable geometry-aware spiking features learning from event streams. The learned event features are fused with the MAV state and goal direction, and then encoded into spike trains via population coding. The resulting spikes are processed by the spiking navigation network and decoded to predict the action. Finally, collision loss, smoothness loss, and goal-reaching loss are defined based on the predicted action, providing physically meaningful supervision for end-to-end optimization of all network modules.

Figure 1: Visual navigation mechanisms across biological, conventional, and neuromorphic paradigms. (A) The biological visual navigation paradigm relies on the retina and neural circuits. Visual information is sensed asynchronously at the pixel level and processed through sparse, eventdriven neural activity to produce navigation behaviors. (B) Comparison between conventional and neuromorphic visual navigation paradigms for MAVs. The conventional visual navigation paradigm relies on frame-based cameras and artificial neural networks. Visual information is acquired synchronously as image frames and processed through dense, clock-driven computation to generate navigation actions. The neuromorphic visual navigation paradigm employs event-based vision sensors and spiking neural networks. Inspired by biological visual processing, it captures visual information asynchronously at the pixel level and processes it through sparse, event-driven computation to generate navigation actions.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors safeguard against misinformation, rendering their failures as much a societal as a technical concern. As generators constantly evolve, detectors trained on static datasets miss newly arising threats, while progressive training interferes catastrophically. Yet, mitigating forgetfulness in terms of accuracy, the prevalent focus of continual learning (CL), is insufficient to reflect real-world impact. We therefore scrutinize the effects of CL methods with respect to evolving fairness. To this end, we analyze four dimensions of fairness across diverse demographics for detectors trained progressively on a chronological sequence of 11 real-world deepfake generation methods. Tracking fairness metrics over time, we expose non-trivial interplays between performance and fairness that depend on both the choice of CL algorithm and demographic intersections. We find accuracy degradation to typically exacerbate unfairness and, conversely, fairness improvements to remain scarce over time. Dissecting the CL method families (rehearsal, prompts, regularization), we observe that inequitable forgetting is not explained by underrepresentation alone, but likely entangled with representation learning. We thus issue a call to action for CL methods to take social outcomes into account when balancing the stability-plasticity tradeoff.

Inequitable forgetting is not explained by underrepresentation alone and may involve representation learning.

papers.abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.

papers.abstract: Recent post-training approaches have shown that self-supervised speech encoders can be adapted to learn a single utterance-level speech attribute through knowledge distillation. In this work, we investigate whether a single speech encoder can simultaneously preserve multiple complementary utterance-level speech representations. We propose a multi-attribute multi-teacher distillation framework that learns semantic, speaker, language, and emotion representations from four frozen teacher models using a shared SSL backbone and attribute-specific branches. Experiments on multilingual semantic retrieval, speaker verification, language identification, and speech emotion recognition show that the proposed model achieves performance close to dedicated single-task students while requiring only a single shared encoder. Furthermore, the learned layer aggregation strategies reveal that different speech attributes naturally emerge at different depths of the SSL encoder, providing new insights into the organization of speech representations.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.

papers.abstract: Vision--language pre-training has enabled substantial progress in image--text retrieval and zero-shot recognition by learning transferable cross-modal representations. However, sentence-level alignment remains insufficient for compositional matching, where captions can describe the same objects and attributes while differing in how these elements are bound. To address this limitation, we propose Flow-CLIP, which refines global image-text alignment through image-conditioned changes in token--patch evidence. Global Compatibility Calibration (GCC) learns a sentence-level similarity metric, while Image-Conditioned Evidence Refinement (ICER) incorporates visual patch context into token queries and uses the resulting change in local matching evidence to adjust the global score. We further introduce Cross-Image Margin Ranking (CIMR), which compares the same positive--negative caption pair across matched and mismatched images, encouraging a larger ranking margin when the image supports the correct description. Experiments on compositional matching and attribute--object binding benchmarks show that Flow-CLIP improves binding accuracy over pretrained CLIP and learned global alignment through local evidence refinement, while cross-image ranking supervision mitigates reliance on language priors. Code will be released at link.
authors: Minghong Wei, Enguang Zhu, Pu Cao, Lu Yang, Qing Song
bullets: Targets sentence-level alignment failures where captions mention the same elements but bind attributes and objects differently.

Improves binding accuracy over pretrained CLIP and learned global alignment on compositional matching and attribute–object binding benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness.

papers.abstract: Language-guided 3D affordance grounding aims to localize functional regions on 3D objects according to interaction intents. However, existing methods exhibit poor generalization to unseen objects. One challenge is the query-target gap: a semantic discrepancy between query features encoding interaction intents and target-region features, leading to inaccurate grounding. End-to-end training favors query representations tailored to seen objects, limiting their compatibility with shifted target-region features on unseen objects. To address this issue, we propose BridgeAfford, a framework that reduces the query-target semantic gap from two complementary perspectives. First, Interaction Region Alignment (IRA) promotes cross-object alignment among geometrically similar interaction regions during training. This enables structures on unseen objects that resemble previously observed ones to produce representations similar to those learned during training, facilitating target-region recognition. Second, Visual Evidence Aggregation (VEA) leverages a 2D affordance model to refine the attention distribution and guide the query toward the correct region, yielding more target-aware queries. Extensive experiments on the LASO and PIAD datasets demonstrate that BridgeAfford outperforms existing methods, particularly on unseen objects, highlighting its robust generalization ability.
authors: Yijie Su, Yakun Zhu, Yi Bin, Pengpeng Zeng, Liang Chen, Guoqing Wang, Jingkuan Song, Heng Tao Shen
bullets: Targets poor generalization caused by mismatched query and target-region representations.

Scope: focuses on generalization to shifted or previously unseen 3D objects.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of BridgeAfford. (b) During initialization, new region features are directly inserted when empty slots are available; otherwise, the two most similar entries are merged to release a slot for the new entry. (c) Visual evidence is incorporated as an attention bias to guide query-to-point attention toward interaction regions.

Figure 1: Motivation for BridgeAfford. (a) Accurate prediction relies on high semantic similarity between the query and the target-region representation. However, shifted local representations on unseen objects may prevent the model from extracting the target region, resulting in query features with low similarity to it. (b) Unseen objects may contain interaction regions that are geometrically similar to those of seen objects. Aligning these regions with geometrically similar regions on training objects promotes consistent representations, helping the model recognize interaction regions and incorporate their semantic information into the query. (c) Objects may contain novel interaction structures that cannot be reliably aligned with those observed during training based on geometric similarity. We therefore use a more generalizable 2D affordance model to directly guide feature extraction, facilitating the generation of target-aware queries.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives, rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based on DINOv3, V-JEPA 2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN. Diagnostic analyses suggest that DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets emphasize absolute position and task identity. We therefore argue that what robot policies learn to predict, and how training is allocated among these targets, should be treated as explicit design choices rather than defaulting to action-dominant training.

papers.abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint. Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept. Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size. Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score. Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920
authors: Lo Gullstrand Heander, Markus Borg, Emma S\"oderberg, Christofer Rydenf\"alt
bullets: CodeHealth negatively predicted agentic review-and-fix token cost across all three tested LLMs, independent of PR footprint.
Each additional CodeHealth point corresponded to 3.5%–6.1% lower token cost.
The association appeared during review, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without producing more comments.
Adjusting for scored-file size removed the association, suggesting file size mediates the relationship.
Two registered code smells predicted fix cost, while batch fixing did not change median CodeHealth.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the study procedure in four phases, with its milestones on a timeline. Takeaway: Hypotheses and sampling were locked after pilot 3, and the pre-registration was finalized after the review agents had started but before the fix agent ran, so no complete row existed at filing (Section 3.12).

Figure 3: Associational path diagram of the registered model, log(tokens total) ∼ health + log(footprint) + language + (1|repo). Takeaway: Change footprint is treated as a mediator candidate sitting on the path from CodeHealth to cost, not as a nuisance covariate to be removed, so RQ1 concerns the direct path c′ that survives conditioning on footprint and RQ2 concerns the decomposition of a, b, and c′; the arrows denote regression paths in an observational design and do not imply causality.

Figure 4: One PR from each CodeHealth tier traced through the measurement instrument, all three from the medium footprint tercile and all three measured with sonnet-5. A pass is one invocation of an agent over its whole input; the iteration counts in each cell are the agent turns taken inside that single pass, so a batch fix pass with no retry can still run many iterations. Each is the PR whose total token cost lies closest to its own tier’s median among PRs with 95 to 125 changed lines, so none is an extreme case. Takeaway: At a nearly identical PR footprint, total cost rises as baseline CH falls, and the rise is not explained by the number of review comments, which are unrelated to CH across the whole sample (ρ = −.03, p = .56). Agent iterations, in contrast, are correlated with CH (ρ = −.16, p < .001). Three PRs illustrate the measurement path and are not evidence for it; the estimates are in Section 4.

Figure 1: The registered answers to RQ1 and RQ2, fitted separately per LLM. Takeaway: Token cost falls with CH for all three LLMs, and CH does not predict footprint, so larger PR footprints do not account for the extra cost of unhealthy code.

Table 12: The registered model form refitted on each pipeline stage separately, one fit per LLM per outcome, on the same PRs as Table 8. Fix-stage fits drop the PRs with zero review comments: n reports the rows that remain. Takeaway: The CodeHealth effect survives removing the fix stage from the outcome entirely, and in fact strengthens for every LLM, so the association lies with the review stage and not with the fix stage that follows it.

Table 13: Decomposition of the review-stage effect, same model form and same rows as Table 12. Because log(review tokens) = log(iterations) + log(tokens per iteration), the first two coefficients in each block sum to that LLM’s review-token coefficient by construction. Comment counts, and the per-comment ratio, are modeled on the PRs with at least one comment. The last row of each block corresponds to the review-token row of Table 12 minus the sixth row of this block, but it is fitted independently on the ratio, on the smaller sample that having at least one comment requires. Takeaway: Lower CodeHealth is associated with more agent turns and more tokens within each turn, and it shows most consistently on the input side, yet it does not correlate with additional review comments, so the additional spend buys no additional output and the cost per review finding rises accordingly.

Table 9: RQ2 three-path decomposition, every path estimated in the registered mixed-model family with a repository random intercept, fitted separately per LLM. Path (a) is log(footprint) ∼ health + language + (1|repo); paths (b) and (c) are the log(footprint) and health coefficients of the primary fit in Table 8. Takeaway: CodeHealth is not associated with PR footprint for any LLM, footprint is the strongest driver of cost for every LLM, and the CH effect on cost persists with footprint held constant, so the effect is direct with respect to PR footprint; Section 4.6.4 examines file size.

Table 1: The three pilot exercises and the main collection. Takeaway: Pilots 1 and 2 failed for sampling reasons rather than pipeline reasons, and each failure influenced the final design; pilot 3 is the main collection at one tenth of the scale, run with the same three LLMs, prompts, and workflow, with small harness updates in between.

Table 10: RQ3 confirmatory test on the main collection: partial Spearman correlation with log1p fix-agent tokens, controlling for log changed lines, Holm-corrected within each LLM’s three-hypothesis family. Takeaway: Complex Method and Complex Conditional are confirmed for all three LLMs; Code Duplication is confirmed for none of them, and its sign even reverses for sonnet-5, so only two of the three pre-registered smell hypotheses are supported.

Table 14: Exploratory refit of the comment-count outcome with both the CodeHealth score and the smell count as predictors on the same rows, controlling for log changed lines, log scored-file lines, log changed files, language, and a repo random intercept. Comment counts are modeled on the PRs with at least one comment, as in Table 13. Takeaway: The number of findings the agents report tracks how many smells CodeScene counted, while remaining unrelated to the CH score those smells produce, so the null in Table 13 reflects the predictor and is not evidence that the agents attend to unrelated properties of the code.

Table 15: The registered model refitted with log total lines of the scored files added, one fit per LLM on the same rows as Table 8. The size coefficient is the change in log tokens per unit of log file lines; it is reported as an estimate and is not part of the corrected family. Takeaway: Adjusting for file size absorbs the CodeHealth association for all three LLMs, which in this sample cannot be separated from the size of the files it is computed over.

Table 2: Achieved cell fill on the 3× 3 CodeHealth by footprint grid, against a target of 56 PRs per cell. Takeaway: Seven of nine cells filled completely. The two short cells are in the unhealthy tier at medium and large footprint, reflecting a real scarcity of low-CH PRs in the AIDev pool.

Table 4: The three LLMs, their serving stacks, versions, and cached input shares. The cached input share is computed as the share of all input tokens served from the prefix cache across the 465-PR collection, pooled over review and fix agents. Takeaway: The three instruments differ simultaneously in provider, quantization, serving stack, and prefix-cache regime, which is why the analysis fits them separately and never compares them inferentially.

Table 3: The four review agents and their primary ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristics (ISO/IEC 2023). Takeaway: The agent set partitions review concerns along an externally defined taxonomy, which makes the choice of roles auditable; the mapping is approximate only for DesignReviewer, which spans two characteristics.

Table 6: Agent-session termination categories and their treatment. Takeaway: A guard-stopped review session is kept because it is instrument behavior and part of the cost being measured; a guard-stopped fix session leaves no completed fix record or post-fix score, so that PR is excluded for that LLM. Infrastructure failures and unexpected errors are retried until success.

Table 5: The three code smells registered as confirmatory hypotheses for RQ3, selected from pilot data by the pre-specified rule. Takeaway: The rule retained the three smells present in enough pilot PRs, with a sign agreed by all three LLMs and the largest mean adjusted correlations; each was then registered with a mechanism of its own.

Table 7: Pilot 3 per-LLM CodeHealth-to-cost slope and the resulting power characteristics at the achieved main-collection design (n = 465, 246 repositories). Takeaway: All three pilot slopes are negative and similar in magnitude, but every LLM’s own required sample size exceeds the achieved 465, which is why no single LLM is designated primary and why the confirmatory claim is a direction-consistency criterion across all three.

Table 16: Run-to-run variance decomposition on the 27-PR replication subsample (three runs per PR per LLM). λ is the run-to-run variance divided by the between-PR variance; ICC(k = 1) is the implied reliability of a single run. Takeaway: qwen3-6’s run-to-run noise is about an order of magnitude larger, relative to its stable PR signal, than either of the other two LLMs, while deepseek-v4-flash and sonnet-5 are both highly reliable at a single run.

papers.selection_reason: Studies the token cost of agentic code review, providing empirical insights into the efficiency of LLM inference pipelines.
papers.title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
papers.tldr: In a pre-registered study of 465 agent-authored PRs, healthier code consistently required modestly fewer tokens for multi-agent review and fixing, largely because it involved smaller scored files.

papers.abstract: Continuous physical human-robot interaction requires robots to rapidly adapt their control behaviour without interrupting task execution. However, existing ROS 2 control architectures rely on stop-to-switch mechanisms that introduce substantial delays and interrupt execution. We present an open-source, sub-millisecond reflex engine based on an enhanced ROS 2-compatible multimode controller that enables deterministic switching between control modalities and integrates reflex behaviours for mitigating contact hazards and kinematic limit violations. Experiments on a Franka Robotics manipulator demonstrate switching delays below 0.1 ms, more than four orders of magnitude faster than conventional ros2_control, while maintaining continuous operation during safety-critical events. In a multi-stage manipulation task, the proposed framework reduced execution time by 3.5% and peak trajectory jerk by more than threefold. By eliminating runtime middleware overhead, controller transitions are implemented as lock-free pointer operations, enabling reflex-level responsiveness within an open-source robotics framework.
authors: Jon \v{S}kerlj, Sami Haddadin
bullets: Addresses delays and task interruptions caused by stop-to-switch mechanisms in existing ROS 2 control architectures.
Uses an enhanced multimode controller with integrated reflexes for contact hazards and kinematic-limit violations.
Implements transitions as lock-free pointer operations to avoid runtime middleware overhead.
On a Franka manipulator, switching delays were below 0.1 ms and continuous operation was maintained during safety-critical events.
A multi-stage manipulation task showed 3.5% lower execution time and more than threefold lower peak trajectory jerk.

papers.tldr: An open-source ROS 2 reflex engine enables deterministic, sub-millisecond control-mode switching during continuous human–robot interaction without interrupting execution.

papers.abstract: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.
authors: Antoine Bergerault, Cyrille Kone, Giorgia Ramponi
bullets: Strategic multi-agent IRL is challenging because rewards that explain observed behavior may not produce optimal decisions.
The paper formalizes this issue through strategic identifiability and shows that observing a fixed policy pair may be insufficient, regardless of the number of expert samples.
It introduces an active IRL algorithm for repeated two-player Stackelberg games, combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design.
Finite-sample guarantees achieve a Stackelberg sub-optimality rate matching the minimax rate up to polylogarithmic factors.
Experiments in an anti-poaching setting show benefits from active exploration for reward recovery and strategic performance.

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
authors: Dongjie Cheng, Ruifeng Yuan, Ran Wei, Ning Song, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Li
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed visual-imagination pipelines, such as novel-view synthesis, for diverse reasoning tasks.
Uses tools and skills to help the VLM decide whether and how to imagine, formulate generation requests, and interpret visual evidence.
Introduces co-evolution of tools, skills, and execution code from feedback while keeping model weights fixed.
Improves over direct reasoning with the same VLM across seven spatial, temporal, causal, and perceptual benchmarks.
Reports relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA; the strongest variant outperforms five evolving baselines across five benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Language priors in MLLMs can override visual evidence, impairing visual perception. Existing benchmarks assume shared priors across models and rely solely on accuracy. However, cross-model prior agreement falls below 80%, and over 15% of items can be answered correctly without any image, causing accuracy to overestimate prior resistance. To address these limitations, we introduce ViSiP-Bench, a benchmark grounded in rare-but-real scenarios across six prior categories, with a model-aware dynamic prior induction protocol and three metrics that more precisely and continuously measure prior resistance than accuracy alone. Evaluating 24 models reveals that prior adherence is pervasive, does not improve with scale, and larger models tend to either strongly override their priors or firmly adhere to them. We therefore propose MAPS, which identifies each model's strongest priors and fine-tunes on factually grounded knowledge to soften excessive prior reliance without disrupting general capabilities.
authors: Li Ma, Yan Zhuang, Jiawen Deng, Fuji Ren
bullets: Existing evaluations overestimate prior resistance because they assume shared priors and rely only on accuracy.
ViSiP-Bench covers six prior categories using rare-but-real scenarios, model-aware dynamic prior induction, and three continuous resistance metrics.
Across 24 models, prior adherence is widespread and does not consistently improve with model scale.
Larger models tend to either strongly override or firmly follow their language priors.
MAPS identifies each model’s strongest priors and fine-tunes on factually grounded knowledge while aiming to preserve general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Sequence models can generalise in fundamentally distinct ways: extrapolating structures seen in training, or using their prompt to adapt to novel tasks. The prevailing strategy determines how the model behaves beyond its training distribution, controlling potential capabilities and risks. Recent work has characterised many different strategies theoretically, and empirically described the transition between them as the quality and quantity of pretraining data vary. However, there is no learning theory for this competition, hence no fundamental understanding of \textit{why} one solution might be favoured over another. Here we provide such a theory in a solvable topic model---documents drawn from a finite mixture of latent topics, mirroring the heterogeneity of modern pretraining data. The dataset comes with two distinct solutions: a specialised predictor, that stores the finite topic mixture, and an in-context one, optimal for topics never seen during training. Our theory predicts their emergence at distinct sample complexities: the in-context predictor is available early, while the specialised one emerges only after the training tokens outnumber the parameters of the data-generating process. Trained transformers reproduce both scales and the separating crossover in remarkable agreement with the theory, with no fitted parameters.
authors: Francesco Cagnetta, Casper L. Christensen
bullets: Studies the competition between distribution-extrapolating specialized predictors and prompt-adapting in-context predictors.
Uses documents sampled from a finite mixture of latent topics, yielding both solution types.
Predicts distinct sample-complexity thresholds: in-context learning appears early, while specialization requires tokens exceeding the data-generating process’s parameter count.
Transformer experiments reproduce both learning scales and their crossover without fitted parameters.

figures.caption: Fig. 3 shows that transformers learn random topic models at the same rate as the Bayesian learner of Sec. 3.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of in-context learning versus specialization in transformers, relevant to Large Language Model learning dynamics.
papers.title: In-Context Learning Before Specialisation: Theory of Learning in a Solvable Topic Model
papers.tldr: A solvable topic-model theory explains why sequence models first learn in-context adaptation and only later specialize as pretraining data grows.

papers.abstract: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71-97.62% overall and 96.67-100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14-55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94-118 tokens per answer, or 48.75-56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their temporal status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information.
authors: Pengfeng Song, Yunkai Zhuang, Liye Shi
bullets: Stores facts as versioned, source-linked records while retaining earlier values for later reference.
Retrieves relevant versions in source order and labels historical records before answer generation.
Combines structured facts with event memory and original dialogue turns to recover missing details.
Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71–97.62% overall and 96.67–100.00% for historical-residence questions.
Used 48.75–56.73% fewer evidence tokens than session-aware RAG; it also outperformed session-aware RAG in a 1,540-question hybrid-memory evaluation.
