papers.title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: TEM is a training-free memory framework that tracks changing facts by preserving version history and temporal labels, improving answers to questions about updated information with compact evidence.

papers.abstract: Surgical teams could benefit from assistants that watch the video for requested events, such as "tell me when the clip applier appears during Calot triangle dissection", and answer questions about what has already happened. We formalise this task as request-driven event detection with exact semantics and causal alert decisions, and present SurgStreamer. It separates procedure-specific perception, which maps the 1-FPS stream to a structured state over tools, actions and phases, from procedure-agnostic reasoning, which evaluates a formal monitoring condition over this state and an event memory, either with exact rules or with a small controller that addresses entities through pointers rather than names. We evaluate this monitoring core with gold conditions. On a pre-registered, sealed test set of 12 laparoscopic cholecystectomies, SurgStreamer reached a macro event-F1 of 0.598 over full procedures. On identical 75-s windows with only the window available to every method, it scored 0.677. The tested configurations of the streaming vision-language model OneStreamer-4B, including ones fine-tuned on SurgStreamer's state or on video with an adapted vision encoder, scored at most 0.540 (Holm-adjusted p <= 0.012). At three external centres, re-training only perception raised performance on held-out procedures from 0.239 to 0.470. On a new procedure, pituitary surgery, controller weights trained on cholecystectomy matched an in-domain controller on oracle state (0.947 vs 0.938). On predicted state they missed the pre-registered non-inferiority margin (-0.024 [-0.040, -0.008]) unless the alert thresholds were re-calibrated. The results support separating perception from reasoning and point to perception under distribution shift as the main limitation.
authors: Bowen Xiang, Jon S. Heiselman, Michael I. Miga
bullets: Formalizes monitoring with exact event semantics, causal alert decisions, structured state, and event memory.
Maps 1-FPS video to tools, actions, and phases, then evaluates conditions using rules or a pointer-based controller.
Achieved macro event-F1 of 0.598 on full procedures and 0.677 on identical 75-second windows.
Outperformed tested OneStreamer-4B configurations, which reached at most 0.540 under the reported evaluation.
Perception under distribution shift remains the main limitation; retraining helped across centres, while cross-procedure transfer required recalibration.

figures.caption: Figure 2: SurgStreamer overview, shown on a sealed Cholec80 test procedure. A natural-language request is compiled once into an executable monitoring condition. Procedure-specific perception (blue) turns the 1-FPS stream into a structured state over a closed vocabulary of tools, actions and phases (decoded flags as lines, probabilities shaded; four of the seven tools shown). Procedure-agnostic reasoning (orange) addresses the entities of the condition through pointers (e1, φ), never by name. Every second, the exact rule controller C-rule, the learned controller C-learn or their per-family hybrid outputs yt , and an alert is issued causally, once the event is confirmed. Here the earlier irrigator onset at 08:35 (×) falls in the clipping phase and is not admissible; the onset at 14:59 (▼) is confirmed and reported at 15:00 (dashed line), as in the reference (decisions of C-rule on the decoded state). The event memory logs episodes and phase transitions causally and answers retrospective requests; the count shown, 3, matches the reference. For a new procedure or centre only the blue components are re-trained; the rule semantics and the C-learn weights are reused unchanged, and only the alert thresholds may be re-calibrated.

Figure 1: Request-driven monitoring on a sealed Cholec80 test procedure (75-s window, equal context: every method has only the window). The request is compiled once into an executable monitoring condition. From the 1-FPS frames, perception computes a structured state: predicted phase, hook probability (shaded) and decoded flag (line); grey: reference presence; orange band: matching tolerance around the reference occurrence; dashed line: its confirmation. Bottom: perframe decisions. SurgStreamer accumulates evidence causally: uncertain at the onset second, a single alert once the onset has persisted K = 2 s, then silence. The strongest state-text baseline (C-LLM) and the vision-adapted VLM (V-VA) stay silent over the whole window, as does V-LoRA (not shown). The example was selected for illustration; Fig. 9 shows a failure, and Section 5 the quantitative results.

Figure 6: A disappearance request on a sealed Cholec80 test window (equal context). The event is the last second the irrigator is visible (“last seen”); it is confirmed only after the instrument has been absent for more than G = 2 s, so the 1-s gap in the reference annotation (annotated) is not an offset. C-learn, which answers this family, briefly outputs uncertain around a dip of the irrigator probability without alerting, and alerts once at the confirmation of the real disappearance. C-LLM stays silent, as does V-LoRA (not shown); V-VA alerts 16 s early, while the irrigator is still visible. Selected to illustrate the failure mode quantified in Fig. 5; layout as in Fig. 1.

Figure 9: A failure on a sealed Cholec80 test window (equal context). At the window start, perception decodes the scissors as present although the reference marks them absent. When this false detection ends (14:58), the decoded state contains an offset, and C-learn alerts at 14:59, 42 s before the reference disappearance; in once mode, the real disappearance is then not reported. C-LLM stays silent; V-VA alerts 34 s early, and V-LoRA (not shown) also too early. The error originates in perception: on the decoded state, an offset had occurred. Layout as in Fig. 1.

Figure 8: The reasoning trained on cholecystectomy, applied unchanged to pituitary surgery (PitVis sealed test). Top: the transfer setting. Perception was re-trained on 15 PitVis procedures; the C-learn weights and alert thresholds are those trained on Cholec80. papers.abstract: Embodied spatial intelligence requires more than visual recognition: models must localize entities, reason about their relations, and express this knowledge in action-relevant forms. Yet joint training can conflate the knowledge needed at different stages because supervision is fragmented across incompatible geometric and semantic outputs. We introduce Anvil, a unified framework for data generation, training, and benchmarking for embodied spatial intelligence. (1) Anvil-Gen is a heterogeneous data flywheel that combines form-specific generation, cross-stage consistency verification, and failure-driven recollection across 11 Ground--Relation--Act forms. (2) Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision for learning diverse embodied spatial capabilities and scene-linked assessments that distinguish stage competence from error propagation. (3) Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student that consolidates heterogeneous spatial knowledge through distillation from specialist teachers. Semantic-first-fault routing targets teacher supervision to the student's earliest decisive failure, while stage normalization controls the loss scale across native outputs of different lengths. We construct 5.8M source-grounded records spanning 160K images, reserving 580K spatial records for held-out evaluation and using the remaining 5.22M records for training. On average across seven public benchmarks, Anvil-MOPD outperforms Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B by 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points, respectively, while reaching 80.67% on VABench-Point. Controlled studies support targeted coverage, selective transfer, and feedback-guided repair as complementary framework components.
authors: Weilin Ruan, Bohan Zhou, Jinghao Li, Yangkai Wei, Wenqian Li, Peiran Dong, Yingjie Xu, Leyi Wu, Haojian Huang, Binghui Xie, Han Yang, Kaiwen Zhou, Yinchuan Li, Ying-Cong Chen, James Cheng
bullets: Addresses fragmented supervision that can mix distinct geometric and semantic reasoning stages.
Anvil-Gen generates and verifies data across 11 Ground–Relation–Act forms, then recollects failure cases.
Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision and evaluations that separate stage competence from propagated errors.
Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student distilled from specialist teachers using earliest-failure routing and stage-normalized losses.
Across seven public benchmarks, it reports average gains of 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points over Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B, respectively; it reaches 80.67% on VABench-Point.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Anvil, a framework for embodied spatial intelligence and robot manipulation, combining data generation, training, and benchmarking.
papers.title: Anvil: Scaling Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Knowledge Recirculation
papers.tldr: Anvil builds embodied spatial intelligence by recirculating verified, failure-driven knowledge across localization, relation reasoning, and action-oriented stages.

papers.abstract: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) addresses decision-making under uncertainty and adverse outcomes. Learning risk-sensitive policies from fixed datasets is important when additional interaction with the environment is costly. Existing work on risk-sensitive RL focuses on online settings or specific risk measures, leaving a general theoretical understanding of its offline setting underdeveloped. In this work, we investigate efficient offline risk-sensitive RL using the optimized certainty equivalent (OCE), a general class of risk measures. We consider two formulations: dynamic-OCE RL, which applies OCE recursively at each step, and static-OCE RL, which applies a single OCE to the cumulative rewards. Under the tabular setting, we develop pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for both formulations and establish tight sublinear suboptimality bounds, explicitly capturing how risk sensitivity, encoded by utility functions, affects learning difficulty. Moreover, we establish minimax suboptimality lower bounds to characterize the problem's fundamental limits. To handle large state spaces, we further develop pessimistic least-squares value-iteration algorithms that incorporate the general OCE risk criterion into linear function approximation. We establish utility-dependent sublinear guarantees with explicit dependence on the feature dimension $d$. To our knowledge, we provide the first offline algorithms along with the first upper and lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.
authors: Hanzhen Wang, Boxiang Lyu, Zhongxiang Dai, Siyang Gao, Dake Zhang, Shuang Qiu
bullets: Addresses offline risk-sensitive RL, where further environment interaction is costly and existing theory is limited beyond specific risk measures.
Studies both dynamic-OCE RL, applying risk recursively, and static-OCE RL, applying one OCE to cumulative rewards.
Proposes pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for tabular problems and pessimistic least-squares value iteration for large state spaces with linear function approximation.
Provides utility-dependent sublinear upper bounds and minimax lower bounds, including explicit effects of risk sensitivity and feature dimension.
Claims the first offline algorithms and upper/lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces TagInsert, a Transformer-based model that challenges the common left-to-right (L2R) generation paradigm in Transformers, for sequence labelling tasks where dependencies may not naturally align with a L2R order. TagInsert lifts the L2R constraint by removing the decoder-side attention mask and enabling the model to decide a preferred order of tag generation at inference time. We experiment on the common Part-of-Speech tagging and the more complex Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) supertagging tasks on multiple languages and low-resource data settings. We show that, although encoder-only models like BERT remain strong performers for tagging tasks, TagInsert frequently outperforms a L2R encoder-decoder model, achieves results comparable to encoder-only models under data-scarce conditions, and shows better results on the long-tail of rare categories. Our analyses show that TagInsert alleviates error propagation typical of autoregressive models by learning to defer difficult predictions to later stages in the decoding process.
authors: Giacomo Bais, Tejaswini Deoskar
bullets: Targets POS tagging and CCG supertagging across multiple languages and low-resource settings.
Removes the decoder-side attention mask so the Transformer can choose which tag to generate next.
Frequently outperforms a left-to-right encoder-decoder model and approaches encoder-only performance in data-scarce settings.
Improves predictions for rare categories and reduces autoregressive error propagation by deferring difficult tags.

papers.abstract: Solving optimal control problems for high-dimensional mechanical systems subject to constraints remains challenging due to nonlinear dynamics and non-convex feasible sets. This paper introduces MAGMA(Multiplier-Augmented Geometric Motion Algorithm), an Affine Geometric Heat Flow (AGHF)-based trajectory optimizer that incorporates an augmented Lagrangian framework solved via a primal-dual flow. A theoretical characterization of the primal-dual AGHF is provided, establishing that MAGMA is a gradient flow on an appropriately defined energy. MAGMA is validated across a variety of challenging trajectory generation problems with obstacles, state limits, and actuation limits. Comparative evaluations against state-of-the-art solvers demonstrate that MAGMA achieves high quality solutions with significantly reduced tuning effort on the hardest problems.
authors: C\'esar E. Ramos Chuquiure, Vansh Thakur, Challen Enninful Adu, Ram Vasudevan
bullets: Targets optimal control with nonlinear dynamics, non-convex feasible sets, obstacles, state limits, and actuation limits.
Uses an augmented Lagrangian framework solved through a primal-dual flow within the AGHF trajectory optimizer.
Provides a theoretical characterization showing MAGMA is a gradient flow of a suitably defined energy.
Experiments across challenging trajectory-generation problems report high-quality solutions with reduced tuning effort compared with state-of-the-art solvers.

papers.selection_reason: Constrained trajectory optimization for high-dimensional mechanical systems, transferable to embodied robot motion planning.
papers.title: MAGMA: Multiplier-Augmented Geometric Motion Algorithm
papers.tldr: MAGMA combines affine geometric heat flow with an augmented-Lagrangian primal-dual flow to optimize constrained trajectories for high-dimensional mechanical systems.

papers.abstract: Generating 3D assets with explicit parts requires two properties at once: geometric detail inside each part and structural coherence across the whole object. Recent image-conditioned 3D generation models adopt a structured 3D representation that anchors tokens to explicit spatial positions, capturing both properties, but their output remains a single fused mesh. We ask how a part-decomposed generation model can inherit both properties of these holistic priors, and answer with STRUCTPARTS, a framework whose core technical contribution is a dual-frame coordinate interleaving mechanism: each shape latent is interpreted under both a part-local and an object-global reference frame, and processed through a global-local inter-leaved transformer that simultaneously reuses the prior's geometric detail at the part scale and its structural coherence at the whole-object scale. As its structural input, STRUCTPARTS uses a segmented mesh scaffold, a coarse mesh paired with a face-level segmentation mask kept entirely within the prior's native 3D representation. With only lightweight finetuning, both intra-part detail and inter-part coherence emerge from the same pretrained weights. On PartObjaverse-Tiny, STRUCTPARTS matches or surpasses prior part-decomposed models at a fraction of their training cost, while naturally supporting part-mesh refinement and part-level editing.
authors: Yiqun Zhao, Binbin Huang, Haobin Duan, Zibo Zhao, Shenghua Gao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining fine intra-part geometry with whole-object structural coherence.
Uses dual-frame coordinate interleaving, interpreting latents in both part-local and object-global frames.
A global-local interleaved transformer transfers geometric detail and structural coherence from pretrained holistic priors.
Conditions generation on a segmented mesh scaffold represented in the prior’s native 3D format.
On PartObjaverse-Tiny, matches or exceeds prior part-decomposed models with substantially lower training cost and supports part refinement and editing.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of STRUCTPARTS’s pipeline. Given a single image, our method first constructs a 3D segmented scaffold using the structure generation model followed by a segmentation model. We then sample points from each part surface to construct the voxel indices in both the per-part normalized space and the shared global-shape space. These voxel indices serve as position embeddings to guide the diffusion model’s sampling process. The segmented scaffold and part meshes depicted here are dataset-provided ground truth (GT), used to illustrate the part-wise data flow. part k, we use local embeddings RoPEL(·) = RoPE(·, I(k)L ) and global embeddings RoPEG(·) = RoPE(·, I(k)G ), which are then injected into the shape latents described next.

Figure 3: Layout-conditioned part decomposition. Comparison among methods that accept an explicit layout (HoloPart, X-Part, FullPart, OmniPart): each row shows assembled shapes for part coherency and exploded views for per-part geometry. Baselines drop fine details, leave incomplete shapes, or introduce floaters; STRUCTPARTS preserves both by reusing the holistic prior.

Figure 5: Ablation on positional-embedding strategies. Three variants compared against STRUCTPARTS’ dual frame: LRoPE only loses global structure (parts treated identically in their own normalized frames); GRoPE only recovers global layout but degrades small or off-center parts under unnormalized coordinates; GRoPE + part embed. (as in prior work) still misses fine geometric detail. Only the dual-frame design recovers both global structure and per-part detail.

Figure 8: Limitations: inaccurate scaffolds. Each example shows the input image, scaffold with segmentation, and exploded generation. Although our method generates geometric detail, inaccuracies in the input scaffold can persist in the generated parts.

Figure 6: Part-mesh refinement. Given a coarse input scaffold, X-Part rigidly follows the input geometry, while STRUCTPARTS recovers fine geometric detail directly from the image by leveraging the holistic prior.
Figure 7: Part-level editing. Merging or splitting segmentation groups on the scaffold yields decompositions at different granularities, training-free at inference time.

Table 4: Training allocation and computational cost. Both methods use 512 tokens per part and the same GPU-hour allocation. Table 8: Cross-dataset evaluation on ABO. A fixed 200-object subset is evaluated with identical inputs and the same whole-shape CD/F-score protocol for all methods. Released and matched-budget X-Part checkpoints are distinguished.

Table 6: Geometry preservation and scaffold perturbations. The input scaffold and generated outputs are evaluated against the same GT shapes with identical normalization and surface sampling. Table 3: Ablation Study of dual-frame positional embedding strategies. Quantitative results evaluated at both part-level and shape-level.

Table 5: Checkpoint quality and training-schedule accounting. Part-level evaluation on PartObjaverse-Tiny. The 40K STRUCTPARTS and 28K X-Part runs use the same GPU-hour allocation; the 20K STRUCTPARTS checkpoint is included to compare quality after fewer optimizer steps and processed parts.

Table 7: Part-level sensitivity to segmentation errors. We corrupt GT boundary labels to retain a known correspondence between each generated and GT part. These results are distinct from the assembled-shape experiment in Tab. 6.

Table 9: Category-wise part-level CD on PartObjaverse-Tiny. Each cell reports mean / median CD, using the six largest evaluation categories. X-Part denotes its released checkpoint.

Differences are STRUCTPARTS minus X-Part. F-score estimates and interval bounds use two decimals; a negative bound that rounds to zero retains its sign. Statistical conclusions use the unrounded intervals.

papers.selection_reason: Reuses holistic 3D priors for part-decomposed generation, fitting 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Seeing Both the Forest and the Trees: Reusing Holistic 3D Priors for Part-Decomposed Generation
papers.tldr: STRUCTPARTS reuses holistic 3D generation priors to produce detailed, structurally coherent, part-decomposed 3D assets with lightweight finetuning.

papers.abstract: Grid foundation models (GridFMs) are graph transformers pretrained on a masked power-flow objective, and evaluate power flow orders of magnitude faster than an iterative solver. Their size, however, targets data-centre inference, whereas low-inertia operation increasingly asks for inference at the edge, next to the measurement, at batch size one and within a single synchrophasor (PMU) reporting frame. We distil a 20.1M-parameter, 12-layer GridFM teacher into a 0.62M-parameter, 6-layer student, a $32.5\times$ parameter reduction at half the message-passing depth, using an objective that combines the masked power-flow loss with output, physics-residual, latent-state and attention transfer. The physics-residual term, which matches the teacher's power-residual profile, has not previously been applied to typed power-grid graphs. We evaluate on a renewable variant of the IEEE 118-bus benchmark grid in which 26 of the conventional (synchronous) generators are replaced by inverter-based renewables with battery flexibility and standardised reactive-power limits (IEEE 1547), giving $97\,529$ physically valid (AC-OPF-feasible) operating scenarios, and we ablate all eight combinations of the transfer terms, reporting accuracy against ground truth and fidelity to the teacher separately. Distillation lowers student error on all four predicted quantities, by up to $48\%$ on active-power dispatch, and every distilled student is more accurate than its teacher on reactive-power dispatch. The gain is largely carried by the output matching term. The physics-residual term, in the layer-aggregated form used here, is consistently harmful, which we attribute to the spatial averaging it applies to a bus-level residual field. The resulting student is $32.5\times$ smaller in parameter count and has half the message-passing depth, making it a candidate for subsequent edge-device benchmarking.
authors: Vlad Alexandru S\u{a}nduleac, Shahariya Rasheed Rayamarakkarveettil Puthanpurayil, Noman Khan, Remus Teodorescu
bullets: Targets real-time, batch-size-one grid inference at the edge within a single PMU reporting frame.
Distils a 20.1M-parameter, 12-layer teacher into a 0.62M-parameter, 6-layer student using output, latent, attention, masked power-flow, and physics-residual transfer losses.
Evaluated on a renewable IEEE 118-bus variant with 97,529 AC-OPF-feasible operating scenarios and separate accuracy and teacher-fidelity analyses.
Student error decreases for all four predicted quantities, with up to 48% lower active-power dispatch error; all distilled students outperform the teacher on reactive-power dispatch.
Output matching provides most of the benefit, while layer-aggregated physics-residual matching is consistently harmful, likely due to spatial averaging of bus-level residuals.

papers.selection_reason: Distillation of a grid foundation model for real-time edge inference directly targets computation and latency reduction.
papers.title: Physics-Aware Distillation of a Grid Foundation Model for Real-Time Edge Inference
papers.tldr: Physics-aware distillation compresses a large GridFM into a 32.5× smaller student that improves power-flow prediction accuracy, though the tested physics-residual transfer term hurts performance.

papers.abstract: Aggressive quantization of neural networks can expose activation functions as bottlenecks for efficient hardware acceleration. Implementing quantized activations as multi-threshold operations has been shown to be a promising optimization, allowing for efficient hardware implementation of few-bit activations. However, current implementations are limited to monotonically increasing functions, quantization schemes with one-dimensional (per-channel) granularity and a small set of predefined activation-quantizer combinations. We formalize the multi-threshold representation to extend it to non-monotonic functions and fine-granular parameters, i.e., multi-dimensional thresholds. For automated conversion of quantized function compositions into threshold representation, we propose a systematic approach via algebraic rules integrated into the ONNX-based compiler infrastructure. We experimentally validate our solution on a selection of monotonic and non-monotonic functions by extending the binary search based multi-threshold operator that is integrated into the FINN framework for end-to-end synthesis of custom-tailored FPGA accelerators. The cost of hardware support for non-monotonicity and fine-granularity is characterized in comparison to an alternative approach utilizing existing operators via graph-level decomposition. We compare our method to prior work as well as the approach taken by the hls4ml framework. As an outlook, we demonstrate the prospects of using the multi-threshold representation during the training of a neural network as a form of quantization aware training.
authors: Christoph Berganski, Felix Jentzsch, Marco Platzner
bullets: Addresses hardware bottlenecks caused by aggressively quantized activation functions.
Formalizes multi-threshold representations for non-monotonic functions and multidimensional thresholds.
Introduces algebraic compiler rules in an ONNX-based infrastructure to automatically convert quantized function compositions.
Validates the approach on monotonic and non-monotonic functions using FINN’s binary-search multi-threshold operator and end-to-end FPGA synthesis.
Characterizes hardware costs against graph-level decomposition, prior work, and hls4ml; also explores multi-threshold representations for quantization-aware training.

figures.caption: Fig. 8: Comparison of functions implemented as multi-threshold functions in terms of lookup table resource utilization over increasing quantization bitwidth β∗. The thresholding bitwidth β results from calibrating the quantizer to the function at the bitwidth β∗. For monotonic functions β = β∗, as indicated by the black horizontal bars. Non-monotonic functions might revisit the same output level, resulting in β > β∗. Functions are ordered from top left to bottom right by average LUTs per output level. The quantization error (mean absolute error) decreases with the quantization bitwidth as indicated below each bar.

To locate the input within the list of seven sorted thresholds, three comparators are required, corresponding to the three levels of the search tree shown on the left.

Fig. 9: Comparison of functions implemented as multi-threshold operators in FINN and a composite lookup-table based approach in hls4ml in terms of LUT count over quantization bitwidth β∗. For FINN, HLS refers to our binary-search backend (Section III) and RTL refers to the backend introduced by SIRA, which requires graph-level decomposition for the non-monotonic functions. Shaded in dark grey is the portion of LUTs used by the multi-threshold operators, which is a more realistic estimate of the resource impact within a streamlined accelerator, where de-quantization occurs only once at the end of the model graph, not after each operation. For hls4ml we set the number of lookup table entries to the same number of thresholds required by our approach – this number is annotated on top of the first group of bars per function. The selected lookup table data type is either floating-point or β∗ bit fixed-point. The two functions on the right are not directly supported as a lookup table in hls4ml and are realized as a composition of a σ(x) lookup table and standalone additions and multiplications.

Fig. 4: Comparison of the hardware implementation to the graph-level decomposition in terms of lookup table resource utilization for increasing number of thresholds N and number of channels covered by parameters. papers.selection_reason: Compiling quantized activations into multi-threshold operators for custom DNN accelerators directly targets efficient AI inference on hardware.
papers.title: Compiling Multi-Threshold Operators for Quantized Non-Monotonic and Fine-Granular Activations in Custom-Tailored DNN Accelerators
papers.tldr: The paper extends multi-threshold activation compilation to support non-monotonic functions and fine-grained, multidimensional quantization for custom FPGA-based DNN accelerators.

papers.abstract: Retrieval tasks are a form of search task where a robot must explore, find an object, and return with it as quickly as possible. Recent work in ergodic control has demonstrated time-optimal path planning for search tasks where visitation is proportionally matched, within some tolerance, to a given target distribution. However, these planners minimize the duration of a full deterministic search, while retrieval missions end their search at an unknown point in the trajectory and must return to a given base. In this work, we propose a new formulation of the time-optimal ergodic search problem that models detection as a Poisson process and minimizes total mission time by including the return phase in the objective. Experimental results show that time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER) achieves up to $19\%$ shorter mission durations relative to ergodic baselines and that this advantage grows as the return phase becomes more costly. Simulation and hardware implementations validate TOER's compatibility with environments of non-convex geometry as well as both 2D and 3D search domains.
authors: Christian Sulana, Christian Hughes, Ian Abraham
bullets: Addresses retrieval missions where detection occurs at an unknown point and the robot must return to a base.
Models object detection as a Poisson process and incorporates the return phase into the optimization objective.
Validated in simulation and hardware for non-convex environments and 2D and 3D search spaces.
Achieves up to 19% shorter mission durations than ergodic baselines, with larger benefits when returning is more costly.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Belief Fidelity Impact on Mission. Search in the room setting from Fig. 3 as the true target is displaced by δ from the given belief. (Left) InfoMax’s detection collapses once the belief is wrong (0.93 → 0.22) while the ergodic methods degrade slowly, since covering the belief’s support leaves detection mass where the target can still be found. (Right) TOER holds the lowest mission time until the target leaves the belief entirely, where its tradeoff between detection speed and terminal position is no longer beneficial.

Fig. 1. Time-Optimal Ergodic Retrieval. A Franka arm executes a full retrieval mission of a green block in an occluded 3D search domain. From its start pose (t0), the arm sweeps the bin along an ergodic trajectory (t1) until the overhead camera detects the target. Once detected, the arm abandons the remaining plan, grasps the object (t2) and delivers it to the base (t3). We propose time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER), which includes the expected return cost explicitly in the objective such that searches prioritize likely detection sites that are closer to the base.

Fig. 6. Computational Scaling of TOER. Log-log wall time for a single solve at fixed iterations (95% CI bands on each slope). TOER and TOES scale identically in trajectory knots N , while the Poisson detection term makes TOER grow linearly in domain samples M while TOES is sublinear.

Fig. 5. Return Bound and Detection Certificate. Validation of the return bound and detection certificate on the non-convex room grid from Fig. 3. (Left) The two return-cost estimates from one detection site. The obstacle-blind bound cuts through walls while the true geodesic routes around them. (Right, Top) Planning against the loose bound costs 0.1% of realized mission time relative to the geodesic bound. (Right, Bottom) With survival ≤ δ imposed, realized survival stays inside the certified region at every δ.

Fig. 2. Expected Mission Time Comparison. Single-target search in an open planar field as the sensor’s detection gain is swept at fixed κ = 6.6. When detection is unreliable, the target is usually not found, thus mission time is dominated by return, and TOES + Return suffers additional return cost at every unsuccessful episode. TOER holds a ≥ 12% advantage over TOES + Return throughout while matching TOES (End @ Base) without imposing a terminal constraint.

Fig. 3. Return Discrepancy Profile. Object search in a planar 12-room lattice. (Left) Search scene with uniform target draws and sensor footprint, occluded by walls. (Right) TOER’s paired mission-time advantage over each baseline vs. return discrepancy κ. Advantage grows logarithmically (R2 = 0.95) toward the ceiling from Prop. 2. The gap to TOER (search-only) isolates the return term, which is null at κ = 1 and 7.9% at κ = 10.

papers.selection_reason: Time-optimal ergodic search and retrieval planning for robot navigation, including the return phase.
papers.title: Time-Optimal Ergodic Retrieval
papers.tldr: TOER plans ergodic search-and-retrieval trajectories that minimize total mission time, including the uncertain detection point and return to base.

papers.abstract: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
authors: Donghoon Han, Minseop Jung, Dong Woo Kwak, SeungJae Lee, Junhoo Lee
bullets: Targets conditional memories whose full embedding table must remain available for lookup.
Encodes each row with a short code and local scale, using a shared Gaussian-trellis reconstruction program.
Adds norm restoration and independently decodable row records for practical access.
Reduces output KL by 41–63% versus 2-bit round-to-nearest quantization.
Cuts DeepSeek table storage from 203GB to 51GB, enabling larger GPU-resident workloads.

papers.selection_reason: Quantizes large LLM n-gram lookup tables with compressed reconstructable codes, drastically reducing model memory footprint while preserving output quality.
papers.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Conditional Program compresses language-model lookup tables to two bits per value while reconstructing requested rows on demand, substantially reducing storage and quantization error.

papers.abstract: Weight quantization below four bits shrinks memory and bandwidth at a perplexity that looks acceptable, but often at the cost of factual knowledge and task accuracy. Ternary weights have mostly been obtained by training from scratch or long fine-tuning. We introduce RoleQ, a quantization framework that places scales by the functional roles of Transformer units rather than by the layout of the weight matrix, as conventional formats do. Vectors that read from the residual stream take one scale per output unit; those that write to it, one per input unit. The rule is structural, needs no search, calibration or stored state, and holds on integer and ternary grids. In a rotated basis it matches a per-layer axis search at half the solver work, and at ternary it cuts perplexity by up to half against layout-based placement in two families at every size from 0.6B to 14B, where per-row scales leave MMLU at chance. Our lightweight post-training pipeline converts an existing checkpoint to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours, a fraction of the cost of learned ternarization, and leads every post-training ternary method at matched or lower memory-resident bits on perplexity, zero-shot accuracy and MMLU, most widely on knowledge. A sparse second ternary plane placed by a per-unit Fisher saliency keeps the matmul multiplication-free and recovers what ternary loses first: at 8B, a fraction of a bit returns about half the MMLU that conversion costs, well ahead of random or Hessian-based placement at equal bits.
authors: Johannes Knittel, Alec Helbling, Hanspeter Pfister
bullets: Targets sub-four-bit quantization, where memory savings often degrade factual knowledge and task accuracy.
Assigns scales by Transformer unit function: residual-stream readers use per-output-unit scales, while writers use per-input-unit scales.
Requires no search, calibration, or stored state, and converts existing checkpoints to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours.
In two model families from 0.6B to 14B parameters, ternary RoleQ reduces perplexity by up to half versus layout-based scaling; per-row scaling leaves MMLU near chance.
A sparse second ternary plane selected by Fisher saliency recovers about half of the lost 8B MMLU performance with a fraction of a bit.

figures.caption: Figure 1: RoleQ aligns scales with the roles. (A) Readers read from the residual stream through rows, writers write to it through columns. (C) Qwen3-14B, ternary at equal bits: the placement alone lifts MMLU from 25.4 (chance) with per-output-channel scales to 38.5.

Random was run at three budgets. (b) The same cells as a ratio to the Fisher placement: its advantage over random decays from 1.96× at +0.15 bits to 1.12× at +0.90, and Hessian × weight overtakes it at +1.20 bits (0.94×). papers.selection_reason: Ternary quantization of LLMs reduces model memory, fitting efficient AI memory-efficiency.
papers.title: RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary
papers.tldr: RoleQ converts pretrained language models to ternary weights using role-aligned scaling, preserving knowledge and accuracy better than layout-based quantization at low memory cost.

papers.abstract: Incremental learning (IL) aims to continually acquire new knowledge (plasticity) while retaining previously learned information (stability). However, striking a balance between plasticity and stability remains a significant challenge for intelligent systems. The human brain achieves exceptional balance, owing to various memory units that collaboratively encode and store information. Inspired by human memory mechanisms, this paper introduces an IL framework with knowledge enCoding, Consolidation, and Integration (Co2In). Co2In is designed as a bi-level memory architecture: a working memory for adaptive knowledge acquisition and a long-term memory dedicated to the persistent retention of information. The two memory modules work cooperatively during IL. The working memory first learns from new data to encode knowledge into parameters. Subsequently, Co2In performs a consolidation process to identify underlying patterns in the learned parameters and re-express them into a compact knowledge representation. Next, the knowledge representation and the identified patterns are transformed into separate network layers and integrated into the long-term memory. These designs empower Co2In to accumulate knowledge with high plasticity and stability. We evaluate Co2In on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet under exemplar-free Class-IL and Task-IL settings. Experimental results show that Co2In achieves state-of-the-art performance with efficient memory consumption.
authors: Wenju Sun, Qingyong Li, Boyang Li, Wen Wang, Siyu Zhang, Yi Wei, Yangliao Geng
bullets: Addresses the plasticity–stability trade-off in continual learning.
Uses working memory for adaptive learning and long-term memory for persistent retention.
Consolidates learned parameters into compact knowledge representations and integrates them as separate network layers.
Evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet under exemplar-free Class-IL and Task-IL.
Reports state-of-the-art performance with efficient memory consumption.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Diagram of memory-based IL methods, Atkinson-Shiffrin human memory model [8], and the proposed Co2In. (a) Memory-based IL methods prevent the model from forgetting when learning by replaying old-task exemplars or restricting gradient directions. (b) In the human brain, information is temporally stored in short-term memory. After repeated rehearsal, the information will be permanently remembered in long-term memory. (c) Inspired by the human brain, Co2In acquires new knowledge with working memory and integrates it into long-term memory for storage.

Fig. 2. Illustration of the learning process of Co2In. (a) The task-t training process of Co2In, including knowledge encoding, knowledge consolidation, and knowledge integration steps. (b) In the knowledge consolidation step, Co2In recognizes new pattern basis and projects the parameters to form compact knowledge representations. (c) In the knowledge integration step, Co2In reorganizes the long-term memory into a unified neural network.

In contrast, the logits output by the quadratic classifier can not only contribute reasonable classification within task-1 samples (c) but is also suitable for task-2 samples (d).

papers.selection_reason: Bi-level memory incremental learning directly fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Co2In: a Bi-level Memory Incremental Learning Framework with Knowledge Encoding, Consolidation, and Integration
papers.tldr: Co2In uses cooperating working and long-term memories to learn new classes while preserving prior knowledge in exemplar-free incremental learning.

papers.abstract: Partial shape matching is a crucial yet underexplored problem in 3D vision, with significant relevance to real-world scenarios where shapes are often only partially observed. Existing feature descriptors face difficulties in this setting, as traditional representations either struggle with the boundaries of partial shapes or heavily depend on the shape's spatial position. While existing approaches have employed DINO features for partial shape matching, these features are not inherently suited for handling partial observations. In this work, we propose a method to refine DINO features using LoRA-based self-supervised learning, enabling the generation of feature descriptors that are robust to partiality. Our features substantially improve performance on partial shape matching compared to traditional or vision foundation features. Additionally, when integrated into existing partial shape matching pipelines, we achieve state-of-the-art results on partial shape matching and left-right prediction benchmarks.
authors: Viktoria Ehm, Dongliang Cao, Riccardo Marin, Daniel Scholz, Weikang Wang, Florian Bernard, Daniel Cremers
bullets: Addresses partial 3D shape matching, where boundaries and spatial-position dependence challenge existing descriptors.
Refines DINO features through self-supervised learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA).
Produces geometry-aware descriptors designed to handle partial observations.
Improves partial shape matching over traditional and general vision-foundation features.
Achieves state-of-the-art results when integrated into existing pipelines on partial shape matching and left-right prediction benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Our Self-Supervised Training Pipeline: Given a full mesh X , we first generate a partial observation Y . After randomly rotating both shapes with different rotation matrices around the Y-axis, we render the partial and full shape from different perspectives with cameras C. For every camera ci ∈ C, we obtain an image IiX of the full shape, which is then passed through a frozen DINOv3 architecture with a LoRA module with rank r to extract pixel-wise features Qi X . These are then backprojected on the shape and averaged to get vertex-wise features FX . Similarly, we proceed for the partial shape Y . Finally, we use the Geodesic-Aware PointInfoNCE contrastive loss to align corresponding vertices of both shapes and separate all others based on geodesic distance. In our experiments we use 4 views for the partial and 9 views for the full shape.

Figure 3. Qualitative Results of Feature Quality: We show colour-coded correspondences based on the features computed with different feature extractors. GeoLoRA exhibits improved performance, especially in left-right predictions.

Figure 14. Qualitative Results of Partial-to-Full Shape Matching Methods: We show two more examples of partial-to-full shape matching on the PFAUST-H and SHREC16 HOLES dataset. We can see improved matching quality with our GeoLoRA features, especially in the extremities of the shapes, such as the left arm of the human and the legs of the horse.

Figure 4. Qualitative Results of Partial-to-Full Shape Matching Methods: We show one qualitative result of partial-to-full shape matching on the SHREC16 CUTS dataset. We can see improvement in the quality of the matching, especially at the arm with GeoLoRA features.

Figure 13. Qualitative Results of Partial-to-Partial Matching: We show colour-coded correspondences for partial-to-partial shape matching methods. We compare DINOv3 features with GeoLoRA features. The red area indicates points that are predicted not to be in the overlapping region. On the BECOS dataset and the PSMAL dataset, we demonstrate improved performance with GeoLoRA features compared to DINOv3 features. On CP2P24 we observe similar matching quality.
Figure 7. Failure Cases: We show two failure cases of our method. The method primarily struggles with shapes in challenging poses, where the shapes are not positioned upright.
Figure 10. 3D Keypoint Matching: Our method can be used for 3D keypoint matching. We show examples of the BeCoS test set.

Figure 11. Qualitative Results of Feature Quality: We show colour-coded correspondences based on the features computed with different feature extractors. GeoLoRA exhibits improved performance, especially in left-right and front-back predictions.
Figure 6. Real-World Scan: We match a real-world partial scan on a template human. DINOv3 struggles to characterise incomplete geometry, while GeoLoRA shows robust performance.
Figure 9. 2D Keypoint Matching: We show examples for keypoint matching on the SPair-71k [42] dataset. Our method shows superior matching results in these examples.
Figure 12. More Qualitative Results: We show more qualitative results of our partial-to-full features.
Figure 5. Qualitative Results of Left-Right Prediction: GeoLoRA shows better chirality prediction than DINOv3 (shapes from BECOS).
Table 7. Overview of Symbols

Table 1. Improvement of Feature Quality Through Our Self-Supervised Pipeline: We show that with GeoLoRA we can improve the feature quality on all partial datasets in terms of the mean geodesic error (×100). BECOS* indicates BECOS without SHREC16 data.

Table 2. Partial-to-Full Shape Matching with GeoLoRA: We show that we can improve the downstream task performance of partial-to-full shape matching with GeoLoRA in comparison to DINOv3 features in terms of mean geodesic error (×100). The numbers in brackets of ULRSSM show the geodesic error after test-time adaptation.

Table 3. Partial-to-Partial Shape Matching with GeoLoRA: We demonstrate that our GeoLoRA features achieve better downstream partial-to-partial shape matching performance than DINOv3, as measured by geodesic error (×100) and Intersection over Union (IoU).

Table 4. Number of Views N with Frozen DINOv3: With an increasing number of views, the time increases linearly, while the geodesic error (×100) already saturates earlier. Thus, we choose 49 views for our experiments.
Table 10. Performance of Different Backbone Scales: We show that with a larger backbone we do not gain significant improvement in terms of geodesic error.

Table 12. Comparison to DINOv2 + Stable Diffusion Features: We compare the chirality (left-right) accuracy of the features used in [58] to our GeoLoRA features. Our method’s features show higher accuracy.
Table 6. Chirality Score for BECOS Partial Shapes: We show that we can improve the left-right prediction of [58] with GeoLoRA in terms of accuracy.
Table 5. PointInfoNCE vs GeoLoRA: We show that our loss formulation decreases the geodesic error (×100) significantly compared to the widely used PointInfoNCE loss.

papers.selection_reason: Self-supervised geometry-aware refinement of DINO features for partial 3D shape matching; relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Teaching DINOv3 About Partial 3D Geometry: A Self-Supervised Geometry-Aware Approach
papers.tldr: A LoRA-based self-supervised adaptation makes DINO features more robust for matching partially observed 3D shapes.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted information from large language models, but existing evaluations often measure forgetting only on a designated benchmark distribution. We argue that such behavioral forgetting is an insufficient standard for privacy-oriented unlearning, and that evaluation should instead test whether forgetting persists across the access paths through which the same information may be recovered. We demonstrate this with a controlled case study of cross-lingual querying: across multiple multilingual model families, forgetting varies substantially when semantically equivalent information is queried in different languages and scripts. A single access path is therefore enough to expose a real gap between behavioral forgetting and information inaccessibility, motivating broader evaluation of access-path generalization and adversarial recoverability alongside in-distribution forgetting.
authors: Tyler Lizzo, Larry Heck
bullets: Machine unlearning evaluations often test forgetting only on a designated distribution.
Privacy-oriented evaluation should examine whether forgetting generalizes across ways of accessing the same information.
A controlled cross-lingual case study finds substantial variation across languages and scripts in multilingual model families.
A single alternative access path can reveal residual information, motivating tests of access-path generalization and adversarial recoverability.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes access-path generalization for evaluating machine unlearning in LLMs, a meaningful contribution to LLM privacy and reliability.
papers.title: Behavioral Forgetting Is Not Privacy in Machine Unlearning
papers.tldr: Behavioral forgetting on one benchmark does not guarantee that private information is inaccessible through other query paths.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation models requires large amounts of interaction data, yet collecting diverse real-robot experience remains costly. Human manipulation videos, in contrast, provide abundant and diverse task experience that could potentially benefit robot learning. However, differences in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms make human motions unsuitable as direct supervision for robot actions, raising a scientific question: what knowledge in human videos should be transferred across embodiments to robot manipulation? To address this question, we analyze subtask transfer through the lens of causal beams, focusing on which contextual conditions and interaction dependencies should be retained to support local task effects. Based on this perspective, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST learns manipulation-related representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations. Within a predefined manipulation model, causal-beam constraints guide contextual information selection by requiring retained assignments to sustain local mechanism outputs while preserving nontrivial responsiveness to retained inputs. The selected semantic information conditions a world-action model, allowing the robot to generate actions from its own observations without requiring human-robot motion correspondence. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show improvements in task success over the corresponding world-action model baselines.

papers.abstract: Sky-image irradiance forecasting is dominated by a two-stage design: a video-prediction model forecasts future sky frames, and a separately trained regressor maps those frames to irradiance. We propose a single-stage alternative that co-denoises the future sky-image and clear-sky-index sequences in one diffusion process, with an irradiance head that reads a denoised preview of the future sky rather than the noised diffusion state. The forecaster needs no regression stage and runs from sky images and deterministic covariates alone, with no measured irradiance at its input --- the situation at a site with a camera but no pyranometer. On 2023 SIRTA data the model reaches a pooled RMSE of $104.1$~W\,m$^{-2}$ and a skill score of $+0.34$ on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) against smart persistence, higher than any of twelve baseline configurations, and retains that skill when retrained on 2021--2022. On the model's own generated frames, a separately trained regressor reaches $150.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$ against the joint head's $104.1$: roughly $46$~W\,m$^{-2}$ that joint training recovers and a cascade discards. Point accuracy is competitive but not best: a deterministic network that also reads measured irradiance attains $97.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$. The model's CRPS skill leads that network's in every sky-condition tertile, by $0.26$ to $0.30$.

bullets: Addresses the limitations of two-stage systems that first generate sky frames and then regress irradiance from them.

On 2023 SIRTA data, achieves 104.1 W m⁻² RMSE and +0.34 CRPS skill versus smart persistence, outperforming twelve baselines; skill transfers when trained on 2021–2022.

A separately trained regressor on the model’s frames obtains 150.6 W m⁻² versus 104.1 W m⁻² for the joint head, indicating roughly 46 W m⁻² of recovered accuracy; deterministic irradiance-informed forecasting remains better for point RMSE.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning enables robots to perform complex tasks by leveraging human-collected demonstrations. However, most existing approaches require labor-intensive data collection with additional teleoperation systems, which hinders scalability. Human videos represent a natural source of data that implicitly contain knowledge of manipulation behaviors. However, transferring them to robots remains challenging due to the visual domain gap and the absence of explicit action labels. In this work, we introduce TDV, a trajectory-based framework that leverages data generation to enable generalizable manipulation. TDV focuses on task-relevant objects by leveraging plug-and-play 6D pose estimation techniques to extract object trajectories from human videos, thereby mitigating the impact of irrelevant backgrounds and varying viewpoints. As a modality-agnostic intermediate representation, trajectories are inherently independent of the visual domains and different embodiments, enabling efficient data generation. Our method outperforms previous approaches on RLBench simulation tasks, achieving near 100\% success rates across seven tasks. In real-world experiments, TDV enables cross-embodiment generalization manipulation from one-shot human demonstrations by leveraging efficient trajectory generation techniques.
authors: Guoping Pan, Xinmiao Yu, Wannan Cao, Jincheng Li, Baolin Jiang, Yizhe Li, Yi Cheng, Houde Liu

During deployment, real-time pose estimation and a switch policy enable closed-loop control and multi-procedure task execution.

papers.abstract: Existing safety benchmarks rely largely on synthetic prompts with loosely grounded taxonomies and offer little focused analysis of severe crime categories. We introduce GUISE, a benchmark of criminal-assistance scenarios sourced from real-world cases and organised under a taxonomy from the UNODC International Classification of Crime for Statistical Purposes (ICCS). Each scenario is rendered under three linguistic framings and evaluated across five distinct cultures. Using our proposed two-tier evaluation framework, which judges both harmfulness and operational uplift, we find that: (i) framing alone drives unsafe compliance, with the mean unsafe compliance rate rising from 28.9% under direct requests to 66.4% under correction seeking (peaking at 97.3%; p < 0.05), as models correcting deliberately distorted details supply executable criminal steps; (ii) culturally adapted prompts elicit significantly more unsafe compliance than literal translations of the same requests in all four non-English languages (+7 to +18 points), a risk that translation-based benchmarks miss; and (iii) unsafe responses from the least-safe models carry strong Anglocentric registers, and the extent of this leakage increases monotonically with response harmfulness ($\rho$ = 0.46 to 0.63 across languages, all p < 0.001). GUISE offers a grounded resource and fine-grained diagnostics for strengthening refusal alignment across languages and cultures. We publish our code and data to facilitate future research.

papers.abstract: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space. Instead of providing multi-view images, videos, or 3D representations to the model, we preserve the native visual encoding of VLMs, i.e., a single image, one at a time, just like humans, and treat the 3D representation only as an environment with which the model can interact through actions (e.g., move left) and observations (rendered images). Each rollout begins from an initial first-person view and a visual question. The model can then iteratively reason, navigate, and reorient its viewpoint before committing to a final answer. Following an initial trajectory-supervised finetuning, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. Crucially, RL provides no direct supervision over which viewpoints the model should visit or which exploration actions it should take. Instead, the model must learn an effective exploration policy solely from the extent to which its interactions improve performance. Across six 3D benchmarks, our model ACT3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2% that improves its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses proprietary Gemini 3.6 Flash. ACT3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50-70% fewer input frames, and generalizes to unseen domains with an average improvement of 5.9% over its supervised initialization. Further analysis reveals adaptive, question-conditioned exploration. Performance gains over the base model increase from 0.6% on questions answerable from the initial view to 16.3% on those requiring extensive exploration. ACT3D searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary exploration, and acquires complementary viewpoints for spatial comparisons. These findings demonstrate that outcome-based RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual evidence, but also to learn when and how to acquire it.

bullets: Uses one rendered image at a time, with actions such as moving and reorienting, rather than preloaded multi-view or 3D inputs.

Learns question-conditioned exploration: it searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary movement, and gathers complementary views for spatial comparisons.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal semantic segmentation benefits from complementary sensors, but this benefit is fragile when some modalities are degraded or missing at test time. Many existing methods rely on dedicated fusion modules or multi-branch cross-modal encoders, and the fusion often becomes unreliable when modalities are absent, leading to substantial performance drops. We propose \textbf{FuseAdapt}, a parameter-efficient framework that performs fusion within the adaptation space of a frozen vision foundation model (VFM), exploring whether VFM priors can serve as an effective shared backbone for multi-modal segmentation. Instead of attaching a standalone fusion network, FuseAdapt assigns each modality a lightweight adaptation branch and performs \emph{adaptation-space fusion} by keeping Q/V low-rank adaptation private to each modality and routing only FFN low-rank residual activations across modalities inside the frozen backbone. The pretrained VFM remains fixed while modality-specific corrections and explicit cross-modal interaction are learned through the adaptation paths. To handle missing modalities, we further introduce \textbf{Predictive Modality Modeling (PMM)}, a direct representation-level objective for cross-modal redundancy. During training, PMM masks a target modality and predicts its embedding from the visible ones, supervised by a teacher target computed under full-modality input. PMM is used only during training and adds no inference-time overhead. Across three multi-modal segmentation benchmarks (MCubeS, DELIVER, MUSES), FuseAdapt consistently improves both modality-complete and modality-incomplete segmentation with a small trainable budget, yielding up to +3.01 mIoU under full modalities and +12.56 mIoU under missing modalities over prior state-of-the-art. Project page: https://devinxzhang.github.io/FuseAdapt-Page/.
authors: Xin Zhang, Robby T. Tan
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when modalities are absent or corrupted at test time.
Uses modality-specific low-rank adaptation branches inside a frozen vision foundation model.
Fuses modalities by routing only FFN adaptation residuals across modalities while keeping Q/V adaptations private.
Introduces Predictive Modality Modeling to reconstruct masked modality embeddings during training without inference overhead.
Improves complete- and incomplete-modality segmentation across three benchmarks, with gains of up to 3.01 and 12.56 mIoU, respectively.

Fusion is thus performed inside the adaptation path while keeping the backbone frozen, and the fused features are sent to a shared segmentation head. For clarity, we show the routing for one modality; the others follow the same design. (b) PMM: To handle missing modalities, an EMA teacher provides the target embedding for a selected modality. papers.abstract: Audio-enabled large language models (AuLLMs) allow users to interact with them simply by talking to them, without the need for an intermediate transcription. This expands the model's accessibility and capabilities by encoding non-verbal cues. However, using non-verbal cues may lead to biased behaviour based on the attributes inferred (or assumed) from them. In this work, we focus on the gender attribute and show that models' perception of it can be unlearned using adversarial methods without a loss in performance on other benchmarked tasks. Such models are useful in situations where gender inference is unwanted. However, in other practical settings, gender perception (without bias) may be desired.As a less radical measure, we distil the gender-agnostic model, creating a model that perceives gender but responds similarly to the gender-agnostic teacher, unless explicitly asked.We apply our newly proposed methods to three AuLLMs and obtain satisfactory results in the gender-unlearning part and partially satisfactory results in the distilling part.
authors: Adnan Al Ali, Jind\v{r}ich Libovick\'y, Anne Lauscher
bullets: Audio-enabled LLMs can infer gender from non-verbal cues, potentially causing biased behavior.
Adversarial training is used to unlearn gender perception while preserving performance on other benchmarked tasks.
Distillation creates models that retain gender perception but aim to respond like a gender-agnostic teacher unless gender is explicitly requested.
The methods are evaluated on three audio-enabled LLMs.
Gender unlearning achieves satisfactory results; distillation is only partially satisfactory.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have accelerated video generation technologies. However, AI-generated videos (AIGVs) remain susceptible to various distortions, highlighting the need for dedicated video quality assessment methods. Content semantics play an important role in AIGV quality assessment, with source prompts typically used as textual references. However, these prompts may not accurately reflect the generated video content, resulting in a discrepancy between the intended textual description and the generated result. To address this limitation, this paper proposes VGCap, an AIGV quality assessment framework guided by visually grounded captions that align better with generated content. Specifically, we introduce two forms of captions: a global caption obtained by minimally revising the source prompt based on multi-frame visual evidence, and prompt-independent segment captions that describe localized temporal content. Together, these captions provide complementary textual evidence for assessing spatial quality, temporal quality, and text-video alignment. Experimental results on the LGVQ and FETV datasets show that VGCap outperforms representative baselines across all three dimensions. Further ablation studies on caption sources and temporal components confirm the effectiveness of visually grounded captions for each quality dimension, while highlighting the benefits of segment-level features for temporal quality prediction. The source of VGCap will be available at https://github.com/lolo123-123/VGCap.
authors: Kehao Zhou, Yixuan Li, Yuxuan Jiang, Fan Zhang
bullets: Source prompts can diverge from the actual video, limiting content-aware quality assessment.
VGCap uses a revised global caption based on multi-frame evidence and prompt-independent segment captions for localized temporal content.
These complementary captions assess spatial quality, temporal quality, and text-video alignment.
Experiments on LGVQ and FETV show VGCap outperforms representative baselines across all three dimensions.
Ablations support visually grounded captions and show segment-level features benefit temporal quality prediction.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overall framework of VGCap. The Text Feature Extractor extracts features from the source prompt, global caption, and segment captions. The Spatial Feature Extractor derives frame-level spatial features. The Temporal Feature Extractor produces whole-video and segment-level motion features. The Adaptive Global Blend Gate fuses the branch-specific video and textual features, which are mapped to their corresponding scores by three quality predictors.

papers.selection_reason: Visually grounded captioning for AI-generated video quality assessment; relevant to video-language understanding and temporal quality evaluation.
papers.title: Beyond Source Prompts: Towards Visually Grounded AI-Generated Video Quality Assessment
papers.tldr: VGCap improves AI-generated video quality assessment by replacing unreliable source prompts with visually grounded captions that better match generated content.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a compelling pathway toward energy-efficient artificial intelligence, fundamentally anchored in presynaptic input-driven sparsity. However, a substantial yet chronically overlooked source of computational overhead persists: the continuous subthreshold dynamics of postsynaptic neurons. Quantitative analysis reveals that up to 44% of neurons in an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18 model reside in a deeply inhibited state, imposing a persistent computational burden despite having a negligible probability of firing. To address this inefficiency, the Dormant Spiking Neuron (DSN) model is introduced. By incorporating a state-driven dynamic gate, the DSN allows a neuron to enter a dormant state when its membrane potential falls below a predefined negative threshold, dynamically pruning redundant computations at the instance level. Crucially, this dormancy mechanism is directly integrated into the neuronal dynamics and trained end-to-end via backpropagation through time using surrogate gradients, enabling the network to actively learn a robust dormancy policy that adaptively preserves critical information flow. Extensive experiments across static and neuromorphic datasets demonstrate that the DSN framework consistently reduces computational energy by 40% to over 70%. Notably, on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, the DSN outperforms state-of-the-art static pruning techniques at comparable reported cost reductions and simultaneously improves the corresponding baseline SNN accuracy by 1.34%. By establishing a trainable, state-driven sparsity paradigm orthogonal to conventional input-driven methods, the DSN unlocks synergistic efficiency gains, presenting an effective approach for advancing neuromorphic computing.
authors: Ruichen Ma, Yicai Chen, Pujun Zhou, Yue Zuo, Chongyang Li, Shuang Liu, Shaogang Hu, Guanchao Qiao
bullets: SNNs incur substantial overhead from continuously updating postsynaptic neurons unlikely to fire; up to 44% are deeply inhibited in an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18.
DSN adds a state-driven gate that places neurons below a negative membrane-potential threshold into a dormant state.
The mechanism is integrated into neuron dynamics and trained end-to-end with backpropagation through time and surrogate gradients.
Experiments on static and neuromorphic datasets report 40%–over 70% lower computational energy.
On ImageNet, DSN exceeds static-pruning performance at comparable reported cost reductions and improves baseline SNN accuracy by 1.34%.

papers.title: The Dormant Spiking Neuron: A State-Driven Mechanism for Efficient Spiking Neural Networks
papers.tldr: Dormant Spiking Neurons reduce SNN computation by dynamically skipping deeply inhibited neurons while preserving—and sometimes improving—accuracy.

papers.abstract: Echo State Networks (ESNs), as lightweight implementations of reservoir computing, provide efficient solutions for temporal data processing in resource-constrained environments. While standard ESNs offer computational efficiency, their dense readout layers inflate the stored model and the per-sample inference cost. This paper introduces a Smooth-L1 regularized ESN (SL1ESN) that promotes sparsity in the readout layer while preserving differentiability for gradient-based optimization. The method employs a twice-differentiable Smooth-L1 approximation compatible with Newton's method, which we exploit both for centralized training and for a second-order (Newton-step) federated aggregation scheme. Under a single fixed shrinkage threshold shared by every dataset and both settings, experiments on seven time-series classification benchmarks show that SL1ESN learns readouts that are $77$--$95\%$ sparse in the centralized setting and $75$--$95\%$ sparse in the federated one, while staying within $0.7$ accuracy points of the strongest dense baseline on five of the seven benchmarks in the centralized setting and within $1.6$ points on the same five in the federated one, and the second-order federated update converges in only a few rounds. The resulting sparsity compresses the stored model, the per-sample inference cost, and the server-to-client broadcast by a comparable factor. These results demonstrate the practical value of sparse readouts for edge computing and IoT deployments.
authors: Gengcheng Lyu, Manuel R\"oder, Frank-Michael Schleif
bullets: Targets the storage, inference, and communication costs of dense ESN readout layers in resource-constrained edge and IoT settings.
Uses a twice-differentiable Smooth-L1 regularizer to promote sparsity while enabling Newton-based centralized training and federated aggregation.
With one fixed shrinkage threshold across datasets and settings, readouts reach 77–95% sparsity centrally and 75–95% federated.
On seven benchmarks, accuracy remains within 0.7 points of the strongest dense baseline centrally and 1.6 points federated on five benchmarks.
The sparse readouts provide comparable reductions in model storage, per-sample inference cost, and server-to-client broadcasts; federated training converges in a few rounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FedSL1ESN training pipeline. The server broadcasts the fixed global reservoir once and a sparse global readout each round (CSR, minimal payload); clients evaluate the local gradient and Gauss-Newton Hessian of their Smooth-L1 loss on private data and return this curvature information for the server’s Newton-step aggregation.

Figure 4: Federated setting; the counterpart of Figure 2. Test accuracy versus readout sparsity for the accuracy-selected global readout obtained by FedSL1ESN, i.e., the model aggregated from five clients that never share data (50 rounds, IID partition, mean over ten seeds, reported at the final round), under the same sweep of the shrinkage threshold τ ; shaded bands are ±1 std across seeds. As in the centralized case, accuracy stays essentially flat out to 75–95% sparsity on most datasets, and collapses only once the readout is driven to near-total sparsity.

Figure 3: FedSL1ESN convergence over communication rounds for each dataset (five clients, IID split, 50 rounds, mean over ten seeds; shaded bands are ±1 std). (a) Test accuracy reaches near-peak within a few rounds on most datasets and is stable thereafter (Strawberry is the slowest, climbing until round ∼ 20). (b) Readout sparsity accrues more gradually over the same rounds, as the continuation schedule sharpens the penalty toward L1, and has largely levelled off by round 50; this is why we fix the budget at 50 rounds and report there. The two panels separate the two timescales of the method, since the cross-entropy fit is reached almost immediately, while the sparsification unfolds over the full round budget. The bands in (b) are wide at early rounds, where seeds sit at different points on the steep part of the curve, and narrow by round 50, which is why the round-50 sparsity is reproducible across seeds.

Figure 2: Centralized setting. Test accuracy versus readout sparsity for the accuracy-selected SL1ESN configuration, trained on the pooled data by a single learner (mean over ten seeds), obtained by sweeping the shrinkage threshold τ ; shaded bands are ±1 std across seeds. Accuracy stays essentially flat up to 80–95% sparsity on every dataset, and collapses only once the readout is driven to near-total sparsity. Figure 4 repeats this sweep for the federated global readout; the two are plotted on the same axes so that the curves can be compared directly, and their similarity is itself the result, indicating that federation does not degrade the sparsity–accuracy trade-off.

Figure 5: One-at-a-time ablation on UCI HAR (mean over ten seeds; shaded bands are ±1 std). Left axis (blue): validation accuracy; right axis (orange): readout sparsity. (a) The shrinkage threshold τ trades sparsity for accuracy cleanly. (b) The penalty strength λ also sparsifies, but sacrifices more accuracy and saturates. (c) Reservoir size NR governs accuracy and saturates around 500. (d) The continuation factor κ leaves accuracy unchanged.

Figure 8: Federated test accuracy (left axis, solid) and readout sparsity (right axis, dashed) as the number of clients K is swept from 2 to 50 (50 rounds, IID partition, shared threshold τ = 0.1, mean ±1 std over ten seeds). The dotted vertical line marks the K = 5 setting used in the main-text experiments. Accuracy is essentially flat in K on every dataset, and sparsity stays in the band observed at K = 5.

Figure 7: Autonomous Lorenz rollout (dashed) against the true attractor (solid) under the four readout variants, at the accuracy-selected configuration. The unregularized, L2, and Smooth-L1 readouts all reconstruct the butterfly and track its two lobes before slowly drifting outward (VPT 277, 270, and 148; Table 7), whereas the L1 readout leaves the attractor earliest, collapsing away from the far lobe (VPT 109). The Smooth-L1 rollout attains the lowest RMSE of the three regularized readouts while, unlike the coordinate-descent L1 solver, remaining compatible with second-order optimization.

Figure 6: Autonomous Mackey-Glass rollout (dashed) against the true test trajectory (solid) under the four readout variants, at the accuracy-selected configuration. The unregularized readout tracks the true trajectory longest (VPT 511; Table 7), followed by the Smooth-L1 readout (VPT 377), whereas the L2 and L1 rollouts lose phase alignment earlier (VPT 176 and 230).
