papers.selection_reason: Sparse readouts in Echo State Networks compress model and reduce inference and federated broadcast costs; relevant to efficient edge AI.
papers.title: Sparse Federated Echo State Networks for Time-Series Classification via Smooth-L1 Regularization
papers.tldr: A Smooth-L1-regularized Echo State Network produces highly sparse readouts for efficient centralized and federated time-series classification with limited accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation is widely regarded as a more faithful way to assess end-to-end (E2E) driving models than open-loop evaluation, and Bench2Drive, built on the CARLA simulator, has become the dominant benchmark for it. We show that its evaluation protocol itself contains pitfalls that can misrepresent the models scored on it. Bench2Drive's comfort metric, adapted from nuPlan, has several implementation errors and a segmentation scheme that rewards standing still, so it mostly measures how long a vehicle stays stationary, correlating with stationary time at r = 0.97 across eight models. We propose a corrected, distance-based metric that cuts that correlation to r = 0.06. Under it, the strong driving-score/comfort tradeoff the original metric reports is no longer detectable once models are compared at matched driving speed, which suggests that comfort trades against how fast a model drives rather than against how well it drives. We also uncover two pitfalls in how the harness supplies navigation signals: the default controller can replace a model's own steering with an angle toward the route target point, and the target point supplied at evaluation time can differ substantially from what a model saw in training. We demonstrate both on UniAD and VAD, where their effects differ sharply, and argue that future closed-loop evaluations should check for them. We will release all fixes as standalone code, so corrected comfort scores can be obtained from logged trajectories without re-running closed-loop simulation.
authors: Thomas Schwarzfischer, Emad Aghajanzadeh, Moritz Thoma, Nael Fasfous, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Pierpaolo Mori, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann
bullets: The original comfort metric contains implementation and segmentation flaws, with comfort strongly correlated with stationary time (r = 0.97 across eight models).
A corrected distance-based metric reduces this correlation to r = 0.06 and removes the apparent driving-score/comfort tradeoff when comparing models at matched speeds.
The reported tradeoff likely reflects driving speed rather than driving quality.
The evaluation harness may override a model’s steering with route-target guidance and provide target points that differ from training inputs.
The authors demonstrate differing effects on UniAD and VAD and release fixes that can recalculate comfort from logged trajectories.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Target-point distance supplied to UniAD in training and at evaluation time, on a logarithmic axis, with statistics (m) for both models below. The shaded band is the training p5 to p95 range, 4.06m to 6.60m, shared by both models. The original planner places UniAD’s target at a median of 64.6m, over an order of magnitude beyond the 4.94m training median, and behind the ego in 13.7% of frames. Ours restores the median for both models, to 6.28m and 6.09m. For UniAD it also removes the tail (p95 130.2m to 20.0m) and the behind-ego frames (13.7% to 0.9%); for VAD it does not, and we report that residual in section III-B.

Fig. 1. Illustration of two closed-loop evaluation pitfalls. In both panels blue marks the model’s own output: its predicted waypoints and the steering vector they imply. (a) Steering overruling: the red vector is the steering the controller substitutes, aimed at the navigation target point (red pin). This can mask a model’s failure to compensate its own steering error (left) and can override a maneuver around an obstacle (right). (b) Target-point mismatch: because the evaluation route planner samples the route differently than the planner that collected the training data, the navigation command switches at a different place along the route at test time (faded red pins) than during training (red pins). Here the ego receives turn right early and begins to rotate, then receives straight at the junction: the command calls for the straight continuation (purple) while its heading and the road geometry support completing the right turn (green), a command-context combination absent from training. Interpolating between the two can produce dangerous behavior. SO: steering overruling; TPM: target point mismatch.

Fig. 3. Sample route of SimLingo [3], showing driving speed over time together with the cumulative comfort scores of the different implementations. We re-project our distance-based implementation on the time axis. The traditional metric considers driving comfortable when and only when the ego vehicle is standing still, marked by the red shaded bands. Even the slight movement from seconds 35 to 38 is deemed uncomfortable. When we apply our fixes, the metric correctly scores segments when the vehicle is driving comfortably, but still incentivizes standing still. Further applying our distance-based segmentation fixes both problems, not changing the comfort score when the ego vehicle is stationary.

Table I. Cumulative impact of removing steering overruling (SO) and aligning target-point sampling (TPM) on driving score (DS) and success rate (SR), on Dev10, against a constant-velocity baseline. ✓ marks a fix applied. TPM is applied on top of SO, not independently.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies and corrects evaluation pitfalls in closed-loop benchmarking of end-to-end driving/navigation models.
papers.title: Comfortably Stuck: Evaluation Pitfalls in Bench2Drive's Closed-Loop Protocol
papers.tldr: Bench2Drive’s closed-loop evaluation can misrepresent driving models because its comfort metric rewards stopping and its navigation inputs may alter or mismatch model behavior.

papers.abstract: As agents powered by foundation models move into open-ended environments, continual learning from experience becomes essential. For agents built on models with fixed parameters, this learning requires reusing prior task experience in context to improve performance and efficiency on future tasks. Existing memory and experience-learning systems typically focus on either retained facts or procedures, and lack a mechanism for establishing the reliability of claims extracted from the ongoing task stream. Indeed, we find that approximately 12--33\% of entries produced by representative systems harm future task performance when reused. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{RIKA} (Reliable Knowledge Acquisition), which combines hierarchical extraction of factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge with Evidence-based Knowledge Admission, which uses source evidence and subsequent experience to govern which claims enter the task agent's context, without additional validation tasks. Across six task streams from Continual Learning Bench and four model backbones, RIKA achieves the highest aggregate score on every backbone.
authors: Yixu Huang, Jiaqi W. Ma
bullets: Existing memory systems often retain facts or procedures without assessing claim reliability.
Unreliable entries can harm future performance; the abstract reports this for approximately 12–33% of entries in representative systems.
RIKA hierarchically extracts factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge.
Its Evidence-based Knowledge Admission uses source evidence and later experience to decide which claims are retained, without additional validation tasks.
RIKA achieved the highest aggregate score across six task streams and all four evaluated model backbones.

papers.abstract: Object manipulation often requires combining non-prehensile actions with grasping. However, existing approaches typically develop these capabilities separately and integrate them by sequencing distinct primitives through prescribed intermediate objectives, limiting the coordination of contact motions and grasping. Their integration also remains sensitive to object and gripper geometry and depends on particular environmental supports, complicating real-world deployment. We present Uni-PNP, a unified policy that jointly learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation for object pose reaching across diverse objects and grippers. To achieve this, we first pretrain a geometry encoder to predict contact-induced object motion using a contact-dynamics dataset constructed from simulated interactions between diverse objects and grippers. We then train the policy in a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum from graspable objects to ungraspable peers, encouraging the discovery of non-prehensile interactions and their integration with grasping. Experiments show 76.39% success on hundreds of seen objects with grippers, and 57.91% on unseen peers, outperforming the strongest pose-reaching baseline by 20.52 and 17.79 percentage points, respectively. We also analyze emergent behaviors, including nonprehensile and prehensile repositioning, grasp acquisition that requires grasping after tipping, and table-assisted reorientation while grasping, and transfer to the real-world scenario. Project page available at lgswdn.github.io/Uni-PNP.
authors: Wenxuan Zhu, Yuze Wang, Jiangran Lyu, Jiayi Chen, Yixin Zheng, Mi Yan, Li Yi, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of separately designed and sequenced prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation skills.
Pretrains a geometry encoder on simulated contact-dynamics interactions to predict contact-induced object motion.
Uses a two-stage reinforcement-learning curriculum progressing from graspable objects to ungraspable peers.
Achieves 76.39% success on seen objects and 57.91% on unseen peers, outperforming the strongest baseline by 20.52 and 17.79 percentage points.
Demonstrates emergent repositioning, grasp-after-tipping, table-assisted reorientation, and transfer to a real-world scenario.

papers.title: Uni-PNP: Unified Prehensile and Non-prehensile Policy Learning for Generalizable Object Pose Reaching
papers.tldr: Uni-PNP learns a unified policy that coordinates pushing, tipping, and grasping to reach target object poses across diverse objects and grippers.

papers.abstract: When an LLM agent misbehaves, a human steps in, and that intervention is usually discarded or replayed as training data. We treat it instead as a measurement: a label pointing at the internal computation that failed. We study it in a controlled agent environment, on one failure (asking a clarifying question when the request was already unambiguous), with labels from a rule-based overseer validated against blind human judgment. Claims cover eligible models, which both over-ask and sometimes act on matched unambiguous requests: five of thirteen qualified (Qwen2.5-3B, gemma-2-2b, OLMo-3-7B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, Phi-4). Four findings. First, the ask-vs-act decision is causally localizable in every eligible family: a direction learned from intervention labels flips 72-100% of held-out over-asks at a definite residual-stream depth, with site and dose chosen on training data, and random directions under the same procedure flip at most one episode. Second, over-asking has two mechanistic signatures: in four families the model demonstrably knows the request is unambiguous (the belief is decodable, causally inert and orthogonal to the decision) and asks anyway; in the fifth, the rare over-asks track different world-representations. Third, steering gated on a probe readout removes most of the simulated oversight burden while legitimate questions survive (bootstrap 95% intervals exclude zero); a prompt instruction makes it worse. Fourth, consolidating the fix into the weights yields a map, not a rule: on one model a LoRA confined to the causal band passes every criterion fixed in advance while behavior cloning on identical data breaks retention; on three families the reverse holds; on the fifth the outcome crosses the boundary across seeds. A geometric rule written down in advance to predict the regime failed on two out-of-family tests; we report the failure and stop rather than fit a replacement.
authors: Cesare Zavattari, Alessandro Tommasi, Giuseppe Prencipe
bullets: Study focuses on one failure: asking for clarification when a request is already unambiguous, using rule-based oversight labels validated by blind human judgment.
Across five eligible model families, intervention-derived directions causally flipped 72–100% of held-out over-asks at specific residual-stream depths; random directions rarely did so.
Most families appeared to know the request was unambiguous but asked anyway, indicating a decision failure rather than missing world knowledge; one family showed different world representations.
Probe-gated steering reduced simulated oversight burden while preserving legitimate questions, whereas a prompt instruction worsened behavior.
Weight consolidation was model-dependent: LoRA and behavior cloning alternated in effectiveness across families and seeds, and a proposed cross-family geometric predictor failed out-of-family tests.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The five-family editing map, every row at three full-pipeline seeds (fresh collection → both LoRAs → both evaluations per seed; gemma at one seed). Each cell: verdict against the four per-arm criteria (a seed passes only if it meets all four; a row is pass only when every seed does, mixed otherwise, with the count), per-seed outcomes, and the failed criterion. The depth column is the test-side peak of the exploratory sweep, the value the two rules were scored on (OLMo-3 53%, Phi-4 55–85% along its plateau); Table 1 gives the frozen-protocol sites. No cheap measurement we tested (cosine column, peak-depth column) predicts the local column — both rules, written down in advance, were falsified out-of-family.

Figure 6: Band-width sweep: retention (top) and IRR (bottom) against edit-band width as a fraction of model depth. Gemma shows the two ordered thresholds — too narrow to fit, wide enough to fit but only unconditionally, wide enough for the conditional policy; Qwen passes at 22% of depth.

Figure 1: Layer-wise causal profiles for the five eligible families: causal flip rate of the behavior-probe direction (extrapolated dose) against relative depth, with the behavior-probe AUC overlaid (it starts well above chance at layer 0, because prompt content is decodable from the start) and, dashed, the largest random-control flip over all sites at the class-mean recipe (one number, not a profile). The probe becomes readable well before the direction becomes causal; the onset of causal leverage is sharp in every family and at a different depth in each. Above the onset the effect is a plateau on gemma, OLMo-3 and Phi-4; on Qwen no site above L28 was tested.

Figure 2: The probe readout that separates the two signatures in our sample. For each family, the mean U-score of over-asked episodes as a fraction of the acted class’s mean distance from the ambiguity boundary. In the four H-caution families, over-asked episodes carry essentially the same “this is unambiguous” belief as acted ones (0.65–0.84); on Phi-4 they sit far closer to the boundary (0.29): its over-asks track genuine internal uncertainty.
Figure 3: Overseer interventions per 200 fresh episodes, per seed (Qwen). Gated steering removes most interventions; the prompt-only instruction increases them on every seed.
Figure 5: Phi-4, local arm: the two criteria, fixed in advance, that it crosses, per seed. Green/check = criterion met, red/cross = missed.

Brackets: Wilson 95% intervals on the extrapolated-dose flip rate; the class-mean column is the same site at the milder of the two doses fixed in advance. In the site column, the percentage is the site’s depth in the stack and the note says where it sits on a causal plateau. Random directions: same site, same unit norm, same target-setting procedure, run at the class-mean recipe (there is no extrapolated random arm), so the dose-matched placebo comparison is the class-mean column against the random column; across all sites and models the largest random-control flip is 1/74 (Qwen, at a causally null layer). On four families the train-side selection reproduces the site of the exploratory test-side sweep; on OLMo-3, whose causal region is a plateau (L17–L21, 72–80%), it lands at L21.

papers.selection_reason: Studies causal localization, steering, and editing of LLM agent computations, contributing to understanding and improving large language model behavior.
papers.title: Human Interventions as Labels: Localizing, Steering, and (Sometimes) Editing the Computations Behind LLM Agent Failures
papers.tldr: Human interventions can label and causally localize the internal computations behind some LLM-agent over-asking failures, enabling targeted steering but only inconsistent weight-based fixes.

papers.abstract: Fixed-function CNN accelerators make edge inference fast and energy-efficient, but they execute only networks that obey a precise numerical contract. On the MAX7800x family, this contract requires power-of-two, per-tensor, symmetric scales, 8-bit activations and biases, integer-only arithmetic, and one statically configured shift per layer. We present ShiftQAT, the quantization-aware training (QAT) flow we developed for this family, which produces networks satisfying the contract by construction. It is the default training path of ai8x-training, the family's open-source training toolchain. ShiftQAT resolves residual, concatenation, and weight-sharing dependencies so that activation scales propagate statically and each layer's requantization reduces to one offline-configured shift. It also trains weights and biases on a joint power-of-two grid that fits the 8-bit bias budget. Among the compared methods, only ShiftQAT satisfies all of the contract's scaling constraints, including signed 8-bit activation storage. Even so, on ImageNet it matches the W8A8 accuracy drop of less constrained QAT methods and stays within 2.9 percentage points of FP32 at W4A8. On MAX78002 silicon, ShiftQAT-trained MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18 classify ImageNet images in 14.6 and 8.4 ms at 5.1 and 2.8 mJ per inference.
authors: Oguzhan Buyuksolak, Osman Erman Okman, Mehmet Gorkem Ulkar
bullets: Targets fixed-function MAX7800x accelerators requiring per-tensor symmetric power-of-two scales, signed 8-bit activations and biases, integer arithmetic, and one shift per layer.
Statically propagates activation scales through residuals, concatenations, and weight sharing, reducing requantization to offline-configured shifts.
Trains weights and biases on a joint power-of-two grid within the 8-bit bias budget.

It is the only compared method satisfying all stated scaling constraints, while matching the accuracy drop of less constrained W8A8 QAT and remaining within 2.9 percentage points of FP32 at W4A8 on ImageNet.
On MAX78002 silicon, MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18 classify ImageNet images in 14.6 ms/5.1 mJ and 8.4 ms/2.8 mJ per inference, respectively.

(b) For a concatenation, the inputs adopt the largest scale among them. (c) For weight sharing, all layers feeding the shared layer adopt the largest scale among them, so that one set of shared weights and one shift serve every invocation.

Figure 2. The ShiftQAT flow. FP32 training is followed by offline initialization, which consists of BN folding, activation-scale proposal, and activation-scale refinement (dependency resolution and propagation). QAT then runs with per-iteration weight/bias scale determination.

The product W ′X ′ is rescaled by Sw and Sx before a full-precision bias is added, and the result is then requantized. (b) The structure the MAX7800x contract requires, as produced by ShiftQAT. Weights and biases share one power-of-two scale Sw, and activation scales are resolved and propagated offline. The only runtime rescaling is a single power-of-two shift per layer (the PoT scaler, Eq. 11).

Figure 4. Static scale propagation on a two-layer network. On the left, each layer’s output carries its real-valued scale. On the right, each layer emits scale-normalized outputs, downstream biases and scales are adjusted offline (Eq. 5), and a single recovery remains at the output. Activations are omitted from the diagram for clarity, but the derivation requires them to be positively homogeneous.

papers.selection_reason: Quantization-aware training enforcing a fixed-function edge CNN accelerator numerical contract, directly targeting efficient inference.
papers.title: ShiftQAT: Quantization-Aware Training for the Numerical Contract of a Fixed-Function Edge CNN Accelerator
papers.tldr: ShiftQAT trains CNNs to meet the MAX7800x accelerator’s strict integer-only, power-of-two quantization contract while preserving strong accuracy and efficient edge inference.

papers.abstract: Biomedical research articles are mainly written for experts and often contain terms that are difficult for the general public to understand. Automated lay summarization has become a solution to make biomedical knowledge easier for patients and the public to understand. However, generating lay summaries from full-text articles requires more computing power because the articles are long and costly to process. Fine-tuning large language models for this task also requires substantial resources. This study asks two questions: (1) whether abstracts contain enough information to produce lay summaries as good as those based on full-text articles, and (2) whether few-shot learning performs as well as task-specific fine-tuning. The study used two public biomedical lay summarization datasets and two recent models, evaluated for readability, factual consistency, semantic similarity, and runtime efficiency. Results show that abstract-based summarization performs better overall. Across both datasets and models, abstract fine-tuning is 4.70 times faster, while abstract zero- and few-shot prompting is 5.31 times faster than full-text methods. These results show that abstract-based prompting reduces runtime cost while maintaining lay summary quality.
authors: Egecan \c{C}elik Evgin, \.{I}lknur Karadeniz, Olcay Taner Y{\i}ld{\i}z

Assesses readability, factual consistency, semantic similarity, and runtime efficiency.
Abstract-based summarization performs better overall across datasets and models.

papers.abstract: Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable. Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences. We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation. Its vision-action-force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution. Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively. Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy. These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.
authors: Yi Qiao, Maolin Zheng, Haoran Sun, Lujia Dong, Wenzhao Lian
bullets: Reactive monitors detect anomalies too late, while vision alone cannot fully reveal physical interactions.
MAIA uses a vision-action-force world model to predict planned-action outcomes and a lightweight head to anticipate anomalies.
CRIA provides 2,852 real-world trajectories across 18 contact-rich tasks with frame-level anomaly annotations.
On seen and novel tasks, MAIA achieves bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 with median warnings 28.0 and 25.1 steps early.
Anomaly-aware action selection raises end-to-end success from 52.6% to 61.5% without policy retraining.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. MAIA Overview. The framework consists of a Vision-Action-Force World Model (VAF-WM) and a predictive anomaly head. VAF-WM extends GE-Base with gated action-force adapters to forecast future visual and force dynamics. The anomaly head fuses these predictions with interaction tokens and uses a temporal transformer to predict anomaly occurrence, temporal prevalence, and localization within the future window.

Fig. 3. CRIA overview. The central ring presents all 18 tasks grouped by interaction category, while the surrounding panels illustrate category-specific interaction characteristics and typical anomaly modes. The hardware setup used for data collection is shown on the right.

Shaded regions indicate correct predictions (green), prediction errors (red), and early warnings (yellow) prior to the true anomaly onset (dashed line). (a) Nominal execution: our method produces fewer false alarms than the baselines. (b) Anomalous execution: our method provides an earlier sustained warning than WCM, while reward-model warnings are intermittent.

Fig. 6. Qualitative modality ablation on representative anomaly cases. The examples illustrate how incorporating physical feedback enables MAIA to distinguish anomalous interactions that remain ambiguous when only visual and action cues are available.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can become off-policy due to training-inference mismatch, mini-batch updates, and asynchronous training.The resulting mismatch is especially harmful in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where rollout--training discrepancies can change routing decisions and lead to router drift. Rollout Routing Replay (R3) mitigates this mismatch by reusing expert selections from the rollout stage during training. Our analysis shows that routing replay introduces gradient bias by losing contributions from experts selected by the training router but not the rollout router. To address this, we propose Router Drift Control (RDC), which uses routing disagreement between rollout and training as a signal of off-policy staleness and selectively rejects high-drift responses. The sequence-level filtering avoids gradient bias introduced by replay while preserving native expert selection and the associated learning signals for retained responses. Experiments show that RDC achieves larger gains as policy staleness increases and remains effective in asynchronous RL. In asynchronous training, RDC combined with Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS) improves the average peak validation accuracy across AIME 2024 and AIME 2025 by 5.5 points over TIS and 4.5 points over R3.
authors: Liangyao Jin, Zhixin Wang, Liming Liu, Mingjun Zhang, Zhengzhou Zhu, Fangcheng Fu, Jinlong Hou, Yuan Cheng, Xiaohe Hu, Ping Zhang, Siyuan Feng
bullets: Off-policy mismatch can cause MoE routing changes and router drift, especially with asynchronous or stale training.
R3 replays rollout-time expert selections but introduces gradient bias by omitting experts selected only by the training router.
RDC uses routing disagreement as a staleness signal and rejects high-drift responses at the sequence level.
This preserves native expert selection and learning signals for retained responses without replay-induced bias.
RDC becomes more effective as policy staleness increases and improves asynchronous RL when combined with TIS.

papers.abstract: Data strategy plays a central role in training large language models (LLMs). It governs the selection, weighting, and scheduling of training data, thereby determining the capabilities a model can acquire from a fixed data budget. We treat high-quality data as having high training-dependent utility, which depends on the target objective, the model, and its training state rather than on the text alone. Research in this area now spans pretraining and post-training, but related ideas use inconsistent terminology and evaluation protocols. This work reviews data strategies across the training lifecycle and formulates them as policies that allocate a training budget over candidate examples. We organise methods by their decision granularity, model dependence, and temporal adaptivity, then compare their computational requirements and empirical support. Fine-grained or state-dependent policies offer more control but incur additional scoring, search, or rollout costs. Evidence for transfer across model scales and comparable end-to-end cost remains limited. A continuously updated list of papers, along with their public implementations, is available at https://github.com/xuyj233/data_strategy_survey.
authors: Yuanjian Xu, Jianing Hao, Tianze Sun, Yongyao Duan, Sam Chen, Jinyi Han, Wanbo Zhang, Yuxuan Sun, Guang Zhang, Zhong Li
bullets: Training-data utility depends on the objective, model, and training state—not text quality alone.
The framework covers data selection, weighting, and scheduling in both pretraining and post-training.

Fine-grained, state-dependent policies provide more control but require greater scoring, search, or rollout costs.
Evidence for transfer across model scales and comparable end-to-end costs remains limited.

papers.abstract: Tokenization is a critical component of the language modeling pipeline, but it is poorly understood. Tokenizers can impact downstream performance, but there is currently mixed evidence about which tokenizer features predict a better language model without requiring a full training run. In this paper, we analyze approximately 200 language models trained on nine different languages. We evaluate both models and their tokenizers and test whether there is a relationship between any proposed intrinsic tokenizer evaluations and model performance, as measured by a wide variety of benchmarks. Despite the quantity and variety of proposed intrinsic tokenizer metrics, we find that none consistently predicts downstream performance across model families, tasks, and languages. This motivates the need for novel tokenizer evaluation metrics and approaches. We propose novel linguistically grounded metric introduced in this work shows that new metrics can capture aspects of tokenizer quality that existing metrics miss, though their predictive power is likely to vary across model families, languages, and tasks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves multimodal reasoning, but group-relative policy optimization broadcasts a single sequence-level advantage to every token of a response, although errors usually localize to a few decisive steps. Recent self-distilled variants refine credit with a teacher--student likelihood gap. However, this signal cannot tell whether it relies on the image or on a language shortcut, and is applied uniformly even when the teacher is uninformative. To address this, we propose Pairwise token contrast and Adaptive trajectory ConfidencE (PACE). Pairwise token contrast scores each response under four teacher views, crossing a correct or incorrect answer hint with the image present or removed, and compares the two hints for every token, which cancels shifts shared by both hints and reveals whether the token's support relies on the image. Adaptive trajectory confidence measures how well the teacher predicts each response given the correct hint and the image, normalizes this score within the batch, and uses it to set how far the token contrast redistributes credit within that response. PACE achieves the best average accuracy on three backbones and ranks first on all evaluated multimodal reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Experiments show that both components matter: replacing pairwise token contrast with a single-view signal underperforms our method, while adaptive trajectory confidence adds further improvement.

Both pairwise contrast and adaptive confidence contribute to the gains.

papers.abstract: We introduce Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D scene generation framework that constructs 4D scenes from separate background and dynamic character representations. Recent advances in generative models have enabled text-driven dynamic scene synthesis, but editable 4D scene generation remains challenging due to the need to preserve spatial geometry and temporal dynamics. Existing approaches typically generate holistic scene videos, where the background and dynamic characters are coupled, making object-level editing and flexible camera control difficult. Edit4D addresses these limitations through a stage-specific generation pipeline. Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage-specific prompts for background, dynamic character, and scene-character composition. Using these prompts, we synthesize multi-view scene images with text-to-image and camera-conditioned generative priors and reconstruct a background 3D Gaussian splatting representation. We then generate a character image, animate it with an image-conditioned video prior, reconstruct a 4D mesh, and bind Gaussian primitives to obtain a character representation. Finally, both components are composed through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization. A global scene refinement is then performed to improve harmonization and rendering consistency. By integrating stage-specific components, Edit4D enables controllable camera motion, flexible object-level editing, and the practical construction of editable 4D scenes. authors: Chanwoo Kim, Tackgeun You, Hwasup Lim

papers.abstract: Small observation or action errors can compound during closed-loop execution and disrupt a trained imitation learning policy. We study whether the original expert demonstrations can improve robustness through test-time hidden-state steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining. Our analysis of a trained policy finds that expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, while the directions capturing this variation differ across regions. Motivated by this geometry, we propose Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states obtained by replaying the demonstrations through the frozen policy. DHS attenuates coordinates with low expert variance more strongly than those with high variance, then maps the modified coordinates back to hidden-state space. This allows steering directions to vary with the current hidden state while retaining every coordinate. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over the unmodified Transformer policies. Controlled comparisons yield higher mean success with learned nonlinear coordinates than with linear coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling. Combining DHS with action smoothing improves mean success rate under observation noise in certain tasks compared with action smoothing alone.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformer architectures have showcased impressive performance on semantic segmentation, yet their quadratic attention complexity hinders practical applications. Recent works have focused on merging tokens to reduce sequence length and thus improve transformer efficiency. However, existing token merging methods primarily rely on feature similarity to identify similar tokens, overlooking spatial consistency, which may introduce segmentation errors in semantic segmentation. In this work, we propose SCMerge, a training-free token merging method that jointly considers feature similarity and spatial consistency in pairing similar tokens. The pairwise tokens are then merged within the encoder, and the resulting token sequences are reconstructed onto the original patch grid after decoding. The proposed method is flexible and can be plugged into existing vision Transformer-based semantic segmentation pipelines. Extensive experiments on the benchmark datasets ADE20K, Pascal Context, and Cityscapes show that SCMerge consistently achieves a better trade-off between segmentation accuracy and efficiency than baseline methods.
authors: Junfeng Ren (Southern University of Science and Technology), Yi Gong (Southern University of Science and Technology), Yuan Zeng (Shenzhen Technology University)
bullets: Addresses the quadratic attention cost of Vision Transformers in semantic segmentation.
Pairs tokens using both feature similarity and spatial consistency to reduce segmentation errors from spatially inconsistent merges.
Merges tokens in the encoder and reconstructs the decoded sequences onto the original patch grid.
Plug-and-play with existing Vision Transformer semantic segmentation pipelines.
Experiments on ADE20K, Pascal Context, and Cityscapes show a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off than baseline methods.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.
authors: Yukun Tian, Junwei Su, Haofeng Xu, Lansong Diao, Zhengping Qian, Weibo Zhao, Wenchao Zhou, Ruiting Zhou, Chuan Wu

Evaluations on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks report up to 2.06× higher training throughput with comparable or better performance.

papers.abstract: Recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods have enabled effective multi-view 3D reconstruction by predicting Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass. However, existing approaches predominantly adopt a pixel-aligned paradigm that predicts one Gaussian per input pixel, coupling the Gaussian count to the input resolution and number of views. This also leads to redundant primitives in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas. We present Anchor3DGS, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that replaces pixel-aligned prediction with a compact anchor-based representation. Guided by information entropy, our method places a set of 3D anchors in the scene, concentrating them in regions of higher visual complexity while maintaining broad spatial coverage. Each anchor performs occlusion-aware aggregation of multi-view image features, exchanges information with other anchors, and is decoded into a set of local Gaussians. A lightweight feature enhancement module further refines the coarse RGB output from Gaussian splatting and improves rendering fidelity. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that our Anchor3DGS achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis quality while only using an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.
authors: Sheng Ye, Jiangke Lin, Fudong Wang, Yi Yuan, Zhen-Hui Dong, Yong-Jin Liu
bullets: Addresses redundant Gaussians in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas.
Uses entropy-guided 3D anchors to concentrate representation where visual complexity is higher while preserving scene coverage.
Anchors aggregate multi-view features with occlusion awareness, exchange information, and decode into local Gaussian sets.
A lightweight enhancement module refines Gaussian-splatting RGB outputs for improved rendering fidelity.
Experiments on diverse benchmarks report state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis quality with an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Anchor3DGS. Given uncalibrated multi-view images, (1) a VGGT-based [28] geometry backbone first predicts the scene’s geometric scaffold. (2) A fixed budget of 3D anchors is then sampled from the scaffold, combining uniform sampling with entropy-guided sampling. (3) Each anchor is projected back into all input views to gather features via occlusion-aware aggregation, and then interacts with other anchors through self-attention. (4) Finally, each anchor is decoded into a set of local Gaussians, which are rasterized and refined to yield the final RGB output.
Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of novel view synthesis. Our method recovers sharper textures and finer details while mitigating artifacts in poorly observed regions.
Figure 5: Rendering metrics under varying anchor count N and decoded Gaussians K (left), and qualitative comparisons of removing the enhancement module and entropy-guided sampling (right).

Figure 3: Uniform sampling ensures broad spatial coverage but wastes anchors (red dots) on uninformative regions (e.g., textureless sky). In contrast, our entropy-guided sampling allocates more anchors to visually complex regions while still maintaining coverage of the scene.

papers.selection_reason: Feed-forward 3DGS with compact anchor-based representation for efficient multi-view reconstruction, fitting 3D vision and efficiency interests.
papers.title: Anchor3DGS: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Compact Anchor-Based Representation
papers.tldr: Anchor3DGS enables pose-free, feed-forward 3D reconstruction with far fewer Gaussians by using entropy-guided scene anchors instead of one Gaussian per input pixel.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable automated preference labeling for robotic manipulation, yet their deployment remains impractical since each query incurs substantial inference cost, while VLMs frequently abstain on visually challenging comparisons. We propose SPEAR, a framework that transforms VLMs into efficient preference oracles via two synergistic mechanisms. First, we design distinguishability-aware query selection to reduce abstention rates by targeting only informative and distinguishable comparisons. Second, we deploy an adaptive reward transition that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement. Experiments on the manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR achieves 88.9% average success, outperforming baselines by 23.3 percentage points, while significantly reducing abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks. SPEAR learns three Mobile ALOHA manipulation tasks fully online on real hardware, demonstrating end-to-end real-world applicability. By addressing query efficiency and exploration challenges, SPEAR establishes VLMs as practical preference oracles for scalable robot learning without manual reward engineering.
authors: Zewen Wu, Ruizhe Liu, Pei Zhou, Feng Chen, Yanchao Yang
bullets: Addresses high VLM query costs and abstentions on visually difficult comparisons.
Uses distinguishability-aware query selection to target informative, answerable comparisons.
Applies adaptive rewards that bootstrap exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement.
Achieves 88.9% average success, 23.3 percentage points above baselines, while reducing abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks.
Demonstrates fully online learning for three real-hardware Mobile ALOHA tasks without manual reward engineering.

Together, these mechanisms enable efficient online learning by ensuring both high-quality query selection and sufficient behavioral diversity for meaningful preference elicitation.

papers.abstract: Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user-specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open-vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact. We propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Guided by a text-promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non-target regions are left untouched. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals. Project page and code: https://lab-of-ai-and-robotics.github.io/target-aware-langmap/
authors: Sibaek Lee, Kyeongsu Kang, Seongbo Ha, Yewon Jeon, Joonyeol Choi, Daegeol Ko, Jaehyuk Hur, Taemin Choi, Minsu Kim, Hyungjoo Ahn, Wonsok Yoo, Hyeonwoo Yu
bullets: Addresses missed user-specified targets in distilled 3D language maps without sacrificing other-word queryability.
Uses a text-promptable segmenter to blend target-region visual embeddings with target text embeddings, leaving non-target regions unchanged.
Computes the smallest effective blending coefficient in closed form, avoiding tuning hyperparameters.
Centers the read-out to remove query-agnostic effects caused by shared components in text embeddings.
Improves open-vocabulary segmentation across three benchmarks, roughly doubling base mIoU on Replica, and transfers to other language maps and real-world robot navigation.

papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) have made substantial progress in audio understanding. However, in high-throughput applications requiring frequent selection, judgment, and scoring, autoregressive text generation introduces additional computational overhead and response latency. To address this limitation, we introduce Qwen-Audio-Jev by augmenting Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next with a dedicated Jev decision head. The model unifies selection, binary judgment, and scoring through three decision primitives: CHOICE, NOUL, and SCORE. Given audio, a natural-language question, and an explicit answer specification, it directly produces a task-conditioned probability distribution or a numerical score through typed decision readouts. Evaluation across 18 labeled configurations covers all three primitives: for CHOICE, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves accuracies of 78.70% on MMAU-mini and 84.06% on MMSU; for NOUL, it achieves an equal error rate of 6.50% on the VoxCeleb1-O speaker verification benchmark; and for SCORE, the model achieves a normalized mean absolute error of 0.1062 on NISQA overall quality assessment, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.8210 and 0.8074, respectively. Compared with the original Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves an approximately 20x inference speedup. It demonstrates its potential for efficient, high-throughput audio decision-making in applications such as large-scale audio screening, speaker verification, and automated quality assessment.
authors: Ying Fang, Zhifu Gao, Qing Gu, Jiajun He, Kangqi Jing, Xiangang Li, Yu Pu, Wupeng Wang
bullets: Supports three typed decision primitives: CHOICE, NOUL, and SCORE, conditioned on audio, a question, and an answer specification.
Evaluated across 18 labeled configurations for audio understanding, speaker verification, and quality assessment.
Reports 78.70% and 84.06% accuracy on MMAU-mini and MMSU, 6.50% EER on VoxCeleb1-O, and 0.1062 normalized MAE on NISQA.
Achieves approximately 20× faster inference than Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next, targeting high-throughput audio applications.

The requested primitive selects the active output; the three readouts do not imply simultaneous multi-question inference.

(b) The optional RLCD-inspired stage initializes from SFT, samples multiple decisions, and uses label-based group rewards for rewardweighted policy-gradient updates. Choice, Noul, and Score are alternative question-conditioned tasks; only the requested primitive is active.

papers.abstract: Learning intrinsic dynamics---the relationship between actions and their consequences---is essential for world models. However, visual variations unrelated to the underlying control process can obscure this relationship in learned representations. We investigate the connection between action predictability, defined as the ability to reconstruct an action from consecutive latent states, and the preservation of intrinsic dynamics. Our central hypothesis is that encouraging action predictability discourages representations from discarding the distinctions between different actions and their consequences. We provide two complementary forms of evidence for this connection. Theoretically, we derive a positive lower bound on squared inverse prediction error when the encoder merges distinguishable outcomes of different actions from the same state and appearance, and show that forward prediction can still be exact on those transitions. Empirically, controlled appearance-diversity comparisons, supervision interventions, and latent probes support the role of action prediction in preserving control-relevant transition information. We instantiate action predictability with Concat IDM, which predicts actions from concatenated latent states and updates the shared encoder using action labels already available in offline trajectories, without changing the test-time planner. Across three independent training runs on Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM increases planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; its paired improvement is 52.9 percentage points larger than that observed with a single appearance. Together, these findings support action predictability as an inductive bias toward intrinsic dynamics and demonstrate the practical benefits of Concat IDM for latent planning under visual diversity.
authors: Jiamin Shi, Yuanhong Zhang, Zhiyang Liu, Jiawei Sun, Jingwen Fu
bullets: Visual changes unrelated to control can cause representations to discard distinctions between actions and their consequences.
The paper links reconstructing actions from consecutive latent states to preserving intrinsic dynamics, with theoretical and empirical support.
Concat IDM predicts actions from concatenated latent states and trains the shared encoder using action labels from offline trajectories.
On Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM raises planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; the reported gain is larger than with a single appearance.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. However, generating each token still involves sequential computation and repeated access to model weights, leading to high decoding latency. Recent pipelined self-speculative decoding methods reduce this delay by drafting tokens from early-loop predictions and asynchronously advancing tokens at different recurrent depths in the same batch, but they do not fully exploit early-loop features for longer lookahead and still spend computation verifying incorrect speculative branches. We introduce \method, a speculative decoding framework for looped transformers that enables earlier drafting of future tokens and assigns complementary roles to different recurrent depths. A lightweight lookahead drafter (LAD) predicts multiple future tokens with early-loop states, and deeper-loop feedback helps decide which draft branches to continue and which to pause, while the full-depth model makes the final token decisions. LoopAhead achieves up to 7.82x decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution.
authors: Zixuan Liu, Nan Xue, Rui Bao, Yuhang Xu, Xiaofeng Cao, Jiangchao Yao, Zhiyong Chen
bullets: Addresses decoding latency from sequential token generation and repeated weight access in looped language models.
Uses a lightweight lookahead drafter to predict several future tokens from early-loop features.
Employs deeper-loop feedback to continue promising draft branches and pause likely incorrect ones.
The full-depth model retains final control, preserving the target model’s output distribution.
Reports up to 7.82× decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a speculative decoding framework that reduces inference latency for looped language models, fitting the efficient AI scope.
papers.title: LoopAhead: Speculating Ahead for Faster Decoding in Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: LoopAhead accelerates decoding in looped Transformers by using early-loop states to draft multiple future tokens while deeper loops selectively verify them.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) have made strong progress in multimodal understanding, yet most treat audio as monaural semantic content, limiting their ability to reason about where sounds originate and how they relate to the visual scene. Recent spatial audio-visual studies address parts of this problem, but often focus on specific abilities, such as spatial correspondence or direction and distance reasoning. In this work, we introduce HLR-AVSceneQA, a comprehensive benchmark with a hear-localize-reason hierarchy that evaluates whether models can recognize what is heard, localize sound sources in egocentric and allocentric views, and use these localized sources to reason about how they relate to the visual scene. We further introduce HLR-LLM, which augments a strong audio-visual foundation model with a binaural spatial audio branch alongside its monaural semantic audio pathway. We train HLR-LLM with a curriculum that incorporates final-stage chain-of-thought supervision for multi-step spatial reasoning. Experiments show that existing AV-LLMs remain limited in spatial grounding and relational reasoning, while HLR-LLM substantially improves spatial audio-visual scene understanding without compromising semantic audio-visual perception.
authors: Kim Sung-Bin, Lee Jung-Mok, Jinwoo Jung, Oh Hyun-Bin, Hyeonggon Ryu, David Harwath, Tae-Hyun Oh
bullets: Addresses AV-LLMs’ limited spatial grounding beyond monaural audio semantics.
Introduces HLR-AVSceneQA, a hierarchical benchmark covering recognition, egocentric/allocentric localization, and scene-relative reasoning.
Presents HLR-LLM with binaural spatial audio and monaural semantic audio pathways.
Uses curriculum training with final-stage chain-of-thought supervision for multi-step spatial reasoning.
Experiments show improved spatial audio-visual understanding without compromising semantic perception; existing AV-LLMs remain limited in spatial grounding and relational reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Architecture and training curriculum of HLR-LLM. (a) HLR-LLM augments a strong AV-LLM with a binaural spatial audio branch, enabling the language model to jointly attend to text, visual, downmixed monaural audio, and binaural spatial audio tokens. (b) The model is trained through a three-stage curriculum: spatial audio alignment, spatial audio-visual instruction tuning, and final-stage CoT tuning for structured spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.
authors: Jing Xia, Changyan Li, Yuduo Wang, Guiyin Tian, Bo Wang, Yifan Liao, Mingjun Li, Shiyan Hu
bullets: Targets service robots entering unmapped buildings without prior on-site traversal or site-specific training.
Uses a floor plan, place clues, and initial topology–odometry alignment instead of a robot-built global SLAM map.
Combines human task constraints and environmental reports with robot-verified physical-state evidence.
Verified node arrivals support translational re-anchoring for visual depth point-goal navigation.
On a Unitree Go2, AVALON completed the reported mission in all 5 runs and avoided timeouts seen with policy-only X-NavDP.

papers.abstract: Decision trees can make vision-language model (VLM) classification interpretable by replacing a single prediction with a sequence of root-to-leaf questions. However, the accuracy cost of this greedy, non-backtracking procedure remains unclear. We introduce \textbf{MYOPIA}, a benchmark comprising four LLM-generated, human-refined decision trees for GTSRB, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and MSCOCO, together with matched prompts, diagnostic protocols, and an evaluation harness. Across GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA-3.2 11B Vision, tree traversal underperforms zero-shot prompting in all 12 dataset--model pairs; paired bootstrap analyses consistently favor zero-shot. Our diagnostics characterize interacting failure modes associated with this gap. Models often recall tree-encoded class attributes more accurately than they ground the same attributes in images: the mean label--image accuracy gaps are 9.5, 13.8, and 12.6 points for GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA, respectively. Incorrect local decisions then irreversibly exclude the correct class, while answer extraction introduces additional model-dependent loss. A node-level audit of the four trees finds that split entropy is weakly but consistently associated with lower node accuracy, whereas depth, branching factor, and within-node grounding differences are less stable. \textbf{MYOPIA} therefore provides a framework for diagnosing hierarchical visual classification and motivates testing tree designs that prioritize perceptual answerability and recovery from early errors. Code is available at https://github.com/islammesabah/VLM_Classification.
authors: Islam Mesabah, Sary Elmansoury, Gerrit Gro{\ss}mann, Peter Neigel, Sebastian J. Vollmer
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of four human-refined decision trees for GTSRB, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and MSCOCO, with prompts, diagnostics, and an evaluation harness.
Tests GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA-3.2 11B Vision across 12 dataset–model pairs; tree traversal underperforms zero-shot prompting in every pair.
Models recall tree-provided class attributes better than they ground those attributes in images, producing model-dependent label–image accuracy gaps.
Local decision errors can permanently remove the correct class, while answer extraction adds further losses.
Higher split entropy is weakly associated with lower node accuracy; effects of depth, branching factor, and within-node grounding are less consistent.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents' tool use or undermines it. We evaluate tool graph memory on nine models and two benchmarks, finding that it seldom improves significantly over baselines, and that its gains, where present, cost over twice the LLM calls. The memory's guidance is often incorrect, and random or no guidance retains most of the gain, implying that the benefit stems from extra computation rather than the memory itself. Moreover, even with the correct next tool suggested, many failures remain, such as giving up without a tool call. Storing the same experience instead as textual insights outperforms tool graph memory with almost no extra LLM calls. This suggests that memory serves better as a soft prior than as a prescription of the next tool, leading to a more effective and generalizable solution.
authors: Uiji Hwang, Richeng Xuan, Taeuk Kim
bullets: Evaluated tool graph memory across nine models and two benchmarks.
Its improvements over baselines are uncommon and cost more than twice the LLM calls when present.
The stored guidance is often incorrect; random or absent guidance preserves most of the benefit.
Correctly suggesting the next tool does not prevent failures such as abandoning tool use.
Textual insights outperform tool graph memory with little extra computation, favoring soft priors over rigid tool prescriptions.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding, but existing benchmarks mainly evaluate whether models can interpret observed visual content. In real-world scenarios, assistants must additionally anticipate what assistance is needed and decide when to provide it. To address this gap, we introduce \textsc{P$^3$IBench}, a benchmark for proactive video understanding in real-life streaming scenarios. It evaluates three complementary capabilities: daily perception, risk prediction and intervention. We benchmark 12 representative open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems. Our evaluation shows that current models struggle to make well-calibrated response decisions. Finally, we construct additional proactive training data and train \textsc{P$^3$I-Assistant-4B}, achieving improvements on several tasks, though gains remain uneven across capabilities. Together, these findings show that effective proactive assistance requires not only visual understanding, but also precise response timing and appropriate restraint.
authors: Boyu Cui, Junhao Luo, Zhihao Wang, Linghan Chen, Zejun Li, Jiwen Zhang, Siyuan Wang, Zhongyu Wei
bullets: Existing video benchmarks focus mainly on interpreting observed content, not anticipating assistance needs or deciding when to respond.
The benchmark measures daily perception, risk prediction, and intervention.
It evaluates 12 open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems.
Current models struggle with well-calibrated response decisions and appropriate restraint.
Training P$^3$I-Assistant-4B with additional proactive data improves several tasks, but gains vary by capability.

papers.abstract: Addressed conditional memory provides a local surface for post-hoc knowledge injection, but a successful write need not transfer to a new question or preserve untargeted behavior. This study combines a controlled GPT-2 comparison with production-memory experiments on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Newly initialized modules attached to frozen GPT-2 are tested in a 2 x 2 design: row-only versus row-plus-projection updates, each with or without fixed module-residual anchoring. All arms reproduce 50 trained completions in each of three sampling seeds. Natural-question target-string hits average 5.3% for both row-only arms, 28.7% for unanchored projection updates, and 22.0% with anchoring, while strict answer scores remain zero. Anchoring lowers measured drift; lexical hits do not establish entity-specific retrieval. In the archived Qwen experiments, gradient writes make the designated first answer token top-ranked for 132 independently reset targets, comprising 93 new promotions and 39 already top-ranked targets. A separate matched 24-target comparison gives 13 new promotions with Adam versus two with SPSA at equal iteration counts but unequal computational procedures. An 80-row case includes saved continuations and a replay record, while reformulations bound its scope. Six DeepSeek zero-order cases yield one new target-token promotion and one regression. These results support bounded writing feasibility and separate trained expression, question-form behavior, and preservation; first-token rankings do not establish complete-answer success or universal conditions for writable memory.
authors: Wei Gao (Shibei Qiyuan AI Technology), Cheng Tian (Shibei Qiyuan AI Technology), Duan Yang (Xi'an Jiaotong University), Jianqing Yin (Shibei Qiyuan AI Technology)
bullets: The study tests whether post-hoc writes transfer beyond a targeted completion while preserving unrelated behavior.
A controlled GPT-2 experiment compares row-only versus row-plus-projection updates, with or without fixed residual anchoring.
Natural-question target-string hits were 5.3% for row-only updates, 28.7% for unanchored projection updates, and 22.0% with anchoring; strict answer scores were zero.
Archived production-memory experiments found 93 new target-token promotions among 132 reset targets, while Adam outperformed SPSA in a matched 24-target comparison.
Results support bounded writing feasibility, but first-token promotions do not establish complete-answer retrieval, entity-specific access, or universal writability conditions.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have steadily demonstrated outstanding performance in high-fidelity, controllable generation across diverse scenarios, following the "pretraining-finetuning" paradigm established in LLMs. Despite these advances, conventional DMs still face critical limitations in sophisticated reasoning, autonomous exploration of generation pathways, and adaptability to complex, human-aligned objectives. Inspired by RLHF's success in LLMs, RL has recently emerged as a pivotal post-training mechanism to iteratively refine DMs through reward-driven trajectory optimization. This paper presents the first comprehensive review of RL-driven DMs and an empirical analysis of how RL reshapes the diffusion process towards experience-centric, goal-directed generation. We propose a novel technical panorama elucidating RL's multifaceted roles in diffusion-based language, multimodal, robotic, and scientific models, with a granular focus on diffusion trajectory optimization and reward engineering. Through extensive experiments on multiple task-specific benchmarks, we systematically evaluate representative methods to intuitively highlight the advantages of different RL post-training strategies. Furthermore, we reveal and dissect three crucial bottlenecks that currently hinder the real-world deployment of RL-driven DMs: reward design fragility, exploration-exploitation trade-off in high-dimensional generation spaces, and training instability under sparse rewards. Based on these perspectives, we provide a principled roadmap for the integration of RL into DMs and outline promising future research directions for robust, interpretable RL-diffusion systems. We also construct a public repository to continuously track the latest developments in this rapidly evolving field: https://github.com/MAIR-Lab-HUST/Awesome-RL-for-Diffusion-Models.
authors: Zhiyuan Ma, Jiabao Wei, Tianyu Wang, Hanqing Wang, Jiadong Pan, Haowen Xu, Liangliang Zhao, Ruixun Liu, Yuhan Wang, Yuwei Zhang, Liang Feng, Junhao Xiao, Kaiyan Zhang, Xuekai Zhu, Daizong Liu, Biqing Qi, Yihao Liu, Ganqu Cui, Ning Ding, Linfeng Zhang, Jianjun Li, Kun He, Xiang Bai, Bowen Zhou
bullets: Identifies limitations of conventional diffusion models in reasoning, autonomous exploration, and complex human-aligned objectives.
Presents a technical panorama of RL’s roles in diffusion models, emphasizing trajectory optimization and reward engineering.
Evaluates representative RL post-training strategies across multiple task-specific benchmarks.
Highlights three deployment bottlenecks: fragile reward design, exploration–exploitation challenges, and instability under sparse rewards.
Proposes a roadmap for robust, interpretable RL-driven diffusion systems and provides a public resource repository.

papers.selection_reason: Reviews RL-driven post-training for diffusion models, including multimodal and generation settings directly relevant to diffusion-based video generation.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning-driven Diffusion Models: Language, Vision, and Beyond
papers.tldr: This paper reviews and empirically analyzes how reinforcement learning post-training makes diffusion models more goal-directed, adaptable, and aligned across language, vision, robotics, and scientific applications.

papers.abstract: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.
authors: Shuoran Jiang, Wentao Zhu, Yang Xiang, Dongfeng Li, Yunan Zhang, Mengchen Zhao, Yuhui Guo, Kai Chen, Youcheng Pan, Xiangping Wu, Qingcai Chen
bullets: Continual learning in LLMs is challenged by catastrophic forgetting and costly global updates.
Gradient-attribution profiling identifies cognition-associated subnetworks with very low mutual overlap.
CiMEO restricts parameter and optimizer-state updates to the subnetwork selected for each training example.
Across 1.4 million sequential instructions and five generative benchmarks, CiMEO achieved the highest average performance among compared methods while mitigating forgetting.
Subspace and principal-angle analyses suggest localized updates help preserve pretrained representations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. localized plasticity in human barin vs. global plasticity in LLMs. (a), Learning recruits and co-activates sparse neuronal ensembles (circles; color indicates activity) across memory-relevant regions, including the hippocampus (HPC), cortex, and subcortical areas, forming an engram. During the first hours to days after learning, synaptic connectivity is preferentially strengthened among HPC engram cells and between HPC and other regions, enabling recent memory expression. Over subsequent days to weeks, systems consolidation supported by hippocampo–cortical replay and synchronized activity (notably involving prefrontal cortex, PFC) promotes maturation of cortical engram cells. This process drives strengthening of synaptic connectivity between corticalcortical and cortical-subcortical engram cells and a progressive shift in the engram cell network toward a higher dependency on cortical engram cells for remote memory expression. (b), Global parameter updates across sequential batches bring memory re-consolidation. During training on successive batches, learning is typically implemented via dense, global weight updates across the network. Lacking a brain-like mechanism of sparse engram allocation and multi-stage consolidation, new batches are absorbed by rewriting shared parameters, which can interfere with or overwrite earlier representations. As a result, the model’s “memory” is continually reconfigured by the order of batches, reflecting a stability–plasticity trade-off and potential forgetting under sequential learning.

Fig. 2. Framework for discovering endogenous cognitive modularity in LLMs and applying it to memory-efficient training. a, We construct a cognitive corpus from the AM-DeepSeek-R1-Distilled-1.4M instruction dataset, where each instruction is annotated with a Bloom’s taxonomy label. b, Cognition-isolated subnetworks are identified via gradient attribution: labelled instructions are fed into the LLM to predict cognition categories, and the gradients accumulated during back-propagation are aggregated to locate cognition-sensitive subnetworks. c, The state-serialized AdamW optimizer maintains a mapping between sparse parameters and their locations in the original dense tensors, so that only cognition-relevant subnetworks are activated and updated during training. d, For continual learning, CiMEO employs a cognitive classifier to assign a cognition label to each input and routes optimization to the corresponding local subnetwork. e, Experiments on five benchmarks report detailed incremental learning and anti-forgetting performance, together with weight-space dynamics during continual learning. f, We further analyze subspace overlap and principal angles across checkpoints to quantify interference and stability in the learned weight subspaces.

Fig. 5. The weight stability analysis. (a), The maximum principle angles between Qwen3-1.5B and all compared methods fine-tuned checkpoints across all layers, and (d) average over layers. (b), The maximum principle angles between Qwen3-1.5B and all compared methods fine-tuned checkpoints across all layers, and (e) average over layers. (c), the subspace overlaps between Qwen3-1.5B and different methods fine-tuned checkpoints across all layers, and (f) average over layers.

papers.title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.
authors: Lichao Ni, Yuhan Liu, Pengfei Li, Guanghuan Fang
bullets: Addresses distribution mismatch at both the environment-observation and intermediate action-flow levels.
Uses frozen domain-specialist teachers to provide velocity supervision along student-generated flow trajectories.
Alternates student updates with fresh environment interaction and action-flow generation, starting from joint supervised fine-tuning.
Improves success rates across LIBERO-40, CALVIN, and Meta-World, with especially larger gains on longer CALVIN sequences.
Produces a single student policy capable of deployment across multiple domains.
