papers.abstract: Language-conditioned humanoid motion generation enables users to create and refine robot movements through natural language. The central challenge is to connect an underspecified request to concrete motion structure that can subsequently be revised relative to an accepted reference. We present TRACE, a generation and editing framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid robot built around typed, measurable kinematic quantities. Our insight is to ground generation conditions in paired training motions and editing goals in the current motion. A language model learns to predict support, root, and hand events from motion-derived supervision; their time-aligned encodings complement the original text in a diffusion generator. Gravity-referenced states and trajectory--contact objectives improve kinematic consistency. For editing, typed requests define body--time scopes and source-relative goals. A separate reference-conditioned diffusion editor uses these goals and revised events to realize changes, while sampling-time projection preserves protected state coordinates. Quantitative evaluation and human assessment show improved semantic alignment and motion quality over the compared methods. Controlled ablations support the value of motion-grounded conditioning and kinematic consistency, while multi-turn editing evaluations demonstrate more reliable execution of successive relative requests under shared preservation constraints. Together, these results support typed kinematic structure as a common basis for motion generation and reference-aware revision.
authors: Zejian Kang, Yifu Luo, Boyang Shen, Jingxuan Li, Zekai Chen, Zekun Shi, Yongxue Xu, Zhenyu Hou, Bingqian Wu, Shaolei Zhang, Wentao Yang, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating underspecified language into concrete, revisable humanoid motion structure.
A language model predicts support, root, and hand events from paired motions; time-aligned event encodings condition a diffusion generator.
A reference-conditioned diffusion editor applies typed body–time goals relative to the current motion, with sampling-time projection protecting selected states.
Gravity-referenced states and trajectory–contact objectives improve kinematic consistency.
Quantitative, human, ablation, and multi-turn evaluations report better semantic alignment, motion quality, and successive relative-edit execution than compared methods.

papers.abstract: When code-repair agents fail, final tests reveal that a patch is wrong but not which earlier commitment caused it or which software obligation failed. Poison Valleys traces this path in 1,844 model requests on two synthetic Python cases: PersistQueue adds atomic batch claiming to a disk-backed queue, while Dijkstra adds source-sensitive filtering to shortest-path search. We define plausible but incorrect software mechanisms, place each in a model's hypothesis, implementation plan, or both, and evaluate the generated code with an Oracle and targeted diagnostic coordinates. Moving the misconception from hypothesis to plan increased failure by 32.2% in PersistQueue and 28.9% in Dijkstra after matching the experimental mix. Different misconceptions produced distinct, model-dependent patterns of violated obligations, although several could converge on the same behavior. This creates a measured connection from upstream misconception to code mechanism and failure form. Code, data, and demo: https://poisonvalleys.org.

papers.abstract: Real-world video denoising for communication systems must handle mixed degradations such as sensor noise, compression artifacts, and motion-induced inconsistency while remaining deployable under tight latency budgets. Purely deep models often achieve high accuracy but come with significant computational cost, whereas classical filters are robust and efficient but insufficiently adaptive. We present FilterFusion, a prior-guided multi-frame denoising framework that combines temporally-aware learned features with an interpretable bank of denoising branches. The model predicts a low-cost guidance signal and uses it to adaptively mix a compact set of denoising responses at the original resolution. The lightweight design uses only 109K parameters and explicitly injects temporal variance and spatial variance cues into the low-resolution controller. On CRVD (real sensor noise), it reaches 34.72 dB PSNR and 0.9330 SSIM with only 0.18 GFLOPs (network-only). Because the filter-bank operations are simple and regular (Gaussian blur, median, weighted sum), a straightforward compiled C implementation of the synthesis path achieves 17.9ms per frame (55.9 FPS) on a single CPU thread at 1080p---exceeding real-time and 122--252 times faster than lightweight CNN baselines that require over 2 seconds per frame. The results demonstrate a strong quality-efficiency-speed trade-off and a practical route to real-time denoising through low-resolution control and explicit filter-based synthesis.
authors: Wenlong Yang, Weihang Yuan, Canran Jin, Jiahao Li, Henrik Turbell, Lifeng Sun
bullets: Targets mixed real-world degradations, including sensor noise, compression artifacts, and motion inconsistency, under tight latency constraints.
Combines temporally aware learned features with an interpretable bank of denoising branches at the original resolution.
Injects temporal and spatial variance cues into a low-resolution controller that predicts adaptive filter mixing.
Uses 109K parameters and 0.18 GFLOPs; on CRVD, achieves 34.72 dB PSNR and 0.9330 SSIM.
A compiled CPU synthesis path processes 1080p frames at 17.9 ms per frame (55.9 FPS), supporting real-time deployment.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of FilterFusion in luma plane. A compact low-resolution predictor estimates pixel-wise fusion weights from the reference frame Yref , temporal mean Ȳ , and variance guidance (Vs, Vt), while a full-resolution filter bank generates multiple candidate responses. The final prediction is obtained by adaptively fusing these responses using the predicted weights. For the chroma planes, the same filter-bank synthesis is applied while reusing the weights predicted from the luma plane, producing the denoised NV12 output with negligible additional cost.

Fig. 1. Multi-dimensional trade-off. papers.abstract: Reusing the attention KV cache across requests is a standard way to cut prefill cost in long-context LLM serving, and production systems increasingly back the per-engine cache with a remote tier shared by every engine. We study such a tier in a disaggregated deployment of GLM-5.3, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention (MLA), on 8xB300 nodes running prefill context parallelism (PCP8). Enabling the remote tier (LMCache with a Valkey store) left median time-to-first-token unchanged but raised the 16k-token p99 from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. Replaying a production request stream on an isolated engine, we find that a remote hit took 0.88 s against 0.31 s to recompute the prompt, and that synchronous loading turned a hit-heavy stream into an unstable queue: p99 83.32 s with the GPUs 7% busy. A two-term cost model explains both: a hit pays off only if the tier delivers more than B* = sR (2.53 GB/s for this model and GPU), and a fixed per-hit engine cost (T0 ~ 0.33 s) means that hits on prompts shorter than about 17k tokens cannot beat recompute at any bandwidth. Guided by the model, we (i) shard the MLA KV store across PCP ranks, with a proof that the existing minimum-over-ranks lookup returns the longest cached prefix and a load protocol that can never desynchronize collectives; (ii) partition the remote tier by rank, one server instance per rank with no coordination, which raises GET bandwidth 6.3x to 10.76 GB/s; (iii) add asynchronous loading to the sharded store; and (iv) fix three client bugs that caused unbounded stalls. On the hit-heavy stream, with 98.5% of prompt tokens served from the remote tier, p99 falls from 83.32 s to 0.67 s. The sharded store raises prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% together with an upstream kernel fix. All changes are submitted upstream to LMCache.
authors: Muhammad Ibrahim
bullets: A remote LMCache/Valkey tier increased 16k-token p99 latency from 3.96 s to 17.3 s, despite unchanged median time-to-first-token.
Remote hits initially took 0.88 s versus 0.31 s for prompt recomputation; synchronous loading caused severe queueing and 83.32 s p99 latency.
A cost model shows caching helps only above 2.53 GB/s and for prompts longer than roughly 17k tokens.
The proposed design shards MLA KV state and the remote tier across PCP ranks, adds asynchronous loading, and fixes three stalling client bugs.
The optimized system reduced hit-heavy p99 latency to 0.67 s, increased prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% with an upstream kernel fix.

papers.abstract: Real-to-sim conversion aims to turn a captured video of a real environment into an editable 3D scene while preserving the geometry and layout of what was observed. Existing methods often follow a one-pass, loosely coupled paradigm: each stage receives only limited feedback from previous stages, allowing errors to propagate without reliable correction and leaving the final scene inconsistent. We present GRASE, an agentic framework that closes this loop by treating the captured multi-view video observations as a standing reference throughout scene modeling. Instead of committing to intermediate estimates, GRASE revises its current hypothesis whenever rendered evidence disagrees with the capture, overcoming the fixed intermediate assumptions of conventional pipelines. Specifically, GRASE first fits the architectural shell and its openings from depth and multi-view cues. An agent then places generated assets in a shared coordinate frame while checking their spatial relationships. Finally, each asset's geometry and placement are refined iteratively to improve agreement across the observed views. By coupling these steps through feedback, GRASE localizes structural discrepancies and revises only the responsible components, while preserving cross-view consistency. The resulting 3D scenes are faithful to the input, consistent across views, and suitable for simulations. In our experiments, GRASE substantially outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, including a direct real-to-sim conversion using GPT6-Astra.
authors: Zhaorui Lin, Haohan Liu, Zhen Chen, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Addresses error propagation and inconsistent geometry in one-pass real-to-sim pipelines.
Uses multi-view video and depth cues to fit the architectural shell and openings.
Places generated assets in a shared coordinate frame while checking spatial relationships.

Produces faithful, cross-view-consistent scenes and substantially outperforms prior methods in experiments, including a GPT6-Astra-based baseline.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents can accumulate interaction feedback, but reliably turning that feedback into reusable experience remains challenging. Existing methods either optimize external experience scaffolds or train experience-related behavior on specific task distributions, leaving open whether experience learning itself can become a transferable model capability. Training such a capability calls for supervision beyond isolated tasks, which mainly support in-episode problem solving rather than revealing what knowledge remains useful across episodes. In this work, we introduce MetaExp, a scalable framework that trains this capability through verifiable task families with controlled cross-task structure. Each family preserves a reusable factor while varying task-specific realizations, enabling transfer without direct solution reuse. We propose two complementary designs: Shared-Tool families keep black-box tools fixed across tasks to elicit operational experience, while Shared-Workflow families preserve latent procedures across changing realizations to elicit procedural experience. We scale environments under both designs, collect and filter sequential interaction trajectories, and fine-tune Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on 4,956 trajectories from 1,000 task families. With parameters frozen during downstream evolution, MetaExp improves by +8.5 points on SpreadsheetBench, peaks at +2.3 on APEX-Agents, and improves by +14.8 on AutomationBench. The gains persist under domain-excluded training, supporting experience learning as a transferable capability for continued non-parametric improvement after deployment.
authors: Renhao Li, Xinjie Shen, Yang Su, Jianhong Tu, Derek F. Wong, Dayiheng Liu, Min Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning reusable experience rather than task-specific strategies or external memory scaffolds.
Uses verifiable cross-task families that preserve either shared black-box tools or latent workflows while varying task realizations.
Trains on filtered sequential interaction trajectories from 1,000 task families and evaluates frozen-model downstream evolution.
Reports gains on SpreadsheetBench, APEX-Agents, and AutomationBench, including improvements after excluding training domains.
Supports experience learning as a transferable capability for non-parametric post-deployment improvement.

papers.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent answers that the supplied context does not support. A compact frozen proxy model can detect such answers by reading the context and another model's response, even from a proprietary generator. Attention-based detectors use summary statistics of the proxy's attention weights, but standard pipelines materialize the attention matrix, whose memory grows quadratically with sequence length. We compute these statistics without materializing attention, by accumulation in the FlashAttention pass, sparse lookups after it, or a second tiled pass over the scores, and classify them by this path into nearly free and costlier ones. On an H100, the statistics of five published detectors add 16% to the latency of a Qwen3-8B forward at 2K tokens, falling to 1.4% at 35K, and store 22.5 KiB per response token. On three benchmarks, probes trained on frozen Qwen3 proxies of 0.6B to 8B parameters prove strong detectors: a 4B proxy outperforms the strongest of nine zero-shot 4-9B LLM judges in F1 on two of the three, the proxies match or outperform specialized grounding checkers of up to 7B parameters, probing each proxy beats prompting it as a judge, and adding attention features significantly improves F1 in half of the 12 benchmark-proxy pairs, never significantly lowering it.
authors: Andrei Volodichev, Maksim Savichev, Nikita Sviridov, Artem Yuliy, Dmitry Simakov, Alexey Zaytsev

Across three benchmarks, frozen Qwen3 probes are strong detectors; a 4B proxy beats nine zero-shot LLM judges on two benchmarks and matches or exceeds specialized checkers.
Attention features significantly improve F1 in 6 of 12 benchmark–proxy pairs and never significantly reduce it.

papers.abstract: In endovascular interventions, physicians rely on planar DSA and X-ray fluoroscopy to interpret vessel anatomy and device motion, yet converting these images into feedback for autonomous navigation remains difficult. A perception and control method is formulated for two-dimensional image feedback. Vessel masks are converted into a labeled centerline graph, and device-tip estimates are projected onto a planned path to obtain progress, deviation, and direction. A rule-based controller uses these quantities for delivery, branch selection, probing, rollback, and recovery. The method was evaluated on a physical dual-device robotic platform in 65 closed-loop runs using simulator-rendered planar images across three paths. All runs reached at least 0.95 maximum observed guidewire progress; two runs (3.1%) met the prespecified failure rule of three or more autonomous stop events. The results establish route-level performance on the tested platform; clinical image sequences and broader anatomy remain to be evaluated.
authors: Sheng Cao, Shuxiang Guo, Yonggan Yan, Jian Guo, Chunying Li, Bin Wang, Mingchao Ding, Yongxin Zhang, Yongwei Zhang, Pengfei Yang, Jianmin Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting planar DSA/X-ray images into feedback for autonomous navigation.
Converts vessel masks into labeled centerline graphs and projects device-tip estimates onto planned paths.
Uses progress, deviation, and direction to control delivery, branch selection, probing, rollback, and recovery.
Evaluated in 65 closed-loop runs on a physical dual-device robotic platform across three simulator-rendered paths.
All runs achieved at least 0.95 maximum observed guidewire progress; 2 runs (3.1%) met the failure criterion.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. System architecture and data flow. Offline, custom device and vessel SE U-Net models are trained, exported to ONNX, and converted to TensorRT engines. Online, device masks provide frame-wise tip and direction estimates, whereas the averaged vessel output is locked as a labeled centerline graph. Operator-selected start and target points define the topology-constrained route. Operator-marked interaction-risk points form a separate early-trigger channel: proximity invokes priority retreat before the delayed off-path condition, without modifying the graph or replanning the route. This heuristic response is not a formal safety guarantee. Projection of both tips onto the route produces the visual state used by the priority controller. A discrete command drives the robot and changes the physical device configuration. Mentice updates the device–vessel interaction and renders the realized motion in the next simulator-rendered image, which closes the visual feedback loop.

papers.abstract: When a vision-language model is finetuned on class-imbalanced data, rare-class recall can fall well below the model's own zero-shot performance. In this regime, we uncover a surprising matched-prompt penalty whereby the standard choice of reusing the descriptive finetuning prompt at inference can yield lower rare-class recall than using a different descriptive prompt. We call this inference-time strategy cross-prompt inference. We evaluate diverse VLMs across six datasets and find that cross-prompt inference consistently recovers rare-class recall, with varying trade-offs in frequent-class recall. The effect reflects a train-eval prompt interaction rather than prompt quality alone, and does not arise with non-descriptive prompt changes. It is strongest when imbalance and visual confusability produce substantial rare-class suppression, and is weak or absent when such suppression does not occur. Using Tuning Contribution (TuCo), which decomposes a model's computation into pretrained and finetuning parts, we find that cross-prompt inference reduces reliance on finetuning-induced computation and shifts the model toward its pretrained component. Reducing that finetuning contribution also substantially reduces the cross-prompt advantage. These results show that rare-class knowledge suppressed by imbalanced finetuning can remain accessible under a different inference prompt.
authors: Emanuel Ben Baruch, Sivan Biham, Alon Shoshan, Yochai Zvik, Avi Ben-Cohen
bullets: Imbalanced finetuning can suppress rare-class recall below the model’s zero-shot performance.
Reusing the finetuning prompt at inference may worsen rare-class recall relative to a different descriptive prompt.
Across diverse VLMs and six datasets, cross-prompt inference consistently improves rare-class recall, sometimes trading off frequent-class recall.
The effect depends on train–evaluation prompt interaction and is strongest under severe imbalance and visual confusability.
TuCo analysis suggests cross-prompt inference shifts reliance away from finetuning-induced computation toward pretrained representations; reducing that finetuning contribution weakens the benefit.

papers.abstract: Every story has two orders: the order in which its events happen and the order in which they are told. A story is nonlinear when the two differ. We introduce a benchmark of 83 published works that measures whether language models can tell nonlinear stories. For each work, we annotate one list of events in both orders, together with a story graph of causal dependencies, character knowledge, and the questions the telling raises and resolves. Given events in chronological order, all 19 models tell them, on average, more chronologically than the published works do; asked for a specific structure, they land within the human range about half the time. We then compare a model's stories of the same events under different conditions, using both an automated judge and 71 human readers. Both prefer the chronological story a model writes by default to the nonlinear one it writes on request, which readers find harder to follow in 81% of decisive judgments. Readers also prefer stories written from the story graph to stories constrained to the published telling order (72% of decisive judgments), a difference the judge does not detect. Our results suggest that following an instruction to reorder a story is not yet the same as telling it well out of order.
authors: Syed Rifat Raiyan, Md. Tariquzzaman, Md Farhan Ishmam, Tenghao Huang
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 83 published works with event orders, causal story graphs, character knowledge, and narrative questions.
Evaluates 19 models on reconstructing published nonlinear structures from chronologically ordered events.
Models default to more chronological storytelling than humans and match requested human narrative structures only about half the time.
Human readers prefer models’ default chronological stories over their requested nonlinear versions in 81% of decisive judgments.
Readers prefer stories generated from causal story graphs over those constrained to the published telling order, suggesting graph-based planning may better support nonlinear narration.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, and speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, and holds the first action that would modify the environment. The strong model then verifies the drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification replaces autoregressive decoding with parallel prefill, the strong model decodes only short verdicts and occasional repairs rather than every step. On $\tau^2$-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the quality gap while lowering both. In an edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. These results suggest that a strong model need not author every step of an agent: reviewing grounded drafts retains most of its quality while cutting both latency and memory traffic.
authors: Zilin Wang, Yinhong Liu, Chao Chen, Qun Liu, Zhijiang Guo
bullets: Addresses the cost of having a strong model generate every tool-calling step in long agent trajectories.

The strong model semantically verifies an entire drafted segment in one prefill pass, commits valid prefixes, and repairs rejected steps.
On τ²-Bench, it comes within one point of the strong model’s success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time.
Across AutomationBench, VitaBench, and MCP-Atlas, it recovers substantial quality relative to weak-only agents while reducing strong-model token generation.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) receive image-generation supervision that exposes them to visual information not fully documented in text. Can learning to generate images expand what pretrained models know? We introduce Knowledge Transfer Probing (KTP), a controlled protocol that supplies new knowledge through image-generation training and tests its accessibility through text-only question answering. Across seven knowledge categories and three UMMs, we observe direct but uneven transfer from visual supervision to language. Motivated by these observations, we successively introduce Textual Alignment and Interleaved Image--Text Alignment, which connect generation and answering through shared knowledge and interleaved responses, respectively. Guidance on selected entities can improve knowledge access on other entities without QA supervision, with additional gains from interleaved alignment. Further analysis shows that knowledge correctly reproduced in images is often more accessible through text, although substantial gaps remain between the two forms of access. These findings support visual generation as a source of knowledge beyond textual supervision, and motivate joint investigation of training data design and model architecture to make this knowledge more broadly accessible.
authors: Wenkai Li, Wenyi Hong, Zhuoyi Yang, Jie Tang
bullets: KTP tests whether image-generation supervision makes visual knowledge accessible through text-only question answering.
Across seven knowledge categories and three models, the study finds direct but variable transfer from visual supervision to language.
Textual Alignment and Interleaved Image–Text Alignment improve access to generated knowledge, including for unguided entities.
Knowledge reproduced correctly in images is generally more accessible through text, but notable gaps remain.
The findings motivate better training-data design and model architectures for broader cross-modal knowledge access.

papers.abstract: While generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models have enabled diverse open-world manipulation, real-world robotic assistance requires two critical capabilities they currently lack: personalization and reliable execution. First, executing an instruction like "make me a sandwich" requires grounding subtask decomposition in persistent user preferences rather than relying on a single generic solution. Second, reliable deployment demands explainable safety assurance that proactively prevents hazards and gracefully recovers from occasional physical failures. To address these gaps, we present CarryOn, a dual-loop harness designed to augment a frozen VLA policy. The planning loop maintains persistent user-level and scene-level context that is continually grounded against new observations and revised through interaction, enabling personalized task selection and execution grounding across conversations and changing scenes. The execution loop actively supervises policy rollouts, shielding actions from predicted hazardous contact. When execution fails, the system invokes reusable control-based recovery skills that restore task progress and are refined through reflection on earlier failures. On a real robot and in simulation, CarryOn dispatches preference-consistent subtasks across users and scenes, reduces the violation rate of an already safety-finetuned VLA from 52.6% to 6.1%, and increases recovery success from 13% to 80% when refined skills are reused.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Yuqi Liu, Yuxin Chen, Sengqiao Yang, Jinhui Ye, Pengguang Chen, Changsheng Lu, Shu Liu, Bei Yu, Jiaya Jia
bullets: Maintains persistent user and scene context to ground task decomposition and execution in preferences across conversations and changing environments.
Supervises policy rollouts and shields actions predicted to cause hazardous contact.
Uses reusable control-based recovery skills after failures, refining them through reflection on prior errors.
Demonstrated preference-consistent task execution on a real robot and in simulation.
Reduced safety violations from 52.6% to 6.1% and increased recovery success from 13% to 80% when refined skills were reused.

papers.abstract: Human face-to-face conversation requires coordinating speech, gestures and expressions across both speaking and listening. We present ELLSA 2, an end-to-end full-duplex dialogue model that jointly optimizes speech interaction and streaming gesture-expression generation. An autoregressive, chunk-wise synthesizer combines pretrained acoustic features with distinct listening and speaking hidden states from the dialogue backbone and speech synthesizer, enabling continuous non-verbal generation even when the model is verbally silent. To translate dialogue understanding into vivid semantic gestures, we introduce contextual semantic calls and template guidance, separating whether to invoke an available semantic gesture from how to realize it. We also establish a curated data and evaluation pipeline for dialog-aware co-speech gesture generation and investigate reference-based multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as automatic judges. Experiments show that ELLSA 2 remains highly competitive with open-source full-duplex speech interaction models and outperforms cascaded baselines across dialog-aware gesture and expression metrics. Semantic template guidance further significantly improves semantic gesture quality. Strong system-level correlations with human judgments support these reference-based scores as useful preliminary metrics for full-duplex and semantic gesture assessment. Together, these results advance dialogue modeling from spoken responses toward coordinated multimodal interaction.
authors: Siyin Wang, Wenyi Yu, Terumi Chiba, Xianzhao Chen, Xiaohai Tian, Jun Zhang, Lu Lu, Chao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating speaking, listening, speech, gestures, and expressions during face-to-face interaction.

Introduces contextual semantic calls and template guidance to separate selecting semantic gestures from realizing them vividly.
Establishes a curated data and evaluation pipeline and explores reference-based MLLM judges for dialog-aware gesture and expression assessment.
Reports strong competitiveness against open-source full-duplex models, improved gesture and expression metrics over cascaded baselines, and further semantic-gesture gains from template guidance.

papers.abstract: We adapt the diffeomorphic coarse-to-fine LapIRN architecture for longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge. The method combines affine pre-registration, multi-modal deformable registration, and test-time instance optimization. We further introduce PET biomarker preservation losses for metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG), including Jacobian-based constraints, and a per-structure rigidity regularization for skeletal structures. The submitted configuration achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with MTV and TLG errors of 3.3% and 3.3%, respectively, on our evaluation protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/koegl/psmareg.
authors: Fryderyk K\"ogl, Anna Reithmeir, Daniel M. Lang, Emily Chan, Rickmer Braren, Julia A. Schnabel
bullets: Targets longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration for the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge.
Adapts a diffeomorphic coarse-to-fine LapIRN pipeline with affine pre-registration, multimodal deformable registration, and test-time optimization.
Adds MTV and TLG biomarker-preservation losses with Jacobian constraints, plus rigidity regularization for skeletal structures.
Achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with 3.3% errors for both MTV and TLG under the reported evaluation protocol.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed registration pipeline. The moving (follow-up) and fixed (baseline) PET/CT scans are first coarsely aligned by an affine pre-registration, and the resulting pair is then passed to the coarse-to-fine LapIRN network, which predicts a dense deformation field (green grid). Finally, after the LapIRN stage, we refine this field per pair by instance optimization (IO) and resample the moving scan with it into the fixed space (warped PET/CT). Both stages are driven by the same objective, a weighted sum of three groups of terms: registration accuracy, PET quantification, and deformation regularization (Sec. 2.3).

Fig. 2. Registration accuracy and biomarker preservation peak at different checkpoints. Validation CT Dice (left) continues to improve after MTV and TLG bias (right) reach their minima. The red dashed line indicates the checkpoint selected using the challenge composite ranking score.

Table 1. Our method against the baselines on the official challenge validation set (n = 20 cases), evaluated against the surrogate labels of Sec. 3.1. Every cell is a mean over the cases, runtime included: DSC and the MTV/TLG errors in %, NDV in ppm, and time in seconds per image pair on the hardware of Sec. 2.7. Bold marks the best value in each column. ∗ marks metrics on which ours (container) is significantly better than the baseline in that row (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank, Holm-corrected within each metric, p < 0.05); runtime is not tested. Dashes mark metrics undefined for a baseline.

papers.tldr: A longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration method preserves PET biomarkers while achieving strong anatomical alignment.

papers.abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner's own arrival. On OpenFly test-seen, no-stop failures account for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state. Flow-GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, X-Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, compared with 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for DreamFly.
authors: Ruibin Ju, Ruifeng Cai, Min Xu, Lin Wang
bullets: Full-chunk execution reduces inference cost from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint, but creates recovery and termination challenges.
Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited states with reconnecting action chunks and STOP targets at the first in-region state.
Flow-GRPO jointly refines the chunked controller and Bernoulli STOP policy using closed-loop task outcomes.
On OpenFly, X-Fly achieves 74.18% test-seen and 51.73% test-unseen success rates, versus 16.45%/18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04%/29.46% for DreamFly.
No-stop errors comprise 47.78% of full-chunk BC failures on test-seen; results are reported with eight controls per decision.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Policy backbone shared by the three training stages. A slow path runs the frozen Qwen3.5-4B VLM on the instruction and causal keyframes; a fast path runs only its visual tower on the current frame. Fused with ten state/anchor/action tokens (ego state, slow-cache anchor, and the last eight executed actions), the representation drives a rectified-flow controller that emits eight 4-D controls (∆x,∆y,∆z,∆ψ) and a separate Bernoulli STOP head; if CONTINUE is sampled, all eight controls are executed.

Figure 1. Accuracy–inference trade-off of X-FLY stages. SR under single-step (k=1) and full-chunk (k=8) execution; x-labels give amortized model inference per executed waypoint. On testseen, full-chunk BC reaches the goal but often does not stop. Recovery DAgger makes full-chunk execution viable, and Flow-GRPO, trained and evaluated at k=8 only, gives the highest SR among the evaluated operating points at 4.7× less amortized model inference time per executed waypoint than single-step execution. Inference timings apply to the X-FLY backbone; DreamFly [9] is shown as an SR reference at k=1.

Figure 2. The full-chunk support gap and how X-FLY addresses it. (a) Full-chunk BC flies eight controls between decisions and visits learner-induced anchors that expert demonstrations cover poorly, with neither a corrective chunk nor an arrival STOP label; the policy overshoots the goal. (b) Recovery DAgger relabels each learner anchor with a chunk whose offset dt decays by a smoothstep (inset) and rejoins the expert route at the chunk end; the first in-region anchor receives STOP. (c) Flow-GRPO samples six free and two STOP-override attempts per task with low-frequency chunk noise (inset: the four cosine modes) and a Bernoulli STOP policy, and uses their relative outcomes to update both.

Figure 5. Flow-GRPO from recovered vs. BC initialization. Source-validation (a) SR, (b) OSR, and (c) NE on a fixed 384-route BigCity panel excluded from Flow-GRPO updates, evaluated every 20 updates; dashed lines mark each initialization. The BC-initialized run was stopped at 680 updates as its OSR and NE kept degrading. ∆: mean change of each run relative to its own initialization over the 35 matched evaluations (shaded window).

Figure 4. Outcome attribution on the same recorded rollouts. Each row splits a policy’s episodes into two success and four failure types and sums to 100; values are expectations under the first-stop distribution (Sec. 4.1), in %. Color encodes magnitude within the success (blue) and failure (orange) groups. STOP / no STOP: success ending with an explicit in-region STOP / inside the region at the control budget. Nav.: no in-region anchor even with STOP disabled; Early/Late: STOP outside the region before/after the first in-region anchor; No-stop: reaches the region, never stops, and ends outside it. Rule in Appendix C; two-decimal values in Table 3.

Table 1. OpenFly test-seen and test-unseen results under the DreamFly-processed benchmark. NE is in meters, other metrics in %. Prior results are as reported with their native stopping policies; every X-FLY row uses the same 128-control cap and Bernoulli STOP policy, evaluated over its first-stop distribution (Sec. 4.1). k: controls executed per fused-policy decision. The two Recovery DAgger rows evaluate the same checkpoint, and its k=8 operating point initializes Flow-GRPO.
Table 2. Data flow of the three training stages. Every stage trains the same modules; the VLM and visual tower stay frozen.
Table 3. Outcome attribution (% of episodes) underlying Fig. 4. Labels follow the rule above. The two success columns sum to SR (Table 1), and all six columns of a split sum to 100 up to rounding.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses full-chunk aerial VLN failures (no-stop) using recovery DAgger and Flow-GRPO.
papers.title: X-Fly: Learning to Reach and Stop in Full-Chunk Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: X-Fly trains aerial VLN agents to recover from off-demonstration states and stop correctly while executing full action chunks, substantially improving navigation success over prior methods.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reason over both structured measurements and free-text records, which makes them attractive for emergency department (ED) prediction. However, most existing LLMs still fall short of conventional ML methods like trees on EHR-based prediction tasks. Our controlled analysis traces this gap to two weaknesses: LLMs do not select informative features, and they misjudge what numerical values imply for risk even when given the right features. We propose TIR-EC, a tool-integrated reinforcement learning framework that addresses both. TIR-EC exposes EHR feature groups as tools the LLM can call. It trains the LLM with rewards from a gradient-boosted tree teacher, which provides a reference set of informative tools and a graded risk target. TIR-EC also distills task-specific clinical skills into the model weights through a reverse curriculum that gradually removes the skills from the prompt during RL process. Evaluation on three clinical prediction tasks shows that our 4B agent achieves the highest macro F1 of all compared models, outperforms conventional ML baselines, and is competitive with much larger frontier LLMs. Further analysis shows that TIR-EC selects more useful evidence with fewer tool calls and combines measurements more effectively.
authors: Pengfei Hu, Chenwei Wu, Qiao Jin, Jun Deng, Zhiyong Lu, Liyue Shen, Yue Ning
bullets: LLMs lag behind tree-based methods because they select uninformative features and misinterpret numerical values.
TIR-EC exposes EHR feature groups as callable tools and uses a gradient-boosted tree teacher to provide tool-selection rewards and graded risk targets.
A reverse curriculum distills clinical skills into model weights by progressively removing those skills from prompts during reinforcement learning.
Across three clinical prediction tasks, the 4B agent achieved the highest macro F1 among compared models, exceeded conventional ML baselines, and matched much larger frontier LLMs.
The agent used fewer tool calls, selected more useful evidence, and combined measurements more effectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TIR-EC. The agent retrieves patient evidence through clinical tools and predicts an outcome. Tree models provide tool targets and risk signals, while clinical skill guidance fades during training. Alternative trajectories for the same patient share retained guidance and receive rewards for agentic RL updates.

Figure 1: Preliminary analysis on 2000 MC-MED patients (Kansal et al., 2025). (a) Disposition AUROC given k of 12 numerical feature groups, averaged over 10 runs. (b) 46 features’ dataset level vs. model-stated change in risk. (c) One decompensation patient. (d) Error decomposition on 100 randomly sampled patients for whom the GBM predicts correctly but Qwen3-4B free selection fails, human-labeled.

Figure 7: General prompt template and interaction protocol for TIR rollout. The figure summarizes the decision process rather than reproducing the runtime prompt verbatim. Blue denotes model reasoning, green a tool call, brown an environment observation, and purple the final prediction.
Figure 5: Feature interpretation. Every model receives the same k randomly drawn feature groups for each patient. Lines show macro AUROC over the three tasks, averaged over 10 random draws at each k.

Figure 3: Selective evidence acquisition. (a) Disposition AUROC when the agent may request up to k feature groups (solid) or is given k random groups (dotted). (b) Macro AUROC versus mean tool calls per patient.

Figure 4: Feature interpretation helps selection. Each arrow is one feature group, from Qwen3-4B (tail) to TIR-EC (head). Only commonly selected features are shown. Lines: least-squares fit across groups.

Table 1: Results on three emergency-care prediction tasks. All LLMs are evaluated in the same agentic feature selection setup as TIR-EC, except Qwen’s "Full Features" rows intakes all features for comparison.
Table 2: Case study of TIR-EC versus GPT.

papers.title: Incentivizing Tool-Use Reinforcement Learning for Post-Arrival Emergency Care Prediction
papers.tldr: TIR-EC improves LLM-based emergency-care prediction by teaching models which EHR features to retrieve and how to interpret their numerical risk.

papers.abstract: Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which assigns depth to the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head, executed on the device, and alternative branches to one SLM pass. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An {\epsilon}-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three Spec-Bench runs per system show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-{\epsilon}. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.
authors: Hanbin Bae, Heejin Choi, Joohyung Lee, Byoung Jin Choi, Sangjun Park, Hoon-Young Cho
bullets: Targets the repeated mobile-NPU passes required to grow deep draft trees in device-cloud speculative decoding.
Assigns draft-tree depth to the model’s native MTP head and alternative branches to one SLM pass, with required server states sent to the device.
Uses quantization, restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window to fit both drafters on a mobile NPU; an ε-threshold can relax exact sampling preservation.
On a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, reduces server GPU time per output token by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization versus server-side MTP self-speculation.
With the same acceptance rule, saves 9.0 percentage points more and delivers 1.9× higher speed than an SLM-only drafter; exact mode still saves 27.7% and 11.9%.

papers.title: HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient Mobile-Cloud Speculative Decoding

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate action sequences that reduce repeated inference, but deciding how much of each sequence to execute is critical to task success. Existing adaptive methods make this decision using generation stability or prediction agreement, yet these signals do not establish whether executing a candidate prefix preserves the ability to complete the task. We introduce a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. Rather than using future prediction to generate actions, our method evaluates existing proposals in the VLA's internal task-conditioned representation space. To learn local judgments from terminal task outcomes, we combine trajectory-level survival supervision with a localization prior that preserves useful behavior within failed rollouts. The resulting validity scores guide execution-horizon selection. Evaluations with pi_0 and pi_0.5 across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success-query trade-offs. These findings point toward a different role for future prediction in robotics, using it to assess how far to trust a policy's proposed actions rather than to generate new ones.
authors: Minkyu Kim, Junhoo Lee, Seungyeon Kim, Suhyun Jeon, Baekseung Kim, Donghoon Han, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Existing adaptive execution methods rely on generation stability or prediction agreement, which may not reflect task-completion potential.
PAV evaluates candidate action prefixes in the VLA’s task-conditioned representation space instead of generating new actions.
It learns local validity judgments from terminal outcomes using trajectory-level survival supervision and a localization prior.
Validity scores guide how many actions to execute at each step.
Experiments with pi_0 and pi_0.5 on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success–query trade-offs.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Policy-aligned predictive verification. The predictor uses the VLA representation and proposed actions to predict future policy representations. The verifier estimates local validity, which is accumulated and normalized to select an execution horizon. The robot executes the selected prefix and replans.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models achieve high-quality image generation but remain computationally expensive due to iterative denoising across many timesteps. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation.
authors: Minkyu Kim, Baekseung Kim, Junhoo Lee, Jangho Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Targets throughput rather than only reducing latency for individual samples.
Fuses multiple samples before the denoising backbone and separates them afterward.
Uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling to adapt fusion factors across denoising stages.
Works across U-Net and transformer diffusion models in pixel and latent spaces.
Composes with existing acceleration methods and enables higher-throughput regimes.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of the ManiFusion framework. K ×B inputs is fused into B representations, jointly processed by a shared denoising backbone, then unfused via the unfusion module into K representations per group, and finally passed through a projection layer to produce K outputs.

Figure 3: Analysis of the representation geometry induced by ManiFusion. (a) Geometric diagnostics measure prediction separation using response-distance ratios, and vector-field consistency and dynamics alignment using cosine similarity. (b) Training dynamics of Fusion Weight Orthogonality for MF-AE with K = 4, showing the development of slot-specific separation during training.

Figure 2: Comparison of throughput vs. quality and diversity on CIFAR-10 (left) and CelebA (right). The table (top) reports FID, sFID, IS, Precision, and Recall across throughput levels for Vanilla and Ours). The plots (bottom) visualize FID (right) and sFID (left) for DDIM, highlighting how Ours (red) compares against Vanilla DDIM (blue).

Figure 5: Empirical local response ratios under multi-sample fusion. We measure local Lipschitz ratios of the denoising dynamics under both near-neighbor and fusion-induced perturbations across fusion factors. The estimated ratios for K=2 and K=4 remain clearly positive while staying well controlled, showing nonzero output responses in the sampled directions. For K=8, the ratio remains positive but becomes noticeably smaller, indicating attenuated responses under more aggressive fusion in this diagnostic.

Figure 4: Clean-capacity and representation-alignment diagnostics under multi-sample fusion. Left. Swiss-roll samples as ambient dimensionD and fusion factorK vary. Right. An affine transformation aligns the visualized fused representations with the single-image reference in this toy setting. papers.abstract: Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) requires robots to respond to sound events by navigating to the associated objects and performing appropriate physical interactions. Existing STMM evaluations primarily vary object layouts within limited architectural structures, leaving challenges to unseen scenes insufficiently explored. We introduce Multi-scene Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (MuSTMM), a dataset that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes with diverse architectures and object layouts. MuSTMM contains 14.36 million precomputed binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs) and a scene-disjoint split for evaluating single-event and multi-event settings in unseen scenes. We further augment the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory that complements acoustic cues with observed geometry. Specifically, we accumulate pose-aligned depth observations in a shared coordinate frame and project this memory into an egocentric Bird's-Eye View (BEV) occupancy map. Fusing map features with sound context produces a goal descriptor that provides both target-location and scene-structure priors, guiding navigation to the target region required for subsequent physical interaction. This policy achieves a 2.60% success rate boost over existing methods, while component ablations further support the effectiveness of spatial memory. MuSTMM and the navigation policy provide a testbed for the new challenge of studying sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes. The code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.

Reports a 2.60% success-rate improvement over existing methods; ablations support the value of spatial memory.

papers.abstract: Learning from interaction experience is essential for enabling large language models to continually improve during deployment. Context distillation offers a promising path: privileged information extracted from experience is provided to a teacher, whose behavior is then distilled into a student model that has no access to it. However, both existing forms of context distillation have limitations. Off-policy context distillation trains the student on teacher-generated trajectories and thus suffers from exposure bias; whereas on-policy context distillation trains on the student's own rollouts, whose states are often uninformative and fail to convey behaviors the student cannot yet produce. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Localized Context Distillation (LoCD). LoCD first localizes the critical spans of a student trajectory that require revision. The teacher then regenerates only these spans from the student's own prefix, and the student is trained on the regenerated segments. LoCD thereby concentrates learning on the most informative states while keeping exposure bias low. Extensive experiments across math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks demonstrate that LoCD consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves more stable training with smaller and sparser parameter updates.
authors: Zhezheng Hao, Yongkang Yang, Xilin Xia, Jiarui Yu, Yi Liu, Fanjunduo Wei, Peijie Dong, Tianfu Wang, Qiang Lin, Can Wang, Hande Dong, Jiawei Chen

papers.abstract: Understanding video content requires reasoning at multiple levels of granularity, from identifying objects to interpreting their interactions and localizing when specific actions occur. This thesis studies three query-guided grounding tasks that answer where key objects are (object-level grounding), how they interact (relationship-level grounding), and when specific moments occur (moment-level grounding). For object-level grounding, we present QDETRv, a query-guided extension of the Detection Transformer for one-shot localization of unseen objects in videos, which combines query-context fusion, a memory module for temporal consistency, and unsupervised pretraining on synthetic object trajectories. We further propose the Temporal Object-Aware Vision Transformer (TOViT) for few-shot video object detection, which builds on a language-aligned open-set vision encoder and propagates high-confidence object features across frames. For relationship-level grounding, we introduce few-shot referring relationships in videos: given a (subject, predicate, object) query and a few support videos sharing the predicate, the entities are localized by optimizing a T-partite random field using a meta-learned relation network with query-conditioned translational embeddings, Global Semantic Aggregation, Local Localization Aggregation, and belief-propagation-based message passing. For moment-level grounding, we propose the Moment Alignment Transformer (MATR) for video-to-video moment retrieval, which uses dual-stage Dynamic Time Warping for pre- and post-fusion alignment, learnable queries for boundary prediction, and self-supervised pretraining with temporal augmentations; MATR also extends to text-to-video moment retrieval with performance comparable to, or better than, the state of the art. These contributions advance query-guided video understanding across spatial, relational, and temporal grounding.
authors: Yogesh Kumar
bullets: Addresses where objects are, how entities interact, and when relevant moments occur in videos.
Introduces QDETRv for one-shot unseen-object localization and TOViT for few-shot video object detection.
Models few-shot referring relationships with a meta-learned relation network and T-partite random-field inference.
Proposes MATR for video-to-video moment retrieval, with an extension to text-to-video retrieval.

Figure 1.1: Thesis Objectives. This work aims to advance query-guided video understanding by addressing three core questions: where objects are present, how they interact, and when specific actions occur. Consider a football match: understanding the play requires (i) identifying key entities such as the ball, goalposts, and the players (where important objects are), (ii) recognizing interactions like “player kicking the ball to a teammate" (how objects interact), and (iii) localizing key events such “goa" moment (when critical actions occur). Together, these tasks enable structured interpretation of complex, fast-paced sports scenes, moving beyond frame-level recognition toward temporally grounded, interaction-aware understanding.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. We ask how a harness can delegate these decisions to a decision model with little loss of success. To evaluate decision models in agentic tasks, we build AgentDecisionBench, which tests them from isolated questions up to control of a running agent, on public benchmarks and our DecisionGym environment. The decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points. Building on these findings, we then design JevAgentHarness, which fits this threshold for each choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it. Because existing decision models never see the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, we train AgentDecision-4B, an open 4B model, on such states with Jev's answers as labels. On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them with AgentDecision-4B and 82.0% with Jev. On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of task success. The models, data, and harness will be released at https://github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness.

papers.title: JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs
papers.tldr: JevAgentHarness enables agents to delegate many tool-choice decisions from LLMs to faster, cheaper decision models while preserving task success through confidence calibration and trajectory-based training.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on generative models for expert execution, workflow planning, and artifact review. Yet many coordination operations require only bounded decisions, such as selecting the next expert or judging artifact quality. Profiling three representative MAS frameworks, we find that routing and review account for 31.7-43.5% of generative-LLM tokens. However, replacing these operations with low-cost decision models introduces two interface gaps: generative planners produce execution plans and handoff instructions (planning gap), while reviewers provide actionable feedback for repairing flawed artifacts (review gap), which bounded decisions alone cannot provide. We introduce Jev-LiteMAS, a multi-agent framework that bridges both gaps by combining a lightweight decision model (Jev) with generative execution and feedback. To address the planning gap, Jev selects experts dynamically from the task and prior expert outputs, using accumulated context to ground subsequent execution without a pre-generated trajectory. To address the review gap, Jev screens intermediate artifacts against task criteria: passing artifacts proceed directly, whereas flagged ones undergo LLM re-review for acceptance or corrective feedback. Across four benchmarks and two backbones, Jev-LiteMAS reduces generative-LLM tokens by 12.7-54.6% over LAS, maintaining accuracy within 1.34 percentage points and lowering latency in seven of eight settings. Grounding routing in substantive expert outputs prevents up to 18.0 points in accuracy loss.

bullets: Routing and review consume 31.7–43.5% of generative-LLM tokens in profiled multi-agent systems.
The framework combines Jev for bounded decisions with generative models for execution and feedback.
Jev dynamically selects experts from task context and prior outputs, avoiding pre-generated workflows.
Jev screens artifacts; only flagged results receive full LLM re-review and corrective feedback.
Across four benchmarks and two backbones, it cuts generative-LLM tokens by 12.7–54.6%, keeps accuracy within 1.34 points, and lowers latency in seven of eight settings.

papers.abstract: Traditional keypoint descriptors, such as SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) and ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF), are computed from local image patches. They may be unreliable in scenes with repetitive patterns or weak textures, where patches at different locations can look similar. We propose the Contextual Line-Assisted Descriptor (CLAD), a keypoint matching method that addresses this problem by using global geometric context from line correspondences. CLAD represents each keypoint with a vector whose elements indicate its proximity to matched lines. It can therefore use the keypoint's spatial relationships to the lines in the scene. We use HOME (Hough-space One-dimensional Matching of Extrema) to detect both clear and weak linear structures and to establish enough line-to-keypoint associations to represent this context. Evaluations on the TUM RGB-D SLAM dataset and outdoor video sequences show that CLAD provides geometrically consistent matches that complement those obtained with traditional local descriptors. In repetitive scenes, where local descriptors may not distinguish similar patches, CLAD uses global structure to improve matching reliability. The method is computationally lightweight and practical to implement.
authors: Masaki Satoh
bullets: Targets ambiguities in local descriptors such as SIFT and ORB when patches look similar.
Builds keypoint vectors from spatial relationships to matched lines, capturing global geometric context.

Designed to be computationally lightweight and practical to implement.

These examples illustrate a limitation of descriptors based only on local image information: in challenging scenes, many local patches may look alike, causing methods such as ORB to confuse different keypoints. In contrast, CLAD uses the global geometric context provided by line correspondences, which helps it find more reliable matches in these cases.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory has become a crucial component of large language model (LLM) agents, with most research focusing on retrieving relevant information accurately and efficiently. However, a dependable memory system must also forget sensitive user data upon request. To evaluate this capability, we introduce MemCut, a systematic benchmark for user-requested forgetting. Its 456 hand-designed secrets in long-horizon conversations have fully annotated evidence trails to test recovery after deletion, including from messages that never state the secrets directly. We propose two recovery metrics. Native recovery measures reader success through the system's retrieval, whereas residual recovery measures the same reader's success when directly given surviving objects traced to annotated disclosures or evidence. We establish three reference deletion baselines to test how far existing retrievers and write models support forgetting across five memory designs and four LLMs. Disclosure removal reduces native recovery far more than residual recovery. LLM-guided deletion of ten additional turns from twenty retrieval candidates leaves 39-76% residual recovery. Subset sweeps (144 facts, three systems, two models) show that widening the pool at a fixed budget reduces residual recovery more than deleting all original candidates. These sweeps identify candidate coverage as a bottleneck in the reference baselines.

papers.abstract: An AI data center is committed years before it draws a watt: a few discrete choices (grid or on-site gas, evaporative or dry cooling, which county to file in) fix its capital, water draw, and carbon path, and LLMs are now asked to help screen them with no test of whether they track what each commitment rules out. We introduce DCBench-440, with two arms reported separately: 200 generative questions over STRIPS worlds for five US deal archetypes, with search-verified gold answers and no tested shortcut above 12% on any question type, and 240 multiple-choice questions grounded in quoted site records, emission equations, and stated scenarios. Across open-weight deployments, accuracy spans 12.5-71.5% (generative) and 58.3-92.5% (multiple choice). One skill fails everywhere: asked to list every action available at a decision gate, no model exceeds 4.0% exact match. The strongest list 72-85% of the actions that would change the project's state but omit most permitted actions that change nothing; with those excused, the best exact match is still 24%. Code, data, and other materials are available upon request.
authors: Pankaj Chouhan, Rajarshi Das, Aditya Dubey, Manminder Tomar, Sreekar Reddy, Samta Sharma, Satyapragnya Kar, PR Panigrahi

papers.abstract: Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs) are fundamental to many real-world applications. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spurred progress in solving these NP-hard problems. However, most existing approaches assume that input instances are error-free, neglecting the presence of faults commonly encountered in real-world data. In this work, we systematically investigate the capability of LLMs to detect (and correct) errors in VRP instances, and identify key limitations, particularly in handling complex instances or errors that substantially increase the LLM's reasoning burden. To overcome these challenges, we propose a self-guided reasoning framework in which LLMs autonomously generate code that provides structured insights to aid in error diagnosis. Experiments across diverse problem settings and LLMs demonstrate that our framework significantly improves error detection performance, achieving near-perfect accuracy.

bullets: Existing LLM-based VRP methods generally assume error-free input data.
The study evaluates LLMs’ ability to detect and correct faults in VRP instances.
LLMs struggle particularly with complex instances and errors that impose high reasoning demands.
The proposed framework generates code autonomously to provide structured diagnostic insights.
Experiments across varied problem settings and LLMs show significantly improved error detection, with near-perfect accuracy.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from internal feedback can improve language models without ground-truth answers or external verifiers. However, confidence and correctness can diverge during training, and continued optimization of average self-certainty can increase confidence while degrading reasoning accuracy. We introduce SIF, a reinforcement learning method that combines comparative reward construction with selective policy updates. SIF compares ranked token-level self-certainty profiles across multiple windows and peers, assigning positive rewards only when both levels of voting provide sufficient support. Sample and group level filtering determines which responses contribute to policy optimization. Experiments on three backbones across 12 mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks show that SIF's final checkpoints achieve higher average accuracy than the best-validation checkpoints of Intuitor and Vigor, with a gain of 4.71 percentage points over Intuitor on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B. Further analyses show better retention of accuracy during continued optimization, while test-time training experiments demonstrate sustained improvements with as few as four rollouts per prompt.
authors: Xun Lu, Shumeng Yang, Xinrui Wang, Songjun Tu, Linjing Li, Daniel Dajun Zeng
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between increasing confidence and actual reasoning correctness during internal-feedback training.
Compares ranked token-level self-certainty across multiple windows and peer responses to construct rewards.
Filters responses at both sample and group levels before policy optimization.
Across three backbones and 12 math/science benchmarks, SIF outperforms reported best-validation checkpoints of Intuitor and Vigor; it gains 4.71 points over Intuitor on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B.
Maintains accuracy better during continued optimization and improves with as few as four test-time rollouts per prompt.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation. Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability. PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions. It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline. We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluate it with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets. Results show that PriorityFEC achieves superior task quality over the compared transport schemes, with its advantages becoming particularly pronounced under stringent deadline constraints. These results demonstrate the importance of jointly optimizing KV-cache utility and deadline-aware transport reliability when reusable LLM state must be handed off across unreliable edge networks.
authors: Han Shen, Qifu Tyler Sun, Fanyang Meng, Ye Wang, Yongsheng Liang
bullets: Addresses redundant prefill computation when shared context moves between agents.
Orders KV blocks by model-side utility so the most valuable information is transmitted first.
Uses feedback-adaptive streaming FEC to schedule repairs before the receiver’s TTFT deadline.
Evaluations on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets show better task quality than compared transport schemes, especially under tight deadlines.
Scope: effectiveness depends on KV-utility estimation, link reliability, and available transmission time.

Fig. 6. End-to-end token-level F1 under different decode-start deadlines on the 100-Mbps burst-loss GE link. PriorityFEC provides substantial gains under ρ = 0.8, where complete loss-free KV serialization is infeasible. As the deadline is relaxed to ρ = 1.0, the performance gap decreases because more KV state can be recovered regardless of source position.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi-billion-parameter model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly than the robot state. We introduce Fast-VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and initial views as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory. During execution, a lightweight online actor fuses learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re-running the foundation model. Fast-VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by 10.9-17.1x and requires 1.22 GiB of post-prefill online resident memory. Task-memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode-matched task memory. These results show that task context can be established once while closed-loop control remains responsive throughout execution. Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA
authors: Kehong Gong, Guanli Hou, Xiaoxu Zheng, Qi Wang, Mingxi Xu, Anbang Zhai, Xiaoyu He, Mingyuan Zhang, Michael Bi Mi

Stores instruction and initial-view context as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory.
A lightweight actor combines current visual/proprioceptive feedback with learned time- and arm-indexed queries to predict action chunks.
Reports strong success across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, with 10.9–17.1× lower amortized RoboTwin inference time than continually conditioned baselines.
Task-memory swaps indicate that performance depends on episode-matched task context.

papers.abstract: Block Influence (BI) ranks Transformer blocks for depth pruning from their input-output cosine change, but the ranking depends on the calibration distribution. We study whether English calibration transfers to Indian languages in Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-1B, and Gemma-2-2B. English, Hindi, Marathi, and Tamil use disjoint Wikipedia articles for calibration and evaluation; every selector receives the same 150-chunk budget, and Tamil is excluded from multilingual aggregation to test cross-script transfer. Across all three models, late-block BI is 20.7-55.5% higher for the three Indian languages than for English, and every predeclared late-minus-middle contrast has a 95% bootstrap interval above zero. This mismatch changes the low-BI blocks selected for removal despite high global rank correlations. Averaging BI over equal English, Hindi, and Marathi budgets mitigates the resulting perplexity damage for Qwen at six removed blocks and for Gemma at all tested depths, including held-out Tamil. The mitigation is not universal: on Llama, balancing improves Hindi and Marathi at two removed blocks but severely harms Tamil, while larger pruning budgets select the same blocks and collapse perplexity regardless of calibration. Rank-mean and minimax-rank aggregators do not dominate the raw mean. These results support a diagnostic claim rather than a universal pruning rule: English-only BI systematically misses late-layer activity for Indian-language text, but multilingual calibration must still be validated per architecture and pruning budget.
authors: Vedant Pandhare, Piyush Dhoka
bullets: BI rankings depend strongly on calibration language, despite high overall rank correlations.

This shifts which low-influence blocks are selected for removal.
Equal-budget English–Hindi–Marathi averaging mitigates perplexity damage for Qwen and Gemma, including held-out Tamil in some settings.
The benefit is not universal: effects vary by architecture and pruning depth, and larger budgets can cause perplexity collapse.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has brought strong gains to language model reasoning, but its improvements on visual tasks remain less consistent. One difficulty is that visual task failures can arise from different sources: the same benchmark may be limited by perception for one model and by reasoning for another. We introduce Perception and Reasoning Attribution (PARA), which measures the remaining perceptual and reasoning headroom of each model--benchmark pair by comparing how many current errors are recovered with more accurate visual information versus a stronger reasoner. Across 4 vision-language models and 17 multimodal benchmarks, PARA broadly agrees with the expected characteristics of existing benchmarks while revealing substantial model-specific variation. More importantly, it shows that RL gains become smaller as perceptual headroom increases, but larger when reasoning explains more of the recoverable errors, suggesting that current RL exploits reasoning headroom more effectively than perceptual headroom. Motivated by this gap, we analyze how existing RL objectives affect visual perception and find that reward- and token-level signals influence visual attention only indirectly. We therefore propose GRAD, a group-relative attention distillation objective that uses the best rollout in each group to directly guide the visual attention of weaker rollouts. GRAD consistently improves performance across two model scales and seven benchmarks, and further complements existing RL methods.
authors: Zeyuan Yang, Zhuohao Chen, Jiaben Chen, Yao Zhang, Maohao Shen, Chuang Gan
bullets: Visual-task failures vary by model: the same benchmark may be perception- or reasoning-limited.
PARA estimates remaining perceptual and reasoning headroom by comparing error recovery with better visual information versus stronger reasoning.
Across 4 VLMs and 17 multimodal benchmarks, PARA finds that RL benefits reasoning headroom more effectively than perceptual headroom.
The authors find existing reward- and token-level RL signals affect visual attention only indirectly.
GRAD distills visual attention from the best rollout to weaker group rollouts, consistently improving results across two model scales and seven benchmarks while complementing existing RL methods.

figures.caption: Figure 5: (a) Changes in perception and reasoning headroom relative to Qwen3-VL-4B.
