papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation by routing each token to a small set of experts, but each selected expert is still used at a fixed precision. We present DPA-MoE, a runtime precision control framework that makes routed experts any-precision. DPA-MoE encodes expert feed-forward weights as prefix-decodable chunks using SharedScale AnyBCQ, profiles per-expert reconstruction residuals offline, and allocates chunks at inference time using live router gate scores. This post-routing allocation lets a single encoded MoE checkpoint operate at multiple effective weight budgets without retraining or re-encoding. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B show that DPA-MoE improves KL divergence and downstream accuracy over uniform chunk allocation at matched budgets, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in our prototype.
authors: Jaeyun Kim, Hoonki Lee, Susie Shin, Hyunmin Kim, Dahyun Lee, Sangyeob Kim
bullets: Addresses the fixed-precision limitation of routed MoE experts.

Outperforms uniform chunk allocation on KL divergence and downstream accuracy at matched weight budgets.
Evaluated on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in the prototype.

papers.abstract: Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable. This letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification, without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a metric world model. Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation. An online Concurrent Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C$^3$BF). An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated assumptions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in $98.3\%$ of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in $93$ of $100$ real-world trials.
authors: Bazeela Banday, Jishnu Keshavan
bullets: Represents collision risk using depth-normalized relative motion inferred from monocular optical flow.
Uses a Concurrent Learning observer to estimate normalized relative velocity and bound estimation error online.
Propagates uncertainty through angular inflation and a robot-footprint margin to construct a robust vision-based collision-cone control barrier function.
An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally adjusts nominal control to enforce safety.
In experiments, the error bound contained measured error in 98.3% of simulation samples, and TurtleBot3 completed 93/100 real-world trials without collisions.

An optimal-decay CBF-QP enforces the resulting safety constraint. The resulting loop performs safety-critical navigation using monocular vision and onboard proprioception, without explicit reconstruction of obstacle position, velocity, or geometry.

papers.abstract: Neural PDE solvers commonly generate multi-step predictions through autoregressive rollout, recursively applying a learned evolution operator and feeding each prediction back as input for the next step. Approximation errors can therefore propagate through the rollout, causing predictions at a shared target time to depend on their temporal origins and rollout depths. For a well-posed deterministic PDE flow, however, states at different times along the same physical trajectory should, under exact evolution, reach the same target state. To this end, we propose Align Latent Rollout (ALR), a regularization approach that promotes consistency across rollout origins through the neural PDE solver's internal representations. A second-order Taylor analysis of latent discrepancy propagation motivates two objectives: zeroth-order latent state consistency, which aligns representations at a shared target time, and first-order latent dynamics consistency, which aligns local evolution responses to shared perturbations. ALR can be integrated into different neural PDE solvers by regularizing suitable internal representations, without modifying their backbone architectures. Experiments across multiple PDE benchmarks and neural-operator backbones show that ALR improves prediction accuracy while reducing shared-target discrepancies across rollout origins.
authors: Xinying Li, Jing Xu, Wenjun Wang, Limei Han, Fenglei Cao, Ruoxi Jiang, Yuan Qi
bullets: Autoregressive rollout errors can make predictions at one target time depend on their starting time and rollout depth.

It uses zeroth-order latent-state consistency and first-order latent-dynamics consistency objectives.
Experiments across multiple PDE benchmarks and neural-operator backbones report improved accuracy and reduced shared-target discrepancies.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) mitigates the performance degradation of source-pretrained models on unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. Recent backpropagation-free token-purging methods address 3D point cloud distribution shifts by filtering unreliable tokens. However, their reliance on predefined purge-size candidates requires multiple forward passes per sample and increases inference cost. We propose SATOR (Sample-Adaptive TOken Routing), a source-free and backpropagation-free 3D TTA framework that eliminates this search by deriving both the partitioning threshold and routing decision directly from each sample. SATOR computes token abnormality scores from complementary attention and geometric relation graphs. It then derives a sample-specific partition into retained and pruned tokens via Otsu-based separability, without evaluating candidate sizes. Keep-ratio-calibrated routing then selects the pruned prediction only when its entropy, penalized by the keep ratio, is lower than that of the original prediction. Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C demonstrate that SATOR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three 3D corruption benchmarks.
authors: Inseok Kong, Geunyoung Jung, Jiyoung Jung
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in 3D point clouds without source data or backpropagation.
Computes token abnormality from attention and geometric relation graphs.
Uses Otsu-based separability to derive each sample’s retained/pruned token partition.
Routes to the pruned prediction only when keep-ratio-penalized entropy favors it.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C.

A keep-ratio-calibrated routing mechanism selects between the original and pruned token sequence predictions, accounting for the keep ratio in the routing criterion.

papers.abstract: Residential design aims to transform existing homes into functional living spaces while satisfying diverse design preferences and physical constraints. However, existing floorplan generation methods typically assume empty building boundaries as input, whereas renovation requires reasoning over existing floorplans. Furthermore, floorplan renovation and furniture layout are commonly addressed as separate tasks, overlooking their inherent spatial dependency. Consequently, practical residential design must preserve immutable structural components while transforming editable spatial elements. It must also optimize furniture placement under design objectives and physical constraints. To address these challenges, we formulate residential design as a design-point-guided conditional generation task and propose RenoLayout, a framework that translates a pre-design residential state together with a design-point set into an executable Geometry-as-Code program. To enable controllable supervision, we construct a Design Map comprising 123 fine-grained design points covering structural renovation and furniture layout. We further introduce Difference-Grounded Design-Point Annotation to derive design-point sets automatically from before--after design pairs with VLM-based consistency verification. RenoLayout is trained using a three-stage CPT--SFT--RL pipeline, progressively improving spatial reasoning, instruction following, and constraint compliance. We also introduce the RenoLayout Benchmark, a set of 200 real-world before--after renovation cases with complete furniture layouts. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first benchmark for unified residential design. These cases include design-critical structural and building-service constraints.
authors: Jingguo Liu, Yuanqing Liu, Chong Zhang, Yue Yang

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on $\pi_{0.5}$ as LTM-$\pi$, our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory-specific semantic annotations or external reasoning-model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM-$\pi$ achieves 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory-specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67% to 87.50%, while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200-token memory budget, success remains 84.00%, versus 87.50% without compression. Finally, real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded-context operation, and real-world robotic control.
authors: Qixin Sun, WenLong Gao, Xiansheng Chen, Zhongyuan Wang, Si Liu, Pengwei Wang
bullets: Stores consecutive-observation transitions in latent form rather than retaining full visual history.
Combines a frozen latent action encoder, lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental, annotation-free inference.

Memory scales effectively: RoboMME success rises to 87.50% with tenfold more demonstrations and remains 84.00% under a 200-token budget.
Real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%; a Cup Swap diagnostic underscores the importance of process supervision for temporal composition.

papers.abstract: Autonomous delivery in large scale buildings requires coordinated planning across multiple spatial levels, including building, floor, and room, while ensuring scheduling efficiency. Existing methods often focus solely on algorithmic development, neglecting integration with physical robotic platforms, and rarely validate performance in real world scenarios. Many approaches also overlook hierarchical building structures and room level privacy constraints, limiting practical applicability. To address these challenges, this paper presents a hierarchical delivery framework based on a Building-Floor-Room abstraction, which decomposes the problem across multiple levels to significantly reduce optimization complexity. We formulate a building aware extension of the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) that explicitly models inter building and inter floor connectivity, room level access constraints, and privacy sensitive areas, enabling globally feasible and privacy compliant task assignment and routing. Based on this hierarchical model, the framework can evaluate delivery efficiency across different building layouts and optimize depot placement for specific configurations. At the execution level, we introduce a novel hardware design for non interactive, privacy preserving delivery, supported by reachability aware distances and a closed loop mapping, localization, and navigation system, ensuring consistency between planned routes and physical navigation. The proposed framework is validated on a real multi sensor robotic platform, demonstrating reliable multi floor delivery with improved path rationality and overall efficiency.

Validated on a real multi-sensor robot, demonstrating reliable multi-floor delivery with improved route rationality and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Efficient synthesis of contact-rich manipulation trajectories is essential for downstream robot learning. Gradient-based planning offers a promising approach, but jointly optimizing motion and contact decisions remains challenging. Meanwhile, many existing planners run on CPUs with limited throughput. We present CQDC-Warp, a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic simulator for batched model predictive control (MPC). We use it to study contact-guided trajectory optimization, in which intended robot--object contacts are specified before planning and encouraged through soft costs, while the simulated dynamics determine contact geometry and frictional response without a prescribed contact-mode schedule. Across $17{,}408$ trials on the $17$-object Allegro in-hand rotation benchmark, our framework achieves $79.8\%$ success, compared with $73.7\%$ for CFree and $65.2\%$ for IMPACT, and reduces mean trajectory-generation time by factors of $27.0$ and $50.2$, respectively. On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with $2{,}048$ parallel worlds, forward and backward throughput reach $2.06\times10^5$ and $2.25\times10^5$ world-steps per second, respectively. Further experiments cover manipulation with LEAP and Shadow hands, environmental contact exploitation, bimanual manipulation, whole-body control, and real-world trajectory replay on a Sharpa hand.
authors: Yanchen Ding, Jiayi Chen, Jianfeng Xu, Wei Zhao, Li Yi, He Wang
bullets: Targets the joint optimization of robot motion and contact decisions, a challenge for gradient-based manipulation planning.
Uses a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic simulator with batched model predictive control (MPC).
Specifies intended contacts through soft costs while allowing simulated dynamics to determine contact geometry and friction without a fixed contact-mode schedule.
On the 17-object Allegro in-hand rotation benchmark, achieves 79.8% success versus 73.7% for CFree and 65.2% for IMPACT.
Demonstrates broad applicability across multiple hands, environmental and bimanual manipulation, whole-body control, and real-world trajectory replay.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts, at the answer position, the content tokens these heads already attend to; both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model's own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks.We evaluate on ECC and GoEmotions across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Across settings, SIAB improves prompt-matched baselines by up to +10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and +5.5 on GoEmotions. Combined with PASTA-style external supervision, it achieves up to +13.84 accuracy points and +12.51 macro-F1 points, while mechanistic analyses trace the gains to sparse, emotion-enriched heads and show that layer proximity affects additivity.
authors: Wenqiu Tang, Zhen Wan, Yihui Wang, Takahiro Komamizu, Ichiro Ide
bullets: Targets implicit emotional states that must persist across topic shifts from sparse conversational cues.
Uses causal localization on synthetic minimal pairs to find affective attention heads.
Boosts, at the answer position, tokens already attended to by those heads—without externally specified target spans.
Improves prompt-matched baselines by up to 10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and 5.5 on GoEmotions across three LLMs.
Combining SIAB with external supervision yields further gains, while analyses link effects to sparse emotion-enriched heads and layer proximity.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) effectively transfers capabilities from a teacher to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts. However, generating complete student rollouts and computing teacher feedback for every token make OPD computationally expensive. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.
authors: Zhengxin Zhang, Maosen Tang, Ning Wang, Changhao Li, Jingren Zhou, Bo Dai, Sainyam Galhotra, Alex Townsend, Claire Cardie
bullets: OPD is costly because it completes student rollouts and obtains teacher feedback for every token.
STOPD samples a stopping position before generation and truncates each rollout at that point or at natural termination.
Blockwise inverse-probability weighting compensates for the reduced chance of retaining later tokens while controlling weight magnitude.
The method preserves Vanilla OPD’s gradient sum in expectation, with update-error bounds derived for SGD, Adam, and Muon.
Across multiple model pairs, domains, and optimizers, STOPD achieves 1.3–2.2× training speedups.

papers.abstract: Multimodal long-document question answering requires models to seek sparse evidence across pages and modalities, understand heterogeneous document content, and reason over the collected evidence. Even advanced vision-language models (VLMs) can overlook sparse evidence and struggle with cross-modal reasoning in a single pass. Existing document agents further introduce multi-step interaction, but some still rely on predefined workflows or coarse-grained actions, limiting the flexibility and granularity of document reasoning. We introduce DocPilot, an agentic document framework that supports expressive orchestration and makes complex document solving learnable by small language models (SLMs). DocPilot orchestrates evidence seeking through page-level navigation and fine-grained evidence localization, and integrates local visual inspection, code-based numerical reasoning, and cross-modal reasoning for multimodal understanding. To transfer these capabilities to small models, we propose curriculum-based agentic training that progresses from single-ability learning to adaptive orchestration through supervision from data-grounded reasoning traces and executable interaction trajectories. Across MMLongBench-Doc, DocBench, FinRAGBench-V, and MADQA, DocPilot achieves strong gains with frontier VLM backbones, while DocPilot-4B delivers competitive performance against substantially larger models, demonstrating strong effectiveness and generalization across diverse long-document reasoning settings. The code is available at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/DocPilot.
authors: Zhuowen Liang, Xiaotian Lin, Yuyu Luo, Haixun Wang, Nan Tang
bullets: Targets sparse, heterogeneous evidence and cross-modal reasoning challenges in long documents.
Uses page-level navigation, fine-grained evidence localization, local visual inspection, code-based numerical reasoning, and cross-modal reasoning.
Trains small language models with a curriculum that advances from individual abilities to adaptive orchestration.
Supervision combines data-grounded reasoning traces with executable interaction trajectories.
Shows strong gains with frontier VLMs and competitive performance from DocPilot-4B across four diverse benchmarks.

papers.title: DocPilot: Interactive Agent Orchestration and Training for Long Visual Document Understanding
papers.tldr: DocPilot improves long visual-document QA by flexibly orchestrating evidence search, visual inspection, numerical reasoning, and cross-modal reasoning, while training small models to perform these capabilities.

papers.abstract: Exact $k$-nearest-neighbor (kNN) search over image descriptors and embeddings underlies visual retrieval, near-duplicate detection, the evaluation of learned representations, and increasingly the memory of LLM agents. However, exhaustive search computes every distance at full precision, whereas approximate indexes return recall below one. We observe that exact search only needs a proof that each excluded vector cannot be a neighbor. Because such a proof only has to be conservative, it can be checked in low precision, much as the retina examines the whole scene at low resolution. We call this principle certified exclusion and realize it in an exact kNN method for GPUs, which we call \certex. Specifically, \certex\ stores a lower-bounding projection of each vector in half precision and folds a rounding certificate into the same tensor-core dot product, so that only the few vectors that the test keeps need exact distances. We prove that \certex\ returns the exact kNN of every query. On sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, \certex\ is exact for every query at 7.1$\times$ to 18.0$\times$ the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 and outperforms quantized and graph indexes whenever every query must be exact.
authors: Dongfang Zhao
bullets: Targets exact visual retrieval, where exhaustive search is costly and approximate indexes may miss neighbors.
Stores conservative lower-bounding projections in half precision and incorporates rounding certificates into tensor-core dot products.
Computes exact distances only for vectors that pass the exclusion test.
Proves that every returned result is the exact kNN set.
Across 16 datasets with up to 100M vectors, reaches 7.1×–18.0× the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 when exactness is required.

papers.selection_reason: Exact kNN acceleration via certified low-precision exclusion; efficiency technique transferable to retrieval and memory systems.
papers.title: CertEx: Exact Visual Retrieval at Scale by Certified Exclusion
papers.tldr: CertEx achieves exact GPU kNN retrieval at scale by cheaply certifying which vectors can be excluded before computing exact distances.

papers.abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) treat the vision encoder as a static feature extractor: it encodes an image once, independently of the question, and leaves subsequent reasoning to the language model. Yet different questions may require different visual operations and processing depths. We present AdaLoop, a framework for question-conditioned visual recurrence in VLMs. AdaLoop adapts visual computation to the question and reuses the encoder's transformations across multiple iterations, with the pretrained vision weights frozen. We also introduce VisRO, a procedural dataset and generation pipeline for training and evaluating vision-centric reasoning. On six VisRO tasks, AdaLoop outperforms standard fine-tuning and question-conditioned single-pass baselines with matched training data and optimizer updates. These gains hold across three VLM families on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution examples. Our findings suggest that pretrained vision encoders can contribute to reasoning through task-directed, iterative visual computation.
authors: Xinran Nicole Han, Yiyang Lu, Katelyn Gan, Todd Zickler
bullets: Addresses the limitation of one-pass, question-independent visual encoding in VLMs.
Adapts visual processing depth and operations to each question through visual recurrence.
Introduces VisRO, a procedural dataset and pipeline for vision-centric reasoning tasks.
Outperforms matched standard fine-tuning and single-pass baselines across six VisRO tasks, three VLM families, and both in- and out-of-distribution examples.
Shows that frozen pretrained vision encoders can support iterative, task-directed reasoning.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a framework for iterative visual computation in VLMs, reusing the vision encoder conditioned on the question. This architectural innovation allows for deeper visual reasoning and is relevant to advancing multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: AdaLoop: Thinking with the Vision Encoder
papers.tldr: AdaLoop enables VLMs to perform question-conditioned, iterative visual reasoning by reusing a frozen vision encoder across multiple computation steps.

papers.abstract: Although Graph Neural Networks are widely used in various domains, they remained mostly unexplored in computer vision. Convolutional Neural Networks and Vision Transformers were leading the field, until the quite recent introduction of Vision Graphs (ViG) that treat images as a set of nodes and apply graph convolution on their k-NN graphs. ViGs show impressive accuracy on image classification but their computational cost remains relatively high. Inspired by optimization methods for GNNs, we present CoViG, a novel approach combining graph coarsening and ViGs. Our method introduces an additional MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks. By simplifying the intermediate graphs and thus decreasing the number of nodes of specific blocks, our approach considerably reduces the computational cost of ViG during inference. We evaluated our approach on ImageNet with several ViG architectures, and we obtained accuracies equivalent to the original ViG models with only about 51\% of FLOPs.
authors: Martial Guidez, Stefan Duffner, Christophe Garcia
bullets: Vision Graphs model images as nodes connected through k-NN graphs, but their computational cost is relatively high.
CoViG adds a MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks.
Graph coarsening reduces the number of nodes processed in selected blocks.
On ImageNet across several ViG architectures, CoViG achieves comparable accuracy using about 51% of the original FLOPs.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces graph coarsening to reduce the computational cost of Vision Graphs (ViGs). This technique of reducing node count is analogous to token pruning and offers a method for improving inference efficiency in vision models.
papers.title: CoViG: Coarsened Vision GNN for Image Classification
papers.tldr: CoViG reduces Vision Graph Network inference cost by coarsening intermediate graphs while maintaining accuracy comparable to standard ViGs.

papers.abstract: Detailed captions transfer visual information into vision-language model supervision, but quality is easily conflated with length: long single-pass outputs still miss small objects, text, and spatial relations or promote uncertain observations into confident claims. We formulate fine-grained captioning as recoverable visual information transfer, in which a teacher acquires missing evidence under a finite observation budget and converts it into reusable supervision. ZoomCap uses a draft caption to route conditional knowledge retrieval, OCR-sensitive reading, coverage-gap recovery, and adaptive visual zooming, allocating deeper crops only to the most complex eligible region, deriving spatial relations from grounded geometry, and fusing non-duplicate evidence. We also introduce FactCycle, which scores caption-derived atomic claims on two blind anchors--source image (truthfulness) and reconstruction (realizability)--separating fabrication from generator loss claim by claim; human and multi-judge comparisons complement this fact-level view. Against Qwen3.5-397B-A17B captions, ZoomCap achieves an 81.9% human tie-adjusted preference score with a teacher over 10x smaller, and FactCycle counts 52.4 transferred claims per image vs. 31.5 for ScaleCap. The evidence also transfers: in continual pre-training, ZoomCap-450K improves the 11-benchmark average by 1.31-2.38 points over the strongest competing corpus and Ling-Tiny-VL-v3 gains 1.4 points on a production document/OCR monitor suite (1.5 on perception) at 60B tokens; in medical pre-training, 2.64M ZoomCap-captioned images improve five VQA benchmarks by 3.04 points (vs. 1.76 for same-image Gemini-3.1-Pro captions).
authors: Hao Shi, Jiafeng Wang, Yuzhuo Fu, Tao Zhang, Jian Bai, Juelu Zhang, Qing Cui, Chao Huang
bullets: Targets missed small objects, text, spatial relations, and overconfident unsupported claims in long single-pass captions.
Routes a draft caption to conditional retrieval, OCR-sensitive reading, coverage recovery, adaptive region zooming, and grounded spatial reasoning under a fixed observation budget.
Introduces FactCycle, which evaluates atomic claims against both the source image and reconstructed scene to distinguish fabrication from information loss.
Achieves an 81.9% human tie-adjusted preference score and transfers 52.4 claims per image versus 31.5 for ScaleCap.
ZoomCap-based pre-training improves general, document/OCR, and medical VQA performance across the reported benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for transferring visual information to VLMs via evidence-routed zooming. This improves the spatial reasoning capabilities of multimodal models by grounding them in specific visual details.
papers.title: ZoomCap: Evidence-Routed Visual Zooming for Recoverable Visual Information Transfer
papers.tldr: ZoomCap uses evidence-guided visual zooming and claim-level verification to produce more detailed, reliable captions that transfer effectively to vision-language model training.

papers.abstract: Predicting cost in a multi-agent world model moves most constrained policy updates into imagination: the stronger model-free baseline needs $10$ to $20$ times CA-MAMBA's interactions on the median SMAC configuration, and CA-MAMBA earns $2.8$ to $12$ times the baselines' MAMuJoCo reward at equal budget. In controlled tests on one task per benchmark, pricing the model's cost advantages at parity more than halves a cost-blind learner's cost and meets a tight continuous-control limit the learned multiplier misses, suggesting the model's cost estimates are not the bottleneck.
authors: Raz Shmueli, Shahaf S. Shperberg
bullets: Moves most constrained policy updates into imagination using a multi-agent world model.
Requires 10–20× fewer interactions than a stronger model-free baseline on median SMAC configurations.
Achieves 2.8–12× the baselines’ MAMuJoCo reward at equal interaction budgets.
Cost-aware pricing more than halves a cost-blind learner’s cost in controlled benchmark tests.
On one task per benchmark, learned cost estimates meet a tight continuous-control limit, indicating cost prediction is not the main bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Multimodal document retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has focused largely on retrieval, yet its answers depend on how well a vision-language model reads the retrieved pages. We find that evidence in retrieved pages remains underused even when the correct pages are retrieved. On SciEGQA oracle pages, five prior methods give the generator 0.7K to 2.7K visual tokens per query on average under a common image processor, yet raising the page-only budget from 1K to 32K improves accuracy by 15.22 points. At a fixed 16K budget, adding ground-truth crops improves accuracy by 3.75 points over page-only input. We study what the generator needs from retrieved pages through two requirements: Loud, making full use of visual token capacity, and Clear, refining the page so that its evidence becomes prominent. For Loud, increasing either the visual token budget or visual fidelity, the image resolution those tokens preserve, improves accuracy with the other held fixed, and full-page scaling outperforms repetition and tiling at matched budgets. For Clear, suppressing surrounding content improves accuracy without enlarging selected regions, and adding OCR of these regions to page images outperforms either input alone. We implement both as Loud and Clear (LoC), which combines higher-resolution pages with OCR from query-relevant regions without ground-truth annotations or additional training. LoC outperforms eight prior methods on SciEGQA, ViDoRe-v3, and MMLongBench-Doc, improving over the strongest, ColQwen3, by 8.88, 3.09, and 4.22 points with the same retriever and generator. It also outperforms its page-only variant under the same visual token budget. These results locate a bottleneck beyond retrieval: how the retrieved pages are given to the generator.
authors: Eunchan Jo, Seounghyun Jang, Sangwoo Mo
bullets: Retrieval is not the only bottleneck: generators often underuse evidence on correctly retrieved pages.
Accuracy improves with larger visual-token budgets, higher image fidelity, and full-page scaling rather than repetition or tiling.
Highlighting relevant regions and combining their OCR with page images makes evidence clearer than either input alone.
LoC combines higher-resolution pages with OCR from query-relevant regions, requiring no ground-truth crops or additional training.
It outperforms eight prior methods across SciEGQA, ViDoRe-v3, and MMLongBench-Doc, including its page-only variant at the same visual-token budget.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses how vision-language models use visual evidence in multimodal document RAG, directly relevant to multimodal LLM reading and reasoning.
papers.title: Loud and Clear: Making Visual Evidence Count in Multimodal Document RAG

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-$\Delta$, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-$\Delta$ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta
authors: Qi Lu, Jiarun Li, Ce Zhang, Miao Pan, Yi Pan, Xu Wang, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
bullets: Most VLA models learn observation-to-action mappings without direct supervision of intermediate physical changes, risking overfitting.
The framework uses current-to-future physical state changes as explicit targets, including task-relevant semantics and visual motion.
A large-scale pretraining dataset provides annotations for these state transitions.
At inference, actions are generated directly from current observations without extra inference overhead.
It is competitive on LIBERO and RoboTwin and outperforms π₀.₅ in real-robot experiments.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Gaussian representations have made high-quality, real-time volumetric video increasingly practical, yet challenging motion can still break their reconstruction: small fast-moving objects may disappear, and fine textures in highly dynamic regions are often lost. In particular, simply training longer or using more Gaussians may still fail to recover small, fast-moving objects. We argue that the key bottleneck is not representational capacity itself, but where and when Gaussian primitives are allocated. Existing allocation strategies rely on current Gaussian locations and often overlook the spatiotemporal destinations of relocated Gaussians. To address these limitations, we introduce two complementary strategies. First, Seed Injection identifies under-reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal appearance changes and reconstruction errors, and initializes new Gaussians at geometrically plausible 3D locations through multi-view observations, independent of existing Gaussian locations. Second, Temporal Biased Relocation uses time-resolved optimization signals to guide the spatiotemporal placement of relocated Gaussians. Both strategies maintain a fixed Gaussian budget without modifying the underlying representation. Experiments across multiple dynamic-scene datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction quality, particularly in highly dynamic regions, recovering small, rapidly moving objects and fine-grained appearance details.
authors: Minhyeok Roh, Minseo Lee, Jun Young Jeong, Byeonghyeon Lee, Lucas Yunkyu Lee, Jaesik Park, Eunbyung Park
bullets: Small, fast-moving objects and fine textures can remain unreconstructed despite longer training or more Gaussians.
The work identifies Gaussian placement across space and time—not capacity—as the key bottleneck.
Seed Injection adds Gaussians to under-reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal changes, errors, and multi-view geometry.
Temporal Biased Relocation guides moved Gaussians using time-resolved optimization signals and their spatiotemporal destinations.
Experiments on multiple dynamic-scene datasets show better reconstruction, especially for rapidly moving objects and fine details.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Seed Injection. We identify under-reconstructed dynamic regions from synchronized multi-view observations and sample candidate pixels from the resulting seed map. The sampled observations are lifted into 3D using multi-view geometry to initialize new Gaussian primitives independently of the existing Gaussian distribution. After optimization, the injected Gaussians provide additional support for dynamic content that is poorly represented or missing in the original reconstruction.

Figure 1: Reconstruction under highly challenging dynamics. Existing 4DGS methods can (a) completely miss rapidly moving objects and (b) lose fine details under fast motion. Our method addresses both failure cases, recovering missing objects while better preserving fine details.

Figure 6: Effect of increased Gaussian capacity and training iterations. Even with twice the number of Gaussians (3M) and training iterations (0.2M), FreeTimeGS fails to recover the rapidly moving ball, while our method successfully reconstructs it with 1.5M Gaussians and 0.1M iterations.

Figure 7: Construction of the dynamic error-based seed map. The reconstruction error map is computed from the difference between the ground-truth and rendered images, while the dynamic mask is obtained from the intersection of temporal difference masks from adjacent frames. The final seed map is obtained by element-wise multiplication of the reconstruction error map and the dynamic mask, highlighting under-reconstructed dynamic regions.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on the CMU Panoptic Juggle sequence. Our method better reconstructs the rapidly moving juggling balls while preserving fine details of the hands.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the representation of dynamic content in volumetric video using Gaussian primitives. This work on dynamic scene representation and allocation is directly relevant to learning and predicting environment dynamics in video world models.
papers.title: Dusting the Phantom: Gaussian Allocation for Fading Dynamic Content
papers.tldr: A fixed-budget Gaussian allocation strategy improves dynamic volumetric video reconstruction by placing primitives where challenging motion and fine detail require them.

papers.abstract: Panoramic 3D reconstruction enables the holistic recovery of complete 360 $^\circ$ scene geometry, offering significant benefits for robotics and AR/VR applications. However, directly estimating geometry from ERP images is inherently challenged by spherical distortions. To reduce spherical projection distortions, a common strategy is to decompose panoramas into distortion-free perspective views, but independently processing these views often introduces cross-view geometric inconsistencies. To address these challenges, we introduce GeoPano, a feed-forward framework for single-view panoramic 3D reconstruction that recovers a geometrically accurate and consistent point cloud from a single panorama. Our approach is driven by two key innovations: First, we propose a panoramic-aware attention aggregator, featuring a streamlined attention architecture equipped with a novel Pano-Attention mechanism, which explicitly exploits the intrinsic spherical geometry of the panorama to guide cross-view interactions, thereby suppressing geometric inconsistencies. Furthermore, we formulate a hybrid supervision strategy to jointly enforce fine-grained local details in perspective space and global structural coherence in spherical space. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous SOTA approaches in reconstruction accuracy, geometric consistency, and visual fidelity.

Uses a panoramic-aware attention aggregator with a Pano-Attention mechanism for geometry-guided cross-view interaction.
Combines perspective-space supervision for local detail with spherical-space supervision for global structural coherence.

papers.title: GeoPano: Towards Geometrically Accurate 3D Reconstruction from a Single Panorama
papers.tldr: GeoPano reconstructs geometrically consistent 3D point clouds from a single panorama by modeling spherical geometry and combining local and global supervision.

papers.abstract: Maintaining small path-tracking errors under moving reference frames is essential for robotic manipulation tasks with tight execution tolerances, such as machining and surgical automation. Conventional time-indexed controllers, including tracking Model Predictive Control (MPC), rely on a fixed temporal correspondence with the reference trajectory and may therefore accumulate path-relative error under abrupt reference-frame motion or timing mismatch. This paper presents MR-MPCC, a Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) framework for velocity-controlled robotic manipulators with 6-DoF end-effector pose regulation under Moving-Reference disturbances. A hierarchical control architecture is adopted, in which an upper-level MPCC optimizes path progress while penalizing contouring and orientation errors, and a constrained resolved motion rate control (RMRC) layer maps the commanded Cartesian twist to feasible joint velocities under joint-level and safety constraints. MR-MPCC is implemented in a ROS2--MuJoCo pipeline and validated on a UR5e platform under moving-reference disturbances, where the path frame is perturbed and tracked by electromagnetic sensors. Compared with PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC under matched disturbance, MR-MPCC achieves lower geometric path-following error and smaller deviations in the moving path frame, demonstrating improved path-following performance under reference-frame motion.
authors: Chonghao Cheng, Tiancheng Li, Jonathan Woolfrey, Liang Zhao, Shoudong Huang
bullets: Targets path-tracking errors caused by abrupt reference-frame motion and timing mismatch.
Uses an upper-level MPCC to optimize path progress while penalizing contouring and orientation errors.
Employs constrained resolved motion rate control to convert Cartesian twists into feasible joint velocities under safety constraints.
Validated on a UR5e in a ROS2–MuJoCo setup with electromagnetic sensing of moving path frames.
Achieves lower geometric path-following error and smaller moving-frame deviations than PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC under matched disturbances.

papers.abstract: Training-free object removal commonly redirects self-attention away from the target region, but on few-step distilled diffusion models this often leaves object-shaped residuals. We identify a temporal mismatch: a structured prediction forms inside the mask at the first forward, and the short trajectory offers few later chances to revise it, while attention rerouting acts mainly in later steps. Across four distilled backbones, magnitude-matched single-forward interventions show that background-directed state correction affects the final result more than attention rerouting. We therefore propose ReState, which corrects the masked clean prediction toward background evidence retrieved from the input using a noise-level-aware weight that vanishes at the final forward. ReState retains object-excluding attention as a complementary constraint and adds no denoiser evaluations. Across two paired benchmarks and two few-step backbones, ReState achieves the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training-free methods, improving PSNR by 3.17 dB on average over the strongest baseline. On OBER-Test, it also outperforms the 50-step attention-forcing reference on all three metrics at 6.7x lower latency. The same configuration transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning. Project page: https://tdrlee.github.io/ReState
authors: Donghwan Lee, Sanghyun Jo, Sihyun Kim, Ziseok Lee, Kyungsu Kim
bullets: Few-step diffusion models can preserve object-shaped artifacts because structured errors arise early, while attention rerouting acts mostly later.
ReState applies noise-level-aware state correction using background evidence from the input, with the correction fading at the final forward.
It retains object-excluding attention as a complementary constraint and requires no additional denoiser evaluations.
Across two paired benchmarks and two few-step backbones, it reports the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training-free methods, with a 3.17 dB average PSNR gain over the strongest baseline.
On OBER-Test, it surpasses a 50-step attention-forcing reference at 6.7× lower latency and transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning.

This committed structure is what attention forcing then fails to remove, leaving a residual (bottom); ReState instead corrects the prediction directly and removes it.

papers.title: ReState: Noise-Level-Aware State Correction for Training-Free Object Removal in Few-Step Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: ReState improves training-free object removal in few-step diffusion models by correcting early masked predictions toward background evidence before later denoising steps.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. We prompt frozen pretrained models to solve problems via CoT and measure the density of each reasoning step with two independent metrics: LP variance (how unevenly information is distributed across steps, computed as the variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood) and the Caveman compression ratio. We then test whether density correlates with, and can be steered to improve, answer correctness. Experiments across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems yield four main findings. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Training paradigm therefore appears more influential than model size in determining density behaviour. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. Finally, we introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), a self-supervised method using token-level Shannon entropy to gate proportional KVcache adjustments during generation, improving accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without any external guidance.
authors: Tanush Kalhan, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Sriram Ranga, Amritendu Mukherjee
bullets: Lower LP variance predicts correctness in SFT models, but the relationship weakens with scale and reverses in RL-distilled models.
Training paradigm influences density behavior more strongly than model size, while models show an intrinsic preference for complexity-favoring distributions.
Directly forcing density patterns during inference sharply reduces accuracy, suggesting natural density structure is important for reasoning.
Pre-generation hint injection plus contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points across both density metrics.
Entropy-Gated Density Routing improves accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without external guidance.

papers.abstract: Code world models represent world dynamics through explicit state and executable rules. We investigate how to coordinate object representations, behavioral revisions, and visual memory within this formulation. We present Mallea, a system for building, steering, and memorizing worlds from text. A coding agent infers object interaction requirements from the prompt and jointly plans object structure, properties, and rules, favoring compact representations that support those requirements. The world evolves under the planned rules; optional user actions steer it, while text requests can edit properties or extend capabilities with unaffected state preserved. Object texture memory retains reusable appearance only for whitebox-defined objects and adapts it as those objects change. The program advances world state, while a generative renderer combines current structure with remembered appearance. By organizing construction, intervention, and memory around the same objects, Mallea conditions subsequent observations on the latest state and compatible appearance. Project page: https://lxycopper.github.io/Mallea.
authors: Xuanyi Liu, Ruiqi Li, Siwei Ma
bullets: Represents world dynamics with explicit object states and executable interaction rules.
Infers object requirements from prompts and jointly plans compact structures, properties, and behaviors.
Supports user interventions and text-based edits while preserving unaffected world state.
Maintains reusable texture memory for whitebox-defined objects and updates it as they change.
Renders each evolving world by combining its current structure with remembered appearance.

Figure 6. Qualitative results. Generated video frames (top) and corresponding display whitebox frames (bottom) for 12 scenes. papers.abstract: Spatial augmented reality (SAR) augments physical environments with projected content, but most systems assume that the projector pose, target region, or motion path has been fixed or specified. We instead make projected light an embodied action: given a language instruction and current visual observations, a system must decide how to move and where and at what scale to place the projection. We introduce LICOA to realize this capability. Its differential-drive chassis provides room-scale approach and repositioning, while a steerable mirror with two degrees of freedom (2DoF) and projection scale provide rapid local control of the beam. A shared interface maps synchronized external and onboard RGB cameras with robot control state to physical optical actions across pretrained action models. Because instruction-conditioned optical action lacks dedicated training data and a common evaluation protocol, we construct a matched simulation embodiment and a corpus with 150 tasks and 7,500 rendered episodes, then evaluate models trained only on this corpus in previously unseen real-world environments. Across 480 complete closed-loop real-world execution trials (rollouts) on 12 tasks, the best adapted action model achieves a 57.50% success rate and 40.64% success weighted by path length, compared with 8.33% and 5.15% for the same architecture trained from scratch. A further 150 real-world ablation rollouts support the need for both camera views and coordinated control of the chassis and mirror. These results establish a physical platform, shared perception and optical action interface, corpus, and real-world evaluation protocol for treating projected light as an embodied action.
authors: Yuchen Deng, Shunkai Zhou, Ruixuan Zhu, Haibin Ling, Bingyao Huang
bullets: Addresses SAR settings where projector pose, target region, and motion path are not fixed in advance.
Combines differential-drive chassis movement with 2DoF steerable-mirror and projection-scale control.
Introduces a shared interface linking synchronized external/onboard RGB observations and robot state to optical actions.
Provides a simulation embodiment, 150-task/7,500-episode corpus, and real-world evaluation protocol.
In 480 real-world trials, the best adapted model achieved 57.50% success and 40.64% success weighted by path length; ablations support using both camera views and coordinated chassis–mirror control.

figures.caption: Figure 3: LICOA makes projected light executable through a shared perception and optical action interface. papers.abstract: Modern agents select tools from registries, but exposing entire registries incurs high token costs and can impair selection as they grow. We present TRACER, a retrieval front-end that indexes observed tool-call sequences in a trie and ranks continuations using a learned blend of empirical and contextual priors. On a mixed retail-and-telecom $\tau^2$ environment, TRACER improves GPT-5.4's tool-selection accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing input tokens per step by 80%, exposing just 5 of 128 tools. In autonomous full-turn execution, it matches GPT-5.4's full-registry task success with 61% fewer input tokens per step. Across six environments and four models, TRACER improves tool-selection accuracy over full-registry selection in 21 of 24 model-environment pairs, with average gains of 6 to 10 points; the three exceptions trail by at most 2.2. We analyze failures in both regimes to identify directions for future work.

papers.abstract: Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that constructs minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one-minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician-informed multiple-choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera-hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.
authors: Zane Durante, Paul Tang, Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Amit Kaushal, Shrinidhi Kowshika Lakshmikanth, Feolu Kolawole, Yu Jun Zheng, Yifan Geng, Shobhit Agarwal, Kevin Schulman, Juan Carlos Niebles, Ehsan Adeli, Arnold Milstein, Li Fei-Fei
bullets: Builds minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical data into hourly reports.
Lets an LLM agent query the hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records.
Evaluated on action detection and clinician-informed QA benchmarks spanning ICU video and records.
Achieves up to 84.8% action-detection accuracy and 61.0% QA accuracy, compared with 49.3% for the strongest same-backbone baseline.
Across 280 patients, detects less purposeful activity among those with positive delirium assessments.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of TRACER. TRACER equips an agent model with hierarchical behavioral representations and tools for understanding multi-day ICU patient trajectories. Vision–language models analyze one-minute bedside video segments to detect atomic actions defined by a clinically informed taxonomy and generate descriptive captions. These outputs are combined with concurrent medication records to generate structured hourly behavioral reports. Through report, timeline, video, and EHR tools, the agent iteratively retrieves evidence and examines relevant video segments to answer retrospective clinical questions. Our evaluation suite assesses atomic action detection on 397 annotated one-minute clips and longitudinal clinical reasoning on 144 multiple-choice questions spanning 264 hours of continuous video.

Figure 2: Per-Category Breakdown of Atomic Action Performance. (a) We plot the per-category F1 scores of the atomic actions used by TRACER. (b) We show the relative frequency of predicted atomic actions with respect to delirium status across a cohort of 280 patients spanning ∼ 60, 000 hours of video data. papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.
authors: Sunghyun Wee, Geunjae Choi, Hyeonjin Kim, Suyoung Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses the coarse base-2 grid of Power-of-Two quantization, which causes severe low-bit accuracy degradation.
Uses a base-√2 weight grid, uniform integer activations, calibration-based grid alignment, and approximate-grid quantization.
Implements √2 with a lightweight one-adder approximation, producing a processing element with fewer gates than a 4-bit multiplier.
On Llama-3-8B, improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning by 8.72% relative to PoT and remains within 0.4 percentage points of the uniform integer baseline.
Generalizes across seven models, three bit-widths, and existing LLM post-training quantization frameworks.

papers.title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.
authors: Sangwu Park, Wonjoong Kim, Yeonjun In, Chanyoung Park
bullets: Prior VLA research mainly evaluates What-level instructions that specify the task, overlooking How-level instructions that specify execution.
The authors find that How-level instructions can reduce task success in current VLAs.
Training with segment-level enriched instructions improves action responsiveness to How-level guidance, but not consistently overall task success.
SIMPLER-IN evaluates instruction-specific success beyond standard benchmarks and reveals poor generalization to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions.
How-level instruction following remains an open challenge.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation enables rectified-flow models with diffusion-transformer architectures to combine task-specific capabilities within a single student. However, matching model outputs does not guarantee that their internal representations are aligned, and it remains unclear where and when additional feature supervision is most useful. We analyze the teacher-student feature mismatch across Transformer blocks and denoising timesteps, and find that the mismatch is concentrated in deeper Transformer blocks during early denoising and persists after OPD distillation, indicating ineffective distillation. Motivated by this observation, we introduce FocusOPD, which augments the base OPD objective with token-wise directional feature alignment restricted to deep layers and early denoising steps. Across two rectified-flow backbones and multiple OPD objectives, FocusOPD improves capability transfer in compositional generation, text rendering, and preference-based evaluation. On the primary benchmark, it improves over DiffusionOPD from 0.953 to 0.967 on GenEval, from 23.797 to 23.944 on PickScore, and from 6.052 to 6.199 on LAION-Aesthetic. Ablations show that selective deep and early supervision is more effective and efficient than alignment over the full network and trajectory.
authors: Xinrui Lin, Shumin Wang, Suqi Song, Fan Li, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Feature mismatches concentrate in deep Transformer blocks during early denoising and remain after conventional OPD.
The method adds token-wise directional feature alignment only in these deep layers and early timesteps.
Evaluated across two rectified-flow backbones and multiple OPD objectives for compositional generation, text rendering, and preference evaluation.
On the primary benchmark, GenEval rises from 0.953 to 0.967, PickScore from 23.797 to 23.944, and LAION-Aesthetic from 6.052 to 6.199.
Ablations indicate selective supervision is more effective and efficient than aligning the full network and denoising trajectory.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based motion planning such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control has become attractive for robotics due to its ability to handle nonlinear dynamics and non-smooth objectives without gradient information, while leveraging parallel rollout computation for real-time performance. However, in real-world robotic systems, the optimized control input is often applied after a non-negligible planning delay, causing a mismatch between the state used in forward simulation and the actual state at control execution, which can significantly degrade planning accuracy and may even lead to unsafe behavior such as collisions. This paper proposes Closed-Loop MPPI with Initial-State Sampling (CLIS-MPPI), which explicitly addresses execution-time state mismatch by modeling planning delay as a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, performing rollout optimization from sampled initial states, and applying a rollout-based local feedback correction during control execution. The proposed method is validated through real-world experiments on a 6-DoF UR5e manipulator in a narrow-passage task involving obstacle avoidance and end-effector target reaching. Across 5 real-world runs of the same task, standard MPPI collided in 2 runs, whereas CLIS-MPPI remained collision-free in all 5 runs. Averaged over all collision-free runs for each method (3 for MPPI and 5 for CLIS-MPPI), CLIS-MPPI reduced the average task completion time from 25.4s to 24.4s and the average end-effector path length from 0.456 m to 0.425 m. It also reduced the overall joint-position and joint-velocity root mean square errors (RMSEs) from 0.100 rad and 0.108 rad/s to 0.017 rad and 0.011 rad/s, respectively. These results demonstrate improved safety, planning-execution consistency, and motion smoothness.
authors: Zidong Liu, Xu Chen
bullets: Execution delays create a mismatch between the planned and actual robot states, potentially causing collisions.
CLIS-MPPI models delay-induced uncertainty as a distribution over execution-time initial states.
It optimizes rollouts from sampled initial states and adds rollout-based local feedback during execution.
On a UR5e narrow-passage task, CLIS-MPPI had 0 collisions in 5 runs, while standard MPPI collided in 2 of 5.
Collision-free CLIS-MPPI runs also showed shorter completion time and path length, with lower joint-position and velocity RMSEs.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed CLIS-MPPI. CLIS-MPPI converts execution delay into an initial-state uncertainty distribution, samples both perturbed initial states and control sequences, and performs parallel forward simulation to obtain rollout trajectories and costs. The weighted rollout distribution is then used to construct a nominal trajectory and extract local feedback gains. Finally, the applied control is computed as a closed-loop combination of the MPPI feedforward term and a state-feedback correction.

During the delay window, the robot continues executing the previous control ui−1. Consequently, when the newly planned control ui actually becomes effective at tsend i , the system state has already evolved to xapply

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has recently been introduced as a promising paradigm for continual learning, where a student policy can be supervised at the token-level. Typically, OPD is performed using a single teacher per prompt rollout (or even per training run). However, this ignores a whole other axis of flexibility that is available due to the on-policy nature - token-level teacher selection during rollouts. Building on this insight, we theoretically explore what makes a teacher and a student compatible for OPD, and leverage our findings to derive several empirical heuristics for teacher selection. In particular, our framework captures several desiderata for OPD: compatible teacher-student reasoning patterns, teacher competence, and induced student diversity. Theoretically, we categorize several types of teacher routing schemes, and we prove that under different scenarios, different routing schemes are likely to be beneficial for optimization and student diversity. We back up our findings with extensive experimental results in domains such as math, coding, kernel generation, and visual reasoning, where we find upwards of 10 percentage points of improvement on pass@$k$ when compared to vanilla OPD and the teacher experts on certain tasks, indicating both capability improvement and diversity over high-quality responses.
authors: Stanley Wei, Jiin Woo, Kaan Ozkara, Youngsuk Park
bullets: Identifies teacher–student compatibility, teacher competence, and induced student diversity as key factors in OPD teacher selection.
Theoretically categorizes teacher-routing schemes and analyzes when different schemes benefit optimization and student diversity.
Derives empirical heuristics for selecting teachers during token-level rollouts.
Experiments across math, coding, kernel generation, and visual reasoning report up to 10 percentage points of pass@$k$ improvement over vanilla OPD and teacher experts on certain tasks.
Results suggest token-level routing can improve both capability and diversity, though benefits vary by scenario and task.

papers.abstract: Unlearning aims to remove selected knowledge from large language models to mitigate privacy and safety risks while preserving useful capabilities. For models that continue to be fine-tuned after release, this goal is insufficient: they must also resist relearning the deleted knowledge while preserving plasticity, the ability to learn new tasks. Existing defenses train against simulated relearning while trying to preserve useful capabilities, but low relearning alone cannot distinguish selective resistance from a general loss of plasticity. Evaluating preservation after an update requires deciding what the updated model should remain close to. A pre-update reference penalizes useful changes induced by the update simply because they depart from earlier outputs. We therefore formulate the reference-timing hypothesis that, at comparable target suppression, an update-matched reference better preserves plasticity than a pre-update one. To test and address this hypothesis, we propose Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU), which applies the same simulated relearning update to the defended model and to an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model, and uses new-task learning to guide model selection. Extensive experiments on TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models show that UMU improves both relearning resistance and plasticity across all three base unlearning methods, lowering harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points. When the reference does not receive the update, relearning remains similarly low but new-task accuracy falls below the base method, supporting the reference-timing hypothesis and showing that robust unlearning should prevent recovery selectively without suppressing learning itself.
authors: Jie Li, Youming Tao, Bowei He, Meng Ding
bullets: Problem: Post-release fine-tuning can recover unlearned knowledge, but defenses must avoid broadly reducing model plasticity.
Method: Apply the same simulated relearning update to both the defended model and an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model.
Model selection uses new-task learning to distinguish selective resistance from general loss of plasticity.
Across TOFU and FaithUn experiments with Llama and Qwen models, UMU reduced harmful and benign relearning and improved new-task accuracy.
A pre-update reference kept relearning low but reduced new-task performance, supporting update-matched evaluation.

papers.abstract: Artificial microbots capable of precise and autonomous navigation could provide versatile platforms for microscale transport, manipulation, and task execution in complex environments. However, reliable navigation becomes increasingly challenging at the micrometre scale, particularly when the surrounding environment changes dynamically. Here, we develop a vision-guided closed-loop navigation framework for light-driven cube-shaped hematite/TiO2 Janus microbots with a characteristic size of approximately 3 {\mu}m. Real-time visual localization using a custom-trained YOLOv11 object-detection model is integrated with discretized waypoint-based magnetic steering to enable precise navigation along complex prescribed trajectories, with more than 90% of the measured trajectory deviations remaining below 6 {\mu}m across the tested path geometries. The framework further enables arbitrary user-defined free-hand trajectories and autonomous navigation through a physically confined maze. In dynamically changing environments, A* path planning enables real-time path replanning while avoiding multiple independently swimming 5 {\mu}m spherical Janus micromotors. Finally, the microbot selectively captures multiple cargo particles and autonomously transports and delivers them to a predefined location while simultaneously avoiding dynamic obstacles. These results establish an integrated platform combining programmable trajectory control, autonomous path planning, real-time environmental adaptation, and task execution within a single light-driven Janus microbot system.
authors: Kanhu Charan Andia, Harsh Prashant Katole, Parth Nitinkumar Bhosale, Hemant Kumar, Dhruv Pratap Singh
bullets: Real-time YOLOv11-based visual localization is combined with waypoint-based magnetic steering.
Over 90% of measured trajectory deviations were below 6 μm across tested path geometries.
The microbots followed user-defined free-hand paths and navigated a physically confined maze.
A* planning enabled real-time replanning around multiple swimming micromotor obstacles.
The system supported selective cargo capture, transport, and delivery while avoiding dynamic obstacles.

papers.abstract: Agentic large language models have been documented to lose reasoning capability when placed inside a harness, the software that mediates their observations and actions. To reconcile these losses, we introduce AutoOnboarder, an autonomous system that adapts an agent to a task the way a trainer onboards a new employee. It places the agent under the supervision of an intelligent ``Onboarder'' coding agent, which iteratively tailors its foundation model, prompt, and harness source code to simultaneously improve performance and decrease cost. Like a real onboarding process, the Onboarder is only given tens of examples, and all evaluation data is isolated on a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage. We report the lessons learned from building and testing AutoOnboarder on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission. Autonomously onboarded agents are able to match or exceed the performance of a Gemini 3.5 Flash baseline at up to 29$\times$ lower costs. However, these agents remain imperfect, and the Onboarding process varies greatly in terms of final performance. We conclude that future Onboarding systems require a robust environment for the Onboarder, including a structured thought interface, (controlled) internet access, and a wide model search space.
authors: Tanay Arora, Cong Liu
bullets: Addresses reasoning losses caused by placing LLMs inside software harnesses.
Uses an intelligent coding agent, the “Onboarder,” to iteratively modify the agent’s foundation model, prompt, and harness code.
Operates with only tens of examples and isolates evaluation data in a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage.
Evaluated on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission; results vary substantially across onboarding runs.
Finds that future systems need stronger Onboarder environments, including structured thought interfaces, controlled internet access, and broader model search.
