papers.abstract: Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance. We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task. PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Our approach also adapts to changes in the user's routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory--routine misalignment after a single memory update. The project page is available at https://davian-robotics.github.io/PAM/
authors: Dohyun Lee, Minho Park, Jeonghoon Park, Dongyoon Hwang, Junha Hyung, Sungwon Hwang, Byungkun Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in proactive assistance, where identical behaviors may indicate different user needs.
Uses a VLM task predictor with Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) to select when and how to assist, and a VLA executor to perform tasks.
Represents routines as a finite-state machine with activity phases, assistance rules, and event-driven transitions.

In a 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, the system improved with experience, achieved the best reported precision, recall, and F1, and reduced first-fire delay from about 5 seconds to 1 second.

papers.abstract: Point-cloud streams are central to autonomous driving and robotics, yet existing segmentation networks process every frame from scratch, although consecutive frames largely overlap. We observe that the intermediate features of point-cloud transformers remain semantically consistent across frames for the same spatial region, especially in deep stages. Building on this, we present SpaceCache, a training-free feature cache that reuses these features across frames. Tokens of previously observed regions skip a sequence of transformer blocks and take their cached features, only the remaining tokens are computed, and the full token layout is restored for dense prediction. Lightweight cache management keeps reused features reliable by limiting each entry's age and evicting low-confidence entries. Unlike token merging, SpaceCache selects tokens at negligible cost and runs its cache operations once per encoder stage. On both outdoor and indoor benchmarks, such as nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet, with two transformer backbones of Utonia and LitePT-B, SpaceCache achieves up to 1.65x speedup with less than 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.
authors: Dongheon Yang, Beomseok Kang, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Addresses redundant frame-by-frame processing caused by substantial overlap in consecutive point-cloud streams.
Uses a training-free cache to let previously observed tokens skip transformer blocks while computing only new or changed tokens.
Maintains reliability by limiting cache-entry age and evicting low-confidence features; cache operations run once per encoder stage.
Evaluated on nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet with Utonia and LitePT-B backbones.
Achieves up to 1.65× speedup with less than a 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.

Cache-hit tokens bypass the selected transformer blocks, while cache-miss tokens are computed through the blocks. papers.abstract: Geometric light detection and ranging (LiDAR)--inertial simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) provides efficient state estimation but lacks the continuous map representation and global refinement capabilities of neural implicit SLAM, while neural implicit methods remain computationally expensive. We propose Lightweight LiDAR--Inertial Neural SLAM (LIN-SLAM), a hybrid method that couples high-rate geometric LiDAR--inertial estimation with neural implicit tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement for accurate real-time onboard SLAM. Experiments on twelve representative sequences from three datasets spanning 32-, 64-, and 128-channel LiDAR configurations show that LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest overall mean absolute trajectory error (ATE) among the evaluated state-of-the-art geometric and neural implicit methods, while substantially reducing runtime compared with existing neural implicit SLAM methods. On a Unitree Go2 equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and a 16-channel LiDAR, LIN-SLAM sustains real-time localization and neural mapping over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory through challenging repetitive corridor environments, with an endpoint closure error of only 0.141~m. To the best of our knowledge, LIN-SLAM is the first LiDAR--inertial SLAM system with a neural implicit backend to achieve real-time online operation on a mobile robotic platform while maintaining state-of-the-art localization accuracy. The code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Shiqi Che, Yijie Liu, Shuo Wang, Wenxin Liu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between efficient geometric SLAM and computationally costly neural implicit SLAM.
Uses high-rate geometric estimation alongside neural implicit tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement.
Evaluated across twelve sequences from three datasets and multiple LiDAR configurations.
Reports the lowest overall mean ATE among evaluated geometric and neural implicit methods, with reduced runtime versus neural implicit baselines.
Runs online on a Unitree Go2 with a Jetson Orin NX over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory, achieving 0.141 m endpoint closure error.

The neural implicit backend uses optimized C++/CUDA computation to reduce processing overhead, fixed-capacity replay storage and local neural windows to control stored data, and preallocated workspaces to reduce repeated allocation. Frontend relative motion initializes neural tracking; continual mapping and loop-based global optimization update the neural map. Backend corrections provide globally corrected poses at the frontend rate.

papers.abstract: Point cloud upsampling is essential for 3D applications but remains challenging due to sparse, under-constrained observations. Multi-view images can resolve geometric ambiguity, but existing multi-modal methods do not fully exploit visual cues. We propose ControlFlow3D, a framework that distills knowledge from pretrained foundation models into a lightweight generation network during training, enabling strong performance without multi-view images available at test time. Specifically, our method performs conditional flow matching in a structured latent space defined by a frozen 3D encoder. Multi-view image tokens and 3D latent tokens are jointly clustered into shared prototypes via unsupervised soft KMeans; the resulting prototypes guide the flow trajectory through velocity control and are aligned by a consistency loss that progressively transfers image knowledge into the base network. A Mamba-based geometry decoder then maps latent features to dense coordinates with linear complexity. We also construct ShapeNetPU, a 35K-object multi-modal benchmark that is 31 times larger than prior datasets. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its strong generalization capability.
authors: Yuang Liu, Zhi Zuo, Zhengkai Zhao, Lirui Zhang, Pan Gao, Hao Feng, Zhengzhe Liu
bullets: Addresses geometric ambiguity from sparse point clouds by leveraging multi-view information during training.

Introduces ShapeNetPU, a 35K-object multi-modal benchmark, and reports strong cross-benchmark generalization.

To distill multi-view knowledge into this network, we introduce an unsupervised prototype-guided velocity controller that jointly clusters image Fimg and 3D tokens F3D into shared prototypes. During inference, the model takes only the sparse point cloud as input and produces the final dense point cloud.

papers.abstract: General-purpose dexterous manipulation requires policies to transfer knowledge from related tasks to new tasks with only a few target demonstrations. Existing benchmarks often provide too many target demonstrations. They also leave the differences between source and target tasks uncontrolled. As a result, they cannot clearly distinguish knowledge transfer from task memorization. Our key insight is the Core-Gen principle. Core tasks are related tasks that share a functional interaction and provide source knowledge, while a Gen task is a novel target within the same functional family that has only a few demonstrations. This setup tests whether a policy can reuse functional interaction knowledge. Based on this principle, we propose Evo-DexBench, which controls both source-task relatedness and target-task exposure. It comprises 30 tasks in six functional families and a VR teleoperation pipeline. The resulting dataset covers three everyday scenes per task. It contains 1,248 multimodal demonstrations collected with simulated Shadow Hands equipped with 123 taxels. Experiments show that even the best-performing method achieves an average success rate of only 38.5%, highlighting the challenges existing methods face in transferring functional interaction knowledge. Further analysis shows that, across the two tasks, joint Core+Gen training improves performance by 12% and 38%, respectively, over training on Core followed by fine-tuning on Gen. This indicates that joint training makes better use of Core knowledge and that functionally matched Core data yields greater gains in success rate than mismatched data. We release the Evo-DexBench dataset and benchmark to support the evaluation of dexterous manipulation policies' generalization across related tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.
authors: Dongyu Gong
bullets: LLMs show human-like N-back behavior: performance worsens with load, especially lure false alarms.
Task-relevant attention heads usually attend to the correct target, including on missed matches.
Linear probes recover target and lure information even when the model’s decision confuses them.
Sharpening attention provides little benefit, while suppressing non-target letter identity generally improves sensitivity.
The finding holds across pretrained models and minimal transformers, with deeper layers alleviating single-layer precision limits.

papers.abstract: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with DeepSeek V3.2 and from 50 to 53 with Kimi K2.7 Code. On disjoint ALFWorld unseen tasks, success rises from 50.75% to 71.64%. Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions, the median code-change ratio is 4.4%. These results support fine-grained execution evidence as a basis for localized, in-place memory-architecture evolution.
authors: Miao Su, Yucan Guo, Zixuan Li, Long Bai, Zhongni Hou, Xiaolong Jin, Jiafeng Guo
bullets: Targets the difficulty of locating failures in long-horizon agent executions using only coarse scores or summaries.
A Patch Agent jointly analyzes raw traces, runtime memory state, and architecture code to identify repair targets.
Applies bounded in-place edits while preserving provider identity and memory compatibility.
Improves performance on GAIA, xBench, and unseen ALFWorld tasks, with a median code-change ratio of 4.4%.

papers.abstract: Synchronous data-parallel training usually assigns every rank the same number of records, even when record costs vary by orders of magnitude. For variable-length models, this converts input variation into idle time because each step waits for its most expensive rank-local batch. We present Batch Cost Lookahead (BCL), a coordination-free data-loading policy that buffers a bounded rank-local window and repartitions it into fixed-cardinality packs with balanced estimated cost. BCL preserves the trainer's record-count contract and requires neither cross-rank metadata exchange nor runtime modification. In simulation over public workload distributions, enabling BCL reduces per-rank estimated batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%. Across 13 NeMo-RL SFT corpora on eight H200 GPUs, rank-local BCL runs 1.050 to 1.167 times faster than pooled MFFD. Compiled H200 measurements on an internal sequence workload show speedups of 1.197 to 1.343 times over packed execution from one to four nodes. We also identify a memory-feasibility boundary: a p99 cap for high-variance or OOM-prone data bounds outliers before BCL balances the rest. These results show that substantial variable-cost imbalance can be removed at the data-loader boundary, while clarifying when data preparation or broader coordination is still necessary.
authors: Tao Huang, Chen Zhu, Antonio Alonso, Daming Li, Adarsh Goura, Jaideep Ray, Yitong Zhou
bullets: Variable-length records can leave ranks idle because each step waits for the most expensive local batch.
BCL buffers a bounded local window and repartitions it into fixed-size packs with balanced estimated cost.
It preserves record-count requirements and operates entirely at the data-loader boundary.
Simulations reduce estimated per-rank batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%; experiments report faster execution across public and internal workloads.
A p99 memory cap is needed for extreme or OOM-prone outliers, and some cases still require data preparation or broader coordination.

papers.abstract: Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, expensive module, and published trigger mechanisms for invoking it lack a shared objective, measured costs, and any standard separating schedule quality from module quality. We provide the missing account: invocation is formalized as a calibrated decision problem whose fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); a renewal baseline proves the optimal schedule periodic under state-independent collapse, with adaptive gains governed by the cost ratio $\rho$ and the dispersion of collapse. Measured systems span three orders of magnitude in $\rho$ (FiS-VLA $0.95$; RoboICL about $10^3$), and a direct test confirms the low-$\rho$ prediction: calibrated gains vanish under homogeneous collapse and grow with heterogeneity. Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($\rho=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points. A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.
authors: Shilin Zhang (North China University of Technology)
bullets: Unifies fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated triggers as special cases of Value of Intervention; periodic scheduling is optimal when collapse is state-independent.
Adaptive scheduling benefits depend on intervention cost relative to fast-policy operation and on heterogeneity in policy collapse.
At intermediate cost (ρ=1.53), the adaptive trigger follows its predicted threshold, but language rewrites fail to improve either LIBERO suite; only reverting failed rewrites avoids net downside.
A leak-free evaluation protocol reduces apparent early-warning AUC from 0.93 to 0.62 across 929 deployment traces.
A detection-limited theorem and compilation loop connect measured intervention value to schedulability and produce refresh periods within 2.4% of a closed-loop oracle.

papers.title: When to Ask for Help: A Decision-Theoretic Account and Measurement Standard for Slow-Module Scheduling in Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Models

papers.abstract: On-screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models' tendency to let an on-screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim-fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open-weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no-claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training-free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2--64.0% to 81.8--85.2% and reduces trap-answer selection from 34.4--50.8% to 11.6--15.0%, while preserving no-claim accuracy.
authors: Huachao Zhu, Junjielong Xu, Sicheng Li, Liang Yang, Mingtao Chen, Zhichao Hu, Li Jiang, Pinjia He
bullets: Introduces a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases spanning 14 claim–fact classes and three versions of each video.
Misleading claims reduce mean accuracy from 90.1% to 51.9%; 42.8% of initially correct answers flip to the trap answer.
Evaluates seven open-weight and four proprietary models, finding that strong performance without claims does not imply claim resistance.
Proposes DEAR, a training-free agent that separates evidence arbitration from reading and answers from a fresh context.
Across 500 videos and three proprietary models, DEAR raises misleading-claim accuracy to 81.8–85.2% and reduces trap answers to 11.6–15.0%.

papers.abstract: Training humanoid whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies requires costly robot demonstrations with aligned robot-view observations and controller-compatible whole-body state-action labels. Egocentric human demonstrations offer scalable supervision but have misaligned views and sparse motion cues. Existing approaches either pretrain policies that still require robot data for adaptation or generate controller-specific commands that limit reuse. Conversion also requires robot-view observations aligned with the generated whole-body motion. We present KODA (Kinematics-Observation Data Alignment), which converts egocentric RGB demonstrations into whole-body VLA training data using a reusable canonical trajectory to guide robot-view synthesis and generate controller-specific whole-body state-action supervision. KODA first generates a simulator-checked whole-body trajectory using a sparse tracker with sampling-based command optimization. This generated trajectory directly determines the onboard camera poses used to synthesize corresponding robot-view observations. The motion, observations, and task instruction form a canonical record. For each deployment controller, KODA optimizes commands to track the stored motion and records the corresponding action labels and proprioceptive states. When switching controllers, KODA retains this canonical record and regenerates whole-body state-action supervision for co-training with matching robot demonstrations. We evaluate KODA on four Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks using two whole-body controllers, SONIC and HEFT. With robot data held fixed, macro-average success on conditions covered by human demonstrations but absent from robot data improves by 45.0 and 46.25 percentage points, respectively. Under both controllers, this metric shows an upward trend across the evaluated human-data budgets, suggesting potential for further scaling.
authors: Zibo Zhou, Yueru Chen, Junsong Wu, Weiji Xie, Qingyao Xu, Sheng Yin, Shiqing Wang, Jiyuan Shi, Siheng Chen, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the costly need for robot demonstrations with aligned observations and whole-body state-action labels.
Generates a simulator-checked canonical whole-body trajectory from sparse human motion using sampling-based command optimization.
Uses the trajectory to synthesize aligned robot-camera observations, then regenerates controller-specific actions and proprioceptive states.
Evaluated on four Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks with SONIC and HEFT controllers.
With fixed robot data, success on human-covered but robot-unseen conditions improves by 45.0 and 46.25 percentage points; performance trends upward with more human data.

The resulting data are combined with matching real-robot demonstrations to co-train a controller-specific vision–language–action (VLA) policy for language-guided humanoid loco-manipulation.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long-horizon histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents. However, existing memory methods often optimize retrieval and memory construction separately, without a shared reward space for evaluating search, writing, and stopping decisions. To address this, we propose All-in-One Memory (AiO-Mem), which organizes these operations as transitions over a shared evidence state and directly evaluates the semantic quality of each action in a unified reward space. AiO-Mem compiles heterogeneous histories into source-traceable multi-view events, providing a shared substrate for retrieval and memory writing. A unified memory policy actor then rolls out complete interaction trajectories over this shared evidence state. A separate trajectory-conditioned process reward model is trained through evidence-grounded supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level DPO to assign process scores to the collected trajectories. These scores are aggregated into an action-balanced trajectory reward and used by Process-Aligned DAPO (PA-DAPO) to optimize the memory policy. Across long-context memory benchmarks, AiO-Mem consistently improves answer accuracy over both static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents.
authors: Bingbing Wang, Jingjie Lin, Weiming Qiao, Jing Li, Ruifeng Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of a unified reward space for memory search, construction, and stopping decisions.

Consistently improves answer accuracy over static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents on long-context benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression-quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately $1.7\times$ expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.
authors: Yingzhuo Deng, Chong Li, Bingxin Liu, Yi Shu, Tianyu Peng, Can Xie, Siyao Song, Shuo Ren, Jiajun Zhang
bullets: Addresses long autoregressive sequences and costly inference caused by tightly coupled generation and synthesis token spaces.
Decouples the token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder.
Uses vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, then deterministically expands compressed tokens before synthesis.
Reports approximately 1.7× faster expanded speech-token generation, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput on bilingual benchmarks.
Supports sustained interaction under limited budgets, transfers across architectures, and complements low-rate tokenization.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich robotic tasks require coordinated motion and impedance under uncertain interaction dynamics and physical constraints. While recent methods on learned policies provide useful interaction strategies, they may fail when contact conditions differ from those encountered during training. Model-based generative methods show promising receding-horizon trajectories optimization results, but often lack structured behavioral guidance and refinement that jointly accounts for constraint geometry and actual contact responses. To this end, we propose Manifold Generative Annealing (MGA), a joint model-free and model-based generative framework for motion--impedance optimization. MGA first organizes pretrained reinforcement learning policies into structured sequence proposals, retaining task-specific interaction strategies without committing to their execution. It then evaluates these proposals alongside exploratory samples through model-based rollouts for refinement or separate execution selection. Crucially, realization-aware manifold refinement aligns updates from the refinement bank with both task constraints and locally achievable physical responses, allowing learned experience to guide online adaptation under changing contact conditions. Experiments cover surface scanning, peg insertion, and humanoid pushing, with improved safety success rate of impedance control under nominal and sensing-shift conditions.
authors: Zhilin He, Guoquan Qi, Changliu Liu
bullets: Targets contact-rich robotic tasks with uncertain dynamics and physical constraints.
Structures pretrained RL policies into sequence proposals that preserve task-specific interaction strategies without directly executing them.
Uses model-based rollouts to refine or select proposals alongside exploratory samples.
Applies realization-aware manifold refinement to respect task constraints and locally achievable contact responses.
Evaluated on surface scanning, peg insertion, and humanoid pushing, with improved impedance-control safety success under nominal and sensing-shift conditions.

papers.abstract: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.

Emphasizes AI that lives on the body, works for the user, and answers to the user.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) dominate video generation but suffer from high inference cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Sparse attention mitigates this by skipping unnecessary computation in the attention matrix, but existing methods apply a fixed sparsity ratio throughout denoising and struggle to accurately determine which computations to skip. To address these limitations, we analyze attention dynamics through attention entropy and mean attention distance, and find that attention becomes increasingly concentrated across denoising steps. We further observe that blocks selected early continue to capture a large fraction of the total attention weight at later steps. These findings suggest two acceleration opportunities: the sparsity ratio should grow as denoising progresses, and earlier search results can be reused to reduce the search space. Based on these findings, we propose Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search (GSRS), a training-free framework that retains more computation early and progressively reduces it later, while restricting subsequent searches to an early candidate set to reduce search overhead. GSRS adopts Top-p selection for adaptive sparsity control, supported by a precise evaluation scheme that computes exact attention weights within the FlashAttention computation at negligible overhead. Experiments on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1 validate that GSRS achieves 1.55$\times$--2.21$\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality comparable to full attention.
authors: Yun Dai, Yuyun Chen, Jiarui Wen, Huiping Zhuang, Cen Chen, Ziqian Zeng
bullets: Video DiTs are slowed by quadratic self-attention, while fixed-sparsity methods poorly reflect changing attention patterns during denoising.
Attention becomes increasingly concentrated over denoising steps, and early-selected blocks retain much of the later attention weight.
GSRS is training-free: it keeps more computation early, reduces it progressively, and restricts later searches to an early candidate set.
Top-p selection provides adaptive sparsity, with exact attention-weight evaluation integrated into FlashAttention at negligible overhead.
Validated on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1, GSRS delivers 1.55×–2.21× speedup while maintaining quality comparable to full attention.

papers.abstract: Sparse KV compression reduces long-context inference costs by retaining selected historical states, yet these states typically keep their coordinates from the full history. Under Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), gaps left by evicted tokens continue to affect query-key matching, potentially limiting the use of retained evidence. We study post-selection positional geometry on a fixed selector-produced cache, examining how positional organization affects the use of retained information and which coordinate and continuation rules improve answer quality. To reorganize this geometry, we propose RoPERelay, which assigns compact, order-preserving RoPE coordinates, relocates cached key phases through inverse rotation and re-rotation, and synchronizes the current query and subsequent generation. It reuses existing K/V without renewed selection, historical re-prefill, or additional cache budget. Across 36 comparisons spanning two models, six sparse selectors, and three long-term memory tasks, RoPERelay improves answer quality in 32 cases. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with BM25 on LongMemEval-S, accuracy increases from 23.6% to 35.4%. Measured complete-request time overhead is approximately 1%-3% in the evaluated configurations. These findings establish positional organization as a distinct optimization dimension for sparse KV caches after content selection.
authors: Wanyang Hong, Zhaoning Zhang
bullets: Sparse KV caches retain selected states, but gaps from evicted tokens can distort RoPE query–key matching.
The method assigns compact, order-preserving coordinates and relocates cached key phases while synchronizing queries and generation.
It operates on a fixed selector-produced cache without renewed selection or historical re-prefill.
Across 36 comparisons, answer quality improved in 32 cases; one reported result rose from 23.6% to 35.4%.
Measured complete-request overhead was approximately 1%–3% in the evaluated configurations.

papers.abstract: Real-time mobile volumetric video enables immersive free-viewpoint experiences, but delivering high-quality 3D content under constrained bandwidth and computation remains challenging. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) systems, such as V$^3$, enable efficient mobile streaming by encoding time-varying Gaussian attributes with commodity video codecs and hardware decoding. However, existing pipelines treat all Gaussians as frame-varying signals, which is poorly suited to full-scene content where large portions remain temporally stable. Our empirical study shows that frame-wise adaptation and video coding of all Gaussians cause quality degradation in complex full-scene content, particularly in temporally stable regions. To address this issue, we propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that processes Gaussians according to their temporal behavior. ResStreamGS identifies residual-sensitive primitives through lightweight probe adaptation and reuses stable Gaussians within each Group of Pictures (GOP). Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP, while only residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in the frame-wise hardware-decodable video stream. Experiments on complex full-scene volumetric videos show that ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51--8.35~dB over a controlled V$^3$-style all-Gaussians baseline, reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5%, and achieves 30.883~FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.
authors: Haoran Liu, Di Wu, Wang Luo, Hengyuan Na, Miao Hu, Guocong Quan
bullets: Targets quality degradation and bandwidth/computation inefficiency when all Gaussians are treated as frame-varying.
Uses lightweight probe adaptation to identify residual-sensitive Gaussian primitives.
Transmits stable Gaussians once per GOP and keeps only residual-sensitive Gaussians in the frame-wise hardware-decodable stream.
On complex full-scene videos, improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51–8.35 dB and reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5% versus a controlled V$^3$-style baseline.
Reaches 30.883 FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full-grid attribution method over position-channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position-channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC-Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.
authors: Haotian Ma, Ruqi Yang, Philip Townsend
bullets: Addresses the limitation of separate spatial heatmaps and global channel scores when channel relevance varies across locations.
Defines a conditional local game over channels at each position while holding surrounding context fixed.
Provides Shapley fairness locally and exactly recovers each position’s contextual contrast when channel attributions are aggregated.
Across three datasets and two baselines, SSI achieves the strongest reported deletion/insertion, spectral, channel, and spatial-localization metrics.
On HLS Burn Scar, it outperforms an MC-Owen estimator using about 6% of its evaluation budget.

papers.abstract: World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video-action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action-conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real-world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.
authors: Yue Su, Bokai Lin, Xinkai Wang, Chubin Zhang, Xiangnan Wu, Kuan Zhang, Weiyang Jin, Jiwen Yu, Yiming Li, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang, Xihui Liu
bullets: Unifies world modeling and policy learning in a shared video-action architecture.
Treats actions as conditions for predicting future worlds and as targets for learning policies.
Evaluates policy learning and world modeling on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa365, and real-world experiments.
Action-conditioned dynamics improve policy performance and generalization across changing scenes.
Action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity, indicating reciprocal benefits.

papers.abstract: Agent memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experiences without updating their parameters. However, semantic similarity alone does not guarantee memory usefulness: downstream performance depends on how memories are selected and presented to the agent. We propose MemComposer, a memory composer that jointly examines the current query and retrieved candidates to decide which experiences to include, how many to select, and how to order them. We train the composer using Experience Policy Optimization (ExPO), a GRPO-based framework that evaluates assembled memory contexts through complete agent interactions and uses task-success feedback to optimize the assembly policy. Across three $\tau^2$-bench domains with two frozen executors, MemComposer outperforms the strongest baseline for each executor while reducing average memory-token usage by 16.9% and 4.9%, respectively. The learned policy also transfers to unseen domains, executors, and memory banks, and benefits from memories generated by stronger models without further training. These results demonstrate the value of learning query-specific memory assembly using downstream task feedback.
authors: Yixuan Xie, Xueqiang Xu, Xinyi Fan, Xinxi Lyu, Tao Feng, Xing Fan, Chenlei Guo, Jie Hao, Shaowen Wang, Jiashuo Sun, Jiawei Han

The learned policy transfers to unseen domains, executors, and memory banks, and can use memories from stronger models without retraining.

papers.abstract: We identify a theoretical incompatibility between 3D point cloud masked autoencoding and SE(3)-equivariant networks. We prove that standard masking triggers a topological collapse, effectively forcing the model to hallucinate orientation without a reference frame. To resolve this, we introduce SIEVE (Scalar Invariant Extraction Via Equivariance), an SE(3)-equivariant self-supervised framework that compresses point cloud geometry into invariant scalar embeddings. At its core is the spherical projection mask, which preserves global pose while obfuscating local semantics, sidestepping the obstruction by construction. Experiments confirm that SIEVE circumvents the predicted collapse where constant and noise masks fail. On downstream point cloud tasks, the resulting embeddings improve over coordinate-based baselines and hand-crafted geometric descriptors, with the largest gains on generalization to unseen shape categories.
authors: Jongann Lee, Sun Woo Park, Yun Young Choi
bullets: Standard masking is theoretically incompatible with SE(3)-equivariant networks because it removes the reference needed to infer orientation.
SIEVE extracts geometry into SE(3)-invariant scalar embeddings.
Its spherical projection mask preserves global pose while hiding local semantics.
Experiments show SIEVE avoids the collapse observed with constant and noise masks.
The embeddings outperform coordinate-based and hand-crafted geometric baselines, especially on unseen shape categories.

figures.caption: Figure 2: SIEVE Framework. SIEVE extracts SE(3)-invariant embeddings using self-supervised reconstruction on an equivariant bottleneck. The equivariant encoder compresses raw point coordinates into an invariant scalar encoding, while the vector pipeline is blocked. The spherical projection mask is applied to the input point cloud and supplied as the new vector embedding. It and the semantic details from the scalar embedding are used by the equivariant decoder to reconstruct the point cloud on a node-level.

Figure 1: Random masking causes representational collapse; spherical projection masking does not. Random masking functions ignore subtle geometric data inherent in point clouds. This imposes topological obstructions in reconstructing the desired non-trivial vector bundles characterizing the underlying geometry of point clouds, as demonstrated in Theorem 2.6. As a result, representational collapse can occur as shown in Section 4.2. SIEVE utilizes a spherical projection mask, thereby possessing capabilities in reconstructing a class of pullbacks of vector bundles defined over a wide variety of 2 and 3-dimensional manifolds as demonstrated in Theorem 3.1.

Figure 5: Reconstruction Comparison and Representational Collapse. We evaluate the reconstruction (blue) of the input point cloud (red) under different masking strategies. Using our spherical projection mask, the model achieves near-perfect reconstruction. Reconstructing with a constant vector mask or the ellipsoid noise mask results in a catastrophic representational collapse. We refer to Appendix A.3 for further discussions.

papers.abstract: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. However, recovering 3D structural features from 2D observations remains a challenging task. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering or involve sophisticated 2D-3D registration which suffers from projection ambiguity, accumulated errors for distal joints and imbalanced learning for different joints. In this work, we propose RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator, which embeds a learnable adjacency map to generate condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss for topological consistency and scale stability, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with mutiple cameras. Besides, we establish a novel cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate the outstanding performance of RoPE-Flow on zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Meanwhile, animated visualizations are shown on the website: ropeflow.netlify.app
authors: Liangjing Shao, Wanhao Liu, Zhiwei Fang, Rulin Zhou, Quanlu Zhang, Changjing Liu, Beilei Cui, Yiming Huang, Hongliang Ren

Uses a learnable keypoint adjacency graph to condition flow matching on relationships among joints.
Introduces bone-length and ray-depth losses with joint-wise weighting for topological consistency and scale stability.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across robot types and cameras, including zero-shot cross-scene evaluation on a new benchmark.

papers.abstract: To address sparse terminal rewards in LLM arithmetic reasoning, we propose a Bellman-consistent trajectory RL method. Our framework introduces Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization (TBRM) to transform sparse rewards into dense token-level signals. We integrate a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) group strategy to reduce gradient variance of Bellman residuals and use hindsight goal relabeling to accelerate intermediate learning. Evaluated on the Countdown task, our method alleviates optimization bottlenecks and stabilizes gradient variance significantly better than GRPO. The TBRM-RLOO framework boosts Pass@1 to 0.55--0.64 and achieves a state-of-the-art Pass@16 accuracy of 76.0--84.0\%, outperforming the SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines. Our approach demonstrates exceptional single-sample efficiency and successfully circumvents standard performance plateaus via test-time scaling.
authors: Lianfa Li
bullets: Targets sparse terminal rewards and optimization bottlenecks in arithmetic reasoning.
Uses Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization to generate dense token-level signals.
Combines RLOO grouping to reduce Bellman-residual gradient variance with hindsight goal relabeling.
On Countdown, reports Pass@1 of 0.55–0.64 and Pass@16 of 76.0–84.0%, outperforming SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines.
Supports improved single-sample efficiency and test-time scaling beyond standard performance plateaus.

papers.abstract: Learned dynamical models can accurately predict trajectories while producing unreliable sensitivities when differentiated or transposed, limiting their use in inverse problems and scientific decision-making. Classical adjoints provide exact local derivatives, but a single adjoint cannot represent the nonlinear response of a system to a family of finite-amplitude perturbations. We introduce SALTO (Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators), a Koopman-based framework for inferring finite-amplitude sources. In the lifted space, the nonlinear dynamics are approximated by a linear propagator, and its transpose carries each sensor backward in a single solve. The result is a reusable lifted adjoint that predicts the measurement produced by any candidate localized event with one encoder pass and an inner product. To give the model the simulator's exact local behavior, SALTO imposes three structural constraints: it anchors the physical-state dynamics to the simulator's linearized propagator, centers the learned observables so that they vanish to second order at the reference state, and uses a block-triangular lifted propagator. These constraints guarantee that the model reduces to the simulator's tangent dynamics and classical adjoint as the amplitude vanishes, while the learned observables carry only the finite-amplitude correction. On three nonlinear PDE systems, SALTO predicts the measurements of finite-amplitude sources to within 2-8% where the classical adjoint is in error by 41-165%, recovers source position and intensity from sparse sensors nearly as accurately as inversion through the solver, and samples the joint posterior of two interacting sources, matching the solver's posterior on reaction-diffusion at a twentieth of its cost. One trained model serves new sensor layouts and measurement times with a single backward solve.
authors: Qi Wang, Rylie Foster
bullets: Addresses unreliable sensitivities from learned dynamical models and the limited nonlinear coverage of classical adjoints.
Uses a lifted linear propagator whose transpose enables reusable backward sensor propagation for candidate events.
Anchors physical-state dynamics to the simulator linearization, centers observables to second order, and enforces block-triangular structure.
On three nonlinear PDE systems, finite-amplitude measurement errors were 2–8% versus 41–165% for classical adjoints.
Recovers sparse-sensor source properties and joint posteriors at substantially lower cost, with one model supporting new sensors and measurement times.

figures.caption: Figure 1: SALTO in one picture. Localized sources S(p) seed a nonlinear flow observed by a few probes. Offline, the solver supplies Lk and the data supply only the finite-amplitude correction, so the lifted model is exact at small amplitude. Online, one backward solve per sensor gives the lifted adjoint Z† j , and every candidate source is scored by an encoder pass and inner products.

Figure 2: (a–d) Space–time evolution of the base flow and of one release, from the solver, the lifted model and the linearized solver. The dashed line is the half-maximum contour of the ground truth. (e) Five representative blocks of the lift, forward in time (top) and adjoint in backward time τ (bottom). papers.abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.
authors: Dingjie Song, Zhiling Yan, Ziqian Zhang, Yuxuan Zhang, Lichao Sun
bullets: ReviewFact benchmarks factual errors in peer-review comments across NLP, machine learning, and natural sciences, while measuring accuracy, cost, and latency.
Whole-comment checking by cheap decision models performs poorly because comments may contain multiple implicit assertions.
PremiseCheck uses an LLM to extract explicit premises without reading the paper, then applies a decision model to verify each premise against the paper.
It achieves accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across three fields at roughly half the cost; for NLP reviews, it uses about one-quarter the cost and less than half the latency.
The framework is evaluated on comments checked independently; its scope beyond this setting is not established by the abstract.

papers.abstract: Tool-using language agents must revise prepared actions when evidence changes or authority is revoked. Selective withdrawal means suspending affected actions, preserving supported work, and resuming only after sufficient repair. We study supervised fine-tuning in NAQD-Env, a synthetic environment with explicit dependencies and a deterministic reference policy. Four LoRA checkpoints of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct compare an original curriculum with an enriched one, the latter under three system-prompt framings with identical views and targets. Three instruction-tuned baselines and all four checkpoints are evaluated under three inference prompts on fresh validation cases, held-out dependency families, and held-out structural combinations. Under the naqd prompt, SFT checkpoints reach decision agreement of 0.77-0.92 and withdrawal recall of 0.46-0.86, versus 0.45-0.63 and at most 0.06 for the baselines. Rule-level diagnostics qualify these gains. The original-curriculum checkpoint wrongly withdraws 26 of 34 actions with surviving alternative support; enriched checkpoints withdraw 0-1. Conversely, all SFT checkpoints narrow prohibited combinations less often than the 7B and 8B baselines, a case absent from both curricula. Delegation results show more withdrawal but poorer preservation of independently authorized actions, and all four checkpoints omit valid event reports. Framing contrasts vary across metrics and splits and do not establish a reproducible advantage or equivalence. One training run per arm, jointly changed curriculum properties, prior evaluation exposure, and baseline-SFT quantization differences limit causal attribution. The contribution is a method for detecting rule-specific regressions that aggregate accuracy can conceal, not evidence that fine-tuning alone ensures agent safety.
authors: Mohamed Abouzahra
bullets: Evaluated four LoRA checkpoints in NAQD-Env against three instruction-tuned baselines across validation, held-out dependency, and structural cases.
SFT checkpoints achieved 0.77–0.92 decision agreement and 0.46–0.86 withdrawal recall under the main prompt, outperforming baselines on these metrics.
Enriched curricula reduced erroneous withdrawal of actions with surviving support, but all SFT checkpoints more often missed prohibited combinations than larger baselines.
Delegation caused more withdrawal but weaker preservation of independently authorized actions; all checkpoints omitted some valid event reports.
Results are limited by single runs, jointly changed curriculum properties, prior evaluation exposure, and baseline quantization differences.

papers.abstract: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) has gained wide attention for its ability to work with limited data. In a proposer-solver loop, a proposer model writes training tasks and a solver model learns to solve them through reinforcement learning. Such loops have succeeded in mathematics and coding, where every answer can be checked automatically. Open-ended expert tasks, like clinical report generations, have no answer key, which makes simple question-answer generation not viable. Here the proposer must also write a rubric that lists the content an answer should include and the errors it should avoid. However, the unique challenge behind model-written rubric is the comprehensiveness of it. For naively generated rubric, solvers tend to exploit it, naming the expected topics without the substance behind them, which corrupts the learning process. To solve this problem, we introduce RRI, Recursive Reward Improvement, which uses a reward hacking adversary to supervise the reward. Before the solver trains on a generated task, an adversary writes an answer that games its rubric while being as useless as possible, the same model writes an honest answer without seeing the rubric, and up to two repair steps revise the rubric to make the honest answer win. The exploits found also rewrite how future tasks and rubrics are generated. On HealthBench Professional, RRI improves the adjusted score over the Generation Only self-improvement baseline by 10.9 points at 9B and 12.4 at 27B, and by 10.3 points without any external model. In particular, the gains are largest on difficult and writing tasks. We show that the 27B model trained on the HealthBench Professional description improves by 6.6 points on PRBench Hard and 8.0 on ProfBench without seeing a task from either. We further analyze the exploitable points of model-generated question-rubric pairs to facilitate future research on open-ended self-play.
authors: Wei Dai, Qianchu Liu, Guanghui Qin, Xing Han, Tristan Naumann, Paul Pu Liang, Sheng Zhang
bullets: Open-ended tasks lack automatically verifiable answers, so proposer-generated rubrics must guide evaluation without being exploitable.
Before solver training, an adversary produces a useless answer that games the rubric, while an honest answer is generated without seeing it.
Up to two repair steps revise the rubric so the honest answer scores higher; discovered exploits also inform future task and rubric generation.
On HealthBench Professional, RRI improves adjusted scores over Generation Only by 10.9 points at 9B and 12.4 at 27B, with gains also achieved without an external model.
A 27B model trained on HealthBench Professional improves on unseen PRBench Hard and ProfBench tasks, indicating transfer beyond the training benchmark.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RRI. The proposer generates clinical tasks and weighted rubrics from medical references. An adversary probes each rubric with an exploit and an honest answer. The repair step keeps criteria that distinguish the better answer from the exploit, then tests the revised rubric with another attack. The solver learns through GRPO using rubric rewards. Training feedback and confirmed exploits guide updates to the generation prompts.

papers.abstract: Machine learning models for tabular prediction typically assume that training data are representative of the population on which they will be deployed. In practice, however, data are often collected based on convenience, availability, or cost, resulting in systematic sampling biases that can distort feature--target relationships and undermine real-world generalization. Existing tabular distribution-shift benchmarks primarily construct out-of-distribution (OOD) settings by partitioning observations across naturally occurring domains. While such partitions may induce changes in P(Y | X), the resulting shifts are neither explicitly controlled nor isolated, and the evaluation distributions themselves are often not representative of the broader target population. We introduce INCONVENIENT, a benchmark designed to study robustness to convenience-sample bias. Rather than relying on naturally occurring domain partitions, INCONVENIENT directly perturbs feature--target relationships in the training distribution while preserving the original population distribution as the deployment environment. This setting more closely reflects real-world scenarios in which models are developed from unrepresentative samples and subsequently deployed on a broader population. The distinction is particularly relevant for large language models (LLMs), whose pretraining may encode population-level knowledge that extends beyond the relationships observed in a biased training dataset. Unlike existing distribution-shift benchmarks, INCONVENIENT provides explicit control over both the direction and severity of relationship shifts, enabling a systematic assessment of robustness to convenience sampling. The benchmark comprises 200 tabular classification and regression datasets spanning diverse application domains and generates around 15,500 shifted training distributions which lead to substantial downstream degradation.
authors: Sara Rezaeimanesh, Chad Klochko, Kundan Thind, Mohammad Ghassemi
bullets: Addresses the gap between representative-data assumptions and real-world training data collected for convenience, availability, or cost.
Creates shifted training distributions by directly perturbing feature–target relationships while keeping the original population as the deployment environment.
Allows explicit control over the direction and severity of relationship shifts, unlike benchmarks based mainly on naturally occurring domain partitions.
Includes 200 tabular classification and regression datasets across diverse domains and about 15,500 shifted training distributions.
The generated shifts cause substantial downstream degradation, supporting systematic robustness evaluation.

The scatter plots reveal substantial performance degradation under convenience-sample bias relative to the in-distribution setting, highlighting the challenges posed by distorted feature–target relationships.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-conditioned embeddings can improve retrieval by progressively refining semantic constraints. However, additional reasoning may introduce over-generalized or semantically noisy abstractions that weaken retrieval specificity. Existing methods largely supervise reasoning through final retrieval outcomes, providing limited guidance over the refinement process itself. We propose AURA, a framework that directly supervises intermediate reasoning states according to how well they separate relevant documents from hard distractors. AURA further trains a lightweight utility estimator over prefix-conditioned embeddings to adapt reasoning depth at inference time. On the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark, AURA-4B achieves 34.7 average nDCG@10 while using 2.8 reasoning steps and 96 generated tokens per query. Under matched deployment conditions, adaptive stopping reduces latency from 4.6 to 0.76 seconds relative to full-trajectory reasoning. Results on MS MARCO further suggest that this specialization need not substantially degrade conventional in-domain retrieval.
authors: Yingtao Luo, Kangyi Zhao, Shiyi Du, Yubo Li
bullets: Reasoning-conditioned embeddings can sharpen retrieval but may become noisy or overly general with additional steps.
AURA supervises intermediate reasoning states by their ability to distinguish relevant documents from hard distractors.
A lightweight utility estimator selects reasoning depth at inference time using prefix-conditioned embeddings.
On BRIGHT, AURA-4B reaches 34.7 average nDCG@10 with 2.8 reasoning steps and 96 generated tokens per query.
Adaptive stopping reduces latency from 4.6 to 0.76 seconds versus full-trajectory reasoning; MS MARCO results suggest limited impact on conventional retrieval.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AURA. Training: A warm-up stage first establishes a retrieval-oriented embedding space. Specificity labels are then constructed from the warmed-up model, the utility estimator is trained on frozen embeddings, and utility-aware weighting is enabled for subsequent joint optimization. Inference: The utility estimator evaluates each state online and terminates reasoning according to the predicted utility, returning the selected embedding for retrieval.

Figure 2: Motivation behind AURA. Existing methods supervise only the final retrieval outcome, while AURA identifies the peak-utility reasoning state before overreasoning weakens retrieval specificity.

Figure 4: Inference-time scaling of AURA on BRIGHT. Greedy selects the best continuation at each step using utility estimator; best-of-k samples k full trajectories and selects the one with highest estimated utility.

papers.tldr: AURA adaptively stops retrieval reasoning when further refinement is no longer useful, improving efficiency while preserving retrieval quality.

papers.abstract: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.
authors: Matteo He, William F. Shen, Alex Iacob, Andrej Jovanovic, Xinchi Qiu, Nicholas D. Lane
bullets: Output-based capability timelines can conflate internal knowledge with the readout’s development.
The authors introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, using checkpoint weights to track structure across every token’s readout row.
In Pythia, the readout reorganizes early in training, and WordNet categories become decodable from its rows during a narrow early window.
Hidden-state probes detect task information before the model’s own predictions do.
Increasing the readout learning rate advances its development and closes this gap sooner, with little change in final loss.

papers.abstract: When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The failed reasoning can nevertheless suggest what to try next. We present Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which turns failed attempts into an additional, tested source of supervision during GRPO training. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening for notes that state the answer, and an admitted replay is distilled into the plain-prompt policy. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.
authors: Sheldon Yu, Tong Yu, Nikki Lijing Kuang, Zhendong Chu, Zhenwei Tang, Sungchul Kim, Lina Yao, Julian McAuley, Junda Wu
bullets: GRPO learns nothing when all attempts for a problem fail because there is no successful exemplar or nonzero group-relative advantage.
RSHD has the policy write a corrective note, re-solve with that note, and admit it only when fresh replay succeeds more often than the original group.
Answer-stating notes are screened out; admitted replays are distilled into the ordinary plain-prompt policy.
The method uses only policy training and outcome verification, with no reference solutions, and requires no notes or extra inference at deployment.
It consistently improves over GRPO across model families, sizes, and two training domains, with gains also transferring out of domain.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RSHD overview. From a scored GRPO group, each failed attempt yields a corrective note (left). The note is screened for answer leaks and replayed; it is admitted only if the replays beat the group’s own success rate, with one revision round (middle). An admitted replay is scored by the same weights with and without the note, and the plain-prompt policy imitates it with detached lift weights, added to the GRPO loss (right).

Each panel’s y-range is fitted to its own curves, so compare gaps within a panel rather than across panels. Plain-prompt success during training (log scale, mean and 95% interval over ten seeds) at three reasoning budgets H , with initial viable-strategy probability 0.01 and note strength 1.6. Every arm is allotted two extra attempts per rollout. Unguided retry imitates accepted retries without a note, repair-biased restart proposes a strategy switch with probability 0.1 and a local repair otherwise, and the strategy-switch note always proposes the other strategy. Success is measured without a note.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo
authors: Yuchen Zhang
bullets: Targets the risk that faulty skill generalizations persist and propagate errors in health-agent answers.
Uses a frozen LLM to propose rules, compares paired skill replacements on shared feedback cases, and ranks rules via least-squares estimates.
Keeps the incumbent skill set as a feasible option and favors incumbents when scores tie.
On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks and 120 held-out cases, it reports 60.00% accuracy versus 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills.
Reported gains are task-dependent, with regressions on some calculations; paired accuracy intervals include zero, and training configurations used 55.6% fewer tokens than SkillOpt.

papers.abstract: Identifying individual dogs from barks in real-world videos remains challenging and largely unexplored. Solving this problem would enable long-term behavioral analysis, veterinary monitoring, and animal welfare monitoring by attributing vocalizations and behaviors to the correct individual. Real-world videos are challenging because multiple dogs may bark simultaneously, become occluded, or move in and out of view. Prior studies show that canine vocalizations and visual appearance contain discriminative identity information, but these modalities have largely been studied independently. We present a multimodal dog-fingerprinting framework combining visual identification, multiple-object tracking, and canine vocal fingerprinting to associate bark events with individual dogs while maintaining persistent profiles. The framework synchronizes bark events with tracked dogs and updates profiles using visual appearance and vocal characteristics, enabling identification despite occlusion, overlapping vocalizations, and off-screen barking. We also introduce a benchmark of 46 real-world videos containing 213 manually annotated bark events. Our framework correctly localizes the active visible dog in 61.83% of visible events at IoU $\geq 0.30$ and achieves a 91.33% F1 score for visible versus off-screen barking detection.

papers.abstract: Data selection reallocates training support across visual concepts, including objects, attributes, color, texture, and backgrounds. Different allocation strategies may produce varied downstream model behavior, especially for tail concepts supported by only a few samples. Discarding them can hurt test-time robustness, while overemphasizing samples lying on category boundaries may introduce unstable training signals. This work explicitly investigates this relationship across fine-grained, spurious-correlation, and general image classification, as well as multimodal pretraining. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract concept activations from individual images. During selection, we accumulate the dataset-level concept support for each added sample. Applying diminishing returns to this distribution down-weights well-represented concepts and shifts the focus to the distribution tail. We then incorporate local support to find samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts. Empirical results show consistent improvements over strong data selection baselines across all benchmarks. We also reveal the connection between concepts our method enhances and the induced behavioral changes, including improved robustness against out-of-distribution and spurious contexts. This work establishes concept support, beyond individual sample importance, as a useful principle for data-efficient and robust learning.
authors: Ziheng Zhang, Neha Hulkund, Colin Lee, Zheda Mai, Hui Shen, Ying Ding, Tanya Berger-Wolf, Sara Beery, Wei-Lun Chao, Jianyang Gu
bullets: Data selection can neglect tail concepts or overemphasize category-boundary samples, harming robustness and training stability.
Sparse autoencoders extract visual concept activations from individual images.
A diminishing-returns objective down-weights well-supported concepts and shifts selection toward the concept-support tail.
Local support helps identify samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts.
The method consistently outperforms strong selection baselines across classification and multimodal pretraining benchmarks, with improved robustness to out-of-distribution and spurious contexts.

We then use local support to locate samples that contribute to filling the distributional gap together with their neighbors. papers.abstract: Diffusion models are notoriously expensive to train, requiring large-scale datasets to learn how to gradually reverse the noise from images over multiple small denoising steps. Current approaches focus on distilling the number of diffusion steps, neglecting potential redundancies of the training data. In this paper, we explore the potential of harnessing eigensamples to train diffusion models on significantly smaller datasets, while preserving model performance. To mitigate the sensitivity to affine transformations of eigenimages, we harness the latent space of a pre-trained CLIP model. We next compute latent eigenvectors by performing principal component analysis (PCA) in CLIP space. Further, we employ eigenvectors as reference points to guide the selection of a representative training set comprising comprising both exemplars (images whose embeddings are closest to eigenvectors) and diverse images. Our comprehensive experiments with different diffusion models applied on multiple datasets indicate that our approach (EigDiff) can reduce training data by up to 14x and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607x, with marginal performance differences.
authors: Andrei Jarca, Vlad Hondru, Florinel-Alin Croitoru, Radu Tudor Ionescu
bullets: Targets redundancy in diffusion-model training data, complementing methods that reduce denoising steps.
Computes PCA eigenvectors in the latent space of a pretrained CLIP model to identify representative samples.
Builds subsets from exemplars closest to eigenvectors plus additional diverse images.
Experiments across multiple diffusion models and datasets reduce training data by up to 14× and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607×.
Reports only marginal performance differences, though results are scoped to the evaluated models and datasets.
