papers.abstract: Passive human videos of everyday activity offer robots access to a massive amount of human experience without requiring a demonstration for each task. However, using this experience requires recovering knowledge from unstructured video recordings and adapting it to a different body (i.e., the robot). To overcome these challenges, we present mobile code-as-policy (MoCaP), an agentic framework that turns passive human video recordings into guidance for an end-to-end mobile manipulation policy. MoCaP extracts spatial memory and cues of how people prepare to interact with objects, which inform navigation and the search for a manipulation-ready configuration. Guided by passive human experience and current observations, MoCaP uses a closed-loop code-as-policy to coordinate planning and tool use primitives to solve motions under the robot's geometry and kinematic constraints. On a real mobile manipulator, MoCaP achieves 80% success on each of two mobile manipulation tasks in an indoor environment whereas existing approaches cannot succeed at the task. Video-derived spatial memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, and human approach prior raises the rate of finding a reachable base pose from 0% to 100% at an unfavorable start location. Videos and code are available on the project website: https://mocap-7.github.io/MoCAP-page/.
authors: Yiyang Cai, Tatsuya Kamijo, Ninghao Lu, Zijin Hu, Sherry Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring knowledge from unstructured human videos to robots with different bodies and constraints.
Extracts spatial memory and human approach cues to guide object navigation and selection of manipulation-ready base poses.
Uses a closed-loop code-as-policy agent to coordinate planning and tool-use primitives under robot geometry and kinematic constraints.
On a real mobile manipulator, achieves 80% success on each of two indoor tasks where existing approaches fail.
Video-derived memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, while human approach priors improve reachable-base-pose discovery from 0% to 100% in an unfavorable start setting.

papers.abstract: Spatial agents have access to reconstruction and segmentation tools, yet inconsistent predictions and fragmented object identities can prevent their outputs from becoming reliable 3D scene information. A simple oracle experiment exposes this perception bottleneck: replacing tool-predicted perception with ground-truth 3D bounding boxes raises an agent to nearly full score across five object-centric VSI-Bench tasks, while retaining the same reasoning tools. Motivated by this finding, we believe the devil of spatial reasoning lies in 3D itself, and introduce DeSpatial(Devil of Spatial), which explicitly decomposes spatial understanding into perception and reasoning. DeSpatial has a shared 3D perception tool to reconcile independent perception outputs into a unified, metric, gravity-aligned 3D scene. This perception tool has two core components: a) a joint segmentation--depth co-refinement module that consolidates masks of the same object and removes projection artifacts caused by inconsistent segmentation and depth within a single frame; b) a cross-view instance fusion module that consolidate voxel-overlapping instances but not allowed to merge same-frame instances. This fusion module additionally fuses spatially disjoint fragments caused by insufficient multi-view observations, by checking their 3D structure and source mask appearance. After receiving the complete and unified 3D scene information, the agent chooses reasoning or computational tools to solve the spatial problem. DeSpatial achieves leading performance on VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial, with additional long-video results on VSI-SUPER, revealing the bottleneck of spatial understanding lies in a precise 3D perception itself.
authors: Yifei Liu, Xiaolong Zhou, Ziyang Gong, Yifan Zhou, Yuanyuan Gao, Yuning Gong, Yuchen Yang, Hongjie Zhang, Xue Yang, Xiao Sun, Zhihang Zhong
bullets: An oracle experiment finds that ground-truth 3D boxes nearly solve five object-centric VSI-Bench tasks, exposing perception as the main bottleneck.
DeSpatial explicitly separates 3D perception from downstream reasoning and computation.
Its shared perception tool builds a metric, gravity-aligned scene using joint segmentation–depth refinement and cross-view instance fusion.
The system prevents erroneous merges while reconnecting fragmented instances using 3D structure and mask appearance.
It achieves leading performance on VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial, with additional long-video evaluation on VSI-SUPER.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of DeSpatial. The VLM receives the video and question and calls our shared perception tool. Joint segmentation–depth co-refinement cleans per-frame observations; cross-view instance fusion associates them into distinguished individual objects. Colors identify individual masks before fusion and persistent instances afterward. Gravity estimation establishes a common vertical direction. The VLM then reasons and answers using reasoning and computational tools.

Figure 3: Cross-view instance fusion. (a) Voxel overlap links partial observations, while sameframe exclusions prevent distinct objects from merging, including through indirect connections. (b) Visual fragment association handles observations without shared voxels. Multiple source views and a common 3D view provide complementary appearance and structural evidence to an identity judge. A positive decision combines the observed fragments and their provenance.

Figure 2: Joint segmentation–depth co-refinement. (a) Same-class mask consolidation unifies highly overlapping masks and visually verified parts of an occluded object. Negative or uncertain identity judgments keep masks separate. (b) Confidence, depth-edge, and 3D outlier filters remove unreliable geometry. Component selection then removes residual detached points that distort the bounding box, retaining the top-k components for k confirmed object parts, usually one.

Figure 4: Human annotation interface for gravity estimation. Both panels show the same scene and eight source views. Green arrows visualize the estimated up direction, and the highlighted button indicates the saved scene-level judgment.

papers.abstract: Improving the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) often relies on post-training with supervision from stronger models. Two common strategies are supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which trains on teacher-generated demonstrations, and on-policy distillation (OPD), which provides teacher feedback on trajectories generated by the student itself. While OPD can be more data-efficient by supervising student-generated trajectories, it is unclear how the teacher's supervision at each state affects the student's learned behavior. To study this question, we conduct a controlled comparison of OPD and filtered SFT across data budgets and tasks where the teacher exhibits different levels of reliability, and analyze how these differences shape student accuracy and completion behavior. Across the two tasks, we find that OPD is effective only when the teacher remains reliable on student-generated trajectories. On ChartQA, where the teacher completes 99% of its solutions, OPD trained on only 10% of the data comes within 1.4 accuracy points of full-data SFT. In contrast, on Geometry3K, where the teacher fails to complete 22% of its solutions, OPD underperforms SFT by 7.9 points, with most of the gap explained by incomplete responses. More strikingly, starting OPD from an SFT student reduces its completion rate from 76% to 62%, effectively erasing the completion behavior learned through SFT. Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT's advantage. These results show that on-policy supervision can transfer not only teacher knowledge but also persistent failure modes on student-visited states. Code is available at https://github.com/ffy208/opd-inherits-teacher-vlm.
authors: Frank F. Yang, Kefei Yan, Yiren Wang, Yiyang Wang
bullets: OPD is compared with filtered supervised fine-tuning across tasks, data budgets, and teacher reliability levels.
On ChartQA, a teacher with 99% completion enables 10%-data OPD to approach full-data SFT within 1.4 accuracy points.
On Geometry3K, a teacher with 22% incomplete solutions makes OPD trail SFT by 7.9 points, largely due to incomplete responses.
Initializing OPD from an SFT student reduces completion from 76% to 62%, while filtering incomplete demonstrations recovers much of SFT’s advantage.
The findings indicate that OPD inherits persistent teacher failures on states visited by the student.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates on-policy distillation for vision-language models, analyzing how teacher reliability affects student behavior, which is relevant to multimodal model training.
papers.title: Do As I Do, Not As I Say: On-Policy Distillation Inherits the Teacher in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: On-policy distillation transfers a teacher’s failure modes as well as its knowledge, working well only when the teacher reliably completes student-generated trajectories.

papers.abstract: Compiler transformations interact, making GPU kernel optimization a search for combinations that preserve the computation while improving performance. We introduce HOW TO TRAIN YOUR LITTLE DRAGON, a training method that teaches a small language model both to construct complete optimization scripts and to improve existing ones. Instead of ranking candidates or generating kernel code, our model generates optimization scripts. We devise a compact, lossless representation whose deterministic decoding reconstructs the exact compiler trace, preserving its transformation parameters and dependencies. We use a compiler framework TVM MetaSchedule to build training data on 54,116 distinct workloads, and construct 108,594 examples in two training sets: 60,236 teach the model to generate an optimized script from an unoptimized kernel, while 48,358 teach it to produce a better script given the kernel and a somewhat optimized script. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to construct and improve optimization scripts from these search-derived examples. We then add reinforcement learning with a shaped reward that combines correctness with measured performance, awarding a latency-based bonus only to numerically correct kernels. We apply this training method to a model with 8 billion parameters. After supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model achieves per-attempt correctness of 91.27% for construction and 92.01% for refinement, while reinforcement learning produces faster kernels than supervised training on 88 of 102 construction tasks and 145 of 170 refinement prompts. With only 8B parameters, our LITTLE DRAGON achieves higher per-attempt correctness and better kernel performance than six frontier LLMs: GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3 among them, each with hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, for which task-specific training is unavailable or expensive.
authors: Annabelle Sujun Tang, Wei Tang, Songyao Jiang, Tianhui Li, Shengzhe Xu, Jiin Woo, Kaan Ozkara, Youngsuk Park, Zhen Jia, Hadi Esmaeilzadeh
bullets: Targets compiler-transformation search by generating optimization scripts rather than kernel code or candidate rankings.
Uses a compact lossless representation that deterministically reconstructs exact compiler traces, including parameters and dependencies.
Trains on 108,594 search-derived examples from 54,116 workloads using TVM MetaSchedule.
Combines supervised fine-tuning with correctness-aware, latency-based reinforcement learning.

Reinforcement learning improves kernel speed over supervised training on most evaluated construction and refinement tasks; the 8B model outperforms six much larger frontier LLMs in reported correctness and kernel performance.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a small language model to construct and refine GPU optimization scripts, reducing latency of ML workloads within efficient AI.
papers.title: How to Train Your Little Dragon: Teaching a Small Language Model to Construct and Refine GPU Optimization Scripts
papers.tldr: Little Dragon trains an 8B-parameter language model to construct and refine GPU optimization scripts, achieving high correctness and faster kernels through supervised learning plus reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Executing heavy-duty physical manipulation in unpredictable environments remains a major challenge for quadrupedal robots lacking dedicated manipulators. This paper presents SOMA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for whole-body non-prehensile manipulation of multi-object stacks using a quadruped robot. Unlike traditional methods restricted to two-dimensional planar pushing, SOMA integrates explicit robot base-height control, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This capability enables the quadruped to manipulate complex payload stacks as a unified system while preventing relative sliding or tipping of upper layers. The architecture factorizes control into a high-level manipulation policy using a Simplified Structured State Space Sequence (S5) encoder to reason over long-horizon temporal history and predict bounded target tracking commands via Beta distributions, and a low-level locomotion policy that dynamically adapts leg stance configurations. In extensive simulation benchmarks, SOMA achieves a $90.3\%$ success rate for single-object reposing and up to $90.1\%$ for dynamic two-box stacks under stringent error margins ($0.05\text{ m}$ position error, $1^\circ$ orientation error). Finally, we validate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot across diverse payload masses and geometries, demonstrating active base-height adjustments to maintain traction and balance during heavy pushing tasks.
authors: Stergios E. Bachoumas, Panagiotis Artemiadis
bullets: Addresses heavy-duty manipulation in unpredictable environments for quadrupeds lacking dedicated manipulators.

Explicit base-height control enables three-dimensional non-prehensile pushing while reducing upper-layer sliding and tipping.
In simulation, it achieves 90.3% success for single-object reposing and up to 90.1% for dynamic two-box stacks under strict pose-error limits.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 across varied payload masses and geometries.

papers.abstract: Large multimodal models have achieved remarkable progress by scaling model capacity and training on massive paired multimodal data. However, this paradigm introduces a fundamental bottleneck: aligned multimodal datasets are expensive to curate, difficult to scale across diverse modality combinations, and increasingly constrain further progress. We introduce Modality Self-Play (MSP), a training framework for multimodal foundation models based on proxy-mediated modality composition. Instead of relying on paired cross-modal data, MSP uses anchor-supporting proxy textual descriptions of unseen modalities as semantic bridges during training. Given an observed modality (e.g., image or audio), the model generates proxy descriptions for complementary unseen modalities, which are then encoded and aligned with the observed modality through learned bridges, enabling cross-modal interaction without real paired non-text supervision. Our central hypothesis is that proxy text, combined with contrastively trained pretrained encoders, provides sufficient semantic structure for multimodal composition to emerge. We show that MSP enables zero-shot modality composition: models trained only with a real anchor modality and accompanying proxy descriptions can integrate and reason over multiple modalities at inference time despite never observing real paired non-text data during training. Empirically, MSP achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on multiple multimodal benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate that learned bridges improve alignment, while anchor-supporting proxy descriptions enable effective cross-modal composition. MSP removes the need for real paired non-text (e.g., audio-vision) supervision, while continuing to rely on modality-text pairs, pretrained contrastive encoders, and modality-distribution bridge calibration.
authors: Robert Moseley, Md Kaykobad Reza, Ameya Patil, Edward Ayrapetian, Salman Asif
bullets: Addresses the cost, limited scalability, and modality coverage of curated paired multimodal datasets.
Uses an observed anchor modality to generate proxy descriptions of complementary unseen modalities.
Encodes and aligns observed modalities and proxy text through learned modality bridges and pretrained contrastive encoders.
Enables zero-shot multimodal composition and reasoning at inference despite no real paired non-text supervision during training.
Reports state-of-the-art or competitive benchmark performance; results still depend on modality-text pairs and bridge calibration.

papers.abstract: Existing long-document QA benchmarks rarely combine large-scale human-authored questions with detailed visual evidence annotations, limiting diagnosis of evidence localization and interpretation failures. We present VELD-QA, a large-scale benchmark for Visual Evidence grounding and question answering in Long Documents. It contains 15,000 fully human-authored question-answer pairs across 5,859 real-world PDFs totaling 372,445 pages, balancing chart, table, and complex-layout tasks. Human annotations identify supporting pages and evidence elements and describe cited visual content, enabling separate retrieval and interpretation evaluation. We evaluate nine vision-language models under four evidence settings and seven retrieval-augmented and agentic systems. Our analysis identifies bottlenecks in evidence localization and interpretation. Retrieval-based methods substantially underperform the oracle setting with ground-truth supporting pages; full-document access does not close the gap. Localization alone is insufficient: oracle accuracy peaks at 81.7%, highlighting persistent visual interpretation and reasoning challenges. Enriching inputs with our visual-element annotations narrows the performance gap by 17-24%, demonstrating value beyond evaluation and motivating data enrichment for multimodal document QA. Our code is available at https://github.com/oracle-samples/veld-qa.
authors: Zhivar Sourati, Marianne Menglin Liu, Rongguang Wang, Zheng Wang, Yazhe Hu, Lan Guo, Yuying Wang, Mengqing Guo, Bhavesh Dnyaneshwar Gore, Shubham Pathak, Ramapriya Ranganath, Sandeep Sharma, Tao Sheng, Sujith Ravi, Dan Roth

Annotates supporting pages, evidence elements, and cited visual content, enabling separate evaluation of retrieval and interpretation.
Evaluates nine vision-language models and seven retrieval-augmented or agentic systems across four evidence settings.
Results reveal major bottlenecks in evidence localization and visual interpretation; full-document access does not eliminate the gap to oracle evidence.
Visual-element annotations improve performance and narrow the gap by 17–24%, while oracle accuracy peaks at 81.7%.

papers.abstract: Safety in agentic systems is inherently sequential: whether an action is safe depends on prior actions, tool outputs, information disclosures, and interactions among agents. Recent work has shifted agent safety guardrails from post-hoc trajectory-level assessment toward step-level action diagnosis and proactive risk prediction, yet existing training objectives provide limited supervision for how step evidence accumulates over time and when it becomes sufficient to justify intervention. We propose \methodlong~(ASPO): a training framework for step-level timely intervention. Pre-fix level stage alignment allows crediting each decision at its own step: it compares each response with the other responses sampled at the same prefix and rewards the action that fits the stage, continuing before the risk is visible, asking while clarification can still avert harm, and stopping before harm is irreversible. Adaptive feedback self-distillation further credits the reasoning behind each decision, with the model itself as a teacher that sees the step annotations on intervention steps and rules mined from its own false alarms on safe steps. Its training data carry a violation taxonomy and an intervention window at every step and are extended through self-evolving multi-agent red-teaming. Finally we present \textsc{StepSafe}, a step-level reasoning guardrail with timely intervention, that achieves the state-of-the-art peformance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks on safety-utility pareto curve with Youden's $J$ of 53.0 (4B) against 46.2.
authors: Siyi Gu, Kunhan Gao, Chao Peter Yang, Sukanta Ganguly, Rex Ying, Arman Cohan
bullets: Targets limited supervision for how step-level safety evidence accumulates and when intervention becomes necessary.
Uses pre-fix level stage alignment to evaluate each action against alternatives from the same interaction prefix.
Applies adaptive feedback self-distillation to teach decision reasoning from intervention annotations and false-alarm rules.
Builds training data with violation taxonomies and per-step intervention windows, expanded through multi-agent red-teaming.
Reports state-of-the-art performance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks, with a Youden’s J score of 53.0 for the 4B model versus 46.2.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots in warehouses and production facilities operate in precisely the environments that defeat point-feature visual odometry: featureless aisles, uniform walls, repetitive racking and specular floors. Such environments are, however, rich in straight-edge structure: rack uprights, door frames, wall junctions and cabinet outlines present high-contrast linear edges stable across wide viewpoint changes. A line-feature extension to cuVSLAM, a CUDA-accelerated visual-SLAM system, is presented that recovers this signal. Lines are parameterised as Pl\"ucker coordinates for geometric transport and as the minimal 4-DOF orthonormal representation of Bartoli and Sturm for optimisation; a Cauchy-robust point-to-line residual with analytic Jacobians is folded directly into cuVSLAM's per-frame Gauss-Newton pose solve, and the same line state is jointly refined in the Schur-complement sliding-window bundle adjustment. An adaptive information weight causes lines to assume more of the estimation burden exactly as point features become scarce, and the extension adds residual blocks to existing solvers rather than introducing a second estimator, reducing exactly to the unmodified point pipeline when disabled. Evaluated in RGB-D mode under SE(3) Umeyama alignment with no scale correction, line features reduce mean absolute trajectory error by 38.5% over the 22 sequences of the TUM RGB-D Freiburg3 collection and by 30.1% over the 8 Replica room and office sequences, where median translation error falls by 38.9% and median rotation error by 66.4%, with zero tracking failures in any configuration tested.
authors: Dara Molloy, Terry Wu, Wonju Lee, Abhilash Nand Kumar, David Adley, Conor Ferguson, Hesam Rabeti
bullets: Targets warehouse and production scenes where point features are sparse but straight structural edges remain reliable.
Represents and optimizes line features geometrically, integrating robust point-to-line residuals and analytic Jacobians into cuVSLAM’s pose solver and sliding-window bundle adjustment.
Adaptively increases line-feature influence as point features become scarce.
In RGB-D evaluations, reduced mean absolute trajectory error by 38.5% on TUM RGB-D Freiburg3 and 30.1% on Replica; no tracking failures occurred.
Scope: evaluated on 22 Freiburg3 and 8 Replica sequences under SE(3) alignment without scale correction.

papers.abstract: Decision models answer typed questions about an input with one probability per option, computed in a single forward pass without generating text. Like the fast System 1 of dual-process theory, they answer at once, but their depth is fixed at training time, so they spend the same computation on easy and hard questions. Models that reason in generated text can think longer, but they pay for every extra step in decoded tokens. We present LEV, a decision model that thinks deeper by rerunning its layers in a loop instead of generating tokens. LEV builds on a language model pretrained as a loop, reads the options after every loop step and trains all steps jointly, so one checkpoint can answer at any depth. On three looped backbones, accuracy rises with depth on the same weights, mostly on hard questions, and a 2.6B LEV goes from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench. On-demand depth, set per question by a small stopper with a threshold fitted on unlabelled requests, saves 15% to 24% of the computation at a cost of under one accuracy point, level with or slightly above a fixed mix of depths. On a locked test set, the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense (non-looped) models and cascades of the same latency below 50 ms.
authors: Dingjie Song, Zhiling Yan, Yuxuan Zhang, Lichao Sun
bullets: Decision models answer typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass but use fixed computation for every question.
LEV reads answer options after each loop and trains all loop depths jointly, allowing one checkpoint to answer at different depths.
Accuracy increases with loop depth, especially on hard questions; a 2.6B model improves from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench.
A learned stopper saves 15–24% computation with less than one accuracy-point cost, using thresholds fitted on unlabeled requests.
On a locked test set, 1.4B and 3B LEV models outperform same-latency dense models and cascades by 5.4–8.8 points below 50 ms.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel architectural approach (looped decision models) for LLMs to balance speed and depth, fitting the large language models subtopic.
papers.title: LEV: Thinking Fast and Deep with Looped Decision Models
papers.tldr: LEV enables decision models to think longer by looping the same layers, improving hard-question accuracy while optionally reducing computation through adaptive stopping.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has driven rapid progress in mathematics, coding, and tool use, but scaling this success to GUI agents remains challenging due to the high cost of interactive environments and the scarcity of realistic training tasks. We introduce MAI-Gym, an open all-in-one platform that unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments. Through a shared rollout pipeline, MAI-Gym ensures consistent agent behavior across evaluation and training, supports ten established benchmarks, and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances. Beyond scalable infrastructure, MAI-Gym enables automated synthesis of diverse GUI applications and challenging tasks, including resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated task verifiers. Using MAI-Gym, we train MAI-Gym-9B, a unified 9B agent for mobile and computer use, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open GUI agents under 10B parameters: 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified. Importantly, RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transfers to its real-world counterpart, improving task success on a phys- ical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%. We release the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint to support repro- ducible research and further advances in scalable GUI agent training.
authors: Panrong Tong, Quyu Kong, Pengxiang Li, Tianyu Xia, Hanzhang Zhou, Lei Wang, Chenglin Cai, Long Li, Long Chen, Jianan Zhang, Zhengwen Zeng, Xu Zhang, Gongjie Zhang, Yue Wang, Steven Hoi
bullets: Unifies evaluation, data collection, and online RL through a shared rollout pipeline across ten benchmarks.
Scales to 20,000 parallel environments and synthesizes diverse apps and execution-validated tasks, including cross-app worlds.
Trains MAI-Gym-9B, a unified mobile-and-computer agent, reporting strong open-agent results under 10B parameters.
RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transfers to its real counterpart, raising physical-phone task success from 28.8% to 48.1%.
Releases the framework, synthesis tools, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and model checkpoint for reproducible research.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents rely on context compaction: when the interaction history outgrows the context window, a compressor replaces it with a natural-language summary. We show that these summaries contain more than a record of what happened. Compaction prompts ask for decisions and next steps, so each summary mixes facts established by the environment with reasoning written by the compressor, and the agent cannot tell the two apart afterwards. In an analysis of a widely used structured compressor, 83% of failed runs trace back to an action that carries out a specific summary entry, most of which no environment output supports. We propose Source-Judged Compaction (SJC), a training-free post-processing step that scores each summary entry for whether it has a source in the environment outputs or the previous summary, and removes the entries that do not. It changes neither the agent nor the compressor and adds one inexpensive judge request per compaction. The judge is Jev, a non-generative decision model that answers the source question with a calibrated probability instead of text. On AppWorld and OfficeBench with two agent models, SJC improves cross-run reliability over the underlying compressor by 2.1%-8.9% without increasing the agent's token usage.
authors: Guanghui Min, Chen Chen
bullets: Long-horizon agents’ summaries mix environment-grounded facts with compressor-generated decisions and next steps.
In an analysis of a structured compressor, 83% of failed runs involved actions based on specific summary entries, usually unsupported by environment output.
SJC scores each entry for a source in environment outputs or the previous summary, then removes unsupported entries.
It is training-free, adds one inexpensive judge request per compaction, and uses a calibrated decision model rather than generating text.
Across AppWorld and OfficeBench with two agent models, SJC improves cross-run reliability by 2.1%–8.9%.

papers.abstract: Agent skills turn procedural knowledge into reusable artifacts, allowing LLM agents to accumulate and refine expertise through experience. Building on this, skill evolution iteratively improves skills using execution feedback. However, improvement may require several interdependent edits, so low-reward versions can still be worth developing. Requiring immediate reward gains can discard useful partial repairs before their benefits emerge. Non-elitist evolution allows new versions to receive further edits despite scoring below earlier ones. For agent skills, this calls for evidence of what to preserve and repair next. We introduce SkillNEO (Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization for Agent Skills), which separately selects a version to use and versions to keep improving. Comparing how related versions perform the same task reveals working steps to preserve and remaining failures to fix. It can also revisit and revise earlier versions using later evidence. Across 86 SkillsBench tasks in eight domains, including software engineering and office work, SkillNEO raises GPT-5.4 Mini's average reward from 49.1% to 66.4%, within GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna's original-skill range. Mini executes tasks, proposes revisions, and edits skills; final evaluation uses the same task instances. Gains span all eight domains. The same skills improve stronger models without further editing. On the 41 tasks with modified skills, reuse improves Luna by 10.5 percentage points and places GPT-5.5 10.6 points above its published original-skill reference. Execution records show these skills can benefit stronger models even when Mini still fails some task requirements. Search histories also show lower-scoring versions leading to skills ultimately selected for use. Together, these findings show that skill evolution can turn a weaker model's partial progress into reusable procedural knowledge for improving more capable agents.

papers.abstract: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.
authors: Anutam Srinivasan, Siddhant Panse, Glen Chou
bullets: Addresses conservative robust adaptive control that ignores guaranteed future parameter learning and struggles with high-dimensional robots.
Uses system-level synthesis to forecast parameter uncertainty and preserve correlations among disturbances, parameter errors, and estimate updates.
Builds tighter guaranteed reachable sets that incorporate expected information gain during planning.
Demonstrates real-time scalability on nonlinear robots, including whole-body control for a 61-state quadruped.
Validates online dynamics learning and stabilization on a physical Crazyflie drone.

papers.abstract: Occupancy predictors rely on large persistent banks of Gaussians or learned queries whose size is fixed by hand. Common pruning proxies, such as opacity, activation frequency, or parameter magnitude, do not measure whether removing a row changes the model's voxel decisions. We introduce Decision-FLIP, a budget-free compilation framework whose scoring and structure selection need only unlabeled calibration inputs. Exact Mean-FLIP scores each persistent row by the number of voxel argmax decisions that change when the row is removed from the readout; a guarded Otsu split of the log-score distribution selects the survivor count without a target and abstains when the split is unsupported; and the survivors are physically compiled into a smaller checkpoint, so camera sampling, attention, and aggregation shrink with the bank. For streaming banks, scores are integrated over each row's lifecycle through warp, death, and refill. Across four Gaussian-bank model-dataset settings and one persistent-query transfer, the automatically selected cuts remove 12-79% of eligible rows and cut bank/query-dependent latency by 7-45% across settings with component profiles, with whole-model savings of up to 8.0% on the primary endpoints bounded by fixed-cost image, voxel, and sensor modules and peak-memory savings of up to 16.6%. Under matched one-epoch recovery controls, semantic mIoU changes by at most 0.18 point. Same-$K$ controls show that the ranking, not only the bank size, matters: random removal collapses GaussianFormer-1 and OccFormer, while label-free Mean-FLIP matches or outperforms supervised Taylor ranking on all five settings where that control was run. The method applies when removable primitives keep a stable checkpoint-row identity; it is budget-free in survivor count, not parameter-free.
authors: Jingxing Li, Anurag Paul, Subhasis Das, Cindy Xu
bullets: Scores each persistent row by how many voxel argmax decisions change when it is removed, rather than using opacity, activation, or parameter magnitude.
A guarded Otsu split selects survivors automatically and abstains when the score distribution does not support a reliable split.
Across five model–dataset settings, it removes 12–79% of eligible rows, reducing bank/query-dependent latency by 7–45% and peak memory by up to 16.6%.
With matched one-epoch recovery, semantic mIoU changes by at most 0.18 point; ranking quality matters, as random removal can collapse models.
Applies to removable primitives with stable checkpoint-row identities; it is budget-free in survivor count, not parameter-free.

papers.abstract: Distillation of reasoning chains from Large Language Models (LLMs) into their smaller siblings is a standard training approach. Frequently, researchers do not have full access to a teacher model and its internal representations, which limits the resulting performance. We propose a recursive offline distillation method combining two components: entropy-based sampling for selective distillation and answer mixing. Specifically, for three open models (3-4B), at each epoch, we sample reasoning chains weighted by entropy difference with an auxiliary medium model (70-72B) and, next, supplement thinking traces with single-token ground truth answers. Our approach consistently outperforms naive distillation with comparable data budgets ($57.15 \pm 1.01$ vs 51.61 on average) and offers a much steeper learning curve. Additionally, we present a comparative analysis of methods to generate and normalize distillation traces.

bullets: Addresses distillation when full teacher access and internal representations are unavailable.
Uses entropy-difference sampling with an auxiliary 70–72B model to select reasoning chains each epoch.
Mixes reasoning traces with single-token ground-truth answers in a recursive offline process.
Across three 3–4B open models, it reports higher average performance than naive distillation under comparable data budgets: 57.15 ± 1.01 vs. 51.61.
Also compares methods for generating and normalizing distillation traces.

papers.abstract: Dementia affects millions of older adults worldwide, yet early detection remains difficult outside clinical settings. Traditional models primarily rely on text or voice-based responses, capturing only a limited view of human cognition despite the inherently multimodal nature of human expression. This work proposes a contactless, multimodal screening framework that leverages video, audio, and text signals collected during structured voice-based interactions with Amazon Alexa. By incorporating these modalities, our approach captures a more holistic representation of human behavior encompassing speech patterns, vocal characteristics, facial expressions, and linguistic structure, which may enable more accurate detection of cognitive decline. Different participants completed three conversational tasks designed to probe spontaneous speech, comprehension, and recall. We pursued three objectives: (1) evaluate which of the three Alexa tasks provides the most informative cognitive signals, (2) compare the effectiveness of unimodal models, and (3) assess the benefits of multimodal fusion models. Task-level analysis shows that the video model achieves its best performance on Command-Reading, with an accuracy of 0.65 (AUC 0.69), while the audio model performs best on Question-Answering, reaching an accuracy of 0.67 (AUC 0.73). In contrast, the multimodal model demonstrates consistently stable performance across tasks, achieving an accuracy of 0.76 (AUC 0.75) on Command-Reading and 0.76 (AUC 0.73) on Question-Answering. These findings demonstrate that multimodal behavioral cues captured through naturalistic interactions can reliably distinguish MCI from healthy aging, highlighting the limitations of traditional diagnostic paradigms and supporting the shift toward multimodal, real-world cognitive assessment frameworks.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative to costly robot demonstra- tions, yet transferring their manipulation priors to robot control remains chal- lenging. The commonly adopted retargeting-based approaches convert human wrist and finger poses into embodiment-specific action commands through hand- crafted geometric mappings. However, such mappings require meticulous recal- ibration across different embodiments and risk propagating hand-tracking errors into downstream robot control pipelines. To this end, we propose EgoJEPA, a three-stage framework that learns embodiment-agnostic representations from ego- centric human videos without rule-based human-to-robot retargeting: 1) Human- action pre-training learns effect-aware latent actions through JEPA-style visual prediction conditioned on hand-motion differences; 2) Latent-action-based world modeling jointly predicts future visual dynamics and latent actions, which decou- ples human prior pre-training from robot-specific control parameterizations; 3) Embodiment-specific tuning adapts the pretrained model to diverse robots through lightweight action adapters. Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of EgoJEPA. It achieves a 74% average success rate under the out-of-domain evalu- ation, compared with 65% for the retargeting baseline, while reducing cumulative cross-embodiment wall-clock cost by 47.2%, from 743.2 to 392.7 hours.
authors: Meng Cao, Can Zhao, Jinjie Wei, Haonan Zhao, Yulong Zhang, Duo Han, Xiaofan Li, Ziwu Song, Rongtao Xu, Ruyi Gan, Hao Wang, Qian Wang, Daolin Ma, Ian Reid, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Addresses the calibration burden and error propagation of human-to-robot retargeting.
Pre-trains effect-aware latent actions with JEPA-style visual prediction conditioned on hand-motion differences.
Learns a latent-action world model that predicts future visual dynamics and actions independently of robot-specific controls.
Uses lightweight action adapters for embodiment-specific tuning across different robots.
On five real-world tasks and three embodiments, reports 74% average out-of-domain success and a 47.2% reduction in cumulative cross-embodiment wall-clock cost versus retargeting.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the EgoJEPA framework. Stage 1: An effect-aware latent action space is learned from ego-centric human video data without embodiment-specific action re-targeting. Specifically, the predictor Pϕ predicts the future representation ẑt+H from the visual context encoded by Eθ and the hand-motion differences ∆mt:t+H−1 encoded by Aψ; Stage 2: A world-action model Wω is trained on ego-centric human video data via joint flow matching to model future visual dynamics and latent human actions extracted by the frozen action encoder Aψ; Stage 3: Using robot demonstration data, the learned action representation is grounded in a target robot embodiment by inserting embodiment-specific input and output adapters Dηr into the action branch, which map between relative robot actions and the shared latent action space.

Figure 1: Training efficiency and scalability of EgoJEPA v.s. retargeting. (a) The retargeting pipeline requires embodiment-specific human-to-robot mappings and repeated calibration, whereas EgoJEPA learns an embodiment-agnostic latent action space in Stages 1–2 and performs embodiment-specific grounding only in Stage 3; (b) Cumulative training cost across robot embodiments. Reusing the embodiment-agnostic models from Stages 1–2 reduces the per-embodiment adaptation overhead of EgoJEPA relative to the retargeting pipeline.

papers.abstract: Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation. Given the task of using a knife to "slice bread," a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for "hand[ing] the knife over," it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff. Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner. Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task- informed prior. This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%. We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects
authors: Manav Kulshrestha, Apoorva Vashisth, Damon Conover, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses limitations of 2D, task-agnostic, and manually annotated task-specific grasping methods.
Uses vision-language reasoning to infer semantic affordances from the task and object geometry.
Refines the task-informed grasp prior with 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency.
Reports a 94% success rate on TaskGrasp, compared with 74% for the best baseline.
Demonstrates zero-shot generalization to real-world objects on a Franka Research 3 robot.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of TGrasp6D. Given a single RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction, a vision-language model identifies and localizes the task-relevant affordance and predicts an image-space grasp orientation. These cues are lifted into 3D to form a task-informed grasp prior, from which candidate 6DoF grasps are sampled and refined for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency, yielding the final task-oriented grasp.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison of different 6DoF TOG approaches on objects from the TaskGrasp [9] dataset. For each method, we show 5 task-oriented grasps per object. Compared to other approaches, our TGrasp6D produces more successful grasps across diverse object types and tasks. For cases like “scoop[ing]” with the “spoon,” most approaches generate feasible grasps. However, performance drops sharply for more challenging cases like doing a “handover” with the “measuring cup.” Of note, compared to the pure vision-language prior (f), grasp-pose refinement (g) appears to visually diversify grasps by generating feasible stable and task-consistent alternates. In some cases, like the “measuring cup,” it even recovers some failures despite noise and missing points due to occlusion in the object point-cloud.

Fig. 1: Example of TGrasp6D producing distinct 6DoF grasps for different tasks on the same real-world object. “handover” task results in grasps that keep the handle clear whereas tasks like “pound” and “cook” that require holding the hammer and pan from the handle are reflected.

Fig. 4: Analysis of failure modes, including the effect of grasp refinement for GPT-5.5. Note the y-axis breaks between 4%-10% and 12%-19% to accommodate Gemini-3.7 (11.0%) and Qwen3.5-35B (19.7%) without compressing the smaller values.

TABLE I: Comparison with baseline methods. Note that fOE and fPE are reported only for grasps marked as failures. All baseline results use unmodified author-released code and, where available, author-provided pretrained weights; we do not alter any baseline’s inference pipeline.
TABLE II: Real-robot task-oriented grasping success rate comparison.

papers.title: TGrasp6D: Task-Informed Vision-Language Priors and Pose Refinement enable Zero-Shot Task-Oriented 6DoF Grasping
papers.tldr: TGrasp6D generates task-appropriate 6DoF robot grasps zero-shot from a task description and one RGB-D image, achieving strong simulated and real-world performance.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning language models on narrowly defined harmful tasks can induce emergent misalignment (EM) across unrelated domains. While prior work has identified shared misalignment-associated representations across independently fine-tuned models, it remains unclear whether these models rely on common computational components. We investigate this question using three LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct trained on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations. Using direction-based activation tracing, we identify three attention-head locations shared among the five highest-ranked heads of all three organisms. Replacing each organism's five selected head contributions with Base contributions reduces free-generation EM from 38.9% to 22.9% for medical, 50.7% to 12.5% for finance, and 41.7% to 11.1% for sports, outperforming layer-matched random interventions without reducing judged coherence. Cross-organism activation transfer further shows that the shared heads exhibit partially interchangeable effects on fixed-response preference. These findings provide evidence that representational convergence in EM extends to shared, causally relevant attention-head components within a common model architecture.
authors: Muhammad Haseeb, Muhammad Tahir
bullets: Three LoRA fine-tunes targeted harmful medical, financial, and extreme-sports advice.
Direction-based activation tracing found three attention-head locations shared among the top five heads across all models.
Replacing selected head contributions with base-model activations reduced free-generation misalignment while preserving judged coherence.
Cross-model activation transfer suggested these shared heads have partially interchangeable effects on response preferences.
The evidence is specific to these fine-tunes and the shared Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct architecture.

papers.abstract: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment remains a critical bottleneck in dementia care, demanding scalable tools capable of capturing subtle behavioral decay. To capture the subtle temporal changes of cognitive decline, we introduce a behavioral dataset collected across seven unscripted multimodal interactions over an 18-month horizon. This dataset formalizes continuous, multi-session interactions into a dense 4D tensor (Batch * Session * Time * Feature) that explicitly preserves concurrent local dynamics alongside long-term changes. To effectively process these complex behavioral patterns, we propose CogDrift-4D: a novel, hierarchical 4D Transformer framework. To capture the complex trajectory of cognitive decline, CogDrift-4D implements a dual-level behavioral fatigue and drift modeling architecture. At the intra-session level, the model computes localized least-squares regression slopes to quantify the acute ``fading'' of frame-level facial action units and acoustic energy. At the inter-session level, a recursive cross-attention feedback encoder acts as a cumulative fatigue accumulator, mapping the patient's continuous behavioral drift across successive sessions. To mitigate environmental noise and track failures across sessions, a localized Quality Gate dynamically filters low-integrity features before final fusion, also an early fusion that integrates semantic insights with raw physical dynamics. Evaluated on structured verbal and linguistic interactions, our architecture successfully detects MCI with a classification accuracy of 0.733 +- 0.13 and an F1-score of 0.716 +- 0.14, outperforming advanced baselines. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, scalable, and robust foundation for home-based, real-time dementia screening.
authors: Sankalp Vaish, Sumukh Veeramalla, Rishank Singh, Caroline Summerour, John A. Batsis, Xiaohui Liang
bullets: Introduces a behavioral dataset spanning seven unscripted multimodal interactions over 18 months.
Represents continuous sessions as a dense Batch × Session × Time × Feature 4D tensor.
Uses hierarchical modeling: intra-session regression slopes capture acute behavioral fading, while inter-session cross-attention accumulates longitudinal drift.
A localized Quality Gate filters low-integrity features and fuses semantic information with physical behavioral dynamics.
On structured verbal and linguistic interactions, achieves 0.733 ± 0.13 accuracy and 0.716 ± 0.14 F1; scope is limited to the reported interaction setting.

papers.abstract: Vehicles that lose control at the handling limit through icing, hydroplaning, or an abrupt evasive maneuver fall outside the operating envelope of production safety systems such as electronic stability control, which focus on preventing instability rather than recovering from it. Expert drivers regain authority in these conditions by drifting. Existing autonomous recovery approaches are validated on idealized scenarios, define "recovered" states empirically and inconsistently, or rely on offline-planned trajectories rather than acting online. We address these gaps by first training a racing policy with reinforcement learning that learns drifting as a time-optimal maneuver, then adapting it to recovery through continued training with a minimum-time reward. We define recovery relative to a phase-plane-grounded stable equilibrium and introduce Gym-Khana for controller training and evaluation. Across 294 initial loss-of-control states, the transferred policy improves recovery by 186.8% over a Stanley path tracker and outperforms both a nonlinear model predictive controller and a recovery-only policy trained from scratch, while also recovering faster on states the baseline can already handle. An ablation shows that racing pretraining, rather than broader initial-state exposure alone, drives this gain. Deployed on a physical 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle using system identification, actuator-lag modelling, and domain randomization, the transferred policy outperforms Stanley on every tested loss-of-control state, including recovering 50% of the time from a hard state the baseline never recovers from.
authors: Teodor Ilie, Kleber Cabral, Sidney Givigi
bullets: Targets failures beyond production electronic stability control, including icing, hydroplaning, and abrupt evasive maneuvers.
Pretrains a policy to drift as a time-optimal racing maneuver, then adapts it for recovery with continued minimum-time training.
Defines recovery using a phase-plane-grounded stable equilibrium and introduces Gym-Khana for training and evaluation.
Across 294 simulated initial states, the transferred policy improves recovery by 186.8% over a Stanley path tracker and outperforms nonlinear MPC and recovery-only training.
On a 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle, it outperforms Stanley on every tested state and recovers 50% of the time from a state the baseline never recovers from.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of the approach. 1. Its actor πrace is transferred unchanged to the recovery task, and its critic is reinitialized. 3. The resulting πrace→rec is deployed on the physical F1TENTH vehicle. Before deployment, system identification, actuator-lag modelling and domain randomization adapt the simulator to the vehicle, and the controller is retrained on it from racing onwards (Sections IV-D and VI). papers.abstract: Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.
authors: Wei-Jer Chang, Zhouchonghao Wu, Akshay Rangesh, Weixin Li, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Wei Zhan
bullets: Addresses the need for realistic multi-agent traffic behavior without relying on human driving demonstrations or logged trajectories.
Jointly trains heterogeneous road users from random initialization using type-specific dynamics and objectives, procedural scenarios, and per-agent randomization.
Outperforms demonstration-free and prior demonstration-assisted self-play baselines on WOSAC while controlling all three road-user types.
Policies trained on nuPlan map geometry maintain comparable realism in zero-shot Waymo evaluation and outperform compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark.
Ablations show that heterogeneous self-play improves both realism and planning, especially in interaction-heavy scenarios.

Each type uses its own dynamics model: jerk-integrated Ackermann dynamics for vehicles, unicycle dynamics for pedestrians, and kinematic bicycle dynamics for cyclists.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification against the target. At ultra-long context it stops paying, because a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup it was meant to provide first erodes and then reverses. The standard response is to build a long-context drafter, by training or fine-tuning one, or by using a multi-token-prediction head shipped inside the target checkpoint. We argue this is unnecessary, because the drafters in use are target-conditioned, reading hidden states the target computed over the entire prefix, so distant context already reaches them without their own attention, and verification corrects what they miss. We therefore freeze released short-context drafters and run them far past their training length under two inference-time mechanisms, one bounding the attention cache they see, which fixes their cost, and one re-basing their rotary position indices into the trained range. No weight is touched and the only tunable saturates early, so one vLLM-side configuration spans 4k to two million tokens, costing at most 0.16x of speedup at short length. We prove when a common index shift leaves the drafter's computation exactly unchanged, and decompose acceptance into two measurable gaps with sharp bounds. Whatever speedup a frozen drafter delivers at short context, it retains out to two million tokens, across three target-drafter pairs and five corpora. The claim concerns the flatness rather than the multiple, and removing either mechanism eliminates it. The gain is conditional on the speculative cost per emitted token staying below the matched target-only cost.
authors: Aref Jafari, Vansh Bhatia, Matt Qin, Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury, Ben Lee, Vikram Appia, Ali Ghodsi, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh
bullets: Long-context drafting becomes uneconomical when the drafter attends over the full prefix.
The approach freezes existing drafters and uses bounded attention-cache visibility plus rotary-position re-basing, with no weight updates.
A single vLLM-side configuration covers 4k–2M-token contexts; tuning saturates early and costs at most 0.16× short-context speedup.
Across three target–drafter pairs and five corpora, the drafter retains its short-context speedup up to two million tokens.
The result concerns stable speedup rather than its absolute magnitude and depends on speculative decoding remaining cheaper per emitted token than target-only decoding.

papers.abstract: Negation is a fundamental aspect of language understanding and it is important vision-language models (VLMs) are able to process it effectively. We investigate how VLMs process negation by analysing attention patterns of different models. We draw comparisons between human gaze and attention in models when processing affirmative vs negated statements. We compare object level model attention to human eye-fixations in both binary and multary settings, evaluating with both synthetic and realistic datasets. We find models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention. While layerwise analysis shows that PaliGemma2-3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism. Additionally, we find that LLaVA-1.5-7B displays a spatial bias towards left-side objects. Our evaluation of models on downstream tasks shows that all models have a discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions highlighting the need to better understand the underlying processing of negation to close this performance gap. All evaluated models perform differently on affirmative versus negated downstream questions, highlighting a persistent negation-processing gap.

papers.abstract: Skill-policy co-evolution, in which an agent's policy model and its skill bank improve each other during training, is a promising paradigm for self-improving agents. Current evaluations score the co-evolved policy on the final bank it trained with (the delivered bank). After deployment, however, skills may be rewritten, added or removed more frequently than the policy model is retrained, leaving the policy to operate on a drifted skill bank that neither the training objective nor existing evaluation protocols address. In this paper, we first establish, through theoretical and empirical analysis, that the fragility hidden by this blind spot is not incidental. The acceptance rule these methods share (cooperative acceptance) ties a policy's competence to the bank it co-evolved with, leaving it fragile once skills drift, regardless of the implementation; empirically, sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution training proceeds. We therefore introduce the CO-evolution Drift Audit (CODA), a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol that simulates skill drift and, alongside success rate under worst-case drift, introduces two new metrics: a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four co-evolution methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5-13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52-93% of the delivered bank's gain over the no-skill baseline. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution, from peak performance on the co-evolved bank to the ability to harness skills however they evolve, and provides a shared standard against which future methods can be audited.
authors: Yujie Feng, Xiaobin Wang, Jinluan Yang, Xiaonan Shi, Pengjun Xie, Philip S. Yu, Xiaoming Wu, Jieping Ye
bullets: Existing evaluations test policies only on the skill bank used during co-evolution, overlooking post-deployment drift.
Theoretical and empirical analysis shows cooperative acceptance intrinsically couples policy competence to its co-evolved bank.
CODA simulates skill drift and measures worst-case success, consistency under meaning-preserving edits, and resistance to corrupted skills.
Across four methods and five benchmarks, drift reduced success by 5–13 points and erased 52–93% of gains over no-skill baselines.
The protocol shifts evaluation from peak performance on a fixed bank to robustness as skills evolve.

papers.abstract: Map generation tasks feature extensive non-structural vectorized data (e.g., points, polylines, and polygons) and thus pose significant challenges to common pixel-wise generative models. Conventional approaches use multiple stages, first segmenting these features at the pixel level and then performing vectorized post-processing, with errors and complexity compounding at each stage. Motivated by the recent success of auto-regressive language modeling, we propose the first map foundation model, named Map Auto-Regressor (MARS), that is capable of generating both multi-polyline road networks and polygon buildings in a unified manner. For training MARS, we collected to our knowledge the largest multi-class map extraction dataset totaling 3.4M examples, which we call MAP-3M. Across four road and building datasets, MARS outperforms or matches the performance of multistage baselines. Additionally, we develop a "Chat with MARS" capability that enables interactive human-in-the-loop map generation and correction, supported by the auto-regressive nature of our end-to-end approach. We release our MAP-3M dataset and project demo page at (1) https://huggingface.co/datasets/bag-lab/MAP-3M and (2) https://huggingface.co/spaces/bag-lab/MARS, respectively.
authors: Qi Zhang, Suvam Bag, Rupanjali Kukal, Lucas Thai, Jacob Kovarskiy, Mike Bianco, Xiaojie Guo, Raphael Tang, Mikael Figueroa, Rishi Madhok, Nikolaos Karianakis, Fuxun Yu

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.
authors: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi, Usha Bhalla, Thomas Icard, Matt Feiszli, Thomas McGrath, Vasudev Shyam, Demba Ba, Leon Bergen, Nina Miolane, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Matthew Kowal, Thomas Fel
bullets: Maps seven task-relevant concepts using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions.
Finds geometries are predominantly multi-dimensional and reflect the constraints under which the robot acts.
Shows joint limits turn wrist orientation into an open arc, while target distance forms separate coarse- and fine-scale subspaces.
Observes similar geometries across two additional VLAs using real-world robot data, suggesting the patterns are not model- or simulation-specific.
Demonstrates that understanding a concept’s geometry enables targeted activation steering.

Instead of rolling about the gripper’s approach axis, we tilt the gripper 30◦ off that axis and orbit the tilt about the vertical. The gripper position is held fixed within 5 cm while the whole arm reconfigures, and we record activations at each step. The arm’s joint limits (clipped to the 1st to 99th training percentile) stop the orbit partway: sweeping both directions from the start covers −70◦ to +158◦ (228◦ of the turn; angles are the realized rotation about the vertical axis). papers.abstract: Damage-recovery algorithms often rank gaits from short trials, yet a gait that performs well briefly may not remain effective during continued execution. In reset-free recovery, each trial also changes the physical state inherited by the next. We introduce persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR), which predicts multiple outcomes over repeated gait execution and uses conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot. Across 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and slot-averaged recovery quality (SRQ) by 0.044 relative to an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final-quality gains occur in all three damage classes. Against no adaptation, PGRR also improves final quality and reduces low-quality failures, whereas the aggregate SRQ difference is inconclusive. Development ablations identify conservative uncertainty handling as the clearest supported contributor to the observed gains. These results show that PGRR can identify stronger post-damage gaits under continuous physical state and that final-gait quality and recovery-summary performance provide complementary evidence for evaluating reset-free recovery.
authors: Minjoong Kim
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between short-trial gait rankings and long-term gait effectiveness after irreversible leg damage.
Uses persistent outcome profiles and conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot.
Evaluated across 108 MuJoCo tasks involving leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock.
Improved final gait quality and reduced low-quality failures versus an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline; gains appeared across all damage classes.
Ablations most strongly supported conservative uncertainty handling, while aggregate SRQ improvement versus no adaptation was inconclusive.

papers.abstract: Evaluator-guided reasoning presents a local control problem at every step: trust the current answer, return a fallback, or spend more inference. We formulate this choice as a compute-aware three-action controller, scoring terminal actions by predicted answer success and expansion by a rollout-based continuation-success surrogate, with compute cost priced explicitly. A local action-gap analysis characterizes when score errors can change a decision, while an expected regret bound accounts for errors along the realized expansion path. Guided by this analysis, we learn and calibrate action-specific confidence estimates, with local uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. On held-out width expansion and revision tasks, the controller improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16%, respectively. Across four Qwen3-8B seeds, compute is lower than fitted Q in both settings, while utility differences are small and mixed. The results frame evaluator-guided reasoning as resource allocation under uncertainty, rather than a uniformly stronger reasoner.
authors: Weida Liang, Kenji Kawaguchi
bullets: Formulates inference control as a compute-aware three-action decision problem.
Scores terminal actions by predicted success and expansion by rollout-based continuation success, with explicit compute costs.
Uses action-gap analysis, pathwise regret bounds, calibrated action confidence, and uncertainty penalties to guide decisions.
Improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16% on two task types.
Results across four Qwen3-8B seeds show lower compute than fitted Q, but only small and mixed utility differences.

papers.abstract: Despite their extensive pretraining knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) struggle to adaptively gather information in experimental design tasks. We study how to amortize sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) into an LLM by explicitly training the reasoning that guides action selection using information-gain rewards. Our approach specifies the experimental generative model independently of the LLM's own beliefs, allowing us to optimize expected information gain under a model of our choosing. We investigate the design choices for amortization, including alternative generative-model constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and computational costs relative to training- and inference-time BED baselines. On Twenty Questions, the resulting policies improve information acquisition and task performance, outperform inference- and training-time BED baselines at substantially lower computational cost, and generalize to unseen categories. We further demonstrate positive transfer from Twenty Questions training to Medi-Q, a real-world clinical dialogue benchmark. These results suggest that information gathering can be learned as a generalizable reasoning skill in LLMs.
authors: Anita Kriz, Antonin Berthon, Nicol\'as Astorga, Mihaela van der Schaar
bullets: LLMs often struggle to adaptively select informative actions despite strong reasoning and pretrained knowledge.
The method amortizes sequential Bayesian experimental design by training reasoning with information-gain rewards under an independently specified generative model.
The study evaluates generative-model design, reward estimation, hypothesis spaces, multi-step objectives, and computational costs.
On Twenty Questions, the learned policies improve information acquisition and task performance, generalize to unseen categories, and use less computation than BED baselines.
Training on Twenty Questions transfers positively to the real-world Medi-Q clinical dialogue benchmark.

papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation requires chain-of-thought (CoT) data with correct answers, but obtaining such data efficiently remains challenging. Forward CoT generation (FCG) followed by rejection sampling (RS) produces verified, question-only responses, yet may require many teacher calls for difficult problems. Reverse CoT generation (RCG) is cheaper because it conditions on the known answer, but access to this answer can lead to post-hoc rationalization and a mismatch with the student's answer-free inference setting. We propose CoTranslator, which learns to translate reverse CoT responses toward the distribution of verified forward responses. Trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward responses, it supports large-scale generation and verification of student training data. Across six student models evaluated on six mathematics benchmarks, CoTranslator improves average accuracy over semantic suppression by up to $5.82$ percentage points. For two 4B students, it retains $95.0\%$ of rejection sampling's average accuracy while using $35.9\%$ of its estimated compute. Without retraining, the same translator transfers to a new mathematics dataset, a different teacher, and STEM problems, improving average STEM accuracy by $4.88$ and $4.31$ percentage points for 4B and 8B students, respectively. These results show that CoTranslator offers an efficient and transferable approach to reasoning distillation.
authors: Zinan Tang, Zhuoshi Pan, Kairui Chen, Ze Yan, Shaomian Zheng, Yukun Zhang, Gang Wang, Biqing Huang
bullets: Problem: Forward CoT generation with rejection sampling is costly, while reverse CoT can rationalize from known answers and mismatch student inference.
Method: Train a translator on a small set of paired reverse and verified forward responses, then use it to generate and verify large-scale distillation data.
Results: Across six student models and six math benchmarks, it improves accuracy over semantic suppression by up to 5.82 percentage points.
Efficiency: For 4B students, it retains 95.0% of rejection sampling’s average accuracy using 35.9% of its estimated compute.
Transferability: Without retraining, it improves STEM accuracy by 4.88 points for 4B students and 4.31 points for 8B students on new settings.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether per-layer, per-task-phase (prompt/reasoning/response) expert-routing statistics in a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model can guide layer-wise mixed-precision quantization of routed-expert FFN tensors (down/gate and up). To attain layerwise routing statistics, we build a routing-capture and profiling pipeline for Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp, derive a composite sensitivity score from routing entropy/decisiveness, coefficient of variation (CV), Jaccard/phase-fragility, and top-1 expert strength, and use coordinate descent to tune a layer allocation that respects a fixed average bits-per-weight budget. Notably, the profiling pipeline is applicable to standard top-k MoE architectures. Across independent experimental conditions (about 4.0 bpw flat, about 2.7 bpw steep, and about 2.7 bpw random allocation as a control), reallocation fails to outperform the uniform baseline within each quality tier. In the flat regime, reallocation is statistically neutral (z about 0.9). For the steep tier, the random reallocation performs within 1 SE of the routing-guided reallocation at the same tier, indicating a structural loss at this quality rung caused by mandatory downgrades and Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) tail injection. This aggressive-budget condition shows a decisive loss (z greater than 4 SE) replicated across three independent weight vectors. We argue that the deeper issue is that routing-behavior statistics are an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.
authors: Yifan Liu
bullets: The study tests whether routing entropy, decisiveness, variability, phase fragility, and top-1 expert strength can guide layer-wise bit allocation.
A routing-capture pipeline profiles Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp and uses coordinate descent under fixed average bit budgets.
Routing-guided reallocation does not outperform uniform allocation in the tested quality tiers; at the flatter budget it is statistically neutral.
At the aggressive budget, mandatory downgrades and KLD-tail injection cause a replicated quality loss, while random reallocation performs similarly to routing-guided allocation.
The results suggest routing behavior is an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.

papers.abstract: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .
