papers.abstract: A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi-agent robotics: N agents, each covering a disc of radius r, spread over a probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent's disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least-squares variance propagation plus a delta-method term for the uncertain arrival time, agreeing with simulation to within 1.8%. The coverage probability of a packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.007 absolute, with a volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at least 2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69% coverage in the plane or 74.05% in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the problem - permitting overlap substitutes Kershner's thinnest-covering density and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p=0.80. Hexagonal packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal-Voronoi configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one-sigma aim-point offset costs 14 points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic placement attains 85% of what the configuration permits while centralised PPO averages 15% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.
authors: Dmytro Babarytskyi
bullets: Closed-form bounds estimate arrival-point uncertainty, mesh coverage, packing limits, and the admissible repositioning commit window.
With non-overlapping agents, coverage is capped at 90.69% in 2D and 74.05% in 3D; overlap removes this separation-induced ceiling above a crossover of p=0.80.
Analytic placement reaches 85% of the applicable ceiling, whereas centralized PPO averages 15% across three training seeds.
Gaussian uncertainty is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but sensitive to bias: a one-standard-deviation aim-point offset reduces coverage by 14 percentage points.
The study validates its formulas by Monte Carlo and argues that feasibility ceilings should accompany learning results.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.
authors: Avishree Khare, Hideki Okamoto, Bardh Hoxha, Georgios Fainekos, Rajeev Alur
bullets: Targets failures in event ordering, timing, and persistence despite correct visual concepts.

Uses score gradients to create attention biases and a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance.
Evaluated on 220 prompts across 11 temporal-constraint categories and five models, improving satisfaction accuracy by 9.5–20 percentage points over CFG.
Requires no external concept classifier or backpropagation through the video transformer, with minimal memory overhead.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner-to-behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL-regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best-of-$K$ reward, minus terms for the raw finite-group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs-target composition and a finite-data final-policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed-reference GGPO scores $32.96$ on the five-benchmark problem-weighted average, versus $46.58$ with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.
authors: Xuanchang Zhang, Tong Zhang
bullets: Addresses learner–behavior policy mismatch, especially the high variance of importance weighting for long responses.

On-policy, the population loss equals the KL-regularized optimality gap; theory gives reward guarantees under coverage and reference-control conditions.
Reference refreshing is important: the reported five-benchmark average rises from 32.96 with a fixed reference to 46.58 with the default schedule.
On mathematical reasoning, GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training–inference mismatch and fixed offline data, and remains effective with increasing policy staleness.

papers.abstract: Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions.Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player's situation and subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual prediction alone. We introduce \rig (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. \rig combines persistent state and configurable rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action-conditioned audiovisual generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and interactions. Further post-training enables \rigarena, an interactive generative first-person shooter (FPS) prototype. Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal interaction between the player and the generated world. Project page: https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/.
authors: Mengfei Li, Yi Zhang, Xingtong Ge, Lunjie Zhu, Fangyu Lin, Peng Li, Guanglu Song, Yu Liu, Wei Xue, Wenhan Luo, Yike Guo
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of sustaining reciprocal, context-aware interactions through audiovisual prediction alone.
Combines persistent state and configurable rules with contextual reasoning and action-conditioned audiovisual generation.
Uses a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning game dynamics and interactions.
Introduces RIGArena, an interactive generative FPS prototype created through further post-training.
Experiments report more reliable combat outcomes and stronger reciprocal interaction between the player and generated world.

papers.abstract: A self-improving agent has to decide which new skills to keep, and in practice it keeps whatever earns a high reward, convinces a judge model, or compresses its library, even when the skill is wrong. That is fine until the answers have to be exactly right: over a table of transactions, a total is either right or wrong. We ask a harder question: can an agent grow what it can compute with no reward, no judge, and no answer key, and still be exactly right? A single frozen model runs two nested loops over a small, exact domain-specific language (DSL). The inner loop answers new questions only when two independently written expressions agree on every record. The outer loop discovers its own missing capability and authors an operator for it, admitted only when an independent second implementation agrees and the result obeys a conservation law, all without ground truth. The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set, and the outer loop self-extends on disjoint starting sets, inventing operators outside the starting closure; a no-induction control answers none of the new questions. The admission rule is empirically sound: it rejects 138 of 138 buggy operator variants under an independent reference, even one written by a different model family, where the admit-if-it-runs, self-consistency, and compression signals the field relies on admit most of them. Unmodified, the same mechanism self-extends on two further domains with unrelated schemas, business-ledger and clinical-encounter question answering, growing their answerable sets more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold. The loop transfers across model families too: run with further proposers, the gate stays sound and independent families self-extend comparably, with only the induction yield tracking each proposer's DSL fluency.
authors: Yun-Shiuan Chuang, Yirou Ge, Yixi Li, Yiming Bian, Zijie Pan, Jenna L. Ballard, Uma Kona, Linsey Pang, Prakhar Mehrotra
bullets: Targets exact answers without rewards, judge models, or answer keys, where incorrect skills cannot be tolerated.
Uses nested loops: agreement between independent expressions answers questions, while agreement between independent operator implementations plus a conservation law admits new operators.
The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set; the outer loop discovers operators beyond the initial DSL closure and fails to expand without induction.
The admission rule rejects all 138 tested buggy operator variants under an independent reference, outperforming simpler admission signals in this evaluation.
The mechanism transfers to business-ledger and clinical-encounter domains, expanding answerable sets by more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The two nested loops, both run by a single frozen model with no ground-truth oracle and no judge. The inner loop (blue) expands the answerable set within a fixed operator set, keeping a question only when two independently written expressions agree on every record (σ(e1) = σ(e2)). The outer loop (green) induces a new operator when a capability gap recurs, admits it through the oracle-free validation gate, and folds it into the library before re-running the inner loop. Detailed in Section 3.

Figure 2: One continuous closed-loop trajectory per domain. Shaded/unshaded bands are successive inner-loop phases; each dashed vertical line is an outer-loop induction (+n operators admitted); the solid line is cumulative answerable types and the dashed orange line the subset whose expression uses an induced operator. Two rounds grow the set 10 → 336 (Merchant, amounts/timing seed), 15 → 162 (BookSQL), and 13 → 248 (EHRSQL) under the same namespace and gate. Discussed in §4.2 and 4.5.

Figure 6: Base-model ablation on the merchant domain across all three starting sets (Amounts & Timing, Top Buyer, Timing), the seed-sensitivity companion to the cross-domain ladder of Figure 3. Five base models per seed, same stacked convention: the light band at the base is the initial seed types (constant across base models), the solid above it is the additional subset expressible with the seed operators alone, hatched is the subset whose expression calls an induced operator, and the label above a bar is the number of operators admitted, shown when at least one answerable type uses them (omitted for zero admissions and for admitted-but-unused ones; e.g. 4B on Amounts & Timing admits four operators that no answerable type ends up using). 4B/8B/14B/32B are Qwen3 dense models, a controlled same-family, same-generation, same-architecture scale sweep; 35B is the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B mixture-of-experts main model (≈3B active parameters, a later generation), shown as a cross-architecture reference point. Discussed in Section 4.4 and Appendix P.

Figure 5: One continuous closed-loop trajectory per starting set, on a fixed validation set (63 merchants). Shaded and unshaded bands mark successive inner-loop phases; a dashed vertical line at each phase boundary is an outer-loop induction, labeled with the number of operators it admits (+n). The inner loop climbs on its current operators (solid), an induction enlarges the library, and it climbs again. The capability each induction closes, in order, is: a most-common-value gap closed by a family of per-group aggregation and counting operators, then a related weighted-mode gap closed by more per-group counting operators (Amounts & Timing); a count gap closed by conditional-filter and per-group count/sum operators, then an equality gap closed by equality-filter and grouped-sum operators (Top Buyer); and a most-common-value gap closed by per-group counting operators, then an argmax gap closed by a single grouped-sum reducer (Timing). The orange dashed line counts only the answerable types whose expression calls an operator admitted this round: it is flat at zero through the first inner phase (no operator to use) and rises only after an induction, so the postinduction gains are genuinely induction-driven, not the inner loop continuing on the base operators. Of the newly answerable types in the first post-induction phase, 76/100 (Amounts & Timing), 178/208 (Top Buyer), and 35/120 (Timing) call an induced operator; the cumulative counts after the second post-induction phase are 116, 254, and 53 respectively. All three starting sets admit new operators at both inductions and keep climbing through a third inner phase; none self-limits within the two induction rounds tested here. Inner phases are capped at eight passes and are still rising at the cap, so these are lower bounds on each phase’s reachable set.

Figure 3: Base-model ablation: the same outer loop run with five base models per domain, in the stacked convention of Figure 2 (light: initial seed types; solid: additional types expressible with the seed operators; hatched: types needing an induced operator; label: operators admitted). 4B/8B/14B/32B are Qwen3 dense models and 35B is the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B main model. Read for gate soundness and whether induction fires, not as a cross-model coverage ranking (absolute coverage is volume-sensitive; §4.4, Appendix P).

Figure 4: Cross-family transfer: the same closed loop, same frozen prompt and gate, with four proposer families (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Mistral-Small-24B, Gemma-3-27B, Llama-3.3-70B) on the three domains, in the stacked convention of Figure 3. The gate stays sound for every family (zero false admits throughout), and two further families self-extend (Mistral on Merchant and BookSQL, Llama on all three). Read for soundness and induction, not coverage ranking; per-family compile rates and the three-seed companion are in Table 11 (§4.4).

Figure 7: Three independent starting sets converge on a shared answerable set. Bars count the quantities answerable in all three runs (the 3-way intersection of their answerable sets, compared by value signature on the shared 63-merchant validation set) at each induction stage. Before any induction the three share 38 quantities, all expressible from their common seed operators and none per-group. After induction the shared core grows to 73, of which 19 are per-group aggregations (hatched) that lie outside every starting set’s closure, so the convergence is in the induced capability, not the seed operators. The three do not collapse into one identical set (each also keeps exploring its own directions; final per-run sizes 326/435/268, pairwise overlaps 102–118); rather, from disjoint seeds they independently acquire the same per-group capability and a common set of exactly-computable quantities.

Table 5: Mutation study of the admission gate. For each admitted operator we generate every single-point mutant of its implementation, discard the ones that still match the original on every input (equivalent mutants), and run the rest through the gate. diff. kills is the uncorrelated model (only the implementation is mutated, the reference stays correct), where differential testing alone should catch the bug. metamorphic and structural kills are the correlated model (the same bug is written into both implementations, so differential cannot catch it), where only the conservation checks or a no-output rejection can catch it. false admits is 0/138 under the uncorrelated (independentreference) model the loop uses, and 10/138 under the correlated worst-case, where the identical bug is written into both implementations so differential is blind and only metamorphic conservation remains. Validation on 63 synthetic merchants.

Table 9: Reach of the admission gate over 384 operator drafts from six induction runs. A draft must pass two filters in turn: the method-free substrate sandbox, then verification (differential and metamorphic). Most drafts are turned away by the substrate, not by verification, because the model reaches for a method call on a harder operator; verification, in turn, rejects almost only wrong operators. Sub-counts are indented.

Table 3: Automated outer-loop induction on three independent starting sets, each from its own minimal operator set (63 validation merchants). Using induced counts new types whose expression calls an operator admitted this round; the control runs amounts/timing with induction skipped (Appendix F).

Table 10: Base-model ablation on synthetic data: the full closed loop re-run with four Qwen3 dense base models on the three starting sets and the fixed 63-merchant validation set, gate-topk K = 3 (Appendix B), the same gate throughout. “inner cov.” is the answerable types the inner loop reaches on the seed operators; “gap” is the top-tallied missing capability the model discovers (each seed is given up to two induction rounds, hence some seeds show two gaps); “drafts” is the operator candidates proposed across all attempted gaps; “admitted” is how many pass the gate; “final” is the total answerable types after all rounds for that seed. The gate is sound at every scale: no false operator is admitted anywhere. Self-extension is not monotone in size: 8B authors no gate-passing operator on any of its 128–192 drafts per seed despite matching or exceeding 4B’s inner coverage, and 4B’s own four admitted operators unlock no further measured coverage in this run; the largest dense model, 32B, admits the most operators overall and is the only dense model to self-extend beyond amounts/timing, on both timing and top-buyer.

Table 1: Gate-component ablation on the mutation/adversarial pool (14 operators, their 138 buggy single-point mutants, and 6 adversarial constructions; 63 merchants), each check toggled independently; the threat model is uncorrelated (independent reference) or correlated (reference carries the same bug). Buggy, Adv., and False rej. count false-admits over the 138 mutants, admits of the 6 adversarial constructions, and wrongful rejections of the 14 correct operators.

Table 13: Text-to-SQL baseline on a third domain, EHRSQL (MIMIC-III): the full verified pools (7,660 compositional and 4,500 retrieval instances) over 300 single-patient contexts. The same frozen base models emit a SQLite query (best-of-5, majority vote over the executed results, temperature 0.4, matching the merchant baseline of Table 8) over a flat per-patient table that mirrors the DSL context one-to-one, so no query needs a JOIN. SQL is granted the median and populationstandard-deviation aggregates SQLite omits, defined to match the DSL. Accuracy is per query (each (question, patient) instance scored against gold). Compositional is the main track (self-generated statistical/ordered questions); Retrieval is a supplementary control of real EHRSQL attribute lookups, where both systems are near ceiling. Numbers are the mean of 3 seeds (per-cell std ≤ 0.01); the DSL is exact by construction. The Compositional (few-shot) column prepends three hand-authored (question, SQL) exemplars (one GROUP BY, one ordered window, one granted aggregate), disjoint from the eval; it lifts most Qwen backbones (4B +0.22, 14B +0.08, 32B +0.07) but is modeldependent: Gemma-3-27B drops (†0.768), where the window exemplar induces an aggregate-overwindow (AVG(LAG()OVER...)) that SQLite rejects, a form it avoided zero-shot with legal self-joins.

Table 6: Adversarial, conservation-preserving wrong operators. Each construction is built to satisfy every relation per group sum or group size declares (relabeling), or is a control that should not (merge). Validated against the same gate as the closed loop, under the two mutation-study threat models. The lone false admit, per group sum + merge under the correlated model, is bold.

Table 11: Cross-family summary: the full closed loop re-run with three additional families (MistralSmall-24B, Gemma-3-27B, Llama-3.3-70B) as the proposer, same frozen prompt and protocol as the main model, across the three merchant seeds and two transfer domains. Final is answerable types after both rounds; compile is the median fraction of proposed expressions that execute (the proposer’s DSL fluency). Every family admits zero wrong operators; discussion in §4.4.

Table 12: Text-to-SQL baseline on a second domain, BookSQL (business-ledger accounts): 3,000 self-generated compositional questions (15 templates across three categories, 200 each) over 300 accounts. The same frozen base models emit a SQLite query (best-of-5, majority vote over the executed results, temperature 0.4, matching the merchant baseline of Table 8 and EHRSQL’s Table 13) over a flat per-account table that mirrors the DSL context one-to-one, so no query needs a JOIN. SQL is granted the median and population-standard-deviation aggregates SQLite omits, defined to match the DSL. Numbers are the mean of 3 seeds (per-cell std ≤ 0.01); the DSL is exact by construction. papers.abstract: A reasoning trace retained at answer time plays two roles: it can raise accuracy, and it can compete with the current evidence when the two disagree. We disentangle these roles by crossing verified evidence versions with the traces generated from each and answering from the same traces and evidence under two configurations: continuation of the model's own thinking and a separate answer call. Across three model families (gpt-oss, Gemma4, Qwen3) on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, the separate call raises evidence-following over continuation by 29.9 to 60.6 points. On the same pairs, removing the trace lowers accuracy by similar amounts under both configurations. Yet continuation repeats the stale conclusion in most conflicts, and the separate call follows the current evidence far more often. Benefiting from a trace and deferring to it are therefore distinct properties. Further analyses show that the final line of a trace carries most of its value, gold evidence helps most before the trace is written, distractors weaken correction under a separate call, and renewed reasoning, unlike a verification instruction, follows the current evidence in most conflicts. Because trace deletion alone cannot reveal which source an answer follows, evaluations should report both properties together with the answer configuration.
authors: Shaoang Li, Yanhang Shi, Jian Li
bullets: Reasoning traces can improve accuracy while also causing models to repeat stale conclusions.
Across three model families on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, separate calls improved evidence-following over continuation by 29.9–60.6 points.
Removing traces reduced accuracy similarly in both configurations, showing that benefiting from a trace differs from deferring to it.
The trace’s final line provides most of its value; gold evidence is most helpful before reasoning is written.
Renewed reasoning corrected conflicts more often than verification instructions, while distractors weakened correction.

papers.abstract: We study continual linear regression in a high-dimensional regime, where a learner observes a sequence of tasks and updates its parameters sequentially. In this setting, we derive an explicit closed-form expression for the generalization loss of a model trained with gradient descent for a fixed number of steps per task, which holds for arbitrary teachers. We prove that the optimal fixed step size decays nearly inversely with the number of tasks, specifically as $\ln T / T$, for a single teacher and, more generally, i.i.d. teachers. Under this scaling, we show that the resulting generalization loss is asymptotically equivalent to that achieved by optimally tuned L2 (isotropic) regularization. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to generalized ridge regression with diagonal regularization matrices, obtaining a closed-form characterization of the generalization loss and identifying necessary and sufficient conditions under which the optimal regularizer is isotropic. Finally, we identify a regime where the optimal step size remains finite even as the number of tasks tends to infinity, thus revealing a non-trivial tradeoff between task variability and implicit regularization, in contrast to the i.i.d. teacher scaling. Our theoretical predictions are corroborated by experiments on both linear models and neural networks, providing practical guidance for the design of continual learning systems.
authors: Gilad Karpel, Daniel Soudry
bullets: Provides a closed-form generalization-loss expression for fixed-step gradient descent across sequential tasks with arbitrary teachers.
For a single teacher or i.i.d. teachers, the optimal step size decreases nearly as ln(T)/T and matches optimally tuned isotropic L2 regularization asymptotically.
Characterizes generalization loss under diagonal generalized ridge regularization and gives conditions for when the optimal regularizer is isotropic.
Identifies a task-variability regime where the optimal step size remains finite as the number of tasks grows, unlike the i.i.d.-teacher case.
Experiments on linear models and neural networks support the theoretical predictions and offer guidance for continual-learning design.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal agents have made significant progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning enables imitation but not active experience organization, while outcome-based reinforcement learning promotes exploration yet underuses intermediate trajectory information. Therefore, we propose EvolvingBrain, which uses an adaptive skill system as the brain for agent self-evolution, consisting of two following components. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution: extracts Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific trajectories, summarizes experience by generating skills, and evolves through multiple interactions with the open world, ultimately forming a Stratified Skill Architecture consisting of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap Skills, which provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and a novel evolution approach. State-Aware Adaptive Execution: summarizes long-horizon interactions into Structured Abstractive Memory and uses it to guide the State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, enabling the agent to utilize knowledge according to its current state. Experiments on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld demonstrate that EvolvingBrain improves success rates on open-world tasks and exhibits generalization capabilities. Our code is provided in the supplementary materials and will be publicly released in the camera-ready version.
authors: Runxuan Liu, Jingqi Shi, Baoxin Wang, Honghong Zhao, Haoyuan Xu, Yueqing Sun, Jiafeng Liang, Tao He, Dayong Wu, Qi Gu, Shijin Wang, Ming Liu, Bing Qin
bullets: Addresses the limits of imitation learning and outcome-only reinforcement learning in organizing and exploiting intermediate experience.
Extracts procedural and problematic patterns from trajectories to generate skills through repeated world interactions.
Builds a stratified skill architecture with domain, plan, and action/trap skills for multi-granularity knowledge storage.
Uses structured abstractive memory and state-aware skill fusion to select and combine skills during long-horizon interactions.
Improves open-world task success rates and demonstrates generalization on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive skill system and structured memory for self-evolving agents in open worlds.
papers.title: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds
papers.tldr: EvolvingBrain enables multimodal agents to self-evolve in open worlds by continually learning structured skills from experience and adapting their use to the current state.

papers.abstract: The closed world asks AI for specialized competence and lets it manufacture the iid data its theory assumes: a fixed criterion licenses collecting examples until the task is covered. The open world asks for versatility --- taking up tasks a machine was not built for, from few examples and with little prior from a human designer --- and offers data that is grouped, not shuffled. Its tasks are not known in advance, so a machine must do inference-time learning (1st requirement). Modeling tasks as sharing latent factors and decomposing the training objective, we derive two more: a *rich representation*, retaining more than iid generalization requires, and a predictive disentanglement that aligns inputs and outputs into matched low-dimensional groups. The analysis further predicts the need for a consistent inner learner, and the benefit of long contexts spanning related tasks. We test these claims on language models up to 8B, asking whether a model has a property (qualitative) rather than how much it wins (quantitative). Models that meet the requirements improve as data from related tasks accumulates; the rest degrade, and neither scale nor layer-type interleaving repairs this.
authors: Jianyu Zhang, L\'eon Bottou
bullets: Open-world settings involve unknown tasks, few examples, and grouped rather than iid data.
The analysis identifies three requirements: inference-time learning, representations richer than iid generalization needs, and aligned low-dimensional input–output groups.
A consistent inner learner and long contexts spanning related tasks are also predicted to help.
Experiments with language models up to 8B find that models meeting these requirements improve as related-task data accumulates, while others degrade.
Neither model scale nor interleaving different layer types fixes failures to meet the requirements.

papers.title: Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements
papers.tldr: Open-world AI requires inference-time learning, rich representations, and predictive disentanglement to improve across previously unseen related tasks.

papers.abstract: Image-to-text (I2T) understanding and text-to-image (T2I) generation are dual tasks in unified multimodal models (UMMs). Reconstructive post-training couples these tasks, but existing reconstruction-based methods remain perception-centric and provide limited supervision for reasoning about structure, intent, and transformation. We propose ReasonUni, a reasoning-augmented reconstructive post-training framework that extends this coupling beyond perception. Given an original image and an editing instruction, the UMM first reasons about what and how to edit and describes the target state, then generates the corresponding target image conditioned on this understanding output. To jointly optimize both modules, we introduce TreeGRPO, a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images per path, then aggregates visual rewards to update both modules under a unified objective. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains in both understanding and generation, showing that reasoning-augmented reconstruction yields genuine mutual gains for UMMs.
authors: Feize Wu, Zhiyuan Yan, Yuhuan Hong, Yuwei Niu, Zongjian Li, Zheyuan Liu, Bin Lin, Jinbo Yan, Jie Qin, Xudong Mao, Limeng Qiao, Guanglu Wan, Li Yuan
bullets: Targets the limited structural, intentional, and transformational reasoning in reconstruction-based multimodal training.
Given an image and editing instruction, the model reasons about the edit, describes the target state, and generates the target image.
Introduces TreeGRPO, which samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images and uses visual rewards to train both modules jointly.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report consistent gains in both multimodal understanding and image generation.
The abstract does not specify numerical results, datasets, or detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed-decision model we compare against, like a standard cross-encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per-system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero-shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine-tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x the per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.
authors: Avdhesh Singh Chouhan, Jack Perry
bullets: Structured attention makes state encoding independent of questions, prevents question interaction, and makes option order irrelevant.
On the typed-decisions benchmark, the 395M model beats the released 421M specialist on soft-label agreement and accuracy across five seeds.
Against a matched fine-tuned baseline, it wins on MultiRC but loses on RACE and BoolQ, where training is unstable.
Question-specific state copies improve RACE and MultiRC by 0.9–3.5 points at 1.4–2.5× latency, but show no measurable benefit on typed decisions.
The study also reports zero-shot references, including a closed general system that outperforms all fine-tuned encoders.

papers.selection_reason: Structured attention mask enables shared state encoding across many questions, reducing per-case latency.
papers.title: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
papers.tldr: Verdict-MQ encodes each case once to answer many typed questions, improving typed-decision calibration and accuracy while trading some performance for lower repeated-processing cost on standard QA tasks.

papers.abstract: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting. In a joint exit-count/calibration-size sweep at n=100, pathwise set size moves only from 3.02 to 3.11 as exits increase from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni degenerates to the full label space for 12 or more exits. Paired comparison against MinSE valid selection at (n,L)=(100,24) gives a set-size difference of 0.80 [0.47, 1.13]. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative boundary, with sets of 7,162-9,620 tokens. Pathwise calibration is most useful when candidate exits are many relative to calibration size, when budgets change after calibration, and when shallow heads return actionable sets.
authors: Adria Binte Habib, Ibne Farabi Shihab
bullets: Naive layerwise calibration loses coverage after data-dependent exit selection; pathwise calibration attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814.
One split-conformal quantile yields nested prefix sets that contain the valid terminal set, supporting any post-calibration label-free stopping policy preserving containment.
Across eight task-backbone cells, average set size was 1.41 with latency fraction 0.71; on CIFAR-100, budget-4 stopping achieved coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57.
Pathwise calibration remained stable as exits increased from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni became degenerate at 12 or more exits; deployment budgets can change without refitting.
The approach is less effective for full-vocabulary decoding, producing sets of 7,162–9,620 tokens, and is most useful with many exits, limited calibration data, or actionable shallow-head sets.

papers.selection_reason: Conformal early-exit calibration for latency-efficient inference.
papers.title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth

papers.abstract: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.
authors: Aiden Swann, Mozes Jacobs, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, David Chanin, Dron Hazra, Usha Bhalla, Curt Tigges, Mac Schwager, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal
bullets: Recover task-relevant features spanning perception, language, proprioception, episode phase, and control variables.
Causal interventions show that steering visual, semantic, and spatial features predictably changes action predictions.
Feature-based data attribution traces failure-recovery behavior to fewer than 1.4% of training tokens.
Results support matching featurizers to representation geometry for more effective robot behavior analysis and modification.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models ($\pi_{0.5}$, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas $\pi_{0.5}$ additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot's action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to $33\%$ while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes ($46.7\%$ vs. $46.9\%$), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Mozes Jacobs, Siddharth Boppana, Tal Haklay, Eric Bigelow, Andrew Lee, Conor Watts, Thomas Icard, Mac Schwager, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal
bullets: Studies how perceptual and semantic representations become actions in three frontier VLA models: π₀.₅, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot.
Activation patching identifies mid-to-late cross-attention layers as the main causal pathway into the action expert.
Early-to-mid representations of target nouns determine object selection, while later text representations encode spatial redirection.
Spatial information is stored differently across architectures, including instruction-following text positions and image-token positions.
Restricting MolmoBot conditioning to 3 of 36 layers cuts inference FLOPs by up to 33% while retaining comparable success; the approach also transfers to real-robot π₀.₅ deployment.

papers.abstract: Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and discover that higher-level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi-step world state prediction, a high-level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT-Image-2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early-stage visual state prediction capabilities on real-world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real-world states.
authors: Wenhao Yan, Haodong Li, Xiaotong Li, Yaxin Luo, Zhengrong Yue, Jialv Zou, Xu Huang, Haojin Yang, Nan Jia, Yan Feng, Peng Pei, Xunliang Cai

papers.abstract: Video generators serve as interactive worlds for exploration and simulation, yet realistic and visually appealing frames do not necessarily depict a consistent 3D world. Existing benchmarks assess selected geometric properties or use vision-language models to judge memory and consistency, leaving systematic 3D evaluation underexplored. We introduce Orbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. Through controlled exploration and revisit, we organize the evaluation into three dimensions: input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency. For input preservation, registered RGB-D references and annotated anchors support appearance, geometry, and spatial stability measurements. For generated-content persistence, we compare revisits to regions absent from the input image with their first generated observations to test whether models preserve what they create. For 3D self-consistency, cross-view depth and feature correspondence, regional scale agreement, and held-out Gaussian rendering test whether generated views describe the same 3D scene. Minute-long exploration and revisits further test long-term consistency. Our construction and annotation pipeline brings together public datasets, self-captured scenes, and simulation, yielding 720 instances across indoor and outdoor environments and six exploration-and-revisit protocols. Evaluation spans 27 text-, action-, and camera-conditioned models through native-interface adapters. Our Orbia benchmark provides a systematic basis for diagnosing 3D inconsistency and developing more persistent video world models.

papers.abstract: Residual context is key to unlocking the speed-quality Pareto frontier of diffusion language models (DLMs) by carrying forward predictive distributions across denoising steps. Yet turning this seemingly simple mechanism into an effective learning paradigm is far from simple: there is no clear recipe for how residual context should be learned. We introduce ORL, a framework for on-policy residual learning in DLMs. Algorithmically, we identify that residual learning is inherently on-policy. ORL learns from model-induced residual trajectories on the fly and introduces an entropy-contraction objective that sharpens predictions as the model revisits its own predictions. System-wise, exact residual supervision requires capturing, retaining, and reprocessing many trajectory-dependent states. ORL co-designs the algorithm with asynchronous residual capture and transport, specialized block-diffusion attention, and packed compute-balanced training, making it practical at scale. On a 4B DLM converted from Qwen3-4B, ORL improves tokens per forward (TPF) by up to 6.2x and, with our dlmrt engine, end-to-end throughput by approximately 6.9x at comparable or better quality. In single-request serving on one H100, this mode achieves a stronger speed-quality Pareto frontier than autoregressive models with EAGLE3 and DFlash speculative decoding under both strict and relaxed verification, running 1.74x faster than DFlash at matched accuracy. ORL also transfers to existing DLMs: on LLaDA-2.1-mini, 36 H100-hours and 4.2M self-generated tokens, about 10x less data than prior LLaDA recipes, yield up to 1.5x higher TPF and up to 3x higher throughput at comparable quality, and on DiffusionGemma, ORL raises TPF by 1.1-1.2x. With dlmrt and NVFP4 quantization, ORL models decode a single request at up to 5,046 tokens/s on one B200, 7,708 on eight B200s, and 2,788 on a consumer RTX 5090, with comparable quality.
authors: Yifan Yu, Yuqing Jian, Jisen Li, Yuezhou Hu, Tianyi Zhang, Xiaoxia Wu, Rui-Jie Zhu, Junxiong Wang, Zhongzhu Zhou, Fan Lai, James Zou, Chenfeng Xu

papers.selection_reason: Presents an on-policy residual learning framework for diffusion language models, improving speed-quality tradeoffs and transfer to existing DLMs.
papers.title: On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: ORL makes diffusion language models substantially faster by learning on-policy residual predictions and supporting them with a scalable systems design, while maintaining comparable quality.

papers.abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
authors: Shiyu Ji, Peng Ling, Chen Lin, Shupeng Li, Yixuan Wang, Qingfu Zhu, Wanxiang Che
bullets: Targets errors in 2-bit MLA KV caches that affect both attention matching and value reconstruction.
Uses offline calibration with a learned shared rotation and coupled quantization thresholds and reconstruction gains.
Supervises calibration through prediction matching and attention-output matching while keeping model weights frozen.
Achieves the highest average accuracy among compared 2-bit methods across three MLA models and six benchmarks.
On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, delivers 3.96× BF16 KV capacity and 2.51× decode throughput at 256K-token inputs in SGLang.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces rotation and range calibration for 2-bit KV cache quantization in MLA, directly targeting memory-efficient long-context inference.
papers.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
papers.tldr: RoLaQ improves 2-bit KV-cache quantization for multi-head latent attention by jointly calibrating rotations and quantization ranges, enabling higher accuracy and greater long-context capacity.

papers.abstract: We introduce TurboMamba, a language-model architecture for faster inference, faster training, and better token prediction. A global Mamba-3 model runs once per completed token block. A small Transformer uses this global context and earlier tokens within the block to predict the next token. Three lightweight additions improve local predictions: direct access to the previous block's last token, a small correction to next-token scores, and a learned mixture with recent-token frequencies. We compare twelve small-scale implementations on public FineWeb-Edu, with comparable parameter counts and shared training-budget caps. The baselines include Transformer, Mamba-3, Jamba, and Zamba. The Jamba and Zamba versions use Mamba-3 in place of their original Mamba modules. TurboMamba achieves the lowest mean test prediction loss (negative log-likelihood, NLL) among all twelve models. Its mean NLL is 9.4% lower than that of Mamba-3, 7.3% lower than that of the Jamba version, and 18.3% lower than that of the Zamba version. End-to-end training throughput is 2.60x that of Mamba-3, 2.81x that of the Jamba version, and 4.82x that of the Zamba version. We measure end-to-end batch latency for a batch of 32 sequences, each with a 256-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. On this workload, TurboMamba achieves a 3.12x speedup over Mamba-3, a 3.53x speedup over the Jamba version, and a 6.21x speedup over the Zamba version.
authors: Hanxin Zhang
bullets: Evaluated twelve small-scale models with comparable parameter counts and shared training budgets on public FineWeb-Edu.
Uses global Mamba-3 processing once per completed token block, while a small Transformer predicts tokens within each block.
Adds previous-block token access, a next-token score correction, and a learned mixture of recent-token frequencies.
Achieved the lowest mean test NLL, with reported reductions of 9.4% versus Mamba-3, 7.3% versus Jamba, and 18.3% versus Zamba.
Reported 2.60×–4.82× higher training throughput and 3.12×–6.21× lower batch latency than the compared baselines, depending on the baseline.

The other models, including the Plain block model, use gray lines and markers, with different line styles and marker shapes.

Once these prefixes are available, the local causal decoders for different blocks can run in parallel. Every target uses earlier token inputs and counts of earlier tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a new hybrid language-model architecture with lexical memory for faster inference and training, directly relevant to LLM architectural advances.
papers.title: TurboMamba: Faster Inference, Faster Training, and Better Prediction with Lexical Memory
papers.tldr: TurboMamba combines block-level Mamba-3 context with a small local Transformer and lexical-memory enhancements to improve prediction quality while substantially accelerating training and inference.

papers.abstract: We expand the exponential kernel of attention into a truncated Taylor series of $n$ terms and factorize each term into a tensor-power inner product, which collapses the causal history into exactly $n$ recurrent states, each updated by one rank-one outer product per token and independent of context length $N$. The recursion is lossless with respect to the truncated kernel ($2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ in float64), and the states are additive across chunks ($5.7 \times 10^{-14}$), so prefill admits a parallel scan. Measured exponents are $t \propto N^{2.28}$ for softmax against $N^{0.91}$ for states, with a crossover at $N \approx 728$ and $20.8\times$ at $N = 8192$; per-token decoding latency is constant at $7.3\,\mu$s against $N^{1.04}$ for softmax, giving $76.0\times$ at $N = 65536$. Accuracy improves exponentially in $n$ while cost grows combinatorially, since the $m$-th state is $\binom{d+m-1}{m}$ wide---a bound confirmed by SVD---so the optimum is second order, $n = 3$, at $6.5 \times 10^{-4}$ error and $9{,}945$ elements per head. Query and key normalization is a prerequisite: without it the argument exceeds the convergence radius and adding terms stops helping.
authors: Zicong Huang
bullets: Approximates the exponential attention kernel with n Taylor terms and tensor-power factorization.
Maintains exactly n recurrent states using one rank-one outer-product update per token, independent of context length.
States combine additively across chunks, enabling parallel-scan prefill and constant per-token decoding latency.
The method scales more favorably than softmax attention for long contexts, with reported speedups up to 20.8× in prefill and 76.0× in decoding.
State width grows combinatorially with order; second order (n = 3) is identified as optimal, while query/key normalization is required for convergence.

papers.selection_reason: Linear-time attention via Taylor expansion with fixed recurrent states.
papers.title: Expanding Attention: A Taylor-Series Route to Linear-Time Transformers with a Fixed Number of Recurrent States
papers.tldr: A truncated Taylor expansion replaces softmax attention with a fixed number of recurrent states, enabling linear-time sequence processing while exposing a cost–accuracy trade-off.

papers.abstract: Sampling from continuous flow-based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FLOWBUDGET, a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FLOWBUDGET normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow~matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler--Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FLOWBUDGET can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget
authors: Zahra Dehghani, Pablo Piantanida, Mohammadhadi Shateri
bullets: Addresses the costly, empirical selection of numerical resolution for pretrained flow-based generators.
Uses training-free, simulation-free interpolation probes of learned dynamics to estimate normalized one-step discretization error.
Derives budget estimators for Euler and Heun ODE solvers and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama SDE sampling.
Maps a target numerical tolerance to an NFE budget using solver order and relates ODE estimates to terminal integration error.
Evaluated across SiT, FlowDCN, and Rectified Flow models and formulations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Analysis of FLOWBUDGET budget estimation.

Table 1: FLOWBUDGET-predicted budgets and corresponding FID, reported as mean ± std over three seeds. Reference FID uses NFE = 250 for SiT-XL/2, FlowDCN-XL/2, and RF-UNet, and NFE = 1 for 1-RF, 2-RF, and 3-RF.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses efficiency in generative models by estimating sampling budgets for flow matching, a technique relevant to both video generation and efficient inference.
papers.title: FlowBudget: Training-Free Sampling-Budget Estimation for Flow Matching Models
papers.tldr: FLOWBUDGET estimates the sampling NFE budget needed by flow-matching models without repeated sample generation or FID-versus-NFE sweeps.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon failures of language models are usually measured as end-task success or as a horizon length. We instead score, step by step, three components of a 400-step ledger task in which every step is easy in isolation and the model's own answers are re-injected into its context: recognising a record already seen 5 to 300 steps earlier, processing the current record locally, and writing a counter incremented at every step. On Qwen3-8B (non-thinking, 20 seeds, replicated on a second machine and backend), with every step scored component by component, two results hold. First, duplicate-recognition errors rise late in the episode -- from 0.0019 to 0.011 per step at risk across step 200 -- while the counter makes no error in 8,000 steps and local processing is descriptively stable; the rise combines long-distance recall errors and rising false alarms. Second, a block of irrelevant content inserted before each step makes the counter fail in 20 of 20 seeds on each machine, against none without it, while its effect on local processing is much smaller and not distinguishable from none. Three pre-registered follow-ups probe the counter. Its value depends on the value present in the response history: a corrupted value persists without correction in every seed, and an exact external reminder, repeated before each message, re-aligns it within one to two steps. Under the irrelevant block, no counter error was observed when an exact compact reminder of the state, supplied externally by an oracle, preceded each message (0 of 20 seeds with an error, against 15 without it), and this reminder outperformed a length-matched neutral text; whether a single reminder suffices was not conclusive, and the absence of damage to the other components was not established. An aggregate or exclusive error classification can hide the difference we report.
authors: Thomas Serval
bullets: A 400-step ledger task separately scores duplicate recognition, local processing, and counter updates with model outputs re-injected into context.
Duplicate-recognition errors increase late in the episode, reflecting both missed long-distance recalls and rising false alarms.
The counter remains error-free without interference, but irrelevant content causes failures in all tested seeds, with little effect on local processing.
Counter errors persist after corruption, whereas exact external state reminders can restore tracking within one to two steps.
Aggregate success or exclusive error metrics can conceal these distinct failure modes; some reminder effects remain inconclusive.

Per-step hazard (probability of an error at step k given no earlier error of the same component) by step slice, for duplicate recognition (R2), local processing (R1, code and sum) and the counter; component-wise scoring. 20 seeds per machine. Error bars: 95% Clopper-Pearson. The R2 rise is decomposed in §5.1 (long distances and false alarms); R1 is descriptively stable; the counter makes no error.

Figure 4: Size map, duplicate-recognition (R2) hazard in time at risk. Seed-level tests are reported in the text before step-level tests.

papers.selection_reason: Component-wise analysis of long-horizon LLM reliability under context re-injection; relevant to long-context behavior and memory.
papers.title: Context Injection and Long-Horizon Reliability: Separating Duplicate Recognition, Local Processing, and Counter Tracking
papers.tldr: Step-by-step evaluation shows that long-horizon failures arise mainly from duplicate-recognition drift and context-sensitive counter tracking, while local processing remains comparatively stable.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) based on large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful way to address complex problems, and their effectiveness depends critically on the collaboration topology that decides which agents participate and how they communicate. Recent work learns to generate this topology from the task query, fitting the generator to corpora of execution-verified graphs. The post-training method for such generators remains a limitation: a corpus lists the graphs that solved a query but never ranks them, leaving continued supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with no per-query preference to exploit. Without such a preference, the generator drifts toward the topologies the corpus contains most often rather than those that suit each query, so a gain on one task can come at a cost on another. We propose PRISM, which recovers per-query signal from the same corpus by learning with privileged information: a teacher reads, through a zero-initialized low-rank branch, a sibling graph that also solved the query and is unavailable at deployment, and the student matches its per-decision targets on trajectories the student samples itself. Across six diverse benchmarks PRISM improves over every topology-design baseline evaluated, and matched-teacher controls support the contribution of privileged query information. Code is available in this link.
authors: Phuong Tuan Dat, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of per-query preferences in corpora containing only execution-verified solution graphs.
Trains a teacher with access to a sibling graph that solved the same query, then distills its per-decision targets to a student on student-sampled trajectories.
Uses a zero-initialized low-rank branch to incorporate privileged information during training without requiring it at deployment.
Improves over evaluated topology-design baselines across six diverse benchmarks; matched-teacher controls support the value of privileged query information.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly used for driving-scene understanding, yet their defensive reasoning under weakly structured Global South traffic remains unclear. We introduce BD-HazardVLM, a diagnostic benchmark of 500 Bangladesh road-scene images, comprising 375 from RSUD20K and 125 from TFP-BD, annotated for hazard presence, primary hazard category, risk timing, severity, defensive actions, visible evidence, and hallucination- and Western-road-bias traps. We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and MiniCPM-V-4.6 using a shared zero-shot task definition and structured output schema. Binary hazard-presence accuracy ranges from 88.0 percent to 89.2 percent, essentially matching the 89.0 percent majority-class baseline. Fine-grained reasoning is substantially weaker: category accuracy remains below 40 percent, risk-timing accuracy ranges from 1.6 percent to 12.4 percent, and exact defensive-action matching remains below 2 percent. Although InternVL3-8B achieves the highest severity accuracy at 61.2 percent, it has zero recall on the 58 high-severity cases. Qwen exhibits severe category mode collapse, while all models show weak latent-hazard anticipation and near-zero self-reported trap recognition. For the evaluated models, these findings show that coarse hazard recognition does not imply reliable fine-grained defensive-driving reasoning and motivate geographically diverse safety evaluation.

papers.abstract: Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks emphasize output-constraint satisfaction but can overlook whether responses meaningfully answer the underlying request, creating an evaluation blind spot. We show that frontier models can receive full credit for responses with little substantive answer content. Using the same verifier-based criterion as a training reward can induce reward hacking, as publicly released checkpoints exhibit higher constraint satisfaction but lower response quality after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. To address this reward hacking, we introduce CALIF, a lightweight method that augments verifier rewards with a calibrated likelihood-based bonus to preserve response quality. CALIF evaluates response likelihood under the request alone using the existing frozen reference policy, requiring no additional judge or learned reward model. Across models ranging from 1.7B to 8B in reasoning and non-reasoning modes, CALIF improves constraint satisfaction on IFBench while maintaining response quality near or above pre-RL levels. It also outperforms corresponding base policies in 40 of 45 model-metric comparisons across three rubric-based instruction-following benchmarks, demonstrating gains beyond training verifiers.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.

papers.selection_reason: Dense progressive reward shaping for long-horizon agentic tasks is a transferable technique for RL-based robot skill learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
papers.tldr: Tev scales long-horizon agent training with verifiable dense progress rewards, enabling stronger performance and generalization across agent benchmarks.

papers.abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.

Yunzhe Qi
Sirui Chen
Federico Bianchi

Pan Lu

Evaluated across 3 model scales and 11 mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic-reasoning benchmarks.
Reports 10.4% higher performance, 35.5–54.7% fewer tokens, 1.8–2.6× faster inference, and 2.7–3.7× lower cost than compared agents and frameworks.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models reconstruct masked tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to autoregressive generation. Yet their Transformer backbones typically carry visible evidence and evolving masked predictions through a single residual stream. We equip masked diffusion models with multiple residual streams that persist through depth and adaptive routing between them, then investigate how they support these complementary roles. On the pretraining task, two streams reduce reconstruction perplexity by 5.71% on validation data and 5.13% on average across external corpora compared with standard residual connections. We observe that, without predefined roles, visible and masked positions learn distinct routing patterns. Causal interventions show that this distinction organizes read and write routing, while token-specific write strength remains important within each role. Guided by these findings, a model trained with role-conditioned routing recovers half the validation gain from adding a second stream. State interventions explain the benefit of the additional stream: it preserves early token representations for later reuse while evidence accumulates at masked positions. This mechanism recurs at a larger model scale, showing how persistent streams support context preservation alongside prediction refinement.

Suren Kazarian
Gleb Molodtsov

papers.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) can capture manipulation priors from action-free videos, but discrete latents usually impose a granularity bottleneck, limiting their ability to represent fine-grained action. Recent continuous alternatives mitigate this, but they are typically used as proxies for world modeling and require a further planning step to produce executable actions. We thus introduce UniLAP, a unified continuous latent-action policy that models the latent space via flow matching and bypasses reliance on future frames during inference. By distilling a LAM teacher with a flow-adaptive objective, UniLAP inherits the teacher's action representation while retaining the multimodal distribution of feasible behaviors. To decouple latent representations from task-irrelevant appearance, we extract a label-free motion target to isolate relevant kinematic cues from spurious visual dynamics. With the established embodiment-agnostic latent manifold, UniLAP can be easily adapted to novel platforms. Pretrained on multi-source videos at a compact 1.1B parameter scale, UniLAP outperforms state-of-the-art latent-action and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines across hand pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.
